Chairman Kudrick read aloud the rules governing the hearing: (1) Applicant will present
its case; (2) Those in favor of the application will speak; (3) Those opposed to the
application will speak; (4) Rebuttal by the applicant and those in favor of the application
will speak; (5) Rebuttal by those in opposition to the application will speak.
He stated that anyone wishing to speak must first give their name, address, and interest in
the case. All questions and comments will be directed to the Chairman. The Board will
base their decisions on facts presented by the applicant. If any of the presented facts are
found to be different than what was presented, the Board reserves the right to reconsider
its approval.
As requested by Chairman Kudrick, the Applicant read the application aloud:
Mr. Jefferson said that presently 24 Kimball Street is a non-square vacant lot. It contains
2 outbuildings on the left-hand side. He would like to demo the existing buildings and
square off the existing structure to 26' x 32' and extend a 6' farmers porch on the front
with the gable end of the home facing the street. It will be a 3 bedroom, 2 bath home.
The present structure only meets the front setback.
The previous structure that was located on the front of the lot burned years ago. The 40°
set back in front meets the requirement. There is only 27' in the rear and the existing
house is only 7' from the property line on the right and 2' from the left. There is a
driveway on the left that goes from the front to the rear of the lot. On the right, there is a
garage and driveway going to the neighbor's fence.
Please give a detailed description of your proposal below. Demo existing house on
lot. Build a new 3 bedroom, 2 bath house. Size of house to be 26' x 32' with additional
farmers porch on front of house. Open concept floor plan on first floor and bedrooms
and at least one bathroom on second floor.

4. The values of surrounding properties are not diminished. The values of

5. Literal enforcement of the provisions of the ordinance would result in an

hardship" means that, owing to special conditions of the property that distinguish it
from other properties in the area: (i) No fair and substantial relationship exists

My request is to rebuild in the same location with the change to be squaring off the new

(B) If the criteria in subparagraph (A) are not established, and unnecessary
hardship will be deemed to exist if, and only if, owing to special conditions of the

be reasonably used in strict conformance with the ordinance, and a variance is
therefore necessary to enable reasonable use of it. With existing non-conforming road
frontage as well as lot size, I would ask to be able to build a new house in same area of

Economic Development Committee
Meeting Minutes
July 6, 2026
Attendance
Members: Sharon Morris, Chair; Jessica Stevenson, Vice Chair; Matt Miller, Selectmen
Rep.; Clint Hanson, Planning Board Rep; Chuck Schmidt; Brendan Williams
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Excused: Chuck Therrien
Business
1. EDC Facebook Page Business Spotlight Posts
The Committee reviewed responses to its Facebook outreach inviting local businesses to
participate in a business spotlight feature. Businesses identified for possible inclusion were
Monroe Plumbing and Heating, Majestic Moonbeam Farm, The Creative Duckling,
Kinstruct Tiny Homes, and Shirley's Kitchen. Members discussed using a short, consistent
question set for each spotlight and favored a brief written post with a business photo rather
than video. The Committee also discussed whether featured businesses should have a tax
ID. Majestic Moonbeam Farm was noted as not yet having one, and members supported
allowing time for that to be resolved while moving ahead with other businesses. By
consensus, the Committee chose to begin with Monroe Plumbing and Heating and to
prepare a standard list of questions that can be reused for future spotlights.
The set of questions that the EDC agreed upon were:
1) Where are you from and what brought your business to Pembroke?
2) Where do your customers come from?
3) How many employees do you have?
4) What do you enjoy most about your job?
5) What piece of advice would you give someone trying to start a business?
Members agreed that a phone call or in-person conversation could be offered if that is
easier for a business owner than replying in writing. A photo of the owner and/or business
will be requested for each post.
Action items:
• C. Cronin will email the final Business Spotlight questions to the members.
• J. Stevenson will contact Monroe Plumbing and Heating.

2. Discussion of Community Organizations on Website
The EDC continued its discussion of whether the town website should include community
organizations, local resources, or business-related information. S. Morris said that a list
developed through the Friends of the Library included organizations such as Scouts and
other clubs. M. Miller reported that he had compiled categories including parks, arts and
craft studios, historical markers, food, conservation areas, retail businesses, services, the
Suncook Rod and Gun Club, and the Town Library after searching Google maps and
online sources. C. Cronin checked the Bow website and they list the athletic club, booster
club, Boy Scouts, Cub Scouts, Garden Club, Men's Club, and Rotary.
Members noted that information about Pembroke amenities is scattered and difficult to
locate. C. Cronin reviewed the town's prior experience with website business listings
becoming outdated when businesses closed, moved, or changed contact information. The
EDC had previously built an internal business list using New Hampshire Secretary of State
data, and chose not to publish it because of maintenance and privacy concerns.
The Committee agreed to defer a final website recommendation until the broader town
website project advances, and to work on a written concept for the Select Board describing
possible categories and a maintenance approach. Members discussed beginning with civic
and community organizations before considering any business listings. The EDC agreed
that permission should be obtained before listing organizations or groups on the website. A
maintenance plan and periodic verification were identified as essential if any listing system
is created on the website.
Action items:
•
M. Miller will email his compiled list to the EDC members.
• The next step is for the EDC to prepare a written proposal for the Select Board
outlining possible categories and how information would be maintained.
3. Bike Rack in Village
The Committee revisited the proposal for a bicycle rack in the village. C. Cronin
summarized prior review of the item and noted that Public Works had previously identified
a landscape island in the parking lot as its preferred location because a sidewalk location
would interfere with winter plowing and ADA access. C. Cronin explained that a resident
had concerns about the location being too secluded and not wanting to park expensive
bikes there. Therefore, the proposal never progressed.
The EDC discussed an alternate location at the small state right-of-way or easement near
Main Street and Glass Street, where there is historical signage, a flagpole, and a cannon.
Several members felt that site would be more visible to cyclists and closer to village
businesses. Discussion included earlier involvement by the American Legion or VFW,
current local maintenance of the area, and ongoing work by Meet Me in Suncook on a
replacement flag and lighting. The Committee agreed that the immediate next step is to
determine the state approval process before taking formal action on a location. No formal
decision was made at the meeting. They will pursue gathering information at this point.

4. Pembroke Bike Tour Discussion
This topic was discussed at the previous meeting. The EDC discussed ideas for a
Pembroke bike tour intended to encourage cyclists to use local roads in lieu of the rail trail,
which is not fully developed, to visit destinations in town. Members favored a simple
approach, such as a Google Maps route with a QR code. Suggested destinations included
White Sands, Memorial Park, the community garden near the Congregational Church,
Pembroke Academy, the Josie Langmaid marker on Academy Road, and town owned
conservation land. Members also noted that local food stops and the planned ice cream
stand could help attract riders to stop in the village. The concept is intended as an
informational guide rather than a formally designated trail. The Committee agreed to
continue the bike tour concept using an informal mapping approach.

5. Promotion and Outreach Plan for Economic Revitalization Zones
The EDC discussed timing for outreach on Pembroke's Economic Revitalization Zones
and agreed that press efforts should begin soon if publicity is desired for August or
September. Members noted that some business owners may not realize they qualify if they
operate in town but live elsewhere. Members identified Rachel Wachman of the Concord
Monitor as a possible contact for a story explaining that Pembroke has two Economic
Revitalization Zones and describing the associated business benefits. C. Schmidt agreed
to make the initial contact, and C. Cronin offered supporting materials for that outreach.

• C. Schmidt will contact Rachel Wachman of the Concord Monitor regarding a
possible news story.
C. Cronin will send Chuck promotional materials and background information on the
Economic Revitalization Zones.

a. Commercial Areas
This item was postponed until the Town website is fully operational again.

There were no updates on this rolling agenda item.

PEMBROKE CEMETERY COMMISSION
July 9, 2026
Minutes
Present: James Garvin, Ellen Paulsen (chair), Victor J. Ranfos (Superintendent of Cemeteries), Zachary
Sawyer, Fleda Young.
1. Chair Ellen Paulsen called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m.
2. On a motion by Fleda Young, seconded by Zachary Sawyer, the minutes of the meeting of June
11, 2026, were approved as submitted.
New business:
3. By a letter dated June 21, 2026, Jane Bates, holder with her husband of burial licenses for Lots
49 A&B in Section 5 of Evergreen Cemetery, requested that the Town of Pembroke repurchase
Lot 49 B because the family no longer has a need for this lot. By unanimous agreement, the
Commission voted to recommend to the Board of Selectmen that the town repurchase Lot 49 B.
The Bates family purchased Lots 49 A&B for $700, the price for two lots, in August 2018. Since
the price for a burial permit for a single lot is $400 and Mr. and Mrs. Bates intend to retain the
permit for Lot 49 A, the Commission will recommend to the Board of Selectmen that the town
offer to repurchase Lot 49 B for the balance of $300, leaving the Bates family in possession of
the license for Lot 49 A. Secretary Garvin will convey this recommendation to the Board of
Selectmen.
4. The Commission discussed the ownership of the French Cemetery on North Pembroke Road.
Earlier research had disclosed that the town assessor's card, prepared by AxisGIS, the contracted
appraiser, indicates that the cemetery is the property of the Town of Pembroke. This is confirmed
by the town tax map (Map ID #2508-00CM-009), which shows that the cemetery, labeled as
"CEM 9," as a town-owned land parcel separate from the adjacent land of the French family.
Zachary Sawyer reported that he had heard that the town had assumed ownership of the formerly
private cemetery during the 1950s. The Commission agreed to assess the current condition and
potential needs of the French Cemetery and to plan to address its care from this time onward.
5. The Commission discussed the guidance for the cleaning and care of gravestones provided by
New Hampshire statutes, which Zachary Sawyer had previously researched and sent to
Commission members. With further study and discussion, the Commission will plan to add
language derived from these statutes to Chapter 155 ("Cemeteries") of the Pembroke Town Code
and make note of the language of the statutes in our next Annual Report for the Pembroke Town
Report for 2027.

2
Old business:
6. Chair Ellen Paulsen reported that she had submitted funding request to the Capital Improvement
Program (CIP) Committee through Town Administrator David Jodoin. Public Works Director V.
J. Ranfos noted that it should not be necessary for Chair Paulsen to attend the upcoming meeting
of the CIP Committee to discuss the request.
7. V. J. Ranfos noted that he had received an inquiry regarding the proposed establishment of a
"scattering garden" for cremation ashes in Buck Street Cemetery. This prompted V. J. to urge that
the Commission move forward with the establishment of such an amenity. We will add the
project to our Six Year Cemetery Plan and will probably begin to add funding for the necessary
landscaping to future CIP Committee proposals, possibly making use of some of the stored
granite that was salvaged from the former front wall of Evergreen Cemetery.
8. Relating to this subject, Secretary Garvin added that he has begun to research the rumored
establishment of a "cremation garden" by the Town of Hooksett. He has learned that the
regulations of the Hooksett Cemetery Commission require that "cremains shall be interred in a
container." At the same time, the Hooksett town website describes Fraser Memorial Park on K
Avenue, which is in a residential neighborhood and is not listed as a Hooksett municipal
cemetery, as a facility that offers grave sites and "cremation gardens." Garvin has left an inquiry
and a request for clarification with the chair of the Hooksett Cemetery Commission and will
report future findings to the Commission.
9. Zachary Sawyer reported that he has been in contact with Nicholas Allan from Celebrate Life
Company. Zachary distributed links to videos that describe the services of the company,
including a quick demonstration video, a video demonstrating the company's administrative
software, and an example of a client's cemetery map. Mr. Allan offered to provide quotes for
services relating to Pembroke cemeteries, noting that some associated fees include an
"onboarding fee" that depends on the size and complexity of the cemetery and an annual service
fee of $1,000 per year. The Commission agreed that we should add cemetery mapping to our Six
Year Cemetery Plan and should consider seeking funding through the CIP Committee but should
not move too far forward without the approval of the Board of Selectmen and relevant town staff.
10. The next regular meeting of the Pembroke Cemetery Commission will be at 6:00 p.m. on
Thursday, August 13 at the Public Works Department headquarters on Exchange Street in
Suncook Village.
11. There being no further business, the meeting was adjourned at 6:50 p.m.
Respectfully submitted.
James L. Garvin, Secretary

Summary: Electricity Supply Contract Renewal - Constellation Energy
Prepared for the Pembroke Select Board - July 15, 2026
BACKGROUND
• Quotes were received through Energy Professionals (the Town's power broker) from 5 different electricity
suppliers for term lengths ranging from 1 to 5 years.
- Pembroke has used Energy Professionals as its broker in the past, including for the current contract with
Constellation Energy, which expires in November 2026 (existing rate: 8.22 ¢/kWh, on a 48-month term).
RECOMMENDATION
• Rates have increased since the previous contract for a variety of market reasons. After evaluating the
available options through Energy Professionals, the Energy Committee recommends extending the Town's
current agreement with Constellation Energy for a new 5-year term.
- This is generally a favorable time of year to shop for a new contract, as supply is plentiful and rates are
relatively low compared to winter, when supply rates typically rise.
- The quoted supply rate is 10.510 c/kWh, but this quote is only valid for 24 hours; the rate at signing may
differ slightly. Once approved, Energy Professionals will confirm the rate is close to what the Select Board
approved, and the Committee will flag any significant deviation.
- The newly implemented Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Initiative (DASI) charge from ISO New England adds
some uncertainty, since it is currently an estimate; the final supply rate will be adjusted to reflect any change
to the DASI charge.
- All quotes received on June 10th are attached for the Board's review.
WHY EXTEND WITH CONSTELLATION
• Constellation is the Town's current supplier, making an extension straightforward.
• The renewal agreement has been reviewed by Town legal counsel and Primex (the Town's insurance
carrier), who recommended minor language changes. Those changes are currently under review by
Constellation Energy as of July 7th.
• Constellation offers several features that are attractive relative to other suppliers:
- 100% Swing: Honors the contracted supply rate even if Pembroke's actual usage exceeds forecast, reducing
risk to the Town. Not all suppliers offer this.
- Blend and Extend: Allows the Town to renegotiate its fixed-rate plan by extending the contract term,
immediately blending the existing (higher) contract rate with the lower current market rate - locking in
savings without waiting for the current agreement to expire. Other suppliers attach more contingencies to
• For reference, savings for the town through our current Constellation Energy supply contract are over
$5,000 for the past 12-month period compared to the default Eversource utility supply rate (details on
second page)
The Energy Committee recommends the Select Board approve a 5-year extension of the Town's supply
agreement with Constellation Energy and welcomes any questions.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
July 15, 2026 6:00 PM
Present: Chair Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Peter Gagyi, Selectman
Matt Miller
Excused: Selectwoman Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
II.
III.
IV.
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM.
Citizens Comment
Scheduled Meetings
Public Hearing Town Code Updates Chapter 138, 152, 154, 165, 167
The Board opened the public hearing at 6:03 PM to consider updates to Chapters 138,
132, 134, 163, and 16/ ot the Town Code. The Chair reviewed that Chapter 138
reflected taxation changes for disability and elderly exemptions previously approved
at Town Meeting; Chapter 152 updated Selectmen bylaws, including committee
representation and recording of meetings; and Chapters 154, 165, and 167 contained
housekeeping updates to cash receipts, financial policies, and the Joint Loss
Management Committee.
During the discussion, David noted that additional revisions to the solid waste chapter
remained under separate review with Gerry Fleury and would be brought forward
later.
No public comment was offered, and the hearing was closed at 6:04 PM. Motion by
Selectman Christiansen, seconded by Selectman Miller to accept the updates as
presented. Motion passed 4-0.
Old Business
Stage/Roof
At the request of the Chair and without objection, the Board took up the stage/roof
update out of agenda order so the attendees present for that item could be heard.
Mark Chevrette, representing Old Home Day and also Public Works, and Dana
Carlucci of the Building Committee reviewed the status of the replacement stage
plans. Dana Carlucci reported that the plans had been distributed, including to Tom

Hebert, and that the current design is for a 16-by-24 structure consisting of beams and
roof only, requiring either a concrete slab or a deck.
Discussion focused on whether to relocate the stage rather than reuse the existing site,
where concerns were raised about uneven ground, wetlands, and the stability of the
existing supports.
Dana Carlucci stated that prior discussions had favored reorienting the stage north-
south facing the basketball courts to reduce the effect of the westerly sun and improve
viewing from the pavilion area near Rose's building. He also noted that Sean Benoit,
who had previously offered to help with the slab, had since died.
Dana advised that available capital funding appeared sufficient for a new slab and
installation, but that delay would likely increase cost as lumber prices rise.
David explained that there would be a joint discussion with the Recreation
Commission members and the Building Committee members on July 30 after the CIP
meeting, and that discussion should come back to the Board for a final decision on
how to proceed at the August 5 meeting.
Energy Committee - Discussion on electric rate renewal
Rich Wengenroth of the Energy Committee presented a recommendation on renewal
of the Town's municipal electricity supply contract, which expires in November 2026.
Rich reported that the Town's broker, Energy Professionals, had obtained updated
market pricing and that Constellation Energy remained the lowest-cost supplier under
consideration. The Energy Committee recommended a 60-month term.
Rich stated that the updated five-year Constellation quote was 10.677 cents per
kilowatt-hour, compared with an earlier quote of 10.51 cents, and noted that current
Eversource supply rates were approximately 14 cents.
The Board discussed the advantages of locking in a lower long-term rate, market
uncertainty, and the concept of a future blend and extend' if prices decline.
Rich reported that Constellation does not include blend-and-extend language in its
standard contract, although the practice may still be available.
The Board also discussed variable ancillary or 'daisi' charges imposed across
suppliers and requested updated monthly comparisons of CPCH and Eversource
rates since CPCH began serving Pembroke.
Legal and insurance review had suggested only minor contract language changes,
which were not included in the current expiring contract and were not viewed as deal-
breakers.
The Board asked that sample contract language from another supplier with an express
blend-and-extend provision be obtained for informational purposes. The Board also

agreed that the quote should be acted on promptly because the pricing was valid for
only about 24 hours.
Motion by Selectman Christiansen to enter into a five year contract with Constellation
Energy at a rate not to exceed 10.677 cents per kilowatt hour, seconded by Chair
Yeaton. Motion passed 4-0.
Rich will request sample blend-and-extend contract language from another supplier
for Board information and provide an updated monthly CPCH versus Eversource
comparison.
Public Works Director - Update on Vehicle and new purchase
VJ Ranfos and David provided vehicle and equipment updates for Public Works.
VJ reported that the previously approved six-wheeler could now move forward, as
staff had delayed execution only long enough to confirm that tariff issues would not
affect the purchase.
On the replacement trash truck for the totaled unit, VJ stated that Sanitary advised the
compacting unit was not the cause of the delay and that the chassis from Lucky's
Peterbilt was now in Vermont being reassembled, with delivery expected within
approximately two weeks.
Staff further reported that the tariff issue had been resolved between the vendors and
that the Town was not expected to bear that cost.
David also confirmed, based on information relayed by Chief Shea's contact that the
approved Ford F-150 would be supplied at the quoted price and was not expected to
be materially affected by tariffs.
VJ Ranfos then updated the Board on the electric trash truck from Battle Motors,
reporting that production was moving again, the smaller battery configuration should
reduce the cost by about $50,000, and an extended warranty had been purchased.
Because of the December 31 grant deadline, VJ had begun the process of seeking a
one-year extension through DES and Governor and Council as a precaution against
further delay.
VJ also reported that Truck 71, the service truck, had suffered a fuel sending unit
failure that was repaired in-house by Corey for about $5,000 compared with a Ford
quote of $17,000, and that the F-600 was ahead of schedule at Viking for plow
equipment installation.
The Board discussed looming CIP pressures for future vehicle replacement and the
possibility of using Sourcewell vendors and nonbinding reservation tools to secure
production slots earlier, subject to contract review.

PEMBROKE EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICE
Capital Improvement Plan for EMS Services
TO:
Town of Pembroke Capital Improvement Committee
Town of Pembroke Board of Selectmen
Town of Pembroke Municipal Budget Committee
David Jodoin, Pembroke Town Administrator
FROM:
DATE:
Christopher Gamache, EMS Director
July 9, 2026
1. SERVICE REQUESTS FOR 2027
1 The Service requests the following amount be depositied into the
Pembroke EMS CIP:
$ 130,000.00
2. SERVICE DESCRIPTION
1) Pembroke Emergency Medical Service (hereafter "Pembroke EMS" or "PEMS") is the municipal ambulance
service for the Town of Pembroke.
2) Pembroke EMS staffs one (1) ambulance, with at least one (1) Paramedic and one (1) other
EMS Provider. The other EMS Provider may be an EMT, Advanced EMT or another Paramedic.
The ambulance is staffed 24/7 and is housed at the Pembroke Public Safety Center.
3) Pembroke EMS responds to approximately 650 to 700 runs per year in the Town of Pembroke and
about 200 runs per year to other communities. This gives the Service an annual call volume of
850-900 runs per year.
3. PEMBROKE EMS CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT PLAN (CIP) SUMMARY:
1) Pembroke EMS' CIP is based upon a 12-year replacement cycle for all equipment and
ambulances.
2) When an ambulance is purchased or replaced, all equipment within the ambulance will
also be replaced. This will include the stretcher, stair chair, cardiac monitor, ventilator,
CPR device, and medication pumps.
3) New ambulances shall be the "Primary" ambulance for six (6) years and will be used on the
majority of the EMS calls responded to by Pembroke EMS during this period. The unit
designator for the primary ambulance in Pembroke shall be "Ambulance 8". This unit designator
is unique in the region and was selected to minimize any confusion over the radio.
4) The second ambulance or rather the older one, shall be held in reserve or back-up for
Pembroke EMS. This ambulance shall be used when the primary ambulance is not available
while maintenance conerns are being addressed OR when it can be staffed by additional
members of Pembroke EMS and qualified members of the Pembroke Fire Department to respond
to 2nd EMS calls. The unit designator for this ambulance shall be "Ambulance 9"
6) Pembroke EMS' CIP projects the anticipated capital expenditures for the total replacement
cycle of all vehicles and equipment using a 5% annual increase in costs.
4. DESCRIPTION OF VEHICLES & EQUIPMENT
1) AMBULANCES: Pembroke EMS shall maintain two (2) ambulances; a primary ambulance and
a reserve ambulance. It is estimated that the Service will respond to approximately 850-900

incidents each year.
Pembroke EMS has created ambulance specifications to ensure our EMS providers have adequate space in
the patient compartment when multiple EMS providers are required to meet the medical needs of our critical
patients. These specifications are also intended to create the safest possible environment for our staff and
patients. The Service uses and intends to continue, to utilize a Ford F-550 4x4 diesel chassis (or complarable
chassis by other manufacturers) for its weight capacity, capabilities and handling.
2) POWER-LOAD SYSTEM: This item is typically part of the ambulance specifications and
allows for the safe loading and unloading of patients within the ambulance by removing all
lifting by EMS providers during this evolution. This decreases the risk of back and extremity
injury for the Service's staff as well as decreased the possibility of patient's being dropped and
injured. Finally, the power-load is a positive, multi-point stretcher securing device. In the
event the ambulance is in a collision and rolls over, the stretcher, with the patient, will remain
locked in place removing the possibility of the stretcher dislodging and further injuring the
patient or causing serious injury to the EMS provider. The power-load is serviced each year by
STRYKER as part of the service agreement.
3) STRETCHERS: Pembroke EMS uses a STRYKER PowerPRO XPS and Power PRO 2 stretchers. This
stretcher has proven to be reliable in the pre-hospital setting and being a mechanical
stretcher, removes the need for EMS staff to lift the patient once they are on the stretcher. The
stretchers are maintained each year by STRYKER as part of the service agreement.
4) STAIR CHAIR: A stair chair is used to remove and carry a person out of their residence in a
seated position. On the 2017 ambulance, there is a STRYKER StairPRO stair chair. The 2025
ambulance has a STRYKER XPEDITION powered stair chair. As with the powered stretchers, the new
stair chair further decreases lifting for the EMS crew while they are moving a patient up or down stairs.
This new device only requires the crew to balance the stair chair during this evolution. Both stair
chairs are maintained each year by STRYKER as part of the service agreement
5) CARDIAC MONITOR: Cardiac monitors are used by advanced providers to monitor a
person's heart rhythm, obtain electro-cardiograms (ECG's), obtain blood pressures, measure
oxygen levels, monitor exhaled carbon dioxide, detects carbon monoxide, defibrilate, used as an AED,
cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing and documenting times of treatments rendered
The 2017 ambulance (Back -up) utilizes a Life Pak 15v4 that was purchased in 2024. The 2025
ambulance is equipped with the Life Pak 35.
The Life Pak 35 provides all the same treatment capabilities as the Life Pak 15. The LP35 is lighter,
utilizes touchscreen technology for ease of use and presents patient data in a formate that is easier
to see and interpret.
6) MECHANICAL CPR DEVICE: Pembroke EMS uses the LUCAS III CPR Device by STRYKER. These
devices are widely used within the region. The LUCAS Ill allows for uninterupted CPR to a
person in cardiac arrest. This frees up EMS providers to perform other treatments while
maintaining a continuous blood flow to vital organs (particularly the brain). Each ambulance has
a LUCAS III CPR device as part of its equipment.
7) VENTILATOR: The Service uses a Zoll Z-Vent Ventilator. This device allows for the mechanical
ventilation of those patients who are not breathing on their own after an advanced airway has been
placed. The ventilator also allows the Service's paramedics to perform CPAP and BiPAP. These
treatments are intended to support a patient's breathing efforts with the goal of improving their
respiratory status and to avoid the need of being intubated and placed on a ventilator. This device
is maintained by Zoll annually as part of a service agreements.
8) MEDICATION INFUSION PUMPS: The Service has two (2) infusion pumps on each ambulance.
nfusion pumps are used to administer certain intravenous medications over a specified period o
ime. Typically, infusion medications are used in the most critical patients or when a specific volume
of fluids are to be administered to a pediatric patient. Pembroke EMS purchased four (4) infusion
pumps in 2025 to replace the older pumps the were used prior.

MINUTES OF THE AUGUST 20, 2026
PEMBROKE CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT (CIP) COMMITTEE MEETING
PEMBROKE TOWN HALL
The CIP Committee held a meeting on August 20, 2026, at 6:00 PM., at Pembroke Town Hall.
The meeting was called to order by Rosemarie Michaud at 6:03 PM. Those present and absent were as follows:
PRESENT:
Rosemarie Michaud
CIP, Resident
David Jodoin
Town Administrator
Karen Yeaton
CIP, Select Board, Alt. Rep.
Kathy Cruson
CIP, Planning Board Rep.
Michael Rodney
CIP, Resident
Gene Gauss
CIP, School Board Rep.
ALSO PRESENT:
VJ Ranfos
Public Works Director
EXCUSED:
Matt Miller
CIP, Select Board Rep.
Approval of Minutes
Motion by Gene Gauss to approve the minutes of August 13th, seconded by Michael Rodney. Select Board
Yeaton abstained. Motion passed 4-0.
Public Hearing - 2027 CIP Requests
Rosemarie Michaud opened the public hearing on the 2021 CIP requests at 6:05 p.m. Rosemarie called to
ublic comment and questions. There were no members of the public so Rosemarie closed the public hearing a
6:06 p.m.
David Jodoin reported that the Energy Committee had reviewed the Library solar proposal and available
incentives and tax credits would require the project to be live, witnessed, and producing by December 31, 2027.
Members discussed questions raised at a prior Select Board meeting, including Select Board Miller's statement
that the estimates were intended as turnkey figures, while also noting remaining questions about structural
review, warranties, interconnection studies, utility upgrades, and any necessary roof reinforcement.

David advised that a structural analysis would be required for the Library roof and also he had a concern on the
Fire side of the Safety Center, while the Police side was not expected to have the same issue.
He further stated that potential savings in the camera project originally developed by Police Chief Gaskell and
now being refined with Fire Chief Paulson for Town Hall, Public Works, Police, Fire, and EMS could leave
additional money available in the Town Facilities and Grounds Capital Reserve Fund.
Members discussed the Library's electric costs, which were estimated at approximately $1,000 per month, and
noted one estimate showing an 8 to 9 year payback period
Ranking of 2027 CIP Requests - Town Facilities and Grounds/Library Solar
Town Facilities and Grounds Capital Reserve Fund Deposit
The first item that the committee reviewed was the proposal to deposit $175,000 into the Town Facilities and
Grounds Capital Reserve Fund.
Rosemarie Michaud asked if these requests could be reduced. David stated the deposit schedule was designed to
support future Town Hall, Library, Safety Center, and related town building needs.
The committee voted as follows on the deposit request. High priority - 2, Medium - 2, and Low -1.
The committee then discussed the proposed Library solar project at an estimated costs of $150,000, exclusive of
any later structural engineering or roof-related work that might be required after further review.
In discussing future building needs, David stated that the current reserve schedule was intended to support the
planned 2029 Safety Center roof and potential solar work, subject to later revision by the Select Board, the
Budget Committee, and Town Meeting.
The committee voted as follows: High priority - 3; Medium - 2
Town Clock Capital Reserve Fund Deposit
The committee reviewed the request for $3,000 to be deposited into the Town Clock Capital Reserve Fund as
well as the next proposed expense in 2032.
Gene Gauss asked what the prior repair costs were. David explained that it was around $35,000 and the money
came out of surplus to pay for it.
The committee voted as follows: High priority - 2; Low - 3
Property Revaluation/Update Capital Reserve Fund Deposit
The committee reviewed the request for $30,000 to be deposited into the Property Revaluation/Update Capital
Reserve Fund.
David explained the current situation in Town where the homes are still selling for much more than we have
them assessed at. If the trend continues commercial property will in effect be paying a higher burden of taxes.

The Board is discussing the possibility of adjusting the values in 2027 to get back in line. Currently the Town's
ratio is at 83% and when we did the revaluation we were at 95%.
Michael Rodney questioned whether the committee even needed to vote on this.
David explained that in the past the same comment had come up and the Chair at the time requested a vote.
The Board voted as follows: High priority - 2; Medium - 1; Low - 2
Statistical Update
Request to withdraw $75,000 from the Property Revaluation Fund
The committee voted High priority - 1; Low - 4
Cemetery Capital Reserve Fund Expense
David explained that there was no need to put any money in the fund this year because they still had enough to
do the proposed work. He also commented that he would like to see the Commission go out at least 10-15 years
with a plan of necessary expenses.
The committee discussed the Cemetery request of $6,000 to repair grave markers.
Rosemarie Michaud commented that some of the expense for the grave marker repairs may also come out of
perpetual care and that would lower the costs.
The committee voted High priority - 5.
Major Fire Equipment Capital Reserve Fund Deposit
The 2027 request was to deposit into the Fund $250,000
The committee reviewed the Fire Department capital schedule and emphasized the importance of maintaining
long-range reserve funding because of sharp increases in apparatus and equipment costs.
Gene Gauss commented that a heavy rescue unit that had cost approximately $169,000 in 1999 would now be in
the range of $1.2 million.
The entire committee voted High priority -5.
David explained that the current CIP plan that the Town uses is one of the best that he has seen over the years,
whether it be as an Auditor or a municipal employee. The Town's Treasurer also hands this out to other
communities as a plan.
He also commented that you can go one Town North or South and you can see what happens when you do not
stick to a plan.

Proposed Changes to Pembroke Town Code 191
Based on citizen complaints received by Pembroke Public Works, Director VJ Ranfos
and I have discussed the need to modify Section 11 of Town Code Chapter 191 to
include times when maintenance is required on any of the Town's Municipal Lots. As
written, the TC does not cover anything other than snow removal operations;
however, there are times when routine maintenance may be needed, such as
paving, line striping, street sweeping, etc. These operational needs require vehicles
to be moved, and, if not moved, towed at the request of the Highway Dept., by way of
the PD. This type of maintenance could, at times, also impact public roadways in the
Town of Pembroke. As a result, we are suggesting that the Board consider changing
the Town Code to encompass other operational needs beyond just snow removal as
follows:
Proposal #1: Change Section 11 to encompass all of the above-listed functions as
follows:
• Change title to Interference with snow removal and routine maintenance
operations (or something similar)
• Change the language in Sub-section A. as follows:
A. Any vehicle which is parked on any public way, or in the town municipal
parking lots, and is interfering with municipal snow removal operations or
properly posted routine maintenance operations may be removed for
safekeeping, by or under the direction of a police officer, to a garage or other
location.
1) Routine maintenance may include but is not limited to: paving, line
striping, street
sweeping, scheduled removal of excess snow in
congested areas, etc.
2) Routine maintenance will be posted at least 24 hours in advance using
static signs in the impacted areas, social media posts, updates on the
Town's website, etc.

MIH-RHTP Project Questions
Hello David,
Dr. David Lapidus is heading up the Mobile Integrated Health (MIH) - Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) for
Concord Hospital. I summarized the questions the Board of Selectmen had and forward that to him. We talked this
after noon and he is preparing a response and an overview of the program. I should have it tomorrow.
To briefly answer Matt's questions:
1. Why is Concord Hospital outsourcing equipment purchases to municipalities & what is the reason the hospital is
trying to share costs of municipal employees instead of hiring new staff?: As stated in a past email, they asked
what will EMS services need to perform the work MIH-RHTP will do. The idea is patients will be more receptive
to receiving care from people they know (familiar EMS providers and vehicles) instead of a Concord Hospital
unit. The intent is a risk free venture for municipalities, with the hospital providing the funds for the staff,
equipment and vehicles needed. Having multiple municipalities involved can cover a larger geographic area
than if the hospital did the project on their own. The goal is to decrease Emergency Department visits, re-
admission rates and improve patient compliance with treatments. The program differs from VNA in the sense,
VNA has strict parameters that it operates under having a low threshold for sending patients to the Emergency
Department. The goal of the program is to graduate patients from MIH to VNA. So MIH isn't doing the job of
VNA, but trying to get patients to a point where they can be managed and care for at home within the
parameters of VNA care. MIH will utilized EMS protocols, tele-health and other components not available to
VNA providers. This MIH will also include the patient's Primary Care Providers to be used as a resource for both
the EMS providers (municipalities) and the patient. By MIH units being attached to their local municipality,
there is a closer working relationship between the MIH unit, Ambulance Crews and the patient. This will allow
for assistance if needed and a seamless transition from MIH to an emergency setting should the patient need
this level of care. Understanding these goals, the hospital feels the MIH model has more benefits than utilizing
2. What are Concord Hospital's expectations regarding the program becoming financially self-sustaining by the end
of the grant? How is the Hospital going to measure/monitor whether the program is making progress towards
financial self-sustainability over the course of the grant? What actions and interventions is Concord Hospital
prepared to do in the event the program is not making sufficient progress towards financial self-
sustainability? The answers to the questions are not fully understood at this time. With talking with Dr.
Lapidus, there are many examples of this type of program around the country. With the goal of increasing
patient compliance and decreasing hospital visits, this data is presented to the health care payors (insurance),
showing the benefit of funding the program and saving on the costs of patients presenting to the Emergency
Department. Dr. Lapidus can elaborate more on this next week.
3. Questions about communications with participating communities and the patients in the event the program does
not succeed and is shut down, and down in a fashion such that people are not surprised and
disappointed. Looking at the intent of the program, this is a short term treatment plan for patients with the
expectation of moving them on to VNA services. There should not be patients who are reliant on this program
for extended periods of time. I do not have further information on this at this time and Dr. Lapidus can provide
more detail at the next BOS meeting.

I know this doesn't fully answer the questions, but this is a new project that is actively being developed. I feel having Dr.
Lapidus (and I believe Dr. Rix) at the next BOS meeting, they can provide a lot more detail and clarification to the Board's
comments and concerns.

Range Roads Subcommittee
Meeting Notes
October 16, 2025
Attendance
Members: Carol Bertsimas, Conservation Commission rep. Matt Miller, Selectboard rep.;
Stephanie Cravotta, Planning Board rep. (via Zoom)
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner, Matt Monahan, Central NH Regional Planning
Commission, Matt Baronas, Central NH Regional Planning Commission
Excused: Bud Curley, Roads Committee rep.
Business
1. Agenda for Event
Carolyn Cronin said the Pembroke Academy auditorium is booked for the event on
Monday, November 17, 2025 at 6:30pm. We are hoping this will be the last subcommittee
meeting before the event because we need time for outreach to advertise and market it.
She and Regional Planning had a conversation about what the agenda for the event would
be and how the event would function. They talked about doing a PowerPoint presentation
at the event and paring it down to 10-15 minutes max, so that people get the information
but we don't lose their attention. We will present an abbreviated version of highlights to
present the issues and explain how the brainstorm session would work.
Matt Monahan said the presentation will lay out the problem statement. We will need to
lead with asking the public for help with what to do with the range roads. We can talk about
the Master Plan survey from 10 years ago that had no consensus. We will lay out some of
the key points.
Matt Miller asked if the presentation will be about the Third and Fourth Range sections, or
will it be range roads in general. Matt Monahan said it will be general, explaining the key
problems with development pressures on the range roads and ask the public how they
would like to address them. We would present high level data. Matt Baronas added that
the last part of the presentation would highlight the visions/scenarios, which demonstrate
what could be done on the range roads, and have the attendees talk about them, and send
them to the stations.
Carolyn Cronin summarized that they would start with the presentation, outline the issues,
let people know what kind of feedback they are looking for, explain how the input will work,
explain the input stations, and people will give written feedback on index cards. We
discussed the possibility of bringing everyone together for a closing statement, but we
think it will work better for people if they can give their feedback and then leave. That way
we don't need a strict end time. This is why the opening presentation is important, because
we won't have the opportunity to talk to them again. We can leave the comment period
open after the event because we want to provide them the full PowerPoint with all the
details. We can post it on the website and have a QR Code available.
T:\Town Planner\Class VI Roads\Range Roads Subcommittee\Minutes\2025\RRMinutes10-16-25.docx
Page 1 of 3

Matt Miller likes leaving the comment period open because people who attend may spread
the word to other people, who then may want to participate and comment. They can review
the information and then email their comments.
Carol Bertsimas asked what happens to all the feedback. Carolyn Cronin said it will be
collected into a report. It will be transcribed as raw data and then we will create an
executive summary of common themes. Carol Bertsimas asked if that will be available to
this group or to the public. Carolyn Cronin said this group will help with that. We will put it
together and then distribute it to the Planning Board, Selectboard, and public. Matt
Monahan added that the town could hold a nonbinding vote on the results, as the
legislative body, to give their ranked preference on the options. That could be how the
results get used rather than a singular course of action. Carolyn Cronin confirmed that this
was the purpose of this event, to get feedback that will inform policy and decision-making.
2. Review Public Input Stations
A draft of the public input stations was circulated to the group. Carolyn Cronin explained
that each station will have a poster board and a committee member assigned to that
station. There will be a photo/visual and a paragraph description of each. We have been
calling them "scenarios," and thank you to Matt Miller for doing the first draft; we are
pivoting to calling them "visions" because it is a vision of the range roads. "Vision" sounds
more broad and open-ended. The attendee of each station should be familiar with the
concept of that station to be able to talk about and answer questions if needed.
Matt Miller suggested adding a metrics box to each poster. For example property tax base,
traffic, development, recreation, etc. to show the expected impact of each of those metrics
for each scenario/station. It will show a comparison so people can see how each scenario
may affect them.
The committee had a detailed discussion on how to rank each, what "impact" meant, how
to assign value, how to quantify the benefits, and what categories made sense to include
in the metrics box.
Matt Monahan will add the metrics box to each station poster and email them for review.
Carolyn Cronin added that there is a section on the poster called "Path," which gives a
general outline of how that vision would be achieved so there are realistic expectations.
3. Review Outreach Plan
a. Review Stakeholders Contact List
b. Delegate who is responsible for different outreach components
Carolyn Cronin put together a Stakeholders Contact List for the committee to review and
comment on. The purpose is to ensure we have an accurate contact list and have not left
anyone out.
T: \Town Planner|Class VI Roads|Range Roads Subcommittee|Minutes\2025\RRMinutes10-16-25.docx
Page 2 of 3

The committee made some additions and clarifications to the stakeholders list. A flyer will
be emailed to each stakeholder.
The event needs to be posted to Facebook groups: Pembroke Speaks, Pembroke
Taxpayers, and Pembroke, NH Community Events. Matt Miller will post the information to
each group once the flyer is finalized.
Everything will be posted on the Town website and easy to link to.
An abutter list was compiled of property owners who abut the Class VI portions of Third
and Fourth Range Roads. A flyer will be mailed directly to them.
Matt Miller asked why not contact the abutters of all range roads, and not just Third and
Fourth. Carolyn Cronin explained that those two will see the biggest impacts because they
have the shortest connections. There are 35 abutters just on those two roads.
Carolyn Cronin asked if an ad in the Concord Monitor would be worthwhile. The committee
decided that the other methods (Facebook, mail) would be more effective.
The committee raised the topic of providing food at the forum. They will explore options for
refreshments (add to the flyer). They should plan for food for 50 attendees. They will need
to request a budget from David.
4. Discussion on PowerPoint Presentation
Matt Monahan will put together a presentation of 5-7 slides with the issues and data points.
He will send around the draft presentation for the committee to review.
The comment period after the public session will be 30 days.
The committee will review the presentation and vision posters, to be sent out, and decide if
they need another meeting. They discussed meeting for a bit immediately before the
event.
Adjournment
The meeting adjourned at 3:45 pm

Range Roads Subcommittee
Meeting Notes
August 11, 2025
Attendance
Members: Carol Bertsimas, Conservation Commission rep. and Matt Miller, Selectboard
rep.
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner, Matt Monahan, Central NH Regional Planning
Commission, Matt Baronas, Central NH Regional Planning Commission
Excused: Stephanie Cravotta, Planning Board rep. and Bud Curley, Roads Committee rep.
Business
1. Update on Senate Bill 281: Building Permits on Class VI Roads
Matt Monahan explained that currently RSA 674:41 states that if you want a building
permit on a Class VI road, you need to go to the Board of Selectmen, and the Planning
Board has to review and comment. If approved, the owner signs a waiver from town
services, including police and fire, and that gets recorded at the Registry of Deeds. We all
know that Police and Fire will try to get there if there is a call, so the applicant talks to the
Road Agent and Fire Chief to see how they can best access the property.
Matt Miller asked who the governing body is and do they still need Planning Board review.
Matt Monahan answered the Selectboard and he believes they do still need Planning
review.
Carolyn Cronin believes they did away with the Planning Board review under the new law.
She explained the new State law takes effect a year from now and to get a building permit
on a Class VI road you would need only to record the signed waiver at the Registry and
provide proof that the buildings and the land are insurable. She doesn't know how you
prove that if the building isn't there yet. Those are the only two requirements. You don't
have to insure the building, just prove that you can. She believes the building permit is
issued automatically with no Selectboard or Planning Board oversight.
Matt Miller asked if the town has its own liability waiver drafted. Carolyn Cronin said yes,
we did that with the town attorney when the Selectboard adopted their Class VI road policy
a couple years ago. It covers trash, recycling, and emergency services.
Matt Monahan said a lot of towns have been dealing with Class VI roads. Bradford just did
a new Class VI road document. This new law means that it's easier to get a building permit
for a single lot. I don't think it changes anything for subdivision, but we don't know for sure.
Carolyn Cronin explained that this is one of a ton of new land use laws that were just
passed. We are in a bit of a gray area because we don't totally know what it all means yet,
if it will be challenged, what case law may come out of it, but it was worth bringing it up to
this subcommittee to keep you informed. It does not negate the need for long-term
comprehensive planning for the range roads, but it's something to be aware of because we
could see impacts of this as soon as next year.
T:\Town Planner\Class VI Roads\Range Roads Subcommittee\Minutes\2025\RRMinutes08-11-25.docx
Page 1 of 5

Matt Monahan added that there were more bills that were pulled, but may reappear in the
next year. For example, there was a proposal for statewide minimum lot sizes and that
may come back again. He showed how lots in the buildout analysis could be affected by
the new building permit law.
Matt Miller commented that continuing with the range road policy project still makes sense
because it's being proactive. He asked how this might affect subdivision. Matt Monahan
admitted that he was not 100% sure, but assumed that the new law did not apply to
subdivisions. He noted that people may be able to get creative with building permits and
try to do things that might result in undesirable development scenarios.
Carolyn Cronin agreed that she did not think this new law would impede Planning Board's
subdivision review process. She noted that building permits may beget more building
permits. She said the impact of this law may not be one big development by a single
developer, but a piecemeal development as the Class VI road becomes more passable
from more people living there.
Matt Monahan described it as patchwork pass-ability as owners improve the road over
time. He said if this were done in a planned way, there would be offsite improvements.
Carolyn Cronin said that New Hampshire Municipal Association (NHMA) did a webinar on
legislative changes. One question that was asked is if the Fire Department still have the
ability to require access upgrades on the Class VI road and the answer was "no". There
are no additional conditions a town can put on the permit, just the waiver and proof of
insurance.
Matt Miller noted that instead of the law that was passed, it probably would have been
better if the State incentivized towns to improve their infrastructure through grants. Carolyn
Cronin said that NHMA shared that same sentiment, that the State should have
incentivized towns rather than slap them on the wrists. The end result is that they've taken
away local control.
Matt Monahan noted that people from out of state are interested in these properties
without realizing you can't actually access the property. So they either have buyer's
remorse or they build out the property with consequences of bad development.
Carolyn Cronin rounded out the conversation with an opinion that this new law flies in the
face of standard State planning language, where the purpose of planning is to prevent
"scattered and premature development". We want development to happen in an orderly
way so as not to overburden town services and taxpayers. This new law is the definition of
scattered and premature development.
2. Agenda for Event
Matt Monahan said the goal is to inform people of the history of development on range
roads, the potential, and the current environment. This history is the San Ken case study.
Matt Miller said he thinks it needs an introduction explaining why this topic is important -
there are undeveloped roads, housing shortages, scattered development, etc. - and
explain that we can be proactive or not.
T:\Town Planner\Class VI Roads\Range Roads Subcommittee\Minutes\2025\RRMinutes08-11-25.docx
Page 2 of 5

Carol Bertsimas added that currently a developer is the only one that can afford to upgrade
the road, and that means a lot more houses than if the individual property owner were
building. Matt Monahan added that we might want a builder to absorb the costs of the
roads as opposed to a TIF district.
Carol Bertsimas asked what the options are for a town to open or pay for a road. Matt
Monahan said one option is the developer requests to open the road and bears the costs
of the upgrades. Or individual property owners could petition the town to open the road at
town meeting and bond the road or do a TIF district. Carolyn Cronin added that there were
a few cases in the past where property owners petitioned to open the road and upgraded it
themselves, but that has become rarer due to the costs of construction.
Carolyn Cronin said that the event will be twofold: give a presentation and get feedback.
What would that feedback process look like? She asked if CHRPC recommend small
group breakout sessions, like a mini Master Plan.
Matt Monahan said the small breakout groups could be focus groups, but there will be a lot
of questions. It will probably be 75% presentation and Q&A and 25% breakout sessions.
Matt Miller had concerns that breakout groups may not be able to cover everything. He
suggested an exhibit/station with a person there to answer questions on each scenario.
Matt Monahan added that the breakout groups could be one theme per group and people
rotate through, so that could be a combination of the two ideas. Matt Miller wanted to
ensure that the breakout groups did not limit feedback.
Carol Bertsimas thought small groups would be more manageable and then they could
share with the full group after. Carolyn Cronin has seen giant flip pads posted around the
room and people could vote with stickers and add comments, each pad is a different topic.
It's a mobile way to give feedback, but you may not be able to get questions answered in
that format. Matt Monahan suggested a facilitator at each station for a set amount of time.
Potential categories for groups/stations were: Third Range Road, Fourth Range Road, Do
Nothing, Conservation/Town Forest, Developer Builds the Road for Developments, Town
Builds the Road, Nonresidential Development, Cluster Development.
Matt Monahan talked about what the zoning permits in those zones. Slides were added to
the presentation showing those uses.
Matt Miller described an example of a nonresidential development. He talked about the
revitalization of the Suncook Village and discussed giving another reason for people to
come to Pembroke. Too much residential makes us a giant suburb and there is no
attraction to live here. We might want something that could attract people to visit or live
here.
Matt Monahan talked about mixed use. Canterbury just adopted a conservation cluster
mixed use ordinance. A mix of the permitted uses there could look like residential with
agricultural uses.

Range Roads Subcommittee
Meeting Notes
May 2, 2025
Attendance
Members: Carol Bertsimas, Conservation Commission rep. and Matt Miller, Selectboard
rep.
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner, Matt Monahan, Central NH Regional Planning
Commission, Matt Baronas, Central NH Regional Planning Commission

Business
1. Information Needed for Community Forum
a. Traffic Study
b. Natural Resource Inventory
c. EMS Response Time Data
d. Updated PowerPoint Presentation
Matt Monahan and Matt Baronas from Central NH Regional Planning Commission
(CHRPC) attended via Zoom. They updated the PowerPoint presentation that was
presented last time. CHRPC added data that was requested at the last meeting. They
added a zoning analysis showing the lot size and frontage requirements in the R1 and R3
zones, which are what the Class VI portions of Third and Fourth Range are zoned as.
CNHPRC also updated the construction cost estimates to upgrade the road from 2023
numbers to 2025 numbers.
Matt Miller asked if this presentation was a draft. Carolyn Cronin clarified that this was a
draft of the presentation to be shown at the event. It will be sent out Committee members
for review and comment after today's meeting.
The San Ken case study and buildout scenarios remain in the presentation. CHRPC
added development constraints (estimated wetland area, conservation land, and steep
slopes.) CNHRPC pulled their traffic count data from locations that could potentially be
impacted by the opening of Third or Fourth Range Rd. They added a table showing the
location of the count, the traffic count, the year the data was collected, and traffic
projections based on each buildout scenario. CNHRPC explained the ITE traffic trip
generation estimate (10/day) for single-family homes.
CHRPC added wildlife habitat to the maps. They also added a graph representing each
buildout scenario with the total parcel acreage and the percent of that acreage estimated
to be impacted by developed area. Matt Miller asked that they label the graph with the
range road that the scenario is referring to.
CNHRPC also added data from the Regional Housing Needs Assessment, which provides
guidance on how many units are required to meet housing needs in the region over a
projected period of time. Matt Miller asked if this was the same data from the Master Plan.
Matt Baronas was unsure if it's in the Master Plan and explained that the Regional
Housing Needs Assessment covers each region and informs a State-wide analysis. Matt
T:\Town Planner\Class VI Roads\Range Roads Subcommittee\Minutes\2025\RRMinutes05-02-25.docx

Miller said that he saw information in the Master Plan that said there would be a decrease
in the number of rental units and projected needing only 3 units per year. It didn't make
sense, so he will look into it again. Matt Monahan explained that the Housing Needs
Assessment is based on population projections and does not address existing housing
deficit. They are including the data to show what the housing need is and how long that
may take to achieve. He suggested that the progress of the San Ken development may be
an indicator of that.
Matt Miller said that in the public meeting, the focus may not be specifically on the number
of homes built. It may be on alternative scenarios of what is possible. He suggested we
present that information as much as the housing information so that the public can think
about all options.
Matt Monahan agreed and asked if it made sense to remove the slide. Matt Miller
suggested instead adding other scenarios beside the single-family development, like
mixed use, town forest, etc. Carolyn Cronin suggested we look at what is currently allowed
in those zones and include that information. She clarified that the focus is heavily on the
single-family residential scenarios because it reflects the pressures and the demand that
the town is experiencing. Carol Bertsimas suggested the presentation should start with an
explanation of what the R1 and R3 are and what is allowed there so people understand.
Matt Miller agreed that we need an introduction to explain why we are looking at this topic
now and why we need public feedback on a variety of possibilities.
Matt Monahan said that he reached out to the NH Municipal Association (NHMA) and
asked if a town can put a question on the ballot that is a resolution, saying what they prefer
but not actually voting to act on it. For example, could Pembroke have a vote asking
opinions about opening Fourth Range Road without actually voting to open the road? You
could get feedback seeing what percentage of voters feel one way or another. NHMA said,
yes, they could have a resolution to get a sense of what the town wants. That could be
helpful here. The Town Attorney would help draft that ballot language.
Carol Bertsimas asked if those types of scenarios ever come about in the practical sense,
where push comes to shove, and the town has to make a choice. Matt Monahan said yes,
scenarios can occur where the town is asked to make a decision. The San Ken case study
speaks to what could happen if the vote went one way or another. Right now the courts
seems to be tipped in the favor of developers, so that's why the town needs to be prepared
and ready to address these scenarios.
Matt Miller asked about a scenario where a developer may do a development that may
block a range road or create an alternative road. He asked what leverage the Planning or
Zoning Board have to deny a project like that if they have knowledge of town plans to do
something different. Carolyn Cronin said that any request for opening or closing a range
road would go to the Board of Selectmen. If the developer were building a new road on
their property, as long as it meets our requirements, the Board would have to approve it.
We couldn't force a developer to build out a range road if it's unrelated to their project.
Carol Bertsimas asked about federal funding for a town to build out a range road. Matt
Monahan said you could apply for the State 10 Year Plan if you make the case that it's an
alternative to Route 3. Alternatively, the town could do a TIF district. The most realistic
scenario is a developer building it out.

The last missing piece of the presentation is the EMS response time data. Matt Monahan
and Carolyn Cronin will set up a meeting to have a discussion with the Fire Chief. The
Committee can take time to review the presentation and give feedback. Matt Miller asked if
we could include property tax impacts to building out the range roads. Matt Monahan said
they could look into that.
At 3pm, CNHRPC had to end the Zoom call because they had another meeting. Matt
Monahan and Matt Baronas left the meeting.
Matt Miller expanded on his thoughts on alternative scenarios. Residential development,
non-residential development, recreational uses, and "do nothing" scenarios should all be
explored. Carolyn Cronin said that ties in with looking at all the permitted uses. We can
add a table to the presentation outlining that. The area has the limitation that there is no
town water and sewer, so that limits the scale of development that could be possible.
Matt Miller asked about how potential State legislation on zoning will tie into this. Carolyn
Cronin said that typically in August or September NHMA will send out a memo to towns
telling us what passed and what that means. She doesn't know if it's worth exploring those
bills in detail at this point. We typically don't amend our zoning right after a bill passes
because there is always the possibility it could be challenged. Regardless of what happens
in Concord, the public input will be valuable for future planning.
We are hoping the public forum will be scheduled in June before school lets out and
people start summer vacation. We need to have a brainstorm session with everyone about
the rest of the agenda items. We need a meeting to do that and finalize the presentation.
The Committee had a brief discussion about existing zoning, open space development,
senior housing, and the cost of housing in general. They are all issues that all towns are
tacing.

Range Roads Subcommittee
Meeting Notes
March 27, 2025
Attendas: Stephanie Cravotta, Planning Board rep: Carol Bertsimas, Conservation
Commission rep.; Bud Curley, Roads Committee rep.; and Matt Miller, Selectboard rep.
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner and Matt Monahan, Central NH Regional Planning
Commission
Business
1. Range Road Issues Recap
Staff explained that a presentation about the development pressures on Class VI roads
(range roads) was shown to the land use boards last summer. Some of those here saw it
and some haven't. We will do a recap for everyone to refresh memories.
This all came about because in summer 2022, the housing market was ramping up and the
planning and building departments were inundated with requests to build on the range
roads. The building inspector cannot issue a permit on a Class VI road. You either need
permission from the Selectboard or to upgrade the road to town spec (paved). It's not
economically feasible for a person to build a road to serve one single-family home. Only a
developer will do that because they recoup the costs from the houses they sell. This issue
creates a conflict between the type of development that is the town's vision for that area
(low density, rural, agricultural) and developers building large-scale housing developments.
At the time, the Planning Board talked about the need to be proactive, not reactive, when
we get these requests to build. They enlisted the help of the Central NH Regional Planning
Commission (CHRPC), who work with other towns on planning issues. They have
excellent staff and resources, and can help with range road planning. The project consists
of three phases: fact finding and data collection, public input, and a final report with
findings and recommendations. This committee will help with the public input process and
compiling the feedback. The feedback can help inform changes to regulations, policies,
and/or zoning. The voters will have the final say as proposals are brought to Town
Meeting.
Staff asked about the members' thoughts on the range roads. C. Bertsimas said that
Conservation sees them as a resource to be enjoyed by all and they are aware of the
pressures to build. Over time, some of the range roads have degraded to almost the point
of being impassable because they are abused. We would like to preserve the range roads.
They add to the town's rural character. I don't know what the answer is. Maybe we choose
one of them to be developed and the leave the rest alone. S. Cravotta explained that she
is new to the Planning Board. As a personal opinion, she echoes Conservation's concerns.
M. Miller recognized that the San Ken example was a good example of not being
proactive. There is some conservation land on the range roads, but they are not
connected. There may be potential to connect them and preserve it as a trail. I've heard
concerns about development leading to increased school costs, but when you have
enough growth it can afford more services. I don't advocate for either way, but it makes
T:\Town Planner\Class VI Roads\Range Roads Subcommittee\Minutes\2025\RRMinutes03-27-25.docx
Page 1 of 2

sense to have a plan in place. I'll be interested to see the outcome of the study. B. Curley
has served on the Roads Committee for 20 years and has seen several occasions where
someone wanted to develop on the range roads. The Roads Committee's perspective is
that the road needs to be built to spec. It's rare, but a homeowner has gone through the
process in the past to build the road for one or two single-family homes.
Staff went through the PowerPoint presentation that was presented last summer. The
presentation raised questions and comments about alternatives to Route 3, pros and cons
of homeowners' associations, acceptance of town roads, assessments and TIF districts,
classifications of roads, and buildout scenarios. (The presentation is available on the
Town website on the Planning Board page. https://www.pembroke-
nh.com/sites/g/files/vyhlif4861/f/uploads/rangeroadspresentation_final.pdf)
2. Function of a Community Forum/Charrette and the Subcommittee's Role
Staff said that the feedback from board members on this issue has been really valuable.
Now we want town-wide feedback through a community forum or charrette. We would like
to see a grassroots outreach effort for community input on this topic. We would like the
chance to educate and inform the larger community with all that we just discussed. We
want to present the facts and solicit meaningful feedback to inform some options/policies
to create that town vision.
M. Miller asked that we create an inventory of the facts so that we can see what has been
gathered and what may be missing. He said there are certain questions from the public
that we can expect. He suggested a traffic study and natural resource inventory would be
useful information for the public forum. M. Monahan added that EMS response times might
be helpful too.
3. Next Steps
Staff suggested that the next meeting should be a discussion about what the outreach
looks like for the public forum. We should talk about groups/stakeholders that should
attend, how we want to publicize it, where and when to hold it, what the presentation
should look like, and what data we need. The committee suggested DPW and the Trail
Dogs Snowmobile Club should be invited. Drainage was asked about. M. Monahan said
that their staff engineer (who is also the Town engineer) could help with technical requests.
This project is funded by NHDOT, so they are paying for the staff time.
4. Next Meeting Date
M. Monahan suggested we need a meeting to plan the event (April/May), then the actual
event (June), and another meeting to recap and compose the findings (Summer). The
Committee agreed to decide on the next meeting date after staff sends out some date and
time suggestions
Adjournment
The meeting adjourned at 7:45pm

Staff presented a revised final draft, which reflected the edits discussed at the last
meeting. Revisions were made to add context and clarity to the information and the figures
and maps. Formatting and appendices were also revised.
Matt Miller suggested moving the public opinion on each Vision from the Options section to
the Public Opinion section that follows. He also suggested moving the Public Opinion
section in front of the Options section.
All agreed it made sense to make the change.
Bob Bourque pointed out a formatting issue on page 29. The "Potential Impact Matrix" box
fell in the middle of the text. It needs to be shifted to the right to keep the text together.
Bob Bourque also pointed out that the text on the maps (the legends and labels) are blurry
and very hard to read. He used a magnifying glass and they were still blurry. Staff talked
about trying to redo the maps if they can. It was suggested that when the maps were
expanded to fit the page, that it distorted the image Staff will look at it.
Carol Bertsimas asked what will happen with the information now that the report is done.
Carolyn Cronin said that the report will be distributed to town board and committees,
posted on the website, and emailed to anyone who submitted email feedback. The hope is
that when the town is faced with questions of whether to open a range road, a lot of the
questions that may arise can be answered by the information in the report. The report has
fact finding, public feedback, and recommendations. The recommendations are applicable
to different boards and departments. The report gives options when faced with different
questions or proposals.
Matt Monahan added that at the next town meeting the town can do a nonbinding
resolution to get more feedback about whether to open a road. Carolyn Cronin also said
that in July, when the new law on issuing building permits on class VI roads takes effect,

Meeting Notes

Attendance
Members: Carol Bertsimas, Conservation Commission rep.; Matt Miller, Selectboard rep.;

Business
1. Review Draft Final Report
a. Discuss how to Present Public Feedback
b. Discuss Recommendations for Report
Carolyn Cronin updated the subcommittee since the last time they met at the public forum
in November. She explained that Stephanie, the Planning Board rep, resigned from the
Planning Board, so Bob Bourque was appointed to replace her. The public forum was in
mid-November, the comment period was open until mid-December and then the holidays
happened, and since then Central NH Regional Planning Commission (CHRPC) have
been working on the bulk of the draft report. She had typed up all the public comments
from the forum and emails. She and CHRPC went back and forth on the report. She
included information about how the public forum operated and the subcommittee's efforts
to plan it. A lot of the report is public comments and information from the PowerPoint
presentation that was previously put together.
Carolyn Cronin explained that there are two tasks left for the subcommittee: finalize the
report and suggest recommendations based on the facts and on the public feedback
collected. The recommendations will be for the Select Board, Planning Board,
Conservation Commission, and other committees that have control over zoning
amendments, master plans, town policies, budgeting decisions, etc. to inform town policies
and regulations, because that is the scope of the subcommittee. The subcommittee's
charge is to decide how you want to process and package the feedback and integrate it
into recommendations.
Staff put together a first stab at feedback analysis and recommendations. Matt Miller also
put together a document with his feedback analysis. He also shared his edits and
comments on the draft report.
Matt Miller explained his suggestions for the report. He recommended the following:
• Adding captions and figure numbers to all the figures in the report.
• Integrating the public comments into the report so it flows better, and possibly
moving some of the data into appendices. For example, some of the detailed data
