like traffic patterns, alternate emergency routes, and lot size requirements can be
moved into an appendix.
Matt Monahan said that the top of the report will have a section for Findings and
Recommendations, which needs to be filled in, and that should help integrate public
feedback into the report.
• The figures for the emergency response were confusing. A caption and a key would
help, and also highlighting where the Class VI portions of the road are.
• The figure of Third Range Road Scenario 2. It's not clear that the Cross Road
alignment is the feature that intends to be highlighted.
• The document raises a few different types of questions about range roads. Some
questions were not addressed, depending what the town decides (traffic, utilities,
etc.)
Matt Monahan agreed that those are good questions for development, generally. He added
that the question might be how those factors are influenced by range roads compared to
other types of roads.
Matt Miller wanted to find a way to call out valid concerns that are raised by the report,
while also acknowledging that those solutions are outside of the scope of the study.
Carolyn Cronin suggested that those types of thoughts would be best suited for the
recommendation section as items that need further examination in relation to a town policy
or when applications to develop are brought forth.
The subcommittee moved on to discussing the public feedback and how to analyze and
present it.
Carolyn Cronin suggested there are a few ways to present the feedback. There could be
summaries for each Vision. She also looked at all the feedback and presented general
themes that came up as frequently mentioned. The challenge is that the data is qualitative,
not quantitative. She said that even comments that were "in favor" or "not in favor" of
certain scenarios were with caveats or concerns. She cautioned that they had to be careful
not to misrepresent the feedback as black and white.
Matt Miller found that for most of the scenarios there was a mixture of feedbacks, except
for Vision 3: Town Forest and Recreation Trails, which had consistent feedback of people
in favor of it.
Bob Bourque suggested both summarizing each scenario's comments and also including
the original comments for anyone to read. It was agreed that the original comments would
be included as an appendix to the report.
Chuck Schmidt explained that he volunteered with one of the master plans years ago. At
that time, the town indicated that they wanted to keep the middle of the town and range
roads as recreation. The philosophy hasn't changed even as new people come into town.
He brought up the new State legislation that allows property owners to build on range
roads, as long as they sign away their liability. He asked why that wasn't mentioned in the
report.

Matt Monahan explained that that legislation relates to single owners of single lots. There
is also the separate issue of subdivision. What we are dealing with more is the subdivision
aspect, as demonstrated in the San Ken Homes example. The question we are looking at
more is what happens with developers of subdivisions, and how does the planning board
balance that, and how does the Select Board treat that request. We are trying to get more
feedback from the last time the town was polled, which was a third in favor of opening the

Matt Miller pointed out that there were comments stating they were not in favor of the town

where the town wants you to spend tax dollars and where they do not want to spend.
That's an important point to inform budgeting decisions and capital improvement plans.
Matt Miller summarized the feedback by each scenario and called out where people

Carol Bertsimas said that there was resounding opposition to high density housing. That
goes back to the issue of wanting a landowner to only build a couple houses, but relying

Does the town open the road to allow fewer houses or does the developer open the road

Bob Bourque suggested either allowing open space development or increasing the

1. CPCNH update (presented by Jackson Kaspari and Andrew Hatch).
1. A PDF of the slides will be included in the meeting minutes.
2. Pembroke Community Power
1. Launched March 2024

Power procured = 24,404 MWh
Customer Savings $157,000 (through June 30, 2025)
4. Current Accounts: 2,650 (2,634 Eversource and 23 Unitil)

5. 65% participation, 20.3% with third party suppliers, 3.3% net metered, and 0.6%
opt-ups.
3. The Pembroke Community Power website is updated periodically to improve
intuitiveness and ease of use. Also there are ways for individual customers to sign up for
news letters, legislative action alerts, rate change notifications etc.
4. Differences in Supply Procurement
1. Utilities
1. PUC has ordered the utilities to procure differently, now they want the
utilities to purchase 50% of their power on the day ahead market
(previously was 0% of power from day ahead market). PUC is wanting
the utilities to increase up to 100% of their procurement from the day
ahead market in the future.
2.
Utilities may reconcile with their customer base in future periods for
under or over collections in the current rate period.
1. The current rates are "proxy rates."
2. Requires utilities to forecast or guess the expected load and the
expected price.
3. There is market exposure and volatility.
2. CPCNH
1. Rate transparency
2. Hedged transactions
3. Rates cover costs--there will be no future reconciliations
4. No surcharges.
5. What is the current understanding of how the utilities will reconcile their under or
over-collections. It is difficult to say because it has been redacted, and only the PUC and
consumer advocate know.
1. Eversource and Unitil claim that their reconciliations have been included into
their August 1 2025 - Jan 31, 2026 rates. Liberty included 4 cents/kwh of
reconciliation for the same period, was rejected by the PUC, and they were told
to remove 50% of their under-collections, and they resubmitted a rate of around
12.8 c/kwh (from 14.8 c/kwh).
2. CPCNH will move towards a cost of service model, meaning that rates will vary
by utility district, or possibly even by CPA (community power aggregation).
Jackson said that although technically possible, rate differences by CPA are
unlikely. Rates will be different by Utility District and by customer class only.
Main reason for the move is that capacity costs, which are charged by ISO-NE,
vary by utility.
6. CPCNH has been improving its load forecasting, financial modeling and cost-of service
analysis.
7. PUC rules for fair market competition in Unitil Docket. The original order from PUC that
utilities shift under-collection costs to non-bypassable charges that all customers would
receive was defeated (for now). So, for now, the precedent that energy costs are not
shifted to distribution/stranded cost charges and to customers in different rate classes.
CPCH played a big role in providing important feedback to the PUC regarding the
under-collection reconciliation process.
8. Benefits of Community power
1. Local control--member driven organization
2. Customer choice--offering electric product options

3. Competition--ensure healthy competition against monopoly utility supply and
traditional third-party brokers
4. Market innovation--promoting a dynamic and modernized energy system that
seeks to unlock greater value for customers
5. Program and project development-locally controlled energy assets can enable
long-term stability, cost savings and greater energy security.
6. Public advocacy-CPCNH works to protect and promote customer and
community interests in legislative and regulatory proceedings.
9. CPCNH has suspended the refresh program, which would automatically enroll new
accounts, until the rates improve and fall below the utility default electricity prices.
10. CPCNH has also not launched any new CPAs until rates improve.
11. Poverty Plains Solar Project in Warner, NH
1. I received the counter signed agreement from CPCH, and I need to turn it in to
David Jodoin.
2. The benefit will be in the form of a cash reimbursement, which Pembroke will
deposit into its general fund. The benefit is calculated as 12.5% of whatever the
default Utility rate is times the amount of power consumed by the 5 qualifying
municipal accounts.
2. Work session to create summary of Solar Generation on Safety Center for CIP Committee on
August 7, 2025.
1. Purpose and benefits
1. Safety Center is biggest electricity consumer, so the PEC was interested in
whether some new energy investment would be an effective way to reduce
costs and improve energy security.
2. Distribution costs are rising--and PUC gave a green light for utilities to increase
the distribution costs without review.
2. Concept
1. A rooftop solar array to generate some fraction of the power used by the Safety
Center, offsetting both electricity supply and electricity demand charges.
2. If possible, a battery system could also charge and discharge in a way that would
shave the peak loads and reduce demand charges. However, our Safety Center
does not have an interval meter, so none of the solar vendors were able to size a
battery system for our demand charges.
3. Additionally, safety center already has a backup generator, so batteries are not
necessary for backup power.
Basic overview of the Proposals
1.
Size (load)
1. Around 60s % seems to be a sweet spot.
2. Location
1. Rooftop
2.
Safety center has excellent roofs and excellent sun exposure.
3.
Costs
1.
GSS $142K for 63% of load offset (110 panels, 59.4 KW system).
2.
Revision
1. $130K for 40% load offset
2.
$250K for 60% load offset
3.
$400K for 100% load offset

3. a. action item review
4. 3. Pembroke Master Plan Discussion with Carolyn Cronin
1. Carolyn presented some slides on the purpose of the Master Plan and how it comes
together, and how it should be used.
1.
It is a guide for decision making and policy making.

2. It has no teeth and cannot be enforced
3.
It is prepared to help guide the development of the municipality.
4. Two sections are required
1. Community vision
2. Land use
3. All other sections are optional and can only be selected from the list
outlined in RSA 674.1-4.
5. Master Plan revisions are recommended every 5 to 10 years. There are
notification requirements every time the document is updated.
6. Pembroke's 2020 Master Plan process.
1. Town survey administered to residents. (300 people responded)
2. Steering Committee made up of town residents organized a
community-wide Visioning forum (1/2 day event at a school) -to solicit
feedback from the town residents on all the topics selected to be
included in the master plan.
3.
The survey results, visioning feedback, and data from CHRPC are
combined and subcommittees are formed to work on each
section/chapter.
4. Finally a review period and final public hearing are held on the draft plan
prior to adoption. The planning board is the owner and the entity that
adopts the plan.
Timeline mid-2017 to early 2021.
6. Pembroke's previous plan was adopted 2004.
1. Note: previous master plans will be reviewed and possibly parts
will propagate and continue into the next master plan.
7. Plan implementation
1. Implementation happens organically based on Town priorities, current
issues, growth patterns or rate of growth in the town.
2. The Master Plan is not meant to be a "to do" list
3. No auditing or reporting when items are completed. Goals are
delegated to responsible parties and given a suggested timeline for ease
of prioritization and implementation.
4. It's a community vision to guide decision-making, not a mandate. The
current Master Plan serves as a barometer of what the community
values and supports.
8.
Energy chapter:
1.
Objective 10.1: keep Pembroke residents and business informed on
energy efficiency. Conservation and renewable energy measures and
where to find additional information and funding.
1.
Energy committee has a role to contribute to the sub objectives
of this objective.
2. Objective 2 (mostly responsibility of Planning Board, Planning
Department, and Building Department): encourage and support energy
conscious development.
1. Town to support an Energy Committee that advises the town on
energy issues...

2. Ensure that the land use regulations do not unduly restrict the
use of alternative energy sources or sustainable construction
techniques.
3. Regularly review and update amendments to the Energy
Building Code and initiate any necessary amendments to ensure
that Pembroke is proactive in addressing emerging energy
efficient construction practices
4. Develop an energy-checklist for any proposed project that
identifies energy efficiency considerations for homeowners,
developers and municipal departments.
5. Amend zoning subdivision and site plan regulations that identify
opportunities for renewable energy installations and address
any potential impacts on surrounding properties.
1. Interestingly, Pembroke does not have any zoning or
ordinance for ground mount solar installations, and
bi-facial solar collectors. It would be useful for the
Energy Committee to advise the Planning Board and
Planning Department on or suggest a solar ground
mount ordinance, or at least parameters that should be
considered by the planning board for a ground mount
solar installation.
3. Objective 3: To reduce municipal usage and costs and improve energy
efficiency in municipal operations. Mostly assigned to the Town
Administrator and Select Board.
1. Actively monitor municipal energy usage and costs to track
progress resulting from energy saving initiatives.
2. Participate in public and private programs that educate and/or
fund the retrofit of municipal buildings and infrastructure.
3. Continue to implement building energy improvement plans to
increase the efficiency of municipal buildings and incorporate
planned improvements into the municipal budgeting process.
4. Investigate options for renewable energy at municipal buildings.

Here is a summary of the current energy section objectives etc.
2. Energy (chapter 10) Note: this is perhaps the least developed chapters of the 2020
Master Plan. It should be revised and augmented by the current Energy Committee.
1. The community survey results showed that Pembroke residents have a strong
interest in energy sustainability and renewables. Over 70% of residents felt it is
important/somewhat important for Pembroke to expand and invest in

renewable energy and over 74% supported ordinances that would encourage
renewable energy options, including solar, electric and wind. On another
question, 88% rated the improvement of energy efficiency of municipal buildings
as important/somewhat important.
Pembroke schools (largely motivated by Josh Coughlin) have identified and
implemented numerous successful energy efficiency projects.
3. Challenges and Opportunities
1. transportation is the leading source of energy use in the state. There is
also the increasing concern for the aging population at both the local,
regional and state levels and its impacts on our abilities to reach
destinations - for recreation, health care and social services. This has a
direct correlation to the land use patterns and infrastructure of our
communities and how we need to get from point A to point B. As New
Hampshire's population continues to age, more compact development
and transportation options become pressing critical needs in many of
our communities. The link between energy efficiency and transportation
is a strong one.
2.
As tax credits, rebates and other incentives continue to evolve and
hopefully stabilize with a consistent funding stream, it is expected that
renewable energy installations will become more prevalent. How to
identify and apply for appropriate financial and informational resources
that exist to help municipalities, business owners, and residents make
positive changes in their energy consumption.

conservation and renewable energy measures and where to find

Types of 3-Phase Current Meters
• Digital Multi-Function Meters: Display voltage, current, power, power factor, etc., often
with data logging and communication.
• Wireless Meters: Use sensors for remote monitoring, sending data via text/email for
alerts (e.g., Monnit ALTA).
• Smart/Submeters: Versatile kWh meters for various 3-phase setups (Delta, Wye) with
optional CTs (e.g., EKM Omnimeter).
• Panel Meters: Designed for panel mounting, offering various features like waveform
capture (Acuvim IIW) or plug-and-play panels (AcuPanel).
Key Components & Setup
• Current Transformers (CTs): Doughnut-shaped devices that go around hot wires to
measure current; two are needed for 3-wire Delta, three for 4-wire Wye.
• Rogowski Coils: Flexible coils that wrap around conductors for non-invasive current
measurement, often used in modern meters.
• Configurations: Meters support 3-wire Delta (2 CTs) or 4-wire Wye (3 CTs) systems.
Common Features & Functions
• Measurement: Current (A), Voltage (V), Power (kW, KVAR), Energy (kWh), Power Factor
(PF), Frequency (Hz).
• Communication: RS485 (Modbus-RTU), Wireless (Zigbee, Wi-Fi), Pulse Outputs.
• Data Logging: Stores historical data for analysis.
• Power Quality: Waveform capture, event logging (Acuvim IIW).

VII. Any New Business: a. Effective July 1, 2025, New Laws governing ADU's:
One ADU per dwelling unit, should be stated in the ordinance if a municipality wishes to implement a
limit. ADU's may be prohibited for multi-family uses such as Town Houses or on rented or leased land.
Sale of an ADU through condominium conveyance is prohibited.
Attached ADU's shall have either an independent means of ingress and egress or ingress and egress
through a common space shared with the principal dwelling. However, the municipality shall not limit
the choice of ingress and egress.
The ordinance may require owner occupancy of either the principle or the accessory dwelling unit, but it
cannot specify which unit the owner must occupy.
The ordinance may establish size limits for ADU's, but it may not limit an ADU to less than 750 sq. ft.
The total living space od the accessory dwelling unit shall not exceed 950 sq. ft. unless otherwise
authorized by he municipality.
Bedroom Limits. A municipality shall not limit an accessory dwelling unit to only one bedroom this
means of course that it may impose a two bedroom limit.
Electrical Service. A municipality shall not deny the establishment of a separate electrical panen and
separate service for the accessory swelling unit.

Malo, Commissioner/Operations Director, Corey Welcome, Operations Associate
Unavailable:

b. Heat Pump: The heat pump is installed and operational at Keith Ave. Next to be installed will
be Pembroke St & Sheep Davis Rd. pump stations.

Pembroke St. first then Sheep Davis Rd second.

b. Review and Sign Late Notice Registers Zone 2 & 3: Late Notice Registers were reviewed and
signed

error from ammeter change out.
A discussion took place on the account.
Motion: Artie made the motion to approve the $30.00 late penalty as a 1 time abatement.
Seconded: by Andy
Page 1|3

Vote: All in favor
d-1. Abatement 96 Sheep Davis Rd. Paulette explained the abatement request for the $587.63 due to an
over charge for Nov. 2024 billing. There was a problem with their pump station working properly. This
has been an issue for a couple of years. The sewer department did inform the property owner to fix the
pump flow meter, this was never done.
A discussion took place on the account.
Motion: Andy made the motion to DENY the abatement for $587.63 due to their failure to fix
the problem.
Seconded: by Artie
Vote: All in favor
d-2. Abatement 96 Sheep Davis Rd. Paulette explained the abatement request for the $1,031.57 due to
an over charge for Feb. 2025 billing. We have worked with the new person overseeing the utilities for
the property. At this time we didn't know that the station wasn't fixed. We asked that they camera the
section in question to make sure that there weren't any defects in the pipe to collect any rain/ground
water coming in. We ask for all the documentation and they did supply us with all information needed.
This is when they looked back into an issue previously and it was found that the repair was not done to
the pump station. Moving forward we will be using water readings from Pembroke Waterworks.
A discussion took place on the account.
Motion: Andy made the motion to accept the abatement for $1,031.57 for the Feb. 2025
Seconded: by Artie

abatement.

2024 in May or June of 2025 and then 2025 cost be invoiced as of Dec. 31, 2025

DATE: March 17, 2025 TIME: 7:00 P.M.
PLACE: 4 Union St.
I. Meeting Called to Order: 7:00 pm
Attendance: Commissioner Jules (Andy) Pellerin, Commissioner Arthur Little, Paulette
Malo, Commissioner/Operations Director, Corey Welcome, Operations Associate
Unavailable:
II. Citizen's Comments: None
III. Scheduled Meetings: None
IV. Old Business: Generator: Keith Ave: The generator is now on line as of today's date. John from
Liberty as well as Artie from A & C Mechanical were there to make sure everything went well and that
there weren't any other issues. The generator was testing as a power failure. All equipment was running
at the same time. It appeared that on the high side it took 20kw and then it dropped to 17 kw while
running under normal circumstance.
A discussion took place if it was necessary to have the new generators 100 kw or would a 75 kw work
just as well and the potential of saving money with a smaller unit.
Action Item: Artie will do a load test at station 3 and 5 to see what size would be needed and
report back at the next meeting if possible.
V. Any Old Business: a. 523-525 Pembroke St. Zoning Proposal: Paulette explained that this is an
application for 5 buildings with 4 units each. Paulette read her response to the ZBA stating that currently
there is sewer capacity at this time for this project to move through the ZBA.
A discussion took place about this project.
VI. New Business: a. Review and Sign Manifest: Manifest was reviewed and signed

b. Review and Sign Warrant 1 Zone 3: Warrant was reviewed and signed
c. Abatement 316 A Meeting House Rd. Paulette explained the abatement request for the $501.29 due
to a billing error from ammeter change out.
A discussion took place on the account.

Seconded: by Artie
Vote: All in favor

Seconded: by Andy
Vote: All in favor
f. Letter to Finance for COLA: Paulette explained that this is the COLA that was budgeted during the
budget process.
Motion: Artie made the motion to accept the COLA as budgeted and to have Andy sign as the
chair the letter to the finance department.
Seconded: by Andy
Vote: 2 in favor, 1 abstained
VII. Any New Business: a. Emergency Heat Pump for Keith Ave.
A discussion took place about the issues with the new generator and Milton Cat saying something about
have 2 apparatuses attached to the gas line. Paulette explained that she got a price to just do Keith Ave
and the got a quote to upgrade all 3 stations to heat pumps with a savings for 3.
Motion: Andy made the motion to accept the quote for 3 heat pumps with a price not to exceed $21,900.
Seconded: Paulette seconded the motion.
Vote: 2 in favor, 1 abstained
b. National Guard: Paulette explained that we are working with them due to an issue with their flow
meter on the pump station. She will let the commissioners know at the next meeting what is found and
what the possible solution is.
c. Election of Officers:
Motion: Artie made the motion to have Andy remain as chair
Seconded: Paulette seconded the motion.

Vote: All in favor

MONTHLY SEWER COMMISSION MEETING
DATE: February 18, 2025 TIME: 7:00 P.M.
PLACE: 4 Union St.
I. Meeting Called to Order: 7:00 pm
Attendance: Commissioner Arthur Little, Paulette Malo, Commissioner/Operations
Director, Corey Welcome, Operations Associate
Unavailable: Commissioner Jules (Andy) Pellerin
II. Citizen's Comments: None
III. Scheduled Meetings: None
IV. Old Business: Generator: Keith Ave: The e-mail from Southworth Milton Cat was reviewed and
discussed. Also discussed the gas pressure. Liberty was great at responding to our request. CAT is still
requiring a few things be done before the start-up such as removal of the heater from inside the station.
Action Item: Paulette will call around to get prices on a split unit to upgrade the heating system in the
pump station.
V. Any Old Business: a. 523-525 Pembroke St. Zoning Proposal: Paulette explained that she sent an
e-mail to the Paul Bacon, Code Enforcement and included Fieldstone Land Consultants with the remarks
for the Special Exception that is in front of the ZBA. In the e-mail she wrote that she spoke to the Sewer
Commissioners personally due to not having a meeting in January. This conversation was about having
the capacity for this project to move forward through the ZBA and the 4 criteria's that will be needed
when they go in front of the Planning Board. Paulette also gave their engineer an estimate of the
potential fees for the sewer connection for the 20 units.
b. 109 Wilkins Ave: Paulette received the amount needed for the escrow for our engineers to review and
comment on the plans submitted to the Planning Board in the amount of $3,000.00 for this phase of the
project. Paulette did contact the Town Planner with the amount of the escrow needed
Page 1|4

VI. New Business: a. Review and Sign Manifest: Manifest was reviewed and signed
b. Review and Sign Warrant 1 Zone 2: Warrant was reviewed and signed
c. Review and Sign Late Notices for Zone 2 & 3: Late Notices were reviewed and signed
d. Abatement 508 Ashley Dr.. Paulette explained the abatement request for the $30.00 late penalty.
A discussion took place on the account.
Motion: Artie made the motion to approve the $30.00 late penalty as a 1 time abatement.
Seconded: by Paulette
Vote: All in favor
e. Correspondence: Were reviewed
f. Accept Minutes of December 16, 2024 Regular Meeting:
Motion: Artie made the motion to accept the minutes of November 18, 2024 as written.
Seconded: by Paulette
Vote: All in favor
g. Accept Minutes of December 16, 2024 Non-Public Meeting:
Motion: Artie made the motion to accept the minutes of November 18, 2024 Non-Public as
written.
Seconded: by Paulette
Vote: All in favor
VII. Any New Business: a. Move Money to PDIP: A discussion took place about how much to money
to move to PDIP. Bank Statements were reviewed with the current amounts in them.
Motion: Artie made the motion to move $200,000.00 to the sewer PDIP operating account.
Seconded: Paulette seconded the motion.
Vote: All in favor
b. New Snow Blower: Corey explained that we are trying to upgrade all the snow blowers at the pump
stations. We have upgraded 2 in past years. Should the commission approve another snow blower this
year we will have 2 snow blowers that can go out for bids. We will keep 1 for the office to remove the
snow along the guard rail to maintain the full parking area.
Motion: Artie made the motion to purchase the Ariens Deluxe snow blower from Greenland Equipment
for the amount not to exceed $1,500.00.
Seconded: Paulette seconded the motion.
Vote: All in favor
Page 2|4

c. 10 Glass St.: Paulette explained that she received an e-mail from the assessing office that they have
noticed that the commercial unit is now occupied. Paulette raised the question as to how this happened
since the last communication from the Town Planner was that any business would need to go in front of
the planning board for approval. Paulette received a response from the Town Planner she contacted the
owner of the building and was satisfied with his response.
A discussion took place about sending an invoice for the unspecified office space being utilized by the
property owner who does not live in the building.
Motion: Artie made the motion to send an invoice for the 75 gpd for the space.
Seconded: Paulette seconded the motion.
Vote: All in favor
d. Coffee Shop at 49 Glass St.: Paulette explained that the proposed renters for the old Lavallee's store
front came in to discuss to potential of opening a coffee shop. They would not be doing any cooking
there. They are proposing to bring in pastries from different town entities such as muffins from Shirley's
Kitchen as well as others. Paulette explained that should they move forward that along with the 3 bay
sink they will also need a grease trap installed. At this time it's unsure as to the number of seats they will
have. Paulette will keep the Commission informed as she gets more information.
VIII. Non-Public Session: None needed
VIII. Motion: Paulette made the motion to adjourn at 7:54 pm
Seconded: Artie seconded the motion.
Vote: All in favor, motion passed
Respectfully Submitted,
Paulette Malo,
Commissioner

Pembroke Planning Board
November 25, 2025
Meeting Minutes
(Approved on April 14, 2026)
Attendance
MEMBERS PRESENT: Brian Seaworth, Chairman; Rick Frederickson, Selectmen's Rep;
Clint Hanson; Kathy Cruson; Stephanie Cravotta; Robert Bourque, Alternate; Joshua
Bursey, Alternate
MEMBERS EXCUSED: Brent Edmonds, Vice Chairman; Angela Delaney
STAFF PRESENT: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner; Kate Castaldo-Rice, Recording
Secretary
Chairman Seaworth called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
Chairman Seaworth asked Alternate Bourque to vote for Member Delaney and asked
Alternate Bursey to vote for Member Edmonds.
New Business
1. Zoning Amendment Request from Resident - 168 Buck Street
Nancy Hurd-Despres was present to discuss her Zoning Amendment Request. She stated
that George Wing's lot is the only lot zoned for business. If this was done, everything east
of Wilkins Avenue would be residential only.
She gave some history on the zoning in the neighborhood and the two houses on the
corner of Smith Avenue and Buck Street. There used to be businesses in the
neighborhood long ago, but they have since been long gone. She stated that the character
of the neighborhood has changed to strictly residential.
She collected signatures from all the abutters, including the property owners, and
submitted a letter to the Planning Board.
Chairman Seaworth explained the two avenues for this request. One would be a Planning
Board Amendment and the other would be a Citizen's Petition Amendment.
Chairman Seaworth discussed the last time they received a request of this nature; it was
for the Silver Hills property. He stated that the Planning Board took about three years
working on that. It eventually was approved as a petition warrant and the Planning Board
eventually had to make a few adjustments a year or two later. A Petition Warrant is more
expeditious.
Alternate Bourque suggested that this change be made to both the lot requested as well as
the Wilkins Avenue lot that was just approved recently.
Chairman Seaworth stated that the current use is for a B-1 lot. If the larger lot were
rezoned to R-1, it would not support the density of the project. He continued that changing
that lot from B-1 to R-1 would make it a non-conforming lot that is grandfathered.
T:\Town Planner \PLANNING BOARD\MEETING MINUTES|2025\11-25-2025 Minutes (Approved).docx
November 25, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 1 of 7

Alternate Bourque asked about the Wilkins Avenue Project. He thought that the B-1 would
be more restrictive than the R-1. Planner Cronin stated that B-1 allows for higher density.
Chairman Seaworth added that there are split zoned lots like this on Third Range Road.
They are part R-1 and part R-3.
Planner Cronin stated that if it is split zoning, you must treat each part of the lot as the
zoning is and can expand by 100-feet whichever portion is a larger portion. In the case of
the Wilkins Ave Project, they factored in the amount of acreage that was R-1 and B-1. Both
were considered.
Chairman Seaworth stated that the impact of the change would need to be considered
individually.
Alternate Bourque expressed that he was confused. He simply questions why the one lot
would be left as part of the B-1 Zone.
Planner Cronin stated that either way, their current uses would be grandfathered non-
conforming. It would just change the zoning for future development.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson asked about Lot 165 across Buck Street.
Ms. Despres' intention was to prevent something like a convenience store from being built
there in the future. She would like it addressed before it becomes an issue.
Alternate Bourque asked if the property owner was in attendance.
Ms. Despres stated that they were not in attendance, but that they signed the letter.
Alternate Bourque asked if this was initiated by the property owner, or Ms. Despres and
she stated that she initiated it.
Chairman Seaworth explained that the Board would need to decide whether they would
take on the amendment or if it would be better to allow Ms. Despres to enter a Petition
Warrant.
He explained that Zoning Amendments are generally started in August or September and
that he was not sure the Board would be able to pull together an amendment that quickly.
Alternate Bourque asked if there needed to be two public hearings. Chairman Seaworth
stated that there would only need to be one unless they were changed.
Member Cruson pointed out that this may affect the property value. She would feel more
comfortable if this was done through Citizens Petition Warrant.
Ms. Despres asked Planner Cronin what she would need to do.
Planner Cronin stated that she would just need to get it stamped by the clerk and Ms.
Despres would not need to do anything.
Member Cruson feels that it may be more fluid this way.

November 25, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 2 of7

Alternate Bourque advised Ms. Despres that it would be more beneficial for her to do this.
Chairman Seaworth added that Ms. Despres should attend the public hearing. She stated
that the abutters didn't attend tonight because she didn't think they would need to. She
assured the Board that they all agreed.
Planner Cronin stated that the Public Hearing would be January 13 at 6:30 pm. She stated
that the public can attend and provide comment, but the Board cannot change the
verbiage of a petitioned amendment.
Old Business
1. Zoning Amendments Town Meeting 2026
a. Legal Review
i. Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs)
Planner Cronin said that Town Legal reviewed the ADU amendments. The lawyer
suggested that the town did not have to define attached and detached ADUs. She
recommended deleting the redundancy of "on the same lot" and "on the same parcel of
land". Town legal was also in favor of establishing an owner occupancy requirement for at
least one of the units.
Planner Cronin spoke about owner occupancy and the possibility of making it a separate
warrant article. The Town Lawyer recommended that one unit should be owner occupied.
Planner Cronin stated that a change to owner occupancy is the only amendment that is not
a State mandate, and so it would make sense to separate that from the vote on mandated
changes.
Chairman Seaworth stated that the lawyer's reasoning for recommending owner
occupancy was like previous discussions that the Planning Board had previously had, as
well as discussions that took place at the Joint Meeting.
Planner Cronin stated that the Town Lawyer noted concerns about the property turning
into a rental with no owners present.
Chairman Seaworth spoke about separating the owner occupancy. The rest of the
changes are solely to come into compliance with statute. The owner occupancy
requirement is a new change. He added that the Zoning Board has consistently been
putting the condition of owner occupancy on ADU approvals.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson stated that this would give the Zoning Board an ordinance
to enforce.
Alternate Bourque explained that this will no longer go to the Zoning Board, but code
enforcement. This is allowed by right now.
Planner Cronin presented a version of the amendment that incorporates the legal
comments.

a. Wetland Ordinance
Planner Cronin stated that at the joint workshop, there was some discussion about this.
There is a contradiction about the buffer being no disturb and the actual wetlands being a
special use permit. The thought was to fix the inconsistencies for this year, but to continue
to collaborate with Conservation on future changes.
Planner Cronin suggests minor changes to make the wetland and the buffer match.

Consultants, PLLC acting as Applicant on behalf of MJ Properties NH, LLC,
owner of Tax Map 266, Lot 117 located at 109 Wilkins Ave. in the Medium
Density Residential (R1) Zone, the Business/Residential (B1) Zone, the

Chairman Seaworth stated that they would be reviewing materials that have been received
since the last meeting. Some of this material was received today. He asked that a
summary be provided. He also stated that the public hearing would also be reopened.
Planner Cronin stated that the last time this application was reviewed was September 23,
2025. The Fire Dept. sent an email on September 23rd commenting that the tower cannot
accommodate the proposed turnaround unless the pavement and shoulder are extended
north another 20 feet long by 28 feet wide. The addition of pavement will likely modify the
stormwater calculations. The Town Engineer issued engineering comments dated
September 23rd. The comments are minor but do not take into account the plan changes
that are required to satisfy the Fire Dept.'s comments on the turnaround.
The applicant agreed to review quotes for a third-party wetland review. Four different
consultants were sent a request for quote, and only one provided a quote. The applicant
reviewed the quote, agreed to the services, and provided escrow on October 16th. Mark
West from West Environmental provided the third-party review and produced a report of

findings. Mark West and the applicant's wetland scientist met onsite on October 23rd. Mr.
West agreed with Fieldstone's wetland scientist on the wetland delineation.
At 6:35 pm, Chairman Seaworth opened the public hearing. He stated that if any member
of the public would like to speak, they would need to provide their name and address and
address all questions to the Board.
John Noonan, Fieldstone Land Consultants, was present to represent the applicant. He
spoke about the wetland scientists' meeting. He also stated that an addition of the
turnaround has been added to the plan. He also added that they are working with
Eversource on the transformer. The other open item is sign off from KV Partners on the
replacement of the catch basins. He also stated that they have increased the size of the
pipe to 15" down Buck Street.
Vice Chairman Edmonds asked if the Fire Department has reviewed or commented on the
updated plan. The applicant stated that the plan adheres to the Fire Department's
recommendation.
Chairman Seaworth stated that there are options that have been presented to the Board
for draft conditions if the Board would like to discuss the final approval at this meeting. He
stated that some things may be treated as conditions, but he expressed some concerns
about certain issues being treated as such. One concern he has is that other boards and
committees, for example the Conservation Commission, have not had a chance to review.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson had some questions on the flow rate as discussed in the
KV Partners letter. KV Partners had concerns about flow occurring in the stone trench
rather than the soils. He asked for further comment from the applicant.
The applicant explained the revised drainage system. There is perforated pipe and 4 feet
of gravel in this area. He feels that the runoff will be held off in the drainage system either
way. He does not foresee it being a maintenance issue for DPW. He suggested a swale as
a possible option. The applicant also spoked about the replacement of the catch basin if
necessary.
Planner Cronin had asked the Town Engineer about the replacement of the catch basin
being an appropriate condition. He felt that it would be an appropriate condition.
Chairman Seaworth asked the Board whether they felt an extension would be appropriate
or a discussion about conditions.
Vice Chairman Edmonds feels that the applicant has done an excellent job on the
application. He did express concerns over the Conservation Commission not having a
chance to comment. He also commented on Mark West and his confidence in his opinion.
He stated that he is ready to move on to conditions if the Board feels that it is appropriate.
Member Cruson spoke about the abutter concerns about water issues that have arisen in
the past with development. She continued that there is a lot of ledge, and this may require
blasting. She asked if there is anything that can be done to protect the abutters if they
have increased water coming off the hillside.

had wanted to get more information from the Fire Department about blasting. As

regulatory responsibility for this.
Planner Cronin stated that she met with Deputy Fire Chief Farley and asked him about
their blasting permit process. She discovered that there are not blasting permits in
Pembroke. In other towns, the scope is for safety. They would not look at abutting
properties. He did note that if it is a reputable blasting company, they generally do this

themselves from liability. He stated that the Board would not know to the extent what

might be impacted by the Wilkins Ave Project.

Selectmen's Rep Frederickson felt that the blasting company would be able to address

Chairman Seaworth feels that the water will go into the stormwater management system.

Pembroke Planning Board
October 14, 2025
Meeting Minutes
(Approved on June 23, 2026)
Attendance
MEMBERS PRESENT: Brian Seaworth, Chairman; Brent Edmonds, Vice Chairman; Rick
Frederickson, Selectmen's Rep; Clint Hanson; Kathy Cruson; Robert Bourque, Alternate;
Joshua Bursey, Alternate
MEMBERS EXCUSED: Angela Delaney; Stephanie Cravotta
STAFF PRESENT: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Chairman Seaworth called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
Member Delaney was unable to attend the meeting, and Chairman Seaworth asked
Alternate Bourque to vote in her place. Member Cravotta was unable to attend the
meeting, and Chairman Seaworth asked Alternate Bursey to vote in her place.
Old Business 00:01:401
1. Zoning Amendments Town Meeting 2026
Planner Cronin presented a draft of the warrant article language and gave a brief overview
of all the amendments. She explained that the manufactured housing amendment is to
correct a reference. The correction to the Table of Dimensional Regulations is because a
word got changed when the table was updated. "Additional" was changed to "any". The
amendment is to change it back.
Planner Cronin explained the change to the Table of Off-Street Parking is to reflect the
change in state law. The town required two spaces per residential unit and now it can only
allow one space per residential unit.
Planner Cronin explained there was discussion about ADUs at the September workshop. A
lot of the changes that are proposed are changes that have to be made because of the
change to state law. One thing discussed at the workshop is something that towns can
require, which is owner occupancy, which isn't currently required. There was no consensus
at the workshop. She put together two different zoning amendments related to ADUs. One
to make the changes mandated by the state and a second on just owner occupancy. That
way, if the owner occupancy does not pass, it does not thwart the changes required by the
state. The planning board can discuss this.
Chairman Seaworth agreed with the proposal. Even if the planning board agrees on owner
occupancy, it is still up to the voters. It's good to keep the optional amendment from
interfering with the necessary amendment.
Planner Cronin mentioned that there was no consensus on In-home Day Care or PFAS at
the workshop.
T:\Town Planner \PLANNING BOARD\MEETING MINUTES|2025\10-14-2025 Minutes (Approved).docx
October 14, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 1 of 9

Planner Cronin gathered from the workshop conversation that the wetlands ordinance will
be a multi-year update. This year the goal is to marry the regulations for the buffer to the
regulations for the wetland.
Alternate Bursey asked about the changes to comply with state law. What happens if the
town votes against it? Planner Cronin said that if voters don't change the town zoning, the
state law still trumps the ordinance, and the ordinance can no longer be enforced.
Someone could try to sue the town if it is enforced.
Chairman Seaworth added that the nature of the change affects how it plays out. For
example, if the state law says a larger ADU size is required and we try to enforce a smaller
one, the applicant would defer to the state law and that would be the end of it. When the
changes are more complex or depend on each other, you can have applicants who say the
ordinance is not compliant, so they don't have to follow the ordinance because it's illegal.
That's when it becomes urgent to make the change and get it done promptly to keep that
from happening. Most of the changes are minor, and if they don't get done this year, staff
would enforce based on the state law.
a. Housekeeping Items
i. Manufactured Housing Table Reference
The planning board had no further discussion on this item.
ii. Correction to Table of Dimensional Regulations
The planning board had no further discussion on this item.
b. State Legislative Changes
i. Table of Off Street Parking
The planning board had no further discussion on this item.
ii. Accessory Dwelling Units
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson wanted to share his opinion on owner occupancy now that
he had put more thought into it. Some of the downfalls of not having the owner occupancy
requirement is that a company could buy houses with ADUs and rent them out. He doesn't
mind a person as a landlord, but when a company buys out a bunch of properties, that
doesn't sit right with him.
Chairman Seaworth spoke about voting against owner occupancy previously, but now has
gone the other way. What the zoning board has been doing is putting this on as a condition
of their special exception. Adding this keeps things the way they have been for many
years. Someone could still request a variance from this requirement. The Zoning Board
would make that final decision.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson spoke about the trend of companies buying a bunch of
properties and "AirBnB"ing them as seasonal rentals. He does not think that's what the
town is looking for. He would prefer a family be able to live there.
T:\Town Planner \PLANNING BOARD\MEETING MINUTES\2025\10-14-2025 Minutes (Approved).docx
October 14, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 2 of 9

Chairman Seaworth presumed this is why the state legislation allowed the towns to have
control over this aspect. He asked if any board members are still up in the air on this topic
or are opposed to adding the owner occupancy requirement.
Member Cruson is not opposed. She asked before if someone could go to the zoning
board for a variance and the answer was yes. If someone could no longer live in the
house, due to a handicap for example, there should be an option for relief from the
requirement, under certain circumstances.
Chairman Seaworth agreed. It sounds that there is a consensus to present them as two
amendments.
Planner Cronin will send the amendment for legal review.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson asked about the "no larger than 750 sf" and asked if the
new state minimum is 950 sf. Planner Cronin agreed there was confusion about that.
Towns cannot be less than 750 sf or larger than 950 sf.
Chairman Seaworth explained that the 950 sf is the state's default if the town does not
prescribe a size. Towns are allowed to go as small as 750 sf or larger than 950 sf.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson pointed out that the town language says "no larger than
750 sl', but the state says no larger than 950 sf. Chairman Seaworth noted that the 950 sf
takes effect if the town is mute on ADU size in their ordinance. The town has the ability to
go larger than 950 sf, but the state says that 750 sf is the limit that a town cannot force
someone to go smaller than.
Upon first reading, Planner Cronin also believed that 950 sf was the new cap, but after
discussing it, it means something different if your town already has an ADU ordinance than
if it did not. She read from an ADU article from the NH Municipal Association (NHMA)
explaining the size limits.
Board members continued to discuss the language of the state law compared to the
language of the town ordinance.
Member Cruson confirmed that ADU applications will only deal with code enforcement or
the zoning board, not the planning board.
Chairman Seaworth asked about having to define "detached" but allowing attached and
detached. He asked if they have to define "detached"? It probably wouldn't hurt, but why
are define "detached" if they are treated the same as attached now?
Alternate Bursey spoke about how the board discussed the requirement of single water
and sewer service. That might change based on whether it's attached or detached.
Planner Cronin said there were state statute changes to how ADU utilities are regulated.
"Detached" was defined because there were multiple references placed throughout the
ordinance where an ADU was defined as attached. Where she had to make changes to
distinguish attached from detached, she had to define detached. The definition language
came from NHMA. She wanted the language to be as clear as possible for homeowners.

Joint Workshop
September 16, 2025
Meeting Minutes
(Approved by Planning Board on October 14, 2025)
Attendance
MEMBERS PRESENT:
Planning Board: Brian Seaworth, Chairman; Brent Edmonds, Vice Chairman; Rick
Frederickson, Selectmen's Rep; Kathy Cruson; Stephanie Cravotta; Robert Bourque,
Alternate; Joshua Bursey, Alternate
Zoning Board: Bruce Kendrick, Chairman; Dana Carlucci, Blakely V. Miner III
Conservation Commission: Ammy Heiser, Chairman; Erin Insley, Co-Chair; Wendy
Weisiger; Carol Bertsimas
STAFF PRESENT: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner; Kate Castaldo-Rice, Recording
Secretary
Chairman Seaworth called the meeting to order at 6:32 pm.
He explained that the workshop's primary goal was to discuss potential zoning changes, to
ensure compliance with new statute, at a high level and to understand each group's
opinion. He also explained next steps of such changes that would be undertaken by the
Planning Board in the future.
Business
Planner Cronin reiterated that zoning amendments would be discussed for approval in
March. These changes would be either to comply with legislation or to make clarifications
to existing ordinances to ensure that they meet the goals of the town.
1. Zoning Amendment Discussion for Town Meeting 2026
a. State Legislation Changes
i. Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUS)
Planner Cronin explained Pembroke's current ADU ordinance and the updated state
legislation pertaining to ADUs. She reviewed changes that are mandated and some
changes that the combined boards may want to consider.
C: \Users|<Williams|AppData|Local\Microsoft|Windows\/NetCache|Content.Outlook|3FVT66LG\09-16-2025 Minutes
(Approved).docx
September 16, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 1 of 5

done through the Building Permit process. This is already in effect.
The ADU can also not be mandated to be less than 750 square feet. There was further
discussion on size requirements and limitations.
There were also changes needed in the ordinance to define both detached and attached
ADUs. Detached ADUs must now be allowed by-right. There were a few other changes
needed where the ordinance alluded to ADUs being attached, including shared utilities and
access to the unit.
In addition, aesthetic requirements cannot be applied to ADUs unless there are standards
for single-family homes. Pembroke does not have aesthetic standards for Single Family
homes and therefore, these can no longer apply to ADUs.
There was also discussion about allowable utility requirements and the ability to build an
ADU simultaneous to the primary residence being built.
Planner Cronin then spoke about owner occupation for ADUs. This is typically a condition
of approval by the ZBA on ADUs. This is not currently in the ordinance. The statute does
allow for this.
Lastly, she explained that existing non-conforming structures can contain ADUs regardless
of compliance with ADU requirements. This can include things like detached garages.
There was discussion on the difference between an ADU and a Duplex and the different
requirements in the zoning ordinance. It was specified that ADUs cannot be added to a
duplex.
Next, separate connections for water and sewer were discussed. It was suggested that the
Water and Sewer Departments should be consulted on their preference. Currently, the
ordinance states that an ADU shall be served by the same water and sewer connection as
the primary dwelling unit. It was determined that there will be no requirement for ADUs to
be on the same water and sewer connection.
There was some discussion on owner occupancy. It is currently not in the ordinance, and
there were varying opinions on if this should be a requirement. Some questioned the
reasoning for requiring an owner-occupied arrangement for ADUs. There were questions
about enforcement of such a requirement, as well. The advantages and disadvantages
were discussed in terms of the Town's interest.
It was also stated that currently, there is only one ADU allowed per lot. An applicant can go
to ZBA for approval for additional ADUs.
There was no agreement reached on the owner-occupancy requirement.
ii. Day Care as an Accessory Use (In-home Day Care)
C: \Users\LWilliams\AppData\Loca/\Microsoft\Windows\/NetCache\Content.Outlook\3FVT66LG\09-16-2025 Minutes
(Approved).docx
September 16, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 2 of 5

Planner Cronin explained that the town can no longer require a special exception for In-
home Day Care. A conditional use permit (special use permit) can be required. This would
now be reviewed by the Planning Board if this were to be adopted.
The number of children permitted for an in-home day care was questioned. Planner Cronin
believes that this is based on state regulation as opposed to town ordinance.
There was a discussion on allowing in-home day cares by right versus through the special
exception process and the Planning Board's role if such a regulation was put in place.
It was mentioned that there would be no public forum for comment, specifically from
abutters if this were to be allowed by right.
Planner Cronin discussed State requirements and clarified that the only change requiring a
decision would be if this was allowed by right. If it is allowed by right, Code Enforcement
and the Fire Department would be responsible for approval.
There was further discussion about abutter feedback. There have not been many
complaints from abutters regarding this of accessory use in the past.
There was no agreement reached on whether to allow in-home day cares by-right or
through a new special use permit process.
b. Aquifer Conservation Ordinance Changes for PFAS
Planner Cronin explained that the Department of Environmental Services (DES) has
drafted a model groundwater ordinance, which includes new regulations on PFAS.
Pembroke already has a comprehensive Aquifer Conservation District Ordinance. Planner
Cronin suggests adding the verbiage about PFAS. These changes would prohibit PFAS
containing firefighting foams, as well as industrial facilities that produce PFAS that may
contaminate groundwater. If PFAS is a by-product of an industrial use, there would be a
special use permit process, and they would need to demonstrate their plan to control
PFAS contamination.
Planner Cronin added that Pembroke Water Works would also need to be involved in the
process and will need to review any suggested changes to the current ordinance.
She explained that this would add a layer of protection in the Aquifer Conservation District
and allow for review of these types of uses.
There was discussion about this ordinance only applying to the Aquifer Conservation
District. It was generally noted that the town may not want PFAS in any area of town. It
was discussed that if there is not an ordinance addressing this, Pembroke may become
more desirable for PFAS producers. The difference between industries that produce PFAS
products as opposed to those that may generate PFAS as a by-product was clarified.
There was further discussion of identifying these PFAS producers and enforcement of the
potential ordinance.

Chairman Seaworth called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.

Alternate Bourque to vote in her place.
Old Business 100:00:531
1. Zoning Amendment Prioritization for Town Meeting 2026
a. Guidance Documents from NHMA
i. Planning & Zoning Laws 2025
Planner Cronin stated that there was a webinar held by the New Hampshire Municipal
Association (NHMA) on updates to state laws that were passed this year. Some of these
impact land use regulations. While some updates would impact Pembroke, others would
not.
Planner Cronin started by explaining HB 631 that deals with mixed use in commercial
zones. This likely does not impact Pembroke, as mixed use is already allowed in
commercial zones.
She then discussed SB 284 that only allows the town to require one parking space per
unit. Currently, Pembroke requires two spaces per unit. This is effective September 13,
2025. After this date, the town must comply.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson asked if the ordinance needed to be updated. Planner
Cronin stated that they probably should update it, but regardless, the law will supersede
the local ordinance.
Member Cruson asked what happens when the occupant has more than one vehicle.
Planner Cronin stated that it does not matter. Chairman Seaworth stated that it could be a
request of the applicant, or they could suggest it to applicants. The applicant would not be
required to comply.
Alternate Bourque noted that there would be a lot of towed vehicles when there is no on-
street parking in the winter. He doesn't feel like this was considered when the law was
C:\Users\LWilliams|AppData\Loca/\Microsoft|Windows\/NetCache|Content.Outlook\3FVT66LG\08-12-2025 Minutes
(Approved).docx
August 12, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 1 of 15

passed. Selectmen's Rep Frederickson stated that some businesses may allow for extra
parking in these types of situations.
Planner Cronin spoke about HB 457, which prohibits municipal zoning ordinances from
restricting the number of occupants of any dwelling unit to less than two occupants per
bedroom. Planner Cronin noted that this does not apply to Pembroke as the town does not
regulate the number of occupants. This is likely aimed at college towns and similar
situations. Chairman Seaworth agreed that this may be targeted to college towns. He
noted that this would not necessarily be applicable to Pembroke's situation.
Planner Cronin discussed SB 283, which applies to floor-area-ratio (FAR) calculations for
any part of a building below or partially below the ground. This does not apply to Pembroke
as the town does not regulate by FAR.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson asked if a finished basement would be included in an
assessment. Chairman Seaworth explained that this is to prevent municipalities from
restricting mixed use. Planner Cronin thinks that this has to do with allowing a maximum
number of units. The below ground units would be included in the calculation.
Planner Cronin spoke about SB 282, which permits buildings up to four floors above grade
to only have one stairway per the building code. This would not apply to the Planning
Board. Member Cruson questioned what fire departments would think of this. Planner
Cronin was unsure if another egress would need to be provided.
Alternate Bourque feels that some of these statutes need to be challenged. Planner Cronin
spoke about the possibility of challenges and a lot of unanswered questions currently.
These have removed a lot of local control and this is unprecedented.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson stated that this does not really apply to Pembroke, because
there is a 35-foot regulation. Pembroke does not have many buildings that are four stories.
Chairman Seaworth responded that the statute is for up to four floors, so it would apply to
the building code in Pembroke. He also spoke about fire department's input being taken
into consideration and past issues with fire suppression requirements. There was some
discussion about the requirement to have two exits in the case of a fire. A decision on SB
282 may be something that ends up determined by the courts.
Next, Planner Cronin spoke about SB 281. This was discussed at the Range Roads
Subcommittee as well. This bill deals with issuing building permits on Class VI Roads.
Previously, the permit would go to the Selectboard first. They would then gather feedback
from Planning Board and other departments. There is a policy in place for this situation.
She continued that now an applicant must only sign and record a waiver of liability for the
town (they will have no town services) and provide proof that the land and building are
insurable. They do not actually need to have insurance. If they meet these requirements,
the Town must issue the building permit.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson asked if they must have a buildable lot. Chairman
Seaworth feels that if the lot is non-conforming, it still does not prevent you from building
on it because presumably the lot was created before whatever prevents it. He thinks it
would be difficult to say the lot is unbuildable.
C:\Users|LWilliams\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\/NetCache|Content.Outlook\3FVT66LG\08-12-2025 Minutes
(Approved).docx
August 12, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 2 of 15

Selectmen's Rep Frederickson noted that currently, it is only a policy on these lots, not an
actual ordinance. Planner Cronin added that the Town cannot require any modifications or
improvements to the road. This could become problematic with emergency services. This
has been the rationale for asking applicants to make upgrades to the road. The NHMA
lawyer did confirm that no upgrades to the road could be required going forward. This will
be effective July 1, 2026. She is unsure that there is anything that can be done to counter
this.
Chairman Seaworth noted that the policy will no longer be able to be applied. He spoke
about applicants coming in prior to the effective date and wondered how the Selectboard
would address these situations.
Alternate Bourque asked if the applicant must prove insurability. Planner Cronin stated that
they would need something like a quote from an insurance company for this proof.
Chairman Seaworth thinks that this is an idea to make the property owner at least think
about it. This ensures that someone has the option to get insurance on their property
and/or building.
Vice Chairman Edmonds asked if Code Enforcement would still get involved. Planner
Cronin stated that they would still need a building permit and must build to code. They
would also need a Town Driveway Permit.
Alternate Bourque asked how a Class VI Road gets upgraded to Class V. Chairman
Seaworth stated that it must be voted on at Town Meeting. Alternate Bourque asked if the
town would be on the hook to build the road. Planner Cronin clarified that this would not
require the town to build the road, it would be just to reclassify it. This would typically be
paid for by the developer.
Planner Cronin added that Regional Planning was at the Range Roads Subcommittee
meeting and stated that this may become a problem for people who are out of state. They
might assume that it is buildable. This may cause some buyer remorse or even creative
building developments.
Alternate Bourque mentioned that a Class VI Road cannot upgraded or maintained by the
town. If the road is changed to a Class V, the town would need to maintain it. Chairman
Seaworth added that even though they are dirt roads, they are still maintained by the town.
He also mentioned that Public Works has tried to push for all roads to be paved because
they are easier to maintain and it makes up for the upfront cost in the long term.
Chairman Seaworth continued that the intent seems to be to phase out Class VI Roads in
favor of developments that will trigger the roads to be upgraded.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson stated that the original plan was to continue to pave those
roads. He feels that this plan is out the window with the new legislation. He believes it will
be 10 to 20 years until everything is paved.
Member Hanson spoke about his experience in Massachusetts. There was massive
development of cheaper land.

Pembroke Planning Board
July 8, 2025
Meeting Minutes
(Approved on August 12, 2025)
Attendance
MEMBERS PRESENT: Brian Seaworth, Chairman; Brent Edmonds, Vice Chairman; Rick
Frederickson, Selectmen's Rep; Clint Hanson; Stephanie Cravotta; Joshua Bursey,
Alternate; Robert Bourque, Alternate
MEMBERS EXCUSED: Kathy Cruson, Angela Delaney
STAFF PRESENT: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner; Kate Castaldo-Rice, Recording
Secretary
Chairman Seaworth called the meeting to order at 6:31 pm.
Member Cruson was unable to attend the meeting, and Chairman Seaworth asked
Alternate Bourque to vote in her place. Member Delaney was not present, and Chairman
Seaworth asked Alternate Bursey to vote in her place.
Old Business [00:01:281
1. Zoning Amendment Prioritization for Town Meeting 2026
Planner Cronin started by stating that the Planning Board would be working on Zoning
Amendment Prioritization for the upcoming year.
Planner Cronin mentioned a webinar by the New Hampshire Municipal Association
(NHMA) at the end of this month on new state legislation that recently passed. She stated
that Planning Board members can also register for the webinar for free if they are
interested.
She spoke about some easy fixes that could be made this year, which include typos and
incorrect references. The substantial changes are all large and require a lot of time, effort
and collaboration with other boards and stakeholders.
She continued that one of the large items would be concerning the Wetlands Protection
District. The Board had spoken about tightening up the criteria. This year, there has been a
lot more Special Use Permits (SUP) applications for the buffer. There have been more
since the change was made from 20 feet to 50 feet. It was a 20-foot no build buffer, but
utilities were allowed. In 2021, the Conservation Commission recommended a 50-foot
buffer. They felt this was the most impactful way to protect the wetland. It also changed
from a no build buffer to a no disturb buffer.
Planner Cronin added that it takes a few years to feel the effects of such a change. She
would like to see if it can be made better based off the applications that the Board has
seen. There are some issues with interpretations of the language. Sometimes, applicants
think that they need a variance, where it needs an SUP. She feels that the Board will need
to work with the Conservation Commission on this and is currently awaiting a response
from them.

July 8, 2025 Planning Board Minutes
Page 1 of 11

Selectmen's Rep Frederickson asked for a list of applications that have requested
Wetlands SUPs since the change.
Chairman Seaworth mentioned that offline, Planner Cronin and he had spoken about how
the SUP has been applied and how it is supposed to be applied. There has been some
confusion. This Board has been thinking of it as a variance. This is a permit, and if they
meet the criteria, they get the permit. He feels that part of this is how wetlands are
regulated, but there is also a technical issue. He feels it would make sense to work on both
at the same time since there is overlap. They do not want to wait until there is potential
legal action.
Alternate Bourque spoke about the 50-foot buffer and it being given an exception,
sometimes down to as low as 10 feet. He questioned why the 50-foot buffer is in place, if
they allow it to be encroached on. Selectmen's Rep Frederickson thought that this would
be Conservation's opinion as well. Chairman Seaworth noted that this is why they have
reached out to Conservation, and he would like to hear what they have to say.
Alternate Bourque stated that he has seen several cases where they have gotten down to
within 10 feet of the wetland. He noted that the golf course was down to 5 feet.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson added that this was the parking lot.
Chairman Seaworth explained what that process would look like for a variance. A hardship
needs to be proven. He noted that SUPs do not function like this. There should be certain
things that you are allowed to do. The SUP should not say what is good, bad or
compromise. It does not fit legally.
Alternate Bourque asked if a variance would be more effective. Planner Cronin explained
the "No Disturb Buffer" but explained how the SUP process works. She noted that the
zoning is a bit contradictory. It says that there is a 50-foot No Disturb Buffer but then states
how to get an SUP for various scenarios.
Alternate Bursey asked what the difference between an SUP and a regulation is.
Planner Cronin explained that there are permitted uses that are "by-right". There are also
prohibited uses which require a variance and a hardship. Last, there are conditional uses
(special use). The SUPs have a set of criteria that must be met and then they are
approved.
Chairman Seaworth spoke about the Aquifer SUP. You cannot put commercial uses in the
aquifer unless you do certain things. This fits the intent of the way that a conditional use is
supposed to work.
Alternate Bourque asked if there should be a joint meeting between Conservation and
Planning Board. Planner Cronin stated that the Board could have a workshop with
Conservation. Selectmen's Rep Frederickson suggested that they allow Conservation to
have a meeting to talk about it first.
Member Delaney arrived at 6:50pm and Alternate Bursey will no longer be voting in her
place.

July 8, 2025 Planning Board Minutes

Chairman Seaworth noted that they needed to determine Conservation's priority. They
have voiced concern about wetlands and open space. Alternate Bourque stated that he
would prefer wetlands because open space will take a while. He suggested a
subcommittee for open space.
Planner Cronin spoke about Open Space Development. The Board has been talking about
this on and off over the last several years. There was a subcommittee at one point. She
spoke about a survey that was done with residents. Alternate Bourque spoke about its
repeal and the subcommittees work on the Open Space.
Planner Cronin spoke about the survey given to residents. It was a divided opinion among
survey respondents. She believes that Open Space was repealed in 2021.
Chairman Seaworth spoke about the survey and trying to decide whether to repeal or fix
Open Space at the time. Planner Cronin stated that the survey was done after the repeal.
Alternate Bourque ask how the survey was advertised. They used Survey Planet, but she
was unsure of how it was advertised. Alternate Bourque thinks that he has notes from the
subcommittee. Planner Cronin also has some notes.
Chairman Seaworth noted that if there is an applicant to do an Open Space development
through the Zoning Board (ZBA), it may not be a good time to write the ordinance. It may
appear like a conflict of interest.
Planner Cronin changed the topic to parking for multifamily developments that go to
Zoning Board and not Planning Board. She gave an example of adding a unit in downtown
Suncook. They would go to the Zoning Board for a special exception. There has been
some butting of heads over who has purview over parking space requirement
enforcement. She thought that a criterion could be added that any additional units must
conform to parking regulations.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson mentioned that they were trying to legislate it to not require
any off-street parking. Planner Cronin added that if you have a certain number of units, you
are only required one parking spot per unit in that case. Currently, Pembroke requires two
spaces per unit. She suggested that they put something in the criteria and the applicant
can request a hardship variance.
Alternate Bourque asked if legislation was passed to not require off-street parking for an
Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU). Planner Cronin and Chairman Seaworth were unsure if
this passed.
Chairman Seaworth added that Pembroke does not currently require specific amount of
parking for any single-family house.
Alternate Bourque stated that Pembroke currently requires off-street parking, but not a
specific number of spaces. He spoke about snow removal.
Planner Cronin stated that every single-family home requires two off-street spaces.
Pembroke requires one off-street parking space for an ADU. She thinks if the ADU
legislation passes, there will need to be many changes.

Chairman Seaworth introduced Jason Menard as a guest speaker to the Board.
Mr. Menard stated that the last time that he met with the Board, they had discussed
updating some of the subdivision road standards to meet new requirements. He prepared
a document for the Board's review. He added that in his line of work, when working with
other towns, he is seeing a lack of defined scopes of work and requirements for what
needs to be done.
He used the reclamation of roads as an example. He spoke about the equipment being
used, requirements for flaggers, shoulder work, and water usage. Instead of having a
foreman or possibly someone they assigned to oversee the project determine the
requirements, Mr. Menard suggests that a document be available outlining the
requirements for projects within the town. This will allow Pembroke to hold a higher
standard in the construction of infrastructure and ensures that they are getting what they
have paid for.
Fortunately, Mr. Menard has been able to oversee some of the projects in Pembroke, as
his company has won the bid, but this may not always be the case. He would like
Pembroke to be in a good position and be aware in any scenario, with anyone who may
win the bid. This would also give Pembroke the ability to ensure compliance with their
regulations when these projects are being worked on. Without regulations and
requirements in place, it can create chaos. The town can lose work quality, and there can
be risks to the workforce or the community.
Mr. Menard would like to see something voted in and routinely updated. This should be
done in house in his opinion. He feels that this would make Town Code updated. He feels
that the standards should be gone through and scrubbed.
Mr. Menard gave an example from Manchester and the details of the manual that they use
and have contractors sign off on. If a contractor does not comply, they can forfeit their

On March 18, 2025, the applicant submitted revised plans, a revised stormwater report, a
response to staff comments, and a letter regarding wetlands.
On March 19th, Water Works issued comments on the revised plans.
On March 21st, the Fire Department commented that they are not in favor of the plan
unless the addressing is corrected, the road is widened to 28 feet, and the turnaround is
constructed.
On April 9th, the Town Engineer issued comments on the revised plans. There are
outstanding issues with the stormwater plan, retaining wall, and he echoed the concerns
about improvements to Wilkins Ave.
Planner Cronin continued by providing an explanation of the Planning Board review
process. By State Statute, the Planning Board has 65 days to review a Planning Board
application. The 65-day review timeclock will expire on May 1st. The hearing on April 22nd
is the last meeting before the expiration. The Applicant was notified of the upcoming
deadline and was asked that they submit an extension request if they wished to continue
with the review process for further opportunity to discuss the application and work through
any outstanding issues.
On the afternoon of April 22nd,
", a request was received from the applicant to continue the
application to the May 27th meeting and to extend the review deadline that the Planning
Board has to that date as well. Planner Cronin suggested that before the Board explored
staff comments and the merits of the plan, the request to extend the review period and
extend the public hearing to May 27t should be reviewed.
Chairman Seaworth noted that in State Law, this is done by agreement with both parties.
Based on the applicant's conversation with Planner Cronin, they have requested an
extension to the next meeting date. The Planning Board must agree to this.
Selectmen's Rep Frederickson asked if the applicant is seeking to have more time to
comply with the outstanding items. Planner Cronin stated that the applicant communicated
to her that they have not completed the revised plans to address the outstanding
comments. Selectmen's Rep Frederickson asked if they still wanted to proceed. Planner
Cronin stated that the applicant would like to continue the process, which is why they have
requested an additional month.
Member Cruson asked Chairman Seaworth if any progress had been made on the many
issues that were relayed to them to be corrected. Chairman Seaworth stated that this could
not be answered since they have not turned anything in. They also have not detailed what
they are working on.
Planner Cronin stated that there has not been any new information since the submittal on
March 18th. Member Cruson asked for confirmation that they had not addressed comments
regarding water issues, the Police Department numbering request, the Town Engineer's
comments, or the Fire Department comments. Planner Cronin stated that they had
addressed some comments but had not addressed most of the comments from town
departments.
