PEMBROKE CEMETERY COMMISSION
January 15, 2025
Minutes
Present: Daniel Chase, James Garvin, Adam Mendozza, Ellen Paulsen (chair), Zachary Sawyer.
1. Chair Ellen Paulsen called the meeting to order at 6:05 p.m. This was a special meeting,
called to consider a citizen's request as described below.
2. On a motion by Dan Chase, seconded by Zachary Sawyer, the minutes of the meeting of
October 10, 2024, were approved as submitted.
3. Chair Ellen Paulsen thanked Public Works Foreman Adam Mendozza for his courtesy in
providing the Public Works conference room for this special meeting.
4. Chair Paulsen described the purpose of the meeting. Colleen Russo of Buck Street has
requested the town's approval to purchase six adjacent burial lots in Buck Street
Cemetery and to use these lots for the scattering of family ashes from cremations. Ms.
Russo wishes to spread these ashes on the surface of the lots without burying them or
covering them with any earth.
Chair Paulsen had previously spoken to Ms. Russo by telephone to determine the details
of her wishes. Commission members asked several questions in order to gauge the
conformity of this proposal with existing town ordinances as stated in Chapter 155
("Cemeteries") of the Town Code and as printed on burial lot licenses issued by the town.
The Commission also had copies of a document entitled "Factors Governing the
Spreading of Human Ashes: New Hampshire and Pembroke," which had been compiled
and distributed prior to the meeting by Secretary James Garvin. This document included
extracts from relevant state statutes, especially RSA 290 "Burials and Disinterments,"
from Chapter 155 of the Pembroke Town Code, and from remarks on the scattering of
ashes posted by the New Hampshire Funeral Directors' Association and the Phaneuf
Funeral Home.
Adam Memdozza distributed a map showing the lots proposed by Ms. Russo for this
purpose: Lots 16 A & B, 17 A & B, and 18 A & B in the eastern ranges of lots in Buck
Street Cemetery near the bank of the Suncook River.
The Commission discussed several aspects of the request, including the stated purposes
of burial lots in town cemeteries, the characteristics of human ashes and their effects on
grass and other vegetation, and current practices of scattering human ashes either in
designated areas such as "scattering gardens" or in natural sites of beauty or significance
to the deceased.

2
Following discussion, the Commission voted unanimously not to approve Ms. Russo's
request. The chief reasons for disapproval were:
a. The stated intent of the Town of Pembroke in providing licenses for lots in the public
mals of refor the shes or mains a cos magich other yes aul hermen t
in individual lots. There is no provision for uses other than burials in these lots, and
uses of lots for other purposes may result in cancellation of the burial license.
b. Licensing six lots for use in scattering ashes rather than burials would forever prevent
the lots from being used for burials. This precedent would preclude the sale of the lots
to other residents of Pembroke for uses that conform to the intended purpose of
"burial of the dead."
c. According to the New Hampshire Funeral Directors' Association, cremated remains
weigh "an average of 7-10 pounds of pulverized bone in the form of calcium
phosphate and sodium.... [and] because of their chemical makeup, cremated remains
are not fertile and, in fact, deter plant root growth." Over the years the Town of
Pembroke has spent time and funds to remove moss and overhanging pine trees,
remove accumulated pine needles, and fertilize this area of Buck Street Cemetery to
encourage the growth of grass. The Commission feared that ashes scattered on the
surface of six lots could prevent the growth of grass on these lots and potentially on
adjacent lots.
5. The Commission asked Secretary Garvin to write to Ms. Russo and state the denial of the
request and explain the reasons for denial.
6. The Commission agreed to consider the possibility of designating appropriate areas for
scattering ashes, separate from formal burial areas, in certain town cemeteries when
regular monthly meetings begin in April 2025.
7. The next regularly scheduled meeting of the Cemetery Commission is at 6:00 p.m. on
Thursday, April 10, 2025 at the Public Works headquarters on Exchange Street in
Suncook Village.
8.
On a motion duly made and seconded, the meeting adjourned at 6:47 p.m.
Respectfully submitted,
James L. Garvin, Secretary

PEMBROKE CEMETERY COMMISSION
September 10, 2026
Minutes
Present: Dan Chase, James Garvin, Ellen Paulsen (chair), Adam Mendozza, Zachary Sawyer,
Fleda Young.
There was no Cemetery Commission meeting in August 2026.
1. Chair Ellen Paulsen called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m.
2. On a motion duly made and seconded, the minutes of the meeting of July 9, 2026, were
approved as submitted.
New Business from the August 13, 2026 Agenda:
3. The Commission discussed the plan to re-pave the roads in Buck Street Cemetery in (or
by) 2031, an item in our Six-Year Cemetery Plan. The Commission is unsure how to the
budget for a project five years in the future and to set aside money in the Capital Reserve
Fund for the project. These questions led to a realization that the Commission does not
know the current balance in the Cemetery Capital Reserve Fund. This uncertainty led to
the discussion outlined below.
Old Business from the August 13, 2026 Agenda:
4. In reply to a question regarding the response of the CIP (Capital Improvements Program)
Committee to the Commission's request for $5,000 for marker repairs in Old North
Pembroke, Pembroke Street, and Evergreen Cemeteries and $1,000 for aluminum lot
corner markers, Adam Mendozza reported the following:
The CIP Committee would like to see our six-year schedule of projects, including paving
the Buck Street Cemetery roads, arranged in chronological order by priority, preferably
with some attempt at estimating project costs. Secretary James Garvin will draft a
timeline for discussion and editing at the next Commission meeting on October 8th.
5. Adam reported that he believes that the Board of Selectmen followed the Cemetery
Commission's recommendations for repurchasing a no-longer-needed burial plot in
Evergreen Cemetery from the Bates family for $300 (see Item 3 in the minutes of the July
9, 2026 Commission meeting).
6. The Commission discussed the degree of maintenance currently needed for the French-
Dearborn Cemetery on North Pembroke Road, which is now recognized as a town

2
property. In a separate memorandum of July 10, 2026, updated on August 11, Secretary
Garvin had stated that the cemetery needs:
•
Leveling of one leaning stone and replacement on its base of one large newer
marble monument that has fallen on its face.
No actual mowing, like the small Cotton and Richardson Cemeteries, but
would benefit from a light cleaning with a string trimmer or scythe once a
year.
Placing and removing two veterans' flags and yearly light trimming of small
vegetation.
The full memorandum is attached to this report.
7. The Commission discussed steps needed to revise Chapter 155 ("Cemeteries") of the
Town Code to include prohibitions on making rubbings of gravestones and on cleaning or
other treatments of monuments except by family or descendants, as specified in Chapter
289.22 and Chapter 635.6 of the New Hampshire Revised Statutes Annotated (RSAs).
Zachary Sawyer had researched these statutes and distributed a memo on the subject on
July 10, 2026. Since revision of Chapter 155 requires approval by the Board of Selectmen
and a public hearing, the Commission concluded that we should begin to draft
appropriate language but that this revision cannot be completed until 2027.
8. The Commission discussed steps needed to establish a spreading garden for cremation
ashes in Buck Street Cemetery as quickly as possible in response to public interest. The
Commission reviewed a handout on the steps to create such an amenity in compliance
with the Pembroke Town Code and New Hampshire State Statutes (RSA 289), compiled
by Zachary Sawyer and first distributed to the Commission on July 10, 2026.
The Commission agreed to study these necessary steps and to give this project high
priority in the Six-Year Plan. Jim Garvin suggested that the garden-like character of the
spreading area might better be achieved by delineating the site with appropriate native
vegetation rather than with granite posts and chains as previously discussed.
Secretary Garvin will outline proposals for location, license wording, and fees before the
October Commission meeting.
New Business from the September 12, 2016 Agenda
9. Public Works Secretary Christine Addington received a call from Donna Young reporting
that a Veteran's marker has been placed inappropriately on the grave of her late husband,
Larry Young, in Buck Street Cemetery. Mr. Young was not a veteran, although the family

3
marks his grave privately with an American flag. The Commission agreed not to place a
veteran's marker at the grave and to let the family treat the grave as they see fit.
10. Public Works Secretary Christine Addington sent the Commission a memo received from
the family of the late Casey James Saggau stating that Mr. Saggau's monument in
Evergreen Cemetery had been moved on its granite base, breaking the seal of silicone
adhesive and causing damage to one edge of the rear face the monument. Adam
Mendozza explained that the mowing contractor has stated that his crew did not impact
the stone. Adam noted that a town crew had been cutting vegetation at the edge of the
cemetery but had not knowingly worked in the vicinity of the stone.
Secretary Addington had received two quotes from Perry Brothers Monument Company:
1) to re-set and re-seal the stone for $100, and 2) to ship the stone to Vermont to have the
damaged edge re-shaved, then re-set and re-seal the stone for $750.
After reviewing a photograph of the slight damage to one rear edge of the stone, the
Commission agreed to offer to pay $100 to have the stone straightened on its base and re-
sealed. If the family wishes to pursue the more costly treatment, they may do so at their
own expense. Secretary Jim Garvin will convey this proposal to Public Works.
11. The Town has received an estimate from New Hampshire Monuments for repairs to
damaged gravestones in Pembroke Street Cemetery for a total cost of $6,850. Chair Ellen
Paulsen checked these graves against our list of Perpetual Care graves and found that
none are covered by the Perpetual Care Trust Fund. In addition, Dan Chase submitted a
photograph of a large, leading granite monument in Evergreen Cemetery that needs
leveling. The Commission agreed that Public Works should proceed to contract for
repairs before the end of the year to the limit of the remaining balance in our Monument
Repair budget line.
12. The next regular meeting of the Cemetery Commission will be at 6:00 p.m. on Thursday,
October 8, 2026, at the Public Works Department headquarters on Exchange Street in
Suncook Village.
13. There being no further business, the meeting adjourned at 7:10 p.m.
Respectfully submitted,
James L. Garvin, Secretary

PEMBROKE CEMETERY COMMISSION
June 11, 2026
Minutes
Present: Dan Chase, James Garvin, Adam Mendozza, Ellen Paulsen (chair), Zachary Sawyer.
1. Chair Ellen Paulsen called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m.
2. On a motion by Zachary Sawyer, seconded by Dan Chase, the minutes of the Cemetery
Commission meeting of May 14, 2026, were approved as submitted.
New business:
3. The Commission discussed the disposition of the veterans' flag holders stored in the Hearse
House at Pembroke Street Cemetery. In addition to new flag holders, the building retains some of
the plastic holders that were used in the early days of the Commission, and a few cast iron Civil
War holders. After discussion, the Commission agreed that the plastic markers may be discarded
or offered to the Pembroke Historical Society if we verify that their threaded aluminum rods do
not fit our current metal holders. If the rods are still useful, we should continue to store them in
the building. The cast iron Civil War holders were removed in error from Pembroke Street
Cemetery some years ago. The Commission should try to return these holders to the graves they
originally marked.
4. Chair Ellen Paulsen distributed photographs of the rear side of the stone wall in front of Old
North Pembroke Cemetery. The wall is composed of very large split granite boulders with their
flat faces toward North Pembroke Road. Behind these large front stones is a sloped buttress of
fieldstones, some of which undoubtedly were removed from gravesites. A few long granite
coping stones have tipped off the front stones and now rest on the sloped stone buttress behind
the wall. The photographs also showed fallen or tipping gravestones.
Following a discussion of other priorities, the Commission decided not to attempt any work on
the Old North Pembroke Cemetery wall at this time but to request funding for gravestone repairs
in that cemetery; see Item 6, below.
Old business:
5. Chair Paulsen reported that she and Secretary Jim Garvin had placed a new flag holder and flag
at the grave of Robert W. Stevens, U.S.N, in Buck Street Cemetery. The Commission thanked
Adam Mendozza and his crew for unearthing this and other flat grave markers that had been
covered by encroaching turf over the years.

2
6. The Commission discussed its funding request to the Capital Improvement Program (CIP)
Committee for 2026. Using price data collected on the cost of aluminum cemetery lot corner
markers and notes on needed grave marker repairs, the Commission proposed the following
request:
a. Grave marker repairs in Old North Pembroke, Pembroke Street, and Evergreen Cemeteries at
$750 per marker:
$5,000.
b. Aluminum lot corner markers: $1,000.
7. Zachary Sawyer observed that there are state statutes that govern the cleaning and care of
gravestones in public cemeteries. He offered to find the citations and suggested that the
Commission propose amending Chapter 155 of the Pembroke Town Code to incorporate
references to these statutes and quote their language. We should also cite these regulations in our
next Annual Report in the Town Report for 2027.
8. Adam Mendozza reported that Superintendent of Cemeteries Victor J. Ranfos had discussed the
concept of a spreading garden for cremation ashes with the Hooksett Cemetery Commission,
which has such an area. The Commission asked Secretary James Garvin to contact the Hooksett
commission to learn more about their approach to the spreading of ashes.
9. Dan Chase mentioned two instances of excessive grave decorations in Evergreen Cemetery,
suggesting that we send notes to the relevant families. We should continue to quote our
regulations in our regular reports for the annual Town Report.
10. Adam Mendozza reported that another solar flag light is available for installation. He will install
it at the Buck Street Cemetery flagpole.
11. Chair Paulsen reported that members of the French family believe that the French Cemetery on
North Pembroke Road is a municipal cemetery. The Commission has always believed that this
cemetery, like the French-Dearborn Cemetery off Borough Road, is private. We will begin to
research the question.
12. The next regular meeting of the Pembroke Cemetery Commission will be at 6:00 p.m. on
Thursday, July 9, 2023, at the Public Works Department headquarters on Exchange Street in
Suncook Village.
13. There being no further business, the meeting was adjourned at 6:55 p.m.
Respectfully submitted,
James L. Garvin, Secretary

PEMBROKE CEMETERY COMMISSION
April 9, 2026
Minutes
Present: James Garvin, Adam Mendozza, Ellen Paulsen (chair), Zachary Sawyer, Fleda Young.
1. Chair Ellen Paulsen called the meeting to order at 6:05 p.m.
2. On a motion by Fleda Young, seconded by Zachary Sawyer, the minutes of the meeting
of October 9, 2025, were approved as submitted.
3. Chair Paulsen distributed a note from Kirsten Rickershauser, Children's Services
Librarian at the Pembroke Town Library, thanking the Cemetery Commission for
participating in the library's townwide scavenger hunt by permitting the placement of
Community Quest Caches at the entrances of Pembroke Hill and Buck Street Cemeteries.
New business:
4. Chair Paulsen distributed a notice from Dignified Cemetery Services, the town's
contractor for burials in the public cemeteries, announcing an increase in burial fees that
will be charged to the town beginning on February 1, 2026. The Commission voted to
have Secretary James Garvin write a letter to the Board of Selectmen outlining the former
and the new fees and recommending new burial charges to be posted by the selectmen in
Chapters 155 and 160 of the Pembroke Town Code.
Old business:
5. Adam Mendozza reported that Public Works Director V. J. Ranfos has discussed potential
projects at Evergreen Cemetery with the individuals who had offered to fund
improvements to the cemetery. Adam announced that the donors have proposed funding
the widening of the middle entrance to the cemetery. V. J. and the donors will meet soon
to discuss the scope and cost of the proposed work.
6. Adam reported that Accurate Tree Service of Bow has completed the removal of trees and
branches from Pembroke Street Cemetery. Sections of a large tree are presently placed
outside the front wall of the cemetery for removal.

2
7. Adam reported on the proposed spreading garden for cremation ashes at Buck Street
Cemetery. He and Superintendent of Cemeteries V. J. Ranfos are leaning toward the back
corner of the cemetery, close to the river and the adjacent state-owned wooded lot. A
small portion of this area has previously been used for indigent burials. V. J. and Adam
have discussed defining the area with posts and providing an entrance that would allow
the periodic use of flail mowers to keep the area clear of pine seedlings and other hazards
to safe access and use by the public. The Commission agreed to this concept and voted to
add initial costs to this year's proposal to the CIP (Capital Improvements Plan)
Committee if we have figures by the June deadline for submission of requests to the CIP
Committee.
8. The Commission also agreed to add the cost of aluminum lot markers to the CIP request
if we have an estimate by June.
9. Zachary Sawyer reported that he had received a message from Celebrate Life Company
of Salt Lake City (https://www.celebratelifeco.com), outlining their range of services for
cemetery administrators. These include digitizing cemetery maps and gravestone
information. The Commission agreed to develop a clear scope of the services needed
from Celebrate Life Company at our May meeting in order to seek cost estimates.
10. There being no further business to be brought before the meeting, on a motion by Fleda
Young, seconded by Zachary Sawyer, the meeting was adjourned at 6:34 p.m.
Respectfully submitted,
James L. Garvin, Secretary

for Suburban and Rural Fire Fighting",

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
December 17, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,
Selectman Rick Frederickson, Selectman Sandy Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
I.
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00pm.
II.
Citizens Comment
None
III.
Scheduled Meetings:
James Colorusso - 477 Fourth Range Road
James Colorusso, 477 Fourth Range Road, is requesting that the requirement to install
sprinkler system in his new build residential home be waived. James explained had
property was surveyed and where they want to build the home is 240 feet from the
road. The current Town Ordinance states that anything over 200 feet from the road
must have a water supply suitable for fire protection services in the form of municipal
water supply, a sprinkler system, or a cistern. James explained that from the property
line, it is 227 feet to the front of the garage and shared he would be willing to make
the driveway amenable to a fire truck.
Selectman Yeaton stated that the Assist. Chief Farley met with James at the Fire
Station 3 weeks ago to discuss this. James said he explained the situation and Assist.
Chief Farley advised him that he did not have the authority to grant a waiver, the
ordinance has been in effect for a number of years, and that he would not support a
waiver because it may set a precedent for future cases.
Selectman Frederickson stated his understanding was that the 200 foot rule is based
on hose and pump length. Assist. Chief Farley stated that that was one of the factors
that was considered during conception of the ordinance. Selectman Frederickson
asked the number 200 is still applicable. Chief Erik Paulsen stated that this ordinance
was put into place before he was chief and was based on the preconnected hose
length. The idea is that should there be an obstruction in the driveway of any kind,
they would need to be able to get a functioning hose to the structure without
connecting additional hoses. Doing so takes time and additional manpower. That is

still the concern and the 200 number is still applicable, Selectman Frederickson stated
that the ordinance could be met in other ways and asked if any of those were
considered. James answered that a cistern is too much money and city water is not an
option. The sprinkler system was quoted at around $30,000 and the company shared
concerns for installing residential sprinklers because they can be set off by cold
temperatures and not always be fire related.
Selectman Miller stated there are homes built before this ordinance without sprinklers
and asked what risks those homeowners have. Assist Chief Farley stated that if they
have long driveways, getting to the fire quickly will be a challenge. There is a finite
amount of water that the truck can carry. Selectman Miller stated those people live
with the risk or they have to invest in a reservoir or a sprinkler system. Whether or
not they have sprinklers is on the homeowners and not on the Town. Selectman
Goulet shared it is a liability on the Town if they cannot get to a home to put out a
fire.
Selectman Christiansen asked who in the area services residential sprinkler systems.
Assist. Chief Farley answered he is unsure. Selectman Christiansen shared that he has
concerns enforcing this ordinance when a homeowner cannot get anyone to service
the system after they are installed
Selectman Yeaton stated the ordinance is 200 feet and the home is 240 feet and asked
if there any opportunity to move the house 40 feet closer and avoid the need for a
waiver. James answered yes but he wanted to put it on the ridge of the land to keep it
further away from the wetlands. James shared he is also confused as to where exactly
the 200 feet starts. Selectman Yeaton stated it is relevant to the driveway length and
asked if the truck shows up, and they need to connect more hoses in order to reach the
house, that time could amount to loss of structure and also the potential for loss of
life. Chief Paulsen stated that is correct.
Selectman Miller stated that his decision comes down to accountability. If the house
burns down, and the homeowner can claim responsibility for the design and as long
as it does not endanger a neighbor, it is their choice and their responsibility.
Selectman Miller asked if anyone knew definitively if the house catches fire and it
cannot be put out, if it is a Town liability. David answered that he is not a lawyer but
thinks that while there is an ordinance that is presently in place, if they were to waive
it, they could run into accountability issues. If the ordinance did not exist, then the
homeowner would be on his own. Assist. Chief Farley interjected that it is important
to remember that the focus here is life safety and residential sprinkler systems are not
designed for property conservation, they are for life safety. People do not die in
residential sprinklered houses. Selectman Christiansen asked how big the water tank
in the basement would be for a sprinkler system. Assist. Chief Farley answered it is
usually a 10-minute supply. Selectman Christansen stated that the Department would
likely not arrive in 10 minutes regardless if there was a system or not. Assist. Chief
Farley explained the 10 minutes is for life safety and to allow the homeowner to get

out and not to save the structure. Selectman Christiansen stated that if he was on the
road, and did not have a sprinkler system, it would be the same outcome in those 10
minutes because the Town is a call department, however, since the ordinance does
exist, it is likely problematic if they waive it.
Selectman Miller suggested speaking to a lawyer before they make the decision.
Selectman Yeaton agreed.
Selectman Frederickson shared there is 600 feet rule for fire safety in the ordinance
with the need for a turnaround. Chief Paulsen stated for a town accepted road vs a
driveway and a major subdivision versus a single family residence.
Selectman Miller asked what the key rules are for a cistern. Assist. Chief Farley
answered there are specifications dependent on the design. The standard tends to be
an underground tank that is around 30,000 gallons.
Selectman Christiansen asked if there are any other town approvals that he still needs.
James answered he received his wetlands waiver and driveway permit, and this is the
last item that needs town approval before submitting plans.
David asked if he looked at costs to build driveway to larger specs and compare the
costs to the sprinkler system. James answered he spoke with a company and was told
it would be cheaper than the sprinkler system.
Selectman Christiansen asked if the whole house has to be within 200 feet or start at
200 feet. Chief Paulsen stated he is unsure and there is some vagueness there.
Selectman Miller stated the key thing for the ordinance is about the water supply so if
the fire truck can make it up there, they still won't have enough water. Selectman
Frederickson stated there is no local supply so they will need to bring it in regardless.
The question is about getting the supply to the home.
The Board tabled the discussion until they heard back from the lawyer.
Officer Scott Pihl - Grant Authorization
Officer Scott Pihl presented the grant authorization from Department of Safety and ask that
the Town act as fiscal agent for the FEMA grant on behalf of the Central New Hampshire
Special Operations Unit. The money is distributed federally, and the dollar amounts are
determined by population, number of call outs, and the size of team. This year, the amount
awarded is $39,119. There is a list of available equipment they can pick from that meet the
requirements of the grant. Officer Piht has been working with the State Grant Administrator
and once they have the paperwork turned in, they submit a list of the equipment they wish to
buy, and he procures the equipment. The invoices would be paid through the town-created
grant account, then it will be submitted to the State, and the State will reimburse within 30
days. David explained they will need to go through the town bid process during the
procurement process. The grant period closes September 30, 2026.

TOWN OF PEMBROKE - DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
SIDEWALK SNOW REMOVAL & CLEARING - 2026
GRANITE WORKZ, LLC is pleased to propose the following for the sidewalk snow removal & clearing for
the winter operation season:
365 DAY/60 HOUR TERM (January 1st 2026 @ 0000 to December 31% 2026 @ 2359) = $9,000.00 =
($150.00 per hour)

VJ Ranfos - Sidewalk Contract
VJ shared that he has worked with Jason Menard, owner of Granite Workz, LLC to
bring the sidewalk plowing contract within the Town budget year rather than per
storm/hours which could straddle two fiscal years. It is typical for contractors with
municipal entities or the state to have contracts that are a weekly/monthly stipend
rather than per hour/storm. He is expected to keep his equipment working and be
ready at all times. Jason took the 3-year average of hours worked and the costs to the
town and came up with a contract for $9,000/season for a total of 60 hours with
payments of $2,250/month due in January, February, March, and April. If 60 hours
has not been used by April 30",
", the remaining balance of the $2,250 will be due
December 15"'. If he goes over 60 hours, the hourly rate is $150/hour:
Selectman Goulet asked if this is considered a fair contract. VJ answered it is.
Selectman Frederickson asked what the difference is in the current practice and this
contract. VJ answered he will be getting a stipend of a minimum of $9,000 for the
season rather than logging hours and billing monthly at a rate of $147/hour.
Selectman Christiansen asked what the 3-year average costs were. VJ answered
roughly $8,800.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to approve the sidewalk clearing contract with
Granite Workz, LLC for 2026 for a fixed cost of $9,000 and $150/hour over 60 hours.
Selectman Miller seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.

Selectman Christiansen asked where they will be installed. VJ explained one will go
on Whittemore Road going down the hill off RT 3 approaching the golf course and
then one leaving the golf course. On Nadine Road, going towards Donna Drive there
is a guard rail with two speed limit signs and those signs will be replaced with the
solar signs.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to accept the contract for $17,200 with East Coast
Signals. Selectman Frederickson seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.
Public Hearing - Flood Maps
Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner, sent an email that the office received correspondence
from the State of NH Office of Planning and Development informing the Town that it
must update the flood map title and date in order to remain compliant with National
Flood Insurance Program. It is a change to the Town Ordinance, so it does require a
public hearing.
Selectman Yeaton opened the public hearing at 6:16pm
Selectman Yeaton closed the public hearing at 6:17pm
Selectman Goulet made a motion to approve the Town of Pembroke Resolution to
adopt New FEMA FIRMS and FIS and the changes to the flood maps as presented.
Selectman Christiansen seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.
Insurance Discussion - Jacob Parol, HealthTrust
Jacob Parol, Benefits Advisor for HealthTrust, and Melisa Briggs, Assistant Benefits
Manager for HealthTrust, discussed the Access Blue and high-deductible health plans
available to employees. The Town can offer up to three different plans. The Town is
currently on the AB20 plan with a 6-tier pharmacy plan and the union is on the 3-tier
benefit plan. It is set up to begin January 1s!. They are offering a special enrollment
period that will begin new coverage March 1s!.
Selectman Goulet asked how the Town can better manage the increase in costs since
the increase was 16.4%. Jacob stated the Town was originally part of the large pool
combined with several other towns and Pembroke chose to switch over to the small
pool. Because of that decision, the rates changed and the rates had to increase in order
to match the pool. This year is anticipated to be a high medical trend year. The 16.4%
rate increase is showing the increase from switching to the small pool, medical

inflation, the actual rate change which is based off claims utilizations, and a 5.3% risk
charge that is added in to rebuild the HealthTrust reserve fund. If the Town had been
in the small group before January 1, 2026, the rate increase would have been between
5% and 6%.
Selectman Goulet stated one of the biggest concerns they heard from employees was
the added costs to prescriptions. Jacob answered that the non-high-deductible health
plans have two pharmacy plan options. Neither option has a pharmacy deductible, just
a co-pay for the prescriptions. In the high-deductible health plans, an employee would
pay the contracted rate of the prescription and it would go towards the deductible.
Selectman Yeaton asked if they have a formulary and if employees needed to see
exactly what tier their prescriptions fell on, would they be able to see that. Jacob said
they absolutely can see it in the benefits package and it is available on the portal as
well. Melisa explained they can price out exactly what their prescriptions will cost on
the enrollee portal and HealthTrust does have a formulary through CVS Caremark
who administers their prescription benefits for the Access Blue plans and Anthem
also has a different formulary for the high-deductible plans. A formulary is a list of
medications covered by the prescription plan that will determine the co-pay.
Selectman Yeaton asked if they have preferred and non-preferred products within
each tier. Melisa answered yes, they have a generic preferred brand and then a non-
preferred brand. The generic filling rate is in the mid 80's.
Selectman Miller asked if the prescription lists change year to year. Jacob stated the
formulary is updated on a quarterly basis. Generics are always tier 1. Selectman
Miller asked if medications can ever fall off the lists. Melisa answered they can, but
the programs administered by CVS Caremark and Anthem use independent
therapeutic committees that make the determinations and the decisions are made
based on not only costs but clinical effectiveness. HealthTrust does not get involved
in those decisions. It is in the contract that they would need to notify the individual
and their physicians within a 60-day time frame if a drug was to be removed from the
list. If the physician determines it is medically necessary that the patient needs this
medication, they can file for a prior authorization. Decisions can be made sooner than
24 hours.
Selectman Yeaton asked if there are certain medications that require preauthorization.
Jacob answered that all the plans the Town is considering have the same formulary
and the same prior authorization guidelines. Nothing should change from what the
employees currently have as long as they stay on an Access Blue plan. If they change
to a high-deductible health plan, they will need new authorizations. There are very
tew prior authorization medications. Melisa explained that Health Trust is unique in
that if the medication costs less than the co-pay, the individual pays the medication's
actual price.
Selectman Yeaton asked if the plans require a referral for specialists. Jacob answered
they do not, but the individual offices may require it.

CHAPTER 133
SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT
[HISTORY: Adopted by Special Town Meeting 4-21-1990 Article No. I. Amendments
noted where applicable. Amended 3-12-2009 Town Meeting; Updated 5/5/14 Board of
Selectmen; Updated 11/18/15; Updated 4/7/21; Updated 5/21/2025; Updated 7/2/2025.]
§ Section 1 - Definitions:
As used in this chapter, the following terms shall have the meanings indicated:
ACCEPTABLE WASTE - Household garbage, trash, rubbish and refuse originating within
the boundaries of the Town, normally collected or disposed of as a result of residential pick
ups or deliveries.
AUTOMATED COLLECTION - shall mean a method of collecting refuse and recycling
through the use of mechanical collection equipment and special carts issued for the storage
and collection of rubbish and recyclables.
AUTOMATED COLLECTION CART (Or approved cart) - shall mean a specially designed
cart with wheels, approved by the Pembroke Board of Selectmen to be used for the storage
of acceptable refuse or recyclables in the automated collection operation.
COMMERCIAL - Commercial entities doing business in the Town of Pembroke, including
but not limited to contractors, multifamily dwellings of more than five (5) units, manufactured
housing parks and commercial establishments of any size such as residential boarding and
lodging homes, convalescent and nursing homes, private schools, motels, inns, restaurants,
lounges, retail sales, service businesses, professional offices, manufacturing or automotive-
related business.
CURB LINE -shall mean the area directly behind or adjacent to the curb; in the absence of a
curb, the area adjacent to the edge of pavement or road
CURBSIDE COLLECTION - shall mean the pick up of acceptable trash and recyclables at
certain residences in the Town.
CUSTOMER - shall mean any resident who receives solid waste &/or recycling service
from the Town.
DESIGNATED COLLECTION POINT - shall mean the place where the automated cart shall
be placed for service, as determined by the Department of Public Works. I
DIRECTOR - shall mean the Director of Public Works or his or her duly authorized
representative.
DWELLING UNIT - shall mean any building or portion thereof that contains living facilities
(which provide for sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation) for not more than one (1)
household.
EXTRA REFUSE - shall mean any refuse placed on, around or in a five-foot radius of the
automated collection cart in excess capacity of the automated cart.
FACILITY - Town designated disposal site.
1

HAZARDOUS WASTE - shall mean hazardous waste as defined in RSA 147-A: 2, as
amended, and the following:
A. Waste containing explosive, toxic or pathological substances;
B. Lithium ion batteries;
C. Waste defined or classified as hazardous waste at any time under federal, state or
local law, or any regulation there under, or waste defined by any applicable federal,
state or local law as low-level or high-level radioactive waste;
D. Waste prohibited for incineration by any local, state or federal agency with jurisdiction
over the waste plant or facility because of its toxic nature;
E. Waste (other than acceptable waste of the character referred to in Subsection A of
the definition of "acceptable waste"), the processing of which would result in
hazardous waste under Subsections A, B, C or D of this definition; or
F. Carts which hold or which previously have held waste described under Subsections
A, B, C or D above.
G. If any governmental entity having jurisdiction shall determine that any substances,
which are not as of the date of this chapter considered harmful or of a toxic nature or
dangerous, are harmful, toxic or dangerous, such substances shall thereafter be
deemed "hazardous waste."
INFECTIOUS WASTE - shall mean waste that has the potential to cause an infectious
disease via exposure to a pathogenic organism of sufficient virulence and dosage, through
a portal of entry in a susceptible host.
MULTI-FAMILY RESIDENTIAL PROPERTY - shall mean more than one (1) but not more
than five (5) dwelling units in a building.
NON-RESIDENTIAL UNIT - shall mean any establishment except those defined under
residential property.
OTHER SOLID WASTE - Residential white metal goods, household appliances,
recyclables, including electronic waste, tires, street sweeping, brush, tree stumps (no tree
stumps will be accepted from commercial haulers), tree limbs and brush under five (5)
inches in diameter and residential demolition debris that is no more than four (4) feet in
length. The above noted items are not accepted at curbside, but are accepted at the
Transfer Station.
OVERLOADED - shall mean that the automated cart is so full of refuse that its lid is not
completely closed, thereby exceeding the automated carts rated capacity.
PERSON - Any natural person, partnership, corporation, association or other legal entity.
RECYCLABLE - shall mean any acceptable material that is collected and handled by the
Town for remanufacture into new products. The Director of Public Works shall determine
which materials are acceptable in the curbside collection program.
RECYCLING (RESOURCE RECOVERY) PROGRAM - The acceptance, processing and
marketing of recyclable materials such as glass, aluminum cans and newspaper.
2

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
November 5, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,
Selectman Rick Frederickson
Excused: Selectman Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00pm.
Il.
Citizens Comment
Gerry Fleury, Solid Waste Committee, stated that as a committee they went and
toured the new facility in Massachusetts. It is clear that Casella has no financial
incentive to maximize revenue from recycling or to mitigate the expense to
customers. An example being that people who do not have intact covers on their
recycling bins allow water to saturate the cardboard which in turn means it weighs
more and the town pays more per ton. It may be worth enforcing the requirement that
everyone has intact covers on their carts. It could be added to the ordinance if the
Selectboard had an interest in it. Selectman Yeaton shared that in October, there was
a 6% increase in the cost of recycling from $141.54/ton to $151.08/ton. Trash
collection is currently at around $117/ton. Gerry explained that trash is adjusted
annually based on the CPI. Selectman Yeaton stated that in April, it was $115.49/ton.
That is a 30% increase in the cost of recycling and Selectman Yeaton expressed
concerns that the increases are hitting a breaking point. Gerry shared that right now,
there is a lot up in the air when it comes to the landfills in New Hampshire. If Dalton
does not open, trash will be shipped a long way away and that could have a huge
impact on the tonnage cost for trash. Year to date, it has cost the Town $8,562.08 for
recycling vs if it was all trash. When the current contract was drafted, an RFP went
out to all potential service providers, and the committee was tasked with the question
of if it was cheaper to continue in town trash collection or outsource. It was a huge
savings to have it in house. David shared that the numbers have recently changed in
favor of outsourcing. Sally Hyland stated that some communities have residents
figure it out and that is much more costly for residents. The transfer station would
remain open, but curbside is on the resident. Selectman Miller stated they should do a
full cost analysis between continuing with curbside and privatization that includes not
only tipping fees but items such as employee wages and benefits and liability
insurance. Sally Hyland stated that since the program began, the Town has saved
around $500,000. Even though the cost per ton for recycling is more, the percentage

III.
of recycling is far lower than that of trash, so trash still technically costs the town
more.
Scheduled Meetings:
Doc Greco - Health Officer
Doc Greco has been the Town of Pembroke Health Officer for 62 years. Doc started
his practice in Town in 1962 and in 1963 the Health Officer past away so the
Selectman asked him to assume the position until they found someone. He has been
in the position ever since. Some of his duties include inspecting all daycare centers,
schools, and foster homes, homes of people adopting, and investigating any health
issues that come up like sewage or septic problems. In schools, Doc checks items like
the temperature of water, that all licensing is current in cafeterias, checks
thermometers in refrigeration, checks that all hazardous materials are in a safe place,
and checks leakage of gases in labs. In daycare centers, he has to check items like
bathroom to kid's ratio, proper ventilation, and hazards on the playground. Code
Enforcement and the Fire Department also go to all daycare centers. Foster homes
have to be checked for items like proper ventilation and hazardous waste/chemicals
are kept out of reach. He also has to deal with complaints between tenants and
landlords for things like poor ventilation and mold. Doc recently handled a call for an
infestation of spiders in a downtown establishment. They investigated and found
spiders so they had to notify the owner, and they must take care of it. If there is any
construction over the aquifer, they have to go over the blueprints with Water Works
and the Town Planner. Selectman Miller asked if they inspect the transfer station for
anything. Doc answered he does not. Selectman Miller asked if he gets a call, what is
the duration from him getting a call to getting there. Doc answered usually within a
day. Selectman Frederickson asked how many hours a week he works. Doc answered
sometimes he has two calls a week and sometimes he has two calls in a month. This
week he had one call. It changes all the time. Selectman Christiansen asked if he does
restaurants. Doc answered no, he does not license restaurants. He recently got a call
that someone found something in their food. He went to the restaurant and checked
out the kitchen and found a lot of problems and he notified the State. He is not a
licensing body but often must do paperwork in order for a license to be issued.
Public Hearing Gerry Fleury - Updates to Solid Waste Chapter 133
Gerry Fleury, Solid Waste Committee, stated that this policy was amended in July to
address businesses in the SB section of downtown using the transfer station. While
working on that update, Gerry noticed the formatting of the chapter was inconsistent
with the rest of the Town Code. Items like section numbers were missing so that was
updated. State laws changed dealing with the disposal of lithium-ion batteries so
prohibited disposal of the batteries was added. There were also some grammar items
such as capitalization of proper nouns that were changed. Violations were clarified
that the Director can suspend repeat offenders from using the transfer station.

IV.
Selectman Yeaton opened the public hearing at 6:39pm.
No public comments were shared.
Selectman Yeaton closed the public hearing at 6:40pm.
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to approve the Solid Waste Ordinance
Chapter 133 as presented. Selectman Miller seconded the motion. Motion passed 4-0.
Public Hearing in accordance with RSA 31:95-b III (a) - acceptance of closeout
monies from Concord Regional Solid Waste
David stated that the Concord Regional Solid Waste is the incinerator in Penacook.
They had land for future expansion, but a developer went in front of the City of
Concord and wanted to build housing. They sold the land, and this check is for the
Town's proceeds of that sale. The Town was once a part of the consortium when this
land was acquired.
Selectman Yeaton opened the public hearing at 6:42pm.
No public comments were shared.
Selectman Yeaton closed the public hearing at 6:43pm.
Selectman Frederickson made a motion to accept the check in the amount of
$53,524.05 in accordance with RSA 31:95-b III (a). Selectman Christiansen seconded
the motion. Motion passed 4-0.
DPW - Street Sweeping Bids
Public Works recommend awarding the bid to GDB Enterprise, LLC for year 2026,
2027, and 2028. The Town currently uses Immaculate Power Sweeping, but they did
not fulfill the requests of the RFP in its entirety.
Selectman Miller asked where they dump what is collected from the streets. Alex
Marrion, DPW, explained they dump it at the transfer station, it gets tested, and then
if cleared, it is dispersed to places like the low spots in Memorial Field.
Selectmen Frederickson made a motion to approve the 2025 street sweeping bid with
GDB Enterprise, LLC for the years 2026, 2027, and 2028 at a rate of $17,850,
Sassed 0, and S18,700 respectively. Selectman Miller seconded the motion. Motion

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
October 22, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Rick Frederickson,
Selectman Goulet
Excused: Selectman Bryan Christiansen
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 pm.
II.
2026 Budget Deliberations
Selectman Goulet made a motion for the Town to move forward with the health
insurance plan as presented at the October 15, 2025 Board Meeting. Selectman Miller
seconded the motion. Motion passed 4-0.
Erik Paulsen, Pembroke Fire Chief, invited the Board to an open house they are
holding at the Safety Center on Saturday from 10-1.
David Jodoin shared the 2025 tax rate has been set and the bills are at the printer. The
rate is $21.84. It is an increase of $2.20 over last year. The town tax went up $0.48,
county tax went down $0.06, local school tax went up $1.87, and the state school tax
went down $0.09. The projection was $22.09 at March Town Meeting.
David shared that after adding health insurance numbers and property liability cost to
each department budget, the overall operational budget that was submitted by the
department heads is up 8.65% which would increase the tax rate by $1.21. David
revised the budgets and is presenting a budget with an overall increase of $0.73.
Selectman Miller asked if in the revised budget the line items change between his
budget and the department head's budgets approximately the same except for
healthcare. David said it is.
Selectman Frederickson asked if the revised budgets have been discussed with each
department head. David said he has gone over the cuts he made with each person.
VJ Ranfos shared that he would like the Board to consider his proposal for the
additional staff member that he made at the last board meeting as they move through
this discussion. Selectman Yeaton asked David if he kept that position in the revised
budget. David answered he did not.

Police Chief Gaskell stated they have an open spots and the revised budget has a 6-
month hold on filling one spot. It is tough on its own to fill an opening and if they
find someone, they want the flexibility to be able to get them in. David stated there is
a lot of movement in that account and his thought was that once the three new
employees pay and benefits are factored in on the original budget, which was made
with full time hours and family plans, there should still be enough in the account to
actually fund the remaining employee for more than 6 months.
Selectman Yeaton read Selectman Christiansen email into the record:
"Although DPW did a great job in their justification for the new position, I would
tend not to support it this year. I would really like to learn more on privatization on
trash pick-up in the coming year so perhaps DPW can get to their headcount that
way. I would put my vote behind David's budget vs. department budget. I would
actually be in favor of a lower budget, but I struggle with the age-old argument of
maintaining the services while keeping the taxes as low as possible. I do not have a
vote tonight but just my two cents. Sorry I can't be there."
Selectman Goulet stated she would like to give DPW the extra person but struggles
with possibility of going private with trash. If they do, is there a need for that
additional person and when will that decision be made. Aside from the DPW new
position, Selectman Goulet supports David's budget.
Selectman Yeaton asked when the current contract with Casella is up. VJ answered
August 2027. Selectman Goulet stated that in light of the contract not being up until
2027, she would support David's budget with the additional DPW position.
Selectman Miller supports a lot of J's reasoning given at the last meeting for the
new employee. Potential privatization does open up staff to other projects. Depending
on what happens with that service, we may not need to hire someone. Solid Waste
Committee should do the full cost analysis of in-house trash collection vs.
privatization. VJ explained the Town of Bow just went to privatization with Casella
and it was roughly $750,000/year and right now it is costing the Town $650,000/year
to pick trash. Selectman Miller stated he would like to have a fairly rigorous analysis
of more exact Pembroke specific numbers.
Selectman Frederickson also shares concerns about adding a person if the Town
privatizes trash collection. If they do go private, the money in the capital reserve will
come back to the Town and asked if there is a way to hold the position until that
discussion happens. David answered they could budget for the position and not fill it
and if they do go private, the money allotted would lapse to surplus at the end of the
year. Selectman Frederickson asked VJ when they would plan to hire the person. VJ
answered the plan was to wait until after Town Meeting. Selectman Miller stated if
they do the analysis before the end of the year on whether or not to outsource trash
collection and if privatization looks better, then they just won't fill the position.
David stated they could cut the position to 6 or 4 months until they are closer to

knowing the actual costs and the cost of the new trash truck. There are still a lot of
moving variables.
Selectman Yeaton supports the need for the new position of DPW but is concerned
about hiring someone, coming to the decision to privatize, and now they need to let
someone go. Selectman Yeaton supports leaving the position in the budget but trim
the term down to 6 months.
Selectman Yeaton asked about the CIP deposit reductions between the two budgets.
David explained that originally, when money was put aside in the Roadway
Improvement Capital Reserve Fund, the money was being built up to save for the
Memorial Park projects which was estimated at $500,000. Then the new estimates are
coming in at about $1.6m so there is a lot of money in the fund for infrastructure
repairs and I feel that's enough. There was a request this year to purchase a 6-wheel
dump truck and a new trash truck. David stated they can always lease a trash truck in
order to give them more time to make this decision. Selectman Yeaton asked if they
are still on track to purchase a new 6-wheel dump truck next year. VJ answered that
they may be in a position to either purchase the 6-wheel or the trash truck next year
but they are hoping to still be able to purchase both. Selectman Yeaton asked if they
do not put enough money in this year, will they have enough to purchase the vehicles.
David answered it completely depends on what the final costs of the trash truck
comes in at. Selectman Yeaton asked if there are any estimates on the 6-wheeler yet.
VJ answered $360,000. David stated right now there is $290,000 in the fund and
$100,000 is reserved for the electric trash truck which leaves $190,000. Then they
have to subtract out $5,200 for the flat bed kit and $58,000 for the lift, that leaves
$126,800. The deposit request was originally $600,000 but the revised budget puts in
$375,000 which would give enough money to buy either the trash truck or the 6-
wheeler.
Selectman Miller stated last year they discussed moving a few hundred thousand
dollars to offset taxes. David stated they moved half a million.
David reviewed highlights of the expected revenues:
• The Town had a portion of land owned by churches as taxable. That will be
coming off the tax rolls due to legislation that was passed
• Motor vehicle revenues are still estimated at $1,600,000
• A Payment in Lieu of Taxes agreement in the amount of $13,000 will no
longer be received from United Church of Christ office building on Rt 106
because of the legislation that was passed.
• The only other real revenue generator for the town is state aid. Meals and
Rooms is estimated at around $400,000
David is presenting warrant articles to make the Selectman agents to expend on the
Sidewalks Capital Reserve Fund and Recreation Capital Reserve Fund.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
October 15, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,
Selectman Rick Frederickson, Selectman Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00pm.
II.
Citizens Comment
None
III.
Scheduled Meetings:
Strategic Contracting - request to waive interest on current use
Police Chief Gaskell shared that they have completed the unlicensed canines under
the civil forfeiter process for the year. To do this, the Tax Collector creates the list of
unregistered canines, the Selectboard signs a warrant, a summons is issued to the
owner, and the owner can either go to court or pay a fine. All summonses are hand
delivered by the Police Department. 95 were issued and 76 responded by paying. 11
did nothing because they no longer have the canine.
Chris Gamache - Collections Policy & Presentation of 2026 Budget
Director Gamache reviewed the Accounts Receivable policy which defines the
billing, write off, and collections practices of Pembroke EMS. Billing rates will be set
by the Bopard of Selectman and shall comply with State and Federal Law. Medical
billing is very complicated and comes with a lot of liability so that service is
contracted out to Comstar. The service charges for details, paramedic intercepts, and
any other EMS activities that they are legal able to receive payments from. Senate
Bill 245 was passed and prohibits ambulance balance billing or "surprise billing"
Essentially, an ambulance service creates a bill for the service provided, that bill is
sent to the insurance company, the insurance company pays whatever that policy
allows, and the patient receives a bill for the balance. The issue arises when a patient
pays for insurance and then the ambulance is out of network. Ambulance services
now have to accept whatever insurance is willing to pay and not pass on the balance.
A caveat to that bill is that ambulance services can charge up to 325% of Medicare
allowable. This year, the rates for BLS(basic life support) are $1,620 and will
decrease to $1,530 next year. The rates for ALS1(a little more of care such as IV's,

medications, EKGs) are $2,420 and will decrease to $1,860. The rates for ALS2 (a
higher-level patient that needs to be intubated, in cardiac arrest, on bipap, etc.) are
$3,550 and will reduce to $2,630. The bulk of the ambulance runs are ALS1. These
figures will affect next year's budget. On average, when factoring in total operational
costs and dividing it per transport, it costs about $1,800 per transport. Medicare pays
around $600. This year, they took what the average of the 50 Services in Southern
NH area charge and amended Pembroke EMS to match.
Hardship cases will be handled on a case-by-case basis. The policy stated that the
EMS Director shall have the authority to reduce a patient's balance to the Medicare
Allowable rates if the patient is a resident of the Town of Pembroke and the patient
does not have health insurance, and the patient has contacted the service with
concerns of having difficulty. The EMS Director shall have the authority to negotiate
a payment plan with the patient or authorized representative. Director Gamache
shared that there is less than a 5% collection rate from people who do not have health
insurance or are "self-pay". The policy further stated that the EMS Director shall
have the authority to write off balances if it meets the requirements of the policy. The
EMS Director shall refer patients to a collection agency when the billing contractor
has exhausted their efforts with collecting on a patient account and the patient does
not or no longer meets the criteria mentioned in this policy. The Board of Selectman
have the authority to accept or deny a person' request for a hardship. Payments are
collected through the service's billing contractor. If someone wants to pay the Service
directly, they will be sent to Town Hall.
At the Board's request the policy will be amended to clarify that not all balances will
be reduced for Town of Pembroke residents by $500 in Section H: Write Offs number
il.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to accept the EMS policy as amended. Selectman
Miller seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.
Director Chris Gamache reviewed the increases and decreases in the Pembroke
Emergency Medical Services' 2026 Budget:
• Fill Time Salaries - 3.58% increase
• Per Diem Salaries - 11.28% increase. Added funds to cover new hires and
training.
• Overtime - 6.18% increase
• Health Insurance - 10.00% increase
• Dental Insurance - 5.00% increase
• Life Insurance - 68.33% increase or $82.
• Contracted Billing Services - 47.62% increase
• Computer Software Maint - 65.57% increase
• Overall budget has a 6.87% increase or $1,143,131.

IV.
Director Gamache shared that Pembroke EMS has answered close to 900 calls this
year as predicted. The response rate for in-town calls is greater than 95%. There were
just under 500 transports which was the predicted amount. 89% of this budget is
payroll and payroll related items.
Selectman Miller asked how much of the per diem increase is due to staffing changes,
call volume, and hourly wage increases. Director Gamache answered none of it is
due to that. The shifts are assigned a dollar value and each shift has different dollar
values within it. The budget is created by looking at those shifts and predicting what
will be needed and when. Then those numbers are calculated by month and by year to
project payroll. This budget includes 5 employees with 40 hours of orientations, 14
hours a month for training, and then holiday pay as well as the increases for COLA,
Merit, training, and education.
David Jodoin clarified that this year, $125,654 was used from the Tri-Town EMS
close out money to offset the costs of the service. The close out total was $449,726.48
and the current balance is $324,072. Selectman Miller asked if there is a target
balance for that special revenue fund. David stated that for Tri-Town, they tried to
keep the surplus fund balance around $250,000. Anything over that would go back
for tax relief. They could keep that process or it could be absorbed into the general
fund budget.
Selectman Yeaton asked if they asked him to reduce the budget by 2-2.5%, what
impact would it have on the Department. Director Gamache answered that they would
try to offset it with fund balance and then he would attempt to bring revenues up
because the majority of the budget is locked. The only line that could be decreased is
supplies. Selectman Goulet stated they are looking for a more specific impact such as
they would have to run 18 hrs. instead of 24 hrs. or a lower level of services. Director
Gamache stated that he would still try and reduce what the Town has to pay before
taking away from the service. Selectman Miller stated that he would like to see other
options other than the special revenue fund to reduce the budget because that is a one
off fund and will be depleted soon. They want to be prepared for Town Meeting in
case there is a motion to reduce the budget. Director Gamache stated that 2.5% is
$29,000. If a per diem is pulled out of the holiday shifts, it is approximately $9,000.
David explained that $29,000 is not even a penny on the tax rate and that is worth
pointing out to the residents.
Old Business
Public Works Director -2026 Budget
VJ Ranfos, Public Works Director, stated that the prior custodian asked for his job
back and he starts on Monday.
The Selectboard sent VJ questions regarding the new hire:

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NE
October 8, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,
Selectman Rick Frederickson
Excused: Selectman Sandy Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
II.
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:02pm.
Citizens Comment
None
III.
Scheduled Meetings:
Chief Gaskell
Police Chief Gaskell shared they have completed the unlicensed canines under the
civil forfeiter process for the year. The process is the Tax Collector creates the list of
unregistered canines, Selectman sign a warrant, a summons is issued to the owner to
court or they pay a fine, and the Police Department hand delivers it. 95 were issued
and 76 responded by paying. 11 did not because they no longer have the canine.
Chief Gaskell - 2026 Budget Presentation
Chief Gaskell and Lieutenant Shea reviewed the increases and decreases in the
Pembroke Police Department 2026 Budget:
• Wages - 3.49% increase
• Health Insurance - 15.76% increase
• Dental Insurance - 10.59%
• Life Insurance - 7.27% decrease
• Expecting all wage and benefit related lines to change before the final
budget.
• Training and Education - 18.52% decrease
• Mental Health and Wellness - 249,900% increase. Lt. Shea stated that
funds were taken out of the training line from last year and will fund the
annual check-in visits for Officers to a culturally competent clinician. It
also gives a little bit of funding for mental health training and allows some

flexibility for the Town to send an Officer in an emergency situation
where a critical incident has negatively impacted an Officer. Selectman
Miller asked how they expect the relationship between the Department and
the healthcare professional to develop. Lt. Shea shared that they have
completed the process this year and all sworn and unsworn staff went for a
visit. The clinician is well versed in first responder and veteran affairs.
The Department is not informed of anything that happens in the session
just whether or not they show up. Further follow up care would go through
the individual's health insurance.
• Dispatch Services - 6% increase
• Fuel - 23.53% decrease
Overall budget has a 4.75% increase or $110,125.
Selectman Yeaton asked if there are any encumbrances for them to consider. David
answered there are not.
Selectman Frederickson asked if removing the funds for mental health and wellness
from the training lines would mean training could potentially suffer. Lt. Shea stated
they have made efforts to bring training in house which makes training dollars go
further than they have in the past.
Selectman Christiansen asked about the reduction in the fuel lines. Chief Gaskell
stated that each year they have been using less and less fuel. 5 years ago it was
calculated at $4/gallon, and the prices have come down.
Selectman Chrisitansen stated the criminal investigations year to date is at $788
dollars and asked if they anticipate to use more. Chief Gaskell stated that line will go
up by the end of the year. They will use it to purchase investigative supplies.
Selectman Miller asked what numbers, outside of the health care numbers, could
change between now and the final budget. David answered workman's comp,
unemployment, property liability, and dental insurance.
Selectman Miller asked if they see a point where the cyber crimes will exceed the
competencies of the Department. Lt. Shea stated they already have to pull outside
resources. The current team dealing with investigations are being sent to training
courses, however, it will be a constant retraining effort. They do not currently have
the ability to do forensics on computers or cell phones. They outsource to the NH
State Police Crime Lab or the different task forces that exist in the State.
Selectman Frederickson asked if they are charged by the State for using any of those
resources. Lt. Shea answered they are not. The law enforcement community is very
collaborative.
Selectman Yeaton asked if technology investigations are part of most major crimes.
Lt. Shea answered that most crimes have an element of technology now a days.

IV.
VI.
Selectman Miller asked for opinions on what they are seeing with E-bikes. Chief
Gaskell stated the category of e-bikes is the deciding factor, but it is not always clear
in the RSA's. Lt. Shea stated it in an under legislated area that makes things difficult.
Old Business
None
Non-Public
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to enter into non-public session in accordance
with RSA 91-A:3 II (b) Hiring Public Personnel. Motion seconded by Selectman
Miller at 6:29 pm.
Roll Call Vote:
Selectman Christiansen
Selectman Yeaton
Selectman Frederickson
Selectman Miller
Yes
Yes
Yes
Yes
The Board came out of non-public session at 6:40 pm.
Motion by Selectmen Christiansen and seconded by Selectmen Frederickson to hire
Vincent Noah Hugo as a new Policer officer at a rate of $33 effective 10/20/25
Adjourn
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to adjourn at 6:42 PM. Selectman Miller
seconded the motion, and it was approved unanimously.
For more detailed information, the meetings are now taped and can be seen on
www.townhallstreams.com click on Pembroke NH and look for the day of the meeting under the
month.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
October 1, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,
Selectman Rick Frederickson, Selectman Sandy Goulet
Excused: Selectman Sandy Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00pm.
IL.
Citizens Comment
None
III.
Scheduled Meetings:
VJ Ranfos - Tree Removal Pembroke Street Cemetery
VJ Ranfos, Public Works Director, shared the back left corner of the Pembroke Street
Cemetery has three dead and failing trees. VJ received quotes from Collins Tree
Service for $17,000, Tree Fellas for $10,218.75, and Accurate Tree Service $7,200.
Department of Public Works and the Cemetery Commission are recommending
awarding the bid to Accurate Tree. They are the lowest bid and DPW has used them
in the past at other cemeteries.
Selectman Miller asked if all the companies were given the same scope of work to bid
on. VJ answered they were. Selectman Miller asked if the bid includes pruning the
trees in front of the cemetery. VJ answered it does.
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to award the tree removal bid to Accurate
Tree Service and to withdraw the funds from the Cemetery Capital Reserve Fund.
Selectman Miller seconded the motion. Motion passed 4-0.
David explained that downtown there is a small park on the corner of Main St. and
Glass St. Meet me in Suncook is looking to take over that piece of property to
beautify but there are trees that need to be pruned and cleaned up. They got a quote
for $1,800 from Girard Tree Services. Girard Tree Services did work for Meet Me in
Suncook at Robert Frost Park on Buck Street. The funds will come from the Public
Works Budget for tree removal. The park is State owned property that the Town
maintains.

VJ Ranfos - Disposition of Town Property
VJ stated there is a 2010 Ford Explorer that DPW would like to send to auction. A
new SUV was handed down from the Police Department, and this one is no longer
needed.
Selectman Frederickson asked what the SUV is used for. VJ explained mainly
administrative tasks.
David asked if the Ambulance service would be interested in the vehicle. VJ
explained the SUV needs too much work for it to be worth it.
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to transfer the listed town property for
disposition to St. Jean Auctioneers. Selectman Frederickson seconded the motion.
Motion passed 4-0.
VJ Ranfos - Winter Sand Bids
VJ explained they received two bids for winter sand. Pike Industries in the amount of
$19.90/ton delivered and $12.45/ton picked up and F.L. Merrill Construction, Inc. in the
amount of $15.92/ton delivered, or $12.00/ton picked up. The last few years, F.L. Merrill has
been the only company to respond to the RFP. Pike Industries did not comply with the
requirements of the bid to provide a sample and a certificate of insurance.
Selectman Miller asked what last year's bids were. VJ answered of $14.67/ton delivered and
$11.00/ton picked up.
Selectman Christiansen asked if they pick up or have the sand delivered more. VJ answered
they try to pick up more than have them deliver but there are occasions when they will have
to have it delivered.
Selectmen Christiansen made a motion to approve the winter sand bid with F.L. Merrill
Construction, Inc. for the price of $15.92/ton delivered and $12.00/ton picked up. Selectman
Christiansen seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.
VJ Ranfos - 2026 Budget Presentation
VJ Ranfos reviewed the increases and decreases in the General Government
Buildings 2026 Budget:
• Wages - 6.60% decrease. Part time custodian retired who was working 20-
hours a week. Selectman Miller asked how the custodial work will get
covered. VJ explained that other employees will be picking up the work until
they are able to hire. The position was budgeted for 25 hours, and they are
advertising for 20 hours.
Electricity has small increases for Safety Center, Town Hall, and Public
Works of 3.75%, 3.47%, and 3.85% respectively.

• Small heating fuel decreases for the Safety Center, Town Hall, and Public
Works of 3.70%, 4.76%, and 3.13% respectively.
• Repair and Maintenance lines for the Safety Center, Town Hall, and Public
Works remained flat. The Library has an increase of 6.25% or $500. The
building is getting older and needs more maintenance.
• Overall budget has a 0.76% decrease or $995
VJ Ranfos reviewed the increases and decreases in the Cemeteries 2026 Budget:
• Mowing Services - 4.04% increase. It is a contracted service.
• Marker Repairs & Cemetery Maint. - 10% decrease.
• All other lines remained flat.
• Overall budget has a 2.57% increase or $1,050.
VJ Ranfos reviewed the increases and decreases in the Department of Public Works
2026 Budget:
• Wages - 12.69% increase or $76,220. VJ is requesting a new position for 8
months. Two positions were eliminated when they began curbside collection,
but the loss of those positions has been felt most in the winter months. VJ is
looking to add one back. It would be advertised as a driver/laborer. They are
currently struggling to be proactive on projects and cover vacations.
• Overtime wages - 3.26% increase
• Part time seasonal wages - 5.23% increase
• Health Insurance - 38.51% increase. Based on a 10% increase, 1 insurance
buyout, and a potential new employee.
• Dental Insurance - 39.70% increase.
• Uniforms - 7.14% decrease
• Training and Education - 25% increase or $500.
• Contracted Services - 5.88% or $500 increase. Mostly the sidewalk plow
company. As sidewalks are added, this is expected to increase.
• Telephone - 3.33% increase.
• Street Sweeping - 102.02% increase. MS-4 regulations mandate the Town
needs to sweep in the Spring and the Fall instead of just in the Spring.
• Meetings & Conferences - 16.67% or $100 increase. There are two
conferences they attend.
• Gas & Fuel - 4.17% or $2,500 decrease. Projected savings from the electric
trash truck.
• Vehicle Maintenance & Repair - 3.90% or $2,250 increase.
• Computer/Software Maintenance - 8.11% or $1,500 decrease
• Union Contract - 100% or $10,935 increase
• Street Lighting - 5.26% decrease
• Solid Waste Department Supplies - 3.13% increase
