Dear HHW Coordinator:
Attached to this e-mail you will find your Fiscal Year 2026 household hazardous waste grant contract package, which
includes a copy of your pre-populated G-1 Grant Contract, and templates of two versions of the required certificate of
authority (by bylaw, or by vote).
1. Complete the certificate of authority that best suits your administrative process.
2. Sign, initial and date the grant contract. Note that the contract must be signed less than 30 days after the
certificate of authorization.
3. Obtain a certificate of insurance that is likely to be valid until the contract approval process is complete
4. Mail a hard-copy completed package with original wet signatures to me at:
NHDES
29 Hazen Drive
P.O. Box 95
Concord, NH 03302-0095
Attn.: HHW Grant Program
Please don't forget:
• Please note that contracts that don't receive final State approval until after your first HHW collection event of
the grant fiscal year are considered "retroactive" and are less likely to be approved. Please submit your
completed contract as soon as possible to avoid this possibility. This is particularly true if you will be holding
collection events in July as the process to approve these grants includes many levels of review; usually including
1

the Governor and Executive Council. Quick turnaround and careful review of the contract submittal greatly
increases the likelihood of review and approval prior to your first collection event.
• Again - Common Error: The contract must be signed and pages initialed and dated less than thirty (30) days
after the certificate of authority is dated. It's OK if they are signed on the same date. This document is officially
stating that the signor of the contract has been granted authority to do so by the grant applicant.
• If the contract is signed more than 30 days after the certificate is signed, there is a likelihood that the
person identified in the certificate is no longer acting in that capacity and therefore not authorized.
• If the contract is signed before the certificate is signed, then it was signed by someone who was not yet
authorized to do so, and we will reject the contract when we review it.
• Please remember to include a copy of your current insurance paperwork including General Liability and
Worker's Compensation with NHDES listed as the certificate holder. More information can be found here. Check
the certificate expiration date to make sure it will be valid long enough to still be in effect at the time of final
grant approval.
Contracts and certificate of authority submitted to NHDES must be hard-copy originals with wet signatures. We
cannot accept photocopies or emailed versions of those documents. Considering the complexity of these
documents, however, you may choose to send it in an email first, so we have a chance to give it a preliminary
read and pick up any obvious errors before you send the hard copy. That would save you time and effort in
mailing a hard copy that will be rejected.
• If you are submitting a certificate of authority by Bylaw, you will need to provide a copy of the bylaw giving the
signor authority to enter into the contract.
• Under Block 1.11, of the G-1 grant contract there are now lines for up to three individuals to sign the
contract. We (NHDES) only require one valid signature for the HHW grant contract. It's OK to leave two
signature lines empty. If you choose to have multiple signatures on your contract, the names and/or positions of
the additional signors must also be identified on the certificate of authority.
• Exhibit B, Paragraph 3 requires the grantee to confirm their third-party vendor's liability coverage, but NHDES
does not require you to submit copies of their certificates.
• NHDES' senior leadership has chosen not to accept digital signatures for financial contracts at this time.
Things that are new this year:
• I currently have tentative plans to retire this summer. As such, I'm in the process of training additional staff in
operating the program. While I will remain the primary contact for the foreseeable future, Ann Astarita
(Ann.s.astarita@des.nh.gov) 603-271-6398 will be an additional contact going forward.
• Ann and l are also working on developing an online presentation to help in completing the forms associated with
the grant process. It isn't ready at the time of this writing, but I will send an email with a link to it when it's
finished. I have no way of knowing when that will be, so don't hold off on submitting your completed contract
because you were waiting for a chance to review the presentation.
If you have any questions, please let me know.
Regards,
NHDES would greatly appreciate your feedback and wants to hear from you. Please take a moment to fill out our short
(5-question) NDES Customer Service Satisfaction Survey.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
April 16, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Sandy Goulet, Selectman Matt Miller,
Selectman Rick Frederickson
Excused: Selectman Karen Yeaton
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
I.
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:02pm.
II.
Citizens Comment
Ill.
Scheduled Meetings:
Acceptance of Household Hazardous Waste Grant in accordance with RSA 31:95-b
III (b)
VJ Ranfos, Public Works Director, explained that the Household Hazardous Waste
Grant is from the NHDES. It is awarded based on the town's population.
Selectman Miller asked who Pembroke contracts with for disposal. VJ explained they
work with the NRRA to contract with a licensed company. Selectman Miller asked
how much of the overall cost the grant will cover. VJ answered the grant will cover
approximately 10%. Last time, $12,500 was budgeted and around $8,000 was spent.
This year, $10,000 is budgeted. Acceptable items are listed on the town website.
Selectman Goulet opened the public hearing at 6:12pm.
No residents were in attendance
Selectman Goulet closed the public hearing at 6:12pm.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to accept the Household Hazardous Waste Grant in
the amount of $1,141 and to authorize the Vice-Chair of the Selectboard to sign the
necessary documents. Selectman Frederickson seconded the motion. Motion passed
4-0.
VJ Ranfos Public Works - Crack Sealing Bid

VJ explained there was only one response to the RFP for crack sealing. It is the same
company the Town has been using, and they have been very happy with the work.
The bid came in $0.04 cheaper per pound than this year.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to waive the bid requirements and to award the
crack sealing bid to Sealcoating Inc. dba indus for the sum of $1.81/per pound not to
exceed $25,000. Selectman Christiansen seconded the motion. Motion passed 4-0.
VJ Ranfos Public Works - Truck Purchase
VJ explained they are asking to purchase a 2025 Ford F660 to replace the 2015 Ford
F550. This is a smaller truck in the fleet used for plowing on tighter roads and various
summer projects. Three companies sent in bids with different options and Public
Works is recommending purchasing from Grappone Ford. Grappone has offered a
$10,000 trade in for the current vehicle. Since the new truck won't be in until next
year, they will reassess next summer and see if the trade in value is higher.
Selectman Frederickson asked if there are any components that can be transferred
from the old truck to the new truck. VJ answered there are not.
Selectman Christiansen asked what they are recommending for a warranty. VJ
answered the Fleet Mechanic Corey Heath suggested the 8-year, 100,000 miles/4,000
engine hours option for $5,170.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to purchase the Ford F600 from Grappone Ford
with the warranty and the current trade in value for $63,430. Selectman Christiansen
seconded the motion. Motion passed 4-0.
VJ Ranfos Public Works - Truck Equipment Purchase
VJ explained the new 2025 Ford F660 will be delivered in the fall of 2025. They will
need to store the truck until Spring while they wait for the equipment to come in.
Once the equipment is in, they will send the truck off and it is expected to be back in
Town with all the equipment installed in August of 2026.
Selectman Miller asked if the quotes for the equipment are firm or can they vary
between now and the Spring of 2026. VJ explained the truck price is locked, and the
equipment is locked barring any future tariffs. He had suggested the Town could pay
extra to cover any potential tariffs, but it would be non-refundable. Selectman Miller
suggested finding out what that number could be. If it is under $5,000, it may be
worth the protection since there is no way to know what tariff amount could
potentially be levied.
Selectman Miller asked if the equipment for the other trucks he received quotes on
would cost the same as this truck. VJ answered they would all have the same
equipment costs.

IV.
VJ explained that the vendors are suggesting that the Towns enter into a program
where they can get in a que for vehicles that they know are up for replacement so that
it would eliminate some potential delays. The Board would like more details on this
plan such as what is the offer and what are the rules and are there any hidden costs to
the Town if funding doesn't get approved. VJ stated that he would try and set up a
time for the vendors to come in and make a presentation.
Selectman Christiansen asked if any of the current equipment has camera feeds. VJ
answered they do. Cameras have been considered standard for the last several years.
There is a backup camera, a camera that shows how much material is in the spreader,
and a camera at the shoot to ensure the material is going out correctly. They are
considering installing dash cams in the trucks starting with the garbage truck.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to approve the purchase of the equipment for the
new truck in the amount of $90,700. Selectman Frederickson seconded the motion.
Motion passed 4-0.
VJ Ranfos Public Works - Lift Purchase
VJ explained the town received bids from Sullivan Tire, Mohawk Lifts, and
Challenger Lifts. DPW is recommending purchasing the lift from Sullivan Tire which
comes with 4 safety jack stands. Corey went and looked at each of the lifts and found
Sullivan had a great service program and had all the accessories they could need. It
also comes with adapters, so they are able to lift the vehicles in a variety of ways
depending on what service they need to complete.
Selectman Christensen asked what the lead time is for delivery. VJ answered it will
be 6 weeks installed. They will hold a class for the employees at DPW on how to
properly use it.
Selectmen Miller asked if they have any vehicles that over the weight capacity for
this lift system. VJ answered that the only truck that may be close to the limit is the
ladder truck.
Selectman Goulet asked if they have ever done business with Sullivan Tire. VJ
answered they currently have an account with them and use them for tires but have
not used this particular division. Selectmen Goulet asked if we will be able to use the
lift on the new electric trash truck. VJ answered he believes they will, but they do not
have the final specs on the trash truck to know its weight.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to purchase the recommended lift from Vehicle
Services Group, LLC and accessories from Lift Works, a division of Sullivan Tire in
the amount of $57,550.68. Selectman Frederickson seconded the motion. Motion
passed 4-0.
Old Business

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
April 2, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Goulet, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman
Matt Miller, Selectman Rick Frederickson
Excused: Selectman Sandy Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
I.
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00pm.
II. Citizens Comment
Sharon Morris, 416 East Meadow Lane, is presenting the opportunity to resurrect the
community Gardens that were once behind the library/church. The gardens were
started in 2014 as a Boy Scout Eagle project located behind the Pembroke Library in
the field. At the time, they had received permission from the Pembroke Selectboard,
Pembroke Library Trustees, and the Pembroke Congressional Church as the
landowner. The goal was to provide a place in the community as an easily accessible
place to grow vegetables, create educational opportunities, and to enhance community
connections. Many residents live in apartments or in areas where there is less than
desirable soil and a community garden provides community members an opportunity
to interact and establish connections to the land. Once the Boy Scouts lost interest,
the garden slowly disappeared. The shed is still there and so are the supplies. The
Trustees of the Church have also shown interest in reviving the community garden. A
Garden Club has been established for residents of Allenstown, Pembroke, and
Suncook that is supportive of this endeavor. Sharon has also contacted the UNH
Horticultural program and they sent over some paperwork on community gardens;
from the ground up.
Selectman Miller asked what would be involved in administering the garden to
continue operations. Sharon answered that a committee needs to be formed. They
have a lot of the original documents that would help the committee. The Committee
would need establish parameters for the garden beds themselves for things such as
what beds are made out of, what can go into them, how much they cost to "rent", does
a contract go year to year, etc.
Selectman Christiansen stated there can be difficulty in getting community volunteers
for committees. Sharon stated one of the reasons the Garden Club was established

III.
was the hopes of getting this community garden off the ground. They have many
members who would likely serve.
Selectman Frederickson asked what she would like the Selectboard to specifically do
tonight. Sharon answered she is looking for guidance. The goal would be for the
garden to be attached in some way to the Town so that if one person stops being able
to manage it, someone else can pick it up.
Selectman Yeaton shared that this may work as a sub-committee attached to an
existing committee such as Recreation or Conservation rather than being its own
Committee. It may also belong with the Women's Club since they handle the flowers
in Town.
David explained the Committee or Club would need something in writing from the
Church for the land that states exactly where the garden would be, and it would need
to be roped off. They would need to figure out water as well. Sharon explained there
is a pump house for water.
Erin Insley, Conservation Commission Chair, stated she would need to look into how
to form a sub-committee. David stated they could have a stand-alone advisory
committee if there is enough interest. Selectman Christiansen stated that with rowing
season starting really soon, it would be faster for them to get moving as a standalone
committee. Sharon will contact the Church as first steps and report back to the
Selectboard
Matt Miller, 229 Brickett Hill Road, submitted information regarding a Federal
Executive Order reducing the Institute and Museum and Library Services and the
impacts the cut in funding will have on the Pembroke Library Services.
Scheduled Meetings:
Katie Booker - Park Bench
Katie Booker, Meet Me in Suncook Committee, shared they are working with the
Library to put a park bench in the George M. Lamiette Square on the corner of Main
and Broadway. The park bench will be funded through a program at the Library
through the company Trex. They take plastic items and turn them into benches. A list
of donatable items is listed at the Library. The Board agrees that will be a great
location for a bench.
Scott Grandmaison - Traffic Issues
Scott Grandmaison, 4 Central Street, shared concerns for cars going the wrong down
Central Street. Central Street is one-way. Scott explained how often, it is vehicles
coming out of the parking lot the wrong way. Scott has requested targeted action in
the past but it hasn't helped curb the situation. Most of the offenders are people who
live and work in the area who do not want to go around. He has been nearly hit

several times throughout the years. Adjusting the angle of the stop sign on Central
Street and changing the parking to head in only parking are suggestions to help curb
the behavior. In the past, his family's vehicle has been damaged by a car driving the
wrong way. There also seems to be a big issue with the pizza delivery drivers. The
Board will discuss this issue with the Police Department. Chief Gaskell stated they
have had direct patrol happening down there and they have had discussions with
people going the wrong way. They can look at signage in the area.
Chief Gaskell - Public Hearing Chapter 191 Vehicles and Traffic
Chief Gaskell presented the updated Chapter 191 Vehicles and Traffic Town
Ordinance.
Corrections:
• Removed the road listing for stop signs and changed it to if there is a stop sign
or yield sign, it is presumed it was approved by the Town of Pembroke or the
State of New Hampshire.
• Speed Zones - If there is no speed sign posted on a town road, the speed limit
is 25 and if it is a state road, it is 30.
• Cleaned up parking violations classes. The fines remained the same, but the
wording is easier to understand. Under the violations, back in parking and
compact car only parking were added to Class II, one-way streets that were
missing from the list were added, and the names of businesses that are no
longer there were removed from the time limit parking listings.
Selectman Frederickson asked if the Town restricts vehicle registration for unpaid
tickets like the City of Concord. Chief Gaskell answered Pembroke does not and at
this point, they do not need to. However, parking passes will not be issued for
municipal lots.
Selectman Christiansen asked if they have discussed crosswalks by the Highschool.
Chief Gaskell stated the Roads Committee has been discussing crosswalks by
Littlefield Condominiums but putting those in would trigger the requirement to add
sidewalks and other crosswalks. David stated that Carolyn Cronin is talking to the
State about putting in a crosswalk by Whittemore and what the costs would be.
Selectman Yeaton opened the public hearing at 7:05 PM.
Kevin who owns Mei Chinese Food, stated that in front of their business, there was
two 15-minute parking spaces, and they have been removed. Some of the people who
now use those spots will stay all day which leads to difficulties for people who are
picking up food. Customers sometimes have to park very far away. This is fine in the
warmer months but not in the winter. Chief Gaskell stated it is hard to enforce 15-
minute parking spaces especially since they are not able to mark tires, which is why
the spots were changed. Kevin is willing to put a camera up and provide the footage
to the police.

Selectman Christiansen seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.
Chief Gaskel! - Chapter 191 Vehicles and Traffic
Chief Gaskell explained that time limit parking has been an issue for Police
Departments since it was deemed a 4' amendment violation to mark tires. The 9th
Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled that the practice is not a 4" amendment violation.
New Hampshire operates out of the 1" Circuit Court of Appeals, and they have not
taken up the case. Which means that technically, there is no judgement on the issue.
Some other Departments in the State still mark tires, some have changed to pay to
park, some have stickers, and some have stopped enforcement all together. There are
62 - 4 hour spots, 57 - 2 hour spots, 4 - 15 minute spots, and 223 free spots.
Chief Gaskell presented updates to Chapter 191 Vehicles and Traffic in the Town
Code:
191-6 Stop Intersections - Removed the street listings and added "All intersections in
the Town of Pembroke, designated as stop intersections whereas any stop sign
erected at an intersection is presumed to have been under authority and approval of
the Town of Pembroke or State of New Hampshire"
191-7 Yield Intersections - Removed the street listings and added "All intersections
in the Town of Pembroke, designated as yield intersections whereas any yield sign
erected at an intersection is presumed to have been under authority and approval of
the Town of Pembroke or State of New Hampshire"

violations. There were no changes but there was language added to clarify what the
violation is and the fee

White Sands. Chief Gaskell stated the facilities parking sticker comes from DPW and
allows you to park at White Sands and go to the dump. The parking permit from the
Police Department allows parking in the municipal lots downtown. The Police
Department will run a check for open parking tickets before giving out a sticker.
191-17 Schedule Ill: Parking Prohibited at All Times - updated language for
accuracy.
Selectman Frederickson stated that the only way to truly enforce timed parking is
with paid parking. Chief Gaskell stated that each machine ranges from $5,000-
$20,000. They were told the Town would need at least 6. There are further
considerations above costs such as collection, maintenance, and power. Selectman
Frederickson asked if there is any data on whether the parking downtown is being
abused. Chief Gaskell stated it is recorded by complaints. Selectman Christiansen
stated the Economic Development Committee is developing a survey of current
businesses and one of the questions is regarding available parking.
Selectman Miller asked if they could charge people who did not pay the ticket for the
officer's time in court. Chief Gaskell doesn't think they can.
Selectman Yeaton asked if anything has changed during the cleanup of this policy.
Chief Gaskell answered that no ordinance rules were changed. Except for the
removal of a handicapped parking spot in front of 24 Kimball Street.
191-21 Schedule VII Speed Zones - Language was added to clarify the length of the
speed zones. If a road is not posted, the speed limit is 25 mph per town ordinance.
The Selectman would like to change the facilities permit to a parking permit for
White Sands.
Old Business
Discussion of Warrant Articles
David explained warrant article 14 for the new cardiac monitor has to pass because
there are no more funds available in the ambulance fund. The Town had appropriated
$450,000 for the vehicle and outfitting. Equipment cannot be moved from the old
ambulance to the new one. The vehicle alone came in at $388,311. After ordering

supplies and other equipment, there is $1,942.09 left in the capital reserve fund. The
ambulance cannot be licensed without a cardiac monitor.

Selectman Goulet made a motion to approve Manifest Two which contains the

Selectman Christiansen abstained.
Minutes 2/19/25 Non-Public 2/19/25
Selectman Goulet made a motion to approve the minutes of February 19, 2025 as
amended. Selectman Frederickson seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to approve the non-public minutes of February 19,
2025 as amended. Selectman Christiansen seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.
V. Town Administrator Report
Tax deeds are in the mail for non-payment of 2022 taxes and tax lien notices have
gone out for those that have not paid their 2024 taxes.

Selectman Christiansen - Planning Board continued the public hearing on the
development on Wilkins Ave. There was a lot of public comment regarding water

town and removed old contact information. The Committee created a 15-question
survey for local businesses to help them set priorities. They are also working on

2. PROJECT TITLE: PFAS Mitigation
3. PROJECT DESCRIPTION
Provide a concise description of the proposed project and the need for the proposed project, including how it will
address public health protection, what alternatives have been considered, and a demonstration of how the
eligibility requirements of RSA 485-H:3, I and Il are met.
Pembroke Water Works (PWW) provides drinking water and fire protection to the Town of Pembroke and the
Village of Suncook in Allenstown, as well as about a dozen homes in Hooksett. PWW is separate from the Town
and receives revenue from user fees/rates and hydrant rentals.
PFAS has been detected in three of PWW's five active wells: Wells #2 and #3 in the Route 3 Wellfield and the
Route 106 well. PFOS has been detected above the MCL in Well #2 several times, and once in Well #3. PWW is
currently blending the flow from Wells #2 and #3, and has reduced the pumping rate. These measures,
combined with the dry summer, allowed them to maintain finished water below the MCL in 2021. No
responsible party has been identified as the source of the contamination. A previous hydrogeological study by
EGGI determined that the contaminants are coming from the north and west of the wells, but they were not
able to identify a definitive source.
In 2021 UE performaed an alternatives analysis to mitigate the PFAS problem. Alternatives evaluated included:
A PFAS water treatment plant for Wells #2/#3,
Blending of Wells #2 & #3 with the Route 106 well (not feasible),
An interconnection with the City of Concord water system to replace Wells #2/#3, and
Establishing a new groundwater supply.
Based on analysis of these alternatives, PWW will begin discussions with the City of Concord to further evaluate
the possibility of an interconnection.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
February 19, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Sandy Goulet, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Goulet, Selectman
Karen Yeaton, Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Rick Frederickson
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00pm.
IL.
Scheduled Meetings:
Public Hearing Water Bond
Kevin Brasley, Chair Pembroke Water Commission, Matt Gagne, Superintendent
Pembroke Water Works are at the meeting to discuss interconnection with the City of
Concord at the public hearing which has been continued from February 5, 2025.
Article 3: To see if the town will vote to raise and appropriate through water fees
(bond/note will be paid for by Water users not through property taxes) the sum of
$10,440,000 (gross budget) for the purpose of all work needed for remediation of
PFAS contaminate of the Pember Water Works Route 3 wellfield that may include:
Inter-municipal connection to the City of Concord Water System, a new well source
or treatment of the Pembroke Route 3 wellfield, and to authorize the issuance of not
more than $10,440,000 of bonds in accordance with the provisions of the Municipal
Finance Act (RSA 33) and to authorize the Municipal Officials to issue and negotiate
such bonds or notes and to determine the rate of intertest thereon; and to apply for,
obtain, and accept any Federal, State, or other aid, grants or additional funding which
may be available for said project (s) to help offset the cost of the bod or note and to
comply with all laws applicable to said project (s) (3/5 ballot vote required)
Selectman Yeaton opened public hearing at 6:30pm.
Matt Gagne stated the Town has been approved for a $1,782,000 grant from DES to
be used towards the project and $1,350,000 in forgiveness. This will leave around
$7,000,000 that will need to be paid back through user fees. This assumes they will
use the entire loan but since costs are not final, this number could come down. They
still need to formally apply for the grant and forgiveness and this warrant article
allows them to do that. If PEAS levels are not brought down, the Town runs the risk
of having their wells shut down. Interconnection is the first option and if that does
not go through, they will look at a new wellfield.

David Jodoin asked if the State will phase the funding. Matt stated they have the
ability to take as they need. If they do not get this approval, they will not be able to
apply for the grants and forgiveness right away which means the Town will receive
less. Right now, Pembroke is ahead of a lot of other towns because Water Works has
been proactive in testing.
Kevin Stribling, 129 Tina Drive, asked if the PFAS problem has been an issue for a
while or is this related to Saint Gobain. Matt stated these chemicals have been used
since the 1940's and were unregulated until 2020. All the years they were in use, they
were dumped in various locations so it's impossible to say how long it has been an
issue but they have been aware of it since 2016. Kevin asked if there have been any
actions taken against Saint Gobain. Matt answered they have been an identified issue
down in Merrimack. The Pembroke Water Works has done some testing to see what
direction the PFAS is coming from but they have no way to go outside of the Town of
Pembroke property. The State has stated concerns it is coming from the airport and/or
the fire testing facility on Route 106 but they are unable to go into the City of
Concord to test. Kevin asked if the interconnection with Concord will make it so
there is more clean water. Matt stated if they cannot produce water from the infected
wells because of the PFAS levels, the interconnection will offset that location. They
will purchase the water they are losing from Concord but if that location is no longer
producing PFAS, then at least the Town will gain capacity from the interconnection.
If they were to treat the well, they could spend millions more and not gain any
capacity. Right now, interconnection is the preferred option. Kevin asked where
Concord gets their water. Matt answered primarily Penacook Lake and when the
water level lowers, they offset with the Contoocook River. They do not have PFAS in
their water but if they did, they have a treatment facility so they have zero
concentration in their water.
Matthew Hanna, 264 Pembroke Street, asked how many wells the Town has. Matt
answered there are 5 wells but only one well has PFAS contamination. In that
location, there are two wells but if they were to shut down the contaminated well, the
PFAS will migrate to the other one. Those two wells cover 40% of the Town's
production. Mr. Hanna asked if Concord has said yes to this proposal. Kevin Brasley
stated they have not yet. The city is in discussions with the Town of Bow for
interconnection and they want to wrap that up first. Mr. Hanna asked if there is a plan
B if Concord says no. Matt answered the options are interconnection with Concord,
treat the wells, or put in new wells at another location. Mr. Hanna asked if it would
make sense for homeowners to put in a filtration system. Matt stated Water Works
could come out or homeowners could come into the office to discuss it. The focus of
the Water Works is on the whole system and not individual homes so they would
need to discuss it on a case-by-case basis. Kevin explained they have not figured out
disposal of PFAS yet so even if a home owner was filtering it out, they are unsure
how to dispose of it.

Selectman Miller stated that when they introduce the item at Town Meeting, they
need to give a very concise update on this issue and the plan. This will be the first
time many are hearing about the issue.
Selectman Yeaton closed the public hearing at 6:16pm.
Tammy Webb - Vachon Clukay & Company 2023 Audit
Tammy Webb presented the 2023 Audit. Tammy explained the Town received an
unmodified opinion which is a clean opinion. The audit is largely focused on risk
assessment. Annually, they update the understanding of internal controls over major
financial cycles such as payroll and accounts payable. Every three years they are
required to test the controls. They will take a sample size and run it through the entire
process to ensure that all policies and procedures are being followed. This year, they
selected a sample of payroll transactions. They found no deviations. They reviewed
all adjusting journal entries, and they found nothing unusual that would require
further inquiries. They reviewed all credit card entries as this is a high fraud risk area.
There were no transactions that needed to be questioned further. They do unexpected
procedures each year. This year, they randomly selected another month of bank
statements to ensure they are being reconciled correctly and timely. They found no
issues. They reviewed the budgetary report. General fund revenues and expenditures
as compared to the budget. The total revenues and financial sources were higher than
the budgeted amount by $188,000 or 2.4%. Which is right on par with where the
Town should be. Total expenditures and other financial uses were less than the
budgeted amount by $671,000 or 7.5%. Which means the Town is able to manage the
Town's finances within the constraints of the budget. The Town continues to have a
healthy financial position. The Town's fund balance policy stated the fund balance
can be 8-17% of general fund operating revenues or no less than two months of
operating expenditures including county and school. On the appropriations side, the
maximum is $4.2m. The total unassigned fund balance as of 12/31/23 was $5.5m so it
is higher than the anticipated amount. In the fall, $500,000 was used to offset the tax
rate which leaves the balance still above the policy. As of 12/31/23, there was still
$651,000 in ARPA funds. Those funds needed to be obligated by 12/31/24 and fully
expended by 12/31/26. There were 2 new GASB pronouncements effective for this
year. One was not relevant to the town and the other was subscription-based
information-based technology arrangements that exceed 12 months. There was only
one agreement that fit the criteria, but it was not material. There were no difficulties
dealing with management to report. In the governance communications is a listing of
any material adjustments that need to be made. A $250,000 tax liability that was
recorded after the 12/31/22 tax year end due to a tax settlement. There were several
adjustments in the sewer funds but those are due to the Sewer Department keeping
their records on a cash basis and they have to bring them to an accrual basis for the
audit. Those are expected every year. No separate management letter was issued this
year.
Selectman Christiansen asked if the town is in the top percentile of her clients.
Tammy answered that the Town is one of the top clients.

Selectboard Members - Yeaton, Goulet, Frederickson, Miller, Christiansen & Town Administrator
Jodoin:
Several years ago, the previous administration was approached by a citizen about marking tires
and how it was illegal. At that time, the enforcement was reduced to actual observed violations
by police or, in which someone (if not a police officer) complained about overtime parking.
Pembroke Police would issue a parking summons based on either the observed violation or the
known credibility of the complaining party, in which case, the complaining party would serve as a
witness. As a result, not too many people continued to complain about the timed parking. When
they do we address it. This current administration has supported this practice however, has also
looked into other ways to enforce the issues at hand.
Current Legal Concerns/Laws
The legality of marking tires with "chalk" is a controversial topic with differing opinions from
different courts.
I have outlined the position of other courts, specifically the 6h and the 9' Circuit Court of Appeals,
which have rendered two separate decisions on the matter:
• Taylor v. City of Saginaw
In 2019, the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that marking tires with chalk violates the
Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches. The court found that
the purpose of marking tires was to raise revenue, not to protect the public from a safety
risk.
• Verdun v. City of San Diego
In contrast, the 9th Circuit Court ruled that tire chalking falls within the administrative
search exception and does not require a warrant. The court found that the primary
purpose of chalking tires is to assist with traffic management and the use of city parking
spots.
• Qualified immunity
In the Taylor v. City of Saginaw case, the court of appeals also ruled that the officer was
entitled to qualified immunity. This means that the officer was shielded from suit
because the law was not clearly established as a violation of the Fourth Amendment.
One of the main arguments against tire chalking is that it violates the Fourth Amendment to the
United States Constitution, which protects citizens from unreasonable searches and seizures.
Some judges have ruled that marking a vehicle's tires without the owner's consent constitutes a
search and requires a warrant.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
February 5, 2025 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Sandy Goulet, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Goulet, Selectman
Karen Yeaton, Selectman Matt Miller
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Excused: Selectman Rick Frederickson
I.
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:03pm.
11.
Scheduled Meetings:
Public Hearing Water Bond
Kevin Brasley, Chair Pembroke Water Commission, Matt Gagne, Superintendent
Pembroke Water Works are at the meeting to discuss interconnection with the City of
Concord. Kevin explained that before the last Commissioner's meeting in January,
the State of New Hampshire told them they would need to get all approvals for the
bond/notes at the 2025 Town Meeting before they can apply. The warrant article
reads bonds or notes but it is not actually a bond, it is a low-cost loan. If they do not
get approvals now, the Town will be sent to the back of the queue and potentially lose
out on grants and partial loan forgiveness. In 2016, when they began testing, the
PFAS in the well was below the allowable levels. The State has since changed the
requirements to be stricter, so Water Works blends the wells in order to dilute the
PFAS and stay below the allowable levels. The City of Concord is in discussions with
the Town of Bow for interconnection and that is taking priority over The Town of
Pembroke. They want to settle the issue with Bow first. In the meantime, there are
concerns that the levels will get too high, and the wells will be shut down.
Selectman Goulet asked if they have a ballpark figure for what the interconnection
will cost. Matt Gagne explained it is still in the design phase and they are about a
third of the way done. The cost was originally $6,000,000 in 2021 but costs have
gone up. Underwood Engineers is doing the design work for the interconnection and
treatment. Another Company is looking into the possibility of digging a new well.
Selectman Yeaton stated that it appears there is $1.8m in loan forgiveness and asked
if that is time sensitive or attached to a specific action they need to take. Matt
explained the $500,000 grant money is guaranteed, and they can use it as soon as it is
officially awarded. The partial loan forgiveness is $1,300,000 and has some items tied
to it and requirements that need to be met. Kevin explained the total bond is for

$10,440,000 but if the grant and loan forgiveness are applied, the total is around
$7,500,000 to be paid by rate payers not taxpayers. Matt explained the
interconnection will also allow them to increase capacity.
Selectman Miller asked if there are constraints on Concord's supply. Matt explained
they can provide a slow feed of 800 gallons per minute, which is larger than our peak
demand in the summer. The larger of the two wells on that side of town is a 600
gallon per minute well. They are looking at putting another well source in the Bear
Brook location that can only produce 300 gallons per minute. So Concord's slow feed
exceeds Pembroke's current demand.
Selectman Miller asked how much water needs to be replaced to achieve PFAS
compliance by 2029. Matt stated that the limit is 15 parts per trillion. Right now, with
the blended wells, they are producing 4 parts per trillion. The new EPA limits are 4
parts per trillion by 2029.
Selectman Miller asked if they have ruled out treatment instead of interconnection
since the methods in place to deal with the waste of treatment are not mature. Matt
stated treatment will cost $19,000,000 and they will have the same capacity. It is
twice the cost of interconnection, but they cannot completely rule it out at this time.
Selectman Miller asked if residential well owners can test their own water. Matt
explained it is around $300 to test and there are only a few companies that do it but
anyone can test their wells.
Selectman Christiansen asked what the impact of this will be on water rates. Kevin
stated there will be increases and they do not know what it will be at this point. They
plan to make the increases gradually in preparation.
Selectman Christiansen asked where the interconnection will be and will the bond
cover road improvements. Matt explained they have looked at a location on Rt 106
but they will likely go with the Route 3 option. Pembroke Water Works already owns
the land on the right before the Nissan Dealership. The original town well is on that
property. That will have a minimal amount of road interruptions but all that will be
accounted for in the design.
Selectman Christiansen asked if this will help with interconnection for sewer. Matt
explained the water works interconnections will help sewer because the City will
already have the approval to go outside city limits.
Selectman Christiansen asked what concord's water source is. Matt stated they get it
from Penacook Lake.
Selectman Yeaton opened the public hearing at 6:33pm.

Ill.
IV.
Selectman Yeaton asked if they foresee any issues in the future working with
Concord. Matt stated they already have a working relationship with all the
surrounding communities and does not see it being an issue going forward.
Nancy Stewart, Pembroke Street, asked if they thought about combining water and
sewer departments to reduce operational redundancy. David stated the Town has
discussed previously combining Water, Sewer, and Public Works. They formed a
subcommittee many years ago probably around 2002, but nothing came of it.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to continue the public hearing for the water bond
until February 19, 2025. Selectman Miller seconded the motion. Motion passed 4-0.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 27, 2024 at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Rick Frederickson, Selectman Sandy Goulet, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,
Selectman Goulet, Selectman Karen Yeaton
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Excused: Selectman Matt Miller
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:03pm.
IL.
Review 2025 Proposed Budget and Budget Committee's request to cut $150,000:
The current proposed tax rate increase over last year is $2.44. The Budget Committee
would like to see the increase reduced to $2.00 which equates to a total reduction of
$500,000 by both the Town and the School District. The Committee has asked the
Town to reduce their budget by $150,000 and the School District to reduce theirs by
$350,000. David stated the Selectboard originally presented the Budget Committee
with a total operational budget of $10,463,817 or a 4.20% increase. After making
additional cuts, the budget was re-submitted to the Committee at $10,305,855 or a
2.90% increase.
David started looking at potential costs to cover the $150,000 and came up with
$25,000 out of the Ambulance Replacement Capital Reserve Fund, $10,000 out of the
Recreation Capital Reserve Fund, $50,000 out of the Town Municipal Facilities
Capital Reserve Fund, and $20,000 out of the Fire Department Major Equipment
cupital Reserve Fund. The operational budget is very lean and can"t sustain more
Selectman Goulet stated she is not in favor of continuing to reduce the Town Budget
at all.
Selectman Christiansen stated he would be comfortable letting the Budget Committee
fulfill their role and vote accordingly but the Town has done their due diligence
regarding the budget, and they do not need to cut further.
Selectman Frederickson stated the Town is below the rate of inflation and the major
money for capital reserves is according to a clear schedule and those purchases will
still be there and need to be made.

Ill.
Selectman Yeaton stated the Budget Committee appeared to be impressed by the
operational budget and it appeared that they understood the cuts would be made to
capital reserves. The capital reserves are not a collection of random rainy-day funds.
They are strategic accounts to support services the voters have voted for. They keep
the tax rate from seeing major fluctuations. If the taxpayers would like to see further
cuts to the budget, they may need to decide what services the Town continues to
offer.
Selectman Yeaton asked what the negative impact of removing the funds from the
capital reserves are. David stated that they are looking at a less expensive version of
the pavilion and Chris Gamache stated he is comfortable with the Ambulance
Replacement Fund reduction. Beyond that, these items will become major budgetary
concerns down the road. The costs will continue to rise and the Town will end up
with shortfalls in funding.
Selectmen Goulet made a motion to reduce the budget by $150,000. Selectmen
Frederickson seconded the motion. Motion failed 0-4.
Adjourn
Selectman Goulet made a motion to adjourn at 6:40 PM. Selectman Christiansen
seconded the motion, and it was approved unanimously.
Karen Yeaton, Chairman

Present: Selectman Rick Frederickson, Selectman Sandy Goulet, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,

Call to Order:

Il. Citizens Comment:
Marie Straiton, 708 Cross Country Road, has a citizen petitioned warrant article she is
requesting the Board put it on their warrant and if not, she will get the required
signatures. The warrant article is titled Property taxes for private education call for
responsible use. Whereas taxpayers have a right to know how money is spent and
deserve clear and verifiable evidence that it is being spent wisely and delivering
results Whereas taxpayers are being diverted from public schools to private and
religious education through education freedom accounts also called vouchers. That
shift does not reduce public school expenses leaving local taxpayers to cover the
difference through higher property taxes and whereas unlike public schools, private
schools' education funded by taxpayers through vouchers lack key accountability
measurers such as reporting how funds are used, tracking student performance,
ensuring services for students with disabilities and conducting background checks for
staff. Therefore, we the voters of Pembroke NH call on our state elected officials to
uphold their duty to fiscal responsibility by rejecting any expansion of taxpayer
funding for private education until we have full accountability transparency and a
sustamable funding plan that ensures no further strain on public schools or local
property taxpayers. We further direct the Pembroke selectboard to deliver this warrant
article and results in writing to the NH governor and member of the state legislature
within 30-days of this vote.
Selectman Yeaton stated she does not support or endorse politically oriented warrants
and that the Town should not be taking a position but rather individuals should
contact elected officials to state their opinions.
Selectman Miller stated there is likely a bill going through the House with public
comment time and that would be the main way to get comments recognized
Selectman Frederickson stated this warrant article would be unclear in what it is

Selectman Frederickson asked if there is enough parking. Max stated they are

Selectman Miller asked if good reviews meant they would not over serve. Chief

Response to questions re: Police Request for Speed Signs
Below are my responses to your questions regarding the Police Department's request to
purchase movable digital radar/speed signs using our Small Equipment Capital
Improvement fund. I hope the information provided will be helpful to you as you
consider our request.
1. Measurable Outcomes
What specific results do we expect these signs to produce for Pembroke residents
(reduction in average speeds, reduction in speeding complaints, improved safety
near schools or nelghborhoods)?
The primary goal of the portable radar signs is to improve voluntary compliance with
posted speed limits in areas where speeding complaints are consistently received.
Research by the Federal Highway Administration has found average speed reductions of
approximately 2-3 mph in many deployments, with substantially larger reductions in the
highest-speed drivers. Though this reduction amount seems minor, a 2-3 mph reduction
in speed can make a meaningful difference in safety. Research done by the International
Transport Forum found that every 1% increase in average speed results in a 2% increase
in all injury crashes, a 3% rise in fatal and severe crashes, and 4% more fatal crashes. A 2-
3 mph reduction is roughly equivalent to a 5% speed reduction, which could translate to a
measurable drop in injury and fatal crashes over time. Other site-specific studies, such as
school zones, have reported reductions approaching 9 mph, depending on roadway
characteristics and deployment location. Areas that seem to have received the greatest
Impact are residential neighborhoods, school zones, parks, and other high pedestrian
traffic areas.
1

:
For Pembroke residents, the expected outcomes include:
• Reduced average vehicle speeds in targeted areas
• Increased driver awareness of posted speed limits
• Improved safety for pedestrians, cyclists, and children
• Fewer citizen complaints regarding speeding
• The ability to collect additional traffic data to guide future enforcement and
roadway safety initiatives
While no single tool eliminates speeding entirely, radar feedback signs have proven to be
an effective, non-confrontational method of changing driving behavior - which is our
ultimate goal.
2. Data & Accountability
How will the department measure and report the effectiveness of the signs (before.
and-after speed data, number of locations addressed, change in complaint volume)?
The signs will allow the department to collect objective traffic data before, during, and
after deployment. The department will track:
• Average vehicle speeds.
• 85"h percentile speeds.
• Traffic volume by date and time.
• Number of locations monitored.
• Citizen complaints before and after deployment.
• Directed enforcement conducted following sign deployment when warranted.
Summaries of this data can be periodically provided to the Board showing where the
signs were deployed, the data collected, and measurable changes in driver behavior.
3. Alternative Uses of the Same Money
Is there any other way we could spend this same $8,400 that would produce better
or more immedlate results for taxpayers, for example, targeted overtime for traffic
enforcement in the highest-complaint areas, additional officer training, or other
traffic-calming tools?
While additional overtime enforcement can temporarily reduce speeding, It provides only
a short-term benefit that ends when the officer leaves the area.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
August 19, 2026 6:00 PM
Present: Chair Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Peter Gagyi, Selectman
Matt Miller
Excused; Selectwoman Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
I.
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM.
II.
Citizens Comment
David Mullen of 418 North Pembroke Road addressed the Board regarding his
property assessment record. Mr. Mullen stated that his tax card contained incorrect
information, including a hot tub assessment he said had been listed since 1997 even
though he has never had a hot tub, and he also referenced a prior siding description
error.
Board members thanked Mr. Mullen for bringing the matter forward and stated staff
would review the tax card history, the current record, and whether the issue could be
corrected before the next tax billing cycle.
The Board discussed the general importance of homeowners reviewing their tax cards
after revaluations and agreed the matter warranted follow-up.
A suggestion was made that a written letter can help create a paper trail when
residents raise assessment concerns.
Scheduled Meetings
Public Hearing to withdraw funds from the Police Small Equipment Capital Reserve
Fund and the Energy Savings Capital Reserve Fund.
The Board opened the public hearing at 6:10 PM on two proposed capital reserve
withdrawals previously discussed on August 5, 2026. Chief Shea reviewed the police
request to purchase movable digital radar speed signs at an estimated cost of $8,400,
with discussion that the authorization should not exceed $8,500 to cover any
incidental costs.
The Board also reviewed the Pembroke Public Library lighting project with KT&T
Electric, noting a total project cost of approximately $21,000, an anticipated rebate of

about $16,000, and a local share of approximately $4,948 to be withdrawn from the
Energy Savings Capital Reserve Fund.
David Jodoin advised the Board that it was suggested that we also look at the other
buildings in Town.
Motion by Selectman Christiansen to approve the withdrawals of a sum not to exceed
$8,500 from the Police Small Equipment Fund, and to further withdraw the sum not
to exceed $5,000 from the Energy Savings Capital Reserve Funds, seconded by
Selectman Miller, Motion passed 4-0.
Police Highway Safety Grant
Chief Shea presented the Highway Safety Grant associated with the speed sign
purchase and related enforcement activity.
The Board was advised that the State would reimburse 75 percent of eligible costs
and that the grant also provides funding for overtime enforcement details related to
speed enforcement, pedestrian and bicycle enforcement, and distracted driving
enforcement.
It was clarified that the enforcement details are not limited to the speed sign locations
and may be deployed elsewhere in town as needed. The Board also reviewed letters
authorizing participation by the Chief and Lieutenant in the reimbursable enforcement
details.
Motion by Selectman Christiansen authorize the Chair to sign the letters with the
New Hampshire Department of Highway Safety permitting participation in the grant-
funded detail work, seconded by Selectman Miller. Motion passed 4-0.
Motion By Selectman Christiansen to accept the terms of the Highway Safety Grant
in the amount of $4,800 and the amended grant terms in the amount of $6,300.60, for
an adjusted total grant limitation of $11,100.60, and to authorize the Board Chair and
Chief Shea to sign the necessary documents, seconded by Selectman Gagyi. Motion
passed 4-0.
Chief Shea/DPW Director Ranfos - Proposed changes to Town Code Chapter 191
section 11
Chief Shea and DPW Director Ranfos presented proposed revisions to Town Code
Chapter 191, Section 11, to expand the existing snow-removal language so it also
covers routine parking lot maintenance operations.
DPW Director Ranfos explained that the current ordinance only addresses snow
removal, while the Highway Department also needs authority to close lots for
sweeping, striping, brush work, and similar work several times each year.
Chief Shea noted that clearer code language and signage would reduce confusion,
improve notice to residents, and better support towing authority when a vehicle must
be removed during maintenance operations.

Two approaches were presented: amending the existing section or using the reserved
Section 12 for a separate maintenance provision. Board members indicated a
preference for revising the existing section.
Public Works estimated parking lot closures for maintenance could occur roughly
four additional times per year, generally posted for 7:00 AM to 3:00 PM, though
many jobs are completed earlier.
The Board discussed resident complaints about temporary sign overlays and the
desire for more professional permanent signage.
Board members favored keeping the ordinance change within the current chapter
structure rather than creating a new section.
Motion by Selectman Christiansen to move Town Code Chapter 191 to public hearing
on September 2, 2026, seconded by Selectman Gagyi. Motion passed 4-0.
Acceptance of Donation from Pembroke Women's Club for Pembroke EMS in
accordance with RSA 31:95-b III (b)
David explained the donation from the Women's Club.
Motion by Selectman Christiansen to accept the $100 donation in accordance with
RSA 31:95-b III (b) from the Pembroke Women's Club for Pembroke EMS,
seconded by Selectman Gagyi. Motion passed 4-0.
Chief Shea - Granite United Way Agreement
Chief Shea presented a Granite United Way reimbursement agreement to support the
Police Department's ACERT team work.
She explained that the town had already chosen to participate in the program because
of its value to Pembroke residents, even before funding availability was clear.
In developing the reimbursement amount, the grant administrator reviewed
experience from the Franklin Police Department, Hooksett Police Department, and
Concord Police Department and estimated a starting level of activity of about one
deployment per month.
Chief Shea said the agreement provides $3,600 in recurring grant funding, beginning
July 1, to reimburse officer wages for deployments and related follow-up work.
She also described the limited reporting requirements and the additional family
support resources available through the program.
The Board discussed correcting the agreement language before signature and
expressed support for the program.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
August 5, 2026 6:00 PM
Present: Chair Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Peter Gagyi, Selectman
Matt Miller, Selectwoman Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM.
II.
Citizens Comment
None
III.
Scheduled Meetings
Public Hearing - Rescinding Prior Class VI/Private Road Building Permit Policy and
Adopting New Private Road Policy.
The Board opened the public hearing at 6:05 PM to consider rescinding the Town's
existing building permit policy for Class VI and private roads and replacing it with a
policy limited to private roads.
The Board reviewed the recent change in RSA 674:41 and discussed counsel's advice
that Select Boards no longer have the same discretion to restrict building permits on
Class VI roads.
It was clarified that the statutory change does not obligate the Town to improve,
maintain, or provide public services on a Class VI road, and that public funds cannot
be expended on a Class VI road unless its status is formally changed.
The Board also discussed the waiver to be signed by applicants and recorded at the
Merrimack County Registry of Deeds, acknowledging the absence of Town
maintenance and related liability.
Selectman Miller wanted to confirm with the Board that if someone built on a Class
VI road that the Town was not obligated to maintain that road and had no liability
associated with it.
David Jodoin stated that was correct and that if someone were to sub-divide their
property on a Class VI roadway then they would need to go to Planning and that
would require a layout provision. Everything would require a waiver which is the
next part of this meeting.

The public hearing closed at 6:06 PM.
Motion By Selectwoman Goulet to rescind the current town policy for building on a
Class VI and private roadways and replace it with building permits on private
roadways per the change in State law, seconded by Selectman Christiansen. Motion
passed 5-0.
Election Inspectors and Checklist Staffing
Iris Altilio of 744 Robinson Road, a Supervisor of Checklist, briefed the Board on
election inspector appointments.
Iris explained that the Democratic Party had appointed five inspectors for the
upcoming election cycle, while the Republican Party had appointed one. Because
additional Republican affiliated workers are needed for ballot clerk and related
election duties, she provided the Town with four Republican volunteers for
consideration and advised that undeclared voters may be used if necessary after
further outreach.
Ms. Altilio stated that party-appointed inspectors serve-two year terms or until
replaced. She also advised that additional staffing will need to needed for the election.
The Board raised no objection to Ms. Altilio proceeding with outreach to the
proposed volunteers.
Timber Harvest Roadwork - Flagg/Robinson Road
Lynn Sweet of Sweets Logging and Land Clearing, 13 Scrivener Road, Stratford,
New Hampshire, appeared on behalf of Nicole Albee and James Bell Tax Map 262-
41 regarding timber harvest access associated with property off Fourth Range Road.
Ms. Sweet stated that the work in the Class VI roadway had been paused after Town
concern was raised, and that a temporary driveway permit had since been obtained.
She described limited brush cutting on the owner side of the roadway, smoothing of
wet spots, possible gravel placement where needed, temporary removal and
replacement of a section of stone wall, and a commitment to keep the Class VI road
open during operations.
Board members discussed documenting existing roadway conditions, protecting
access for others, and the need for a more consistent Town policy for timber related
work on Class VI roads. VJ Ranfos and staff reported that a site visit showed little
change in roadway condition and a well-prepared landing area.
Ms. Sweet estimated approximately 20 loads of pine, about one load of hardwood,
and additional biomass/chip loads for roughly 40 to 50 heavy loads over about one
month.
The Board discussed, but did not impose, a restoration bond for this project; members
indicated a broader policy should be developed for future requests.

Motion by Selectwoman Goulet to approve minor trimming of trees in the right of
way and to bring in the necessary fill to access the site, seconded by Selectman
Miller. Motion passed 5-0.
Class VI Roadwork and Building Permit - David Arsenault
David Arsenault of 214 King Boscawen appeared regarding access and improvements
on Sixth Range Road and a building permit request for a proposed single-family
residence on land that he owns.
He provide photographs showing exposed boulders in the roadway and requested
permission to perform minor work, primarily by jackhammering rock rather than
removing it entirely, to make access passable.
The Board, VJ Ranfos, and Fire Chief Erik Paulsen discussed coordination with
Public Works, the need to keep the roadway open for emergency access, and the
possibility of minor fill after the rock work is completed.
The Board then reviewed the building permit request under RSA 674:41 and
reiterated that, for a Class VI road, the applicant must execute and record a waiver at
the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds acknowledgement that the Town will not
maintain the road or accept liability for lack of services.
The Board also noted that existing seasonal range-road weight restrictions remain in
effect and will need clarification from legal on how that will now be handled with the
new law,
Mr. Arsenault stated that this is for a single family home and not a sub-division.
The Board agreed that proof of recording of the waiver must be provided to the Town
before the building permit is issued and the Town will also verify that proof of
insurance is required before a permit can be pulled.
Motion by Selectwoman Goulet to approve minor work in the roadway to remove
boulders to access the site which will be reviewed by Public Works, seconded by
Selectman Christiansen. Motion passed 5-0.
The Next discussion concerned the application for a building permit
The Board discussed the building permit phase and reminded Mr. Arsenault that the
permit would need to be recorded at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds at his
expense before the permit could be issued. In addition the Board would need to verify
with legal if a letter of guarantee must be provided from an insurance carrier that the
home will be insurable.
Motion by Selectwoman Goulet to issue the building permit to Mr. Arsenault for a
single family residence located at 401 Sixth Range Road. In order to get the permit
the applicant must record the waiver at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds at
their cost and provide proof to the Building Inspector before the actual permit issued.

Insurance Letter from Committee

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
March 18, 2026 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,
Selectman Peter Gagyi, Selectman Sandy Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
I.
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00pm.
II.
Citizens Comment
None
III.
Scheduled Meetings:
Jenn Miskovic and Paulette Malo - Health Insurance Presentation
Jenn started by explaining the process and how they identified three plans with
Healthtrust to present to the Board. The Committee is suggesting that the Town retain
the current AB20 plan for those who want a non-deductible plan and are willing to
pay the extra costs. The next plan was the AB15 plan that would have a deductible for
the users, and lastly was a high deductible HSA plan.
The Committee discussed what other municipalities are paying including the school
and the need for plans that will retain employees as well as what each plan would
cover.
Also as part of the discussion the Committee suggested upgrading the Towns Dental
coverage which would costs a little over $2,882 a year extra but would provide better
coverage to the employees.
Selectmen Miller asked how the formulary plan compared on the policies for
prescriptions. Jenn explained that the AB 15 plan would have the same coverages as
the AB 20 plan and that the only change would be the High deductible Lumenos plan.
Paulette advised the Board that Healthtrust would be coming in to discuss the plans
with the employees and even have one on one sessions with them.
Selectman Christiansen asked if the $2,882 was per employee or per month. Paulette
confirmed that the amount was for six months.

Selectmen Gagyi asked how many employees were covered under the current plans.
Jenn advised 33.
Chairman Yeaton asked how this would affect the retirees. Jenn responded that the
retirees would still be on the plans because they pay 100% of the costs.
Selectmen Miller asked what the feedback was from the employees on the different
plans.
Selectmen Goulet stated that there wasn't much feedback from the employees at this
time.
Selectman Gagyi asked how many took the buyout. David responded about 6
employees.
The Board discussed if they would approve this evening or not. Selectmen Miller
stated that he felt the information presented was good and that he would like the
employees to meet with Healthtrust the sooner the better and the Board can then work
on the Towns costs sharing on the plans at a future meeting.
Motion by Selectman Goulet to accept the committee's recommendations as
presented, for both the health and dental plans, seconded by Selectmen Christiansen.
Motion passed 5-0
VJ Ranfos Post Closure Monitoring Contract
VJ was in to discuss the contract with KV Partners to continue monitoring the site.
This is a housekeeping item that we have to do every year. We are required to
monitor the transfer station.
Selectmen Gagyi asked how many monitoring wells does the Town Have, VJ
responded that there are about five monitoring wells that are checked as well as air
quality.
Selectmen Goulet made a motion to authorize the Public Works Director to sign the
contract with KV Partners for land fill post closure monitoring, seconded by
Selectmen Christiansen. Motion passed 5-0.
Generator Contracts
VJ explained that these are the Towns annual monitoring contracts for the generators.
Motion by Selectmen Goulet to accept the contracts with Milton Cat and to authorize
the Public Works Director to sign the contract, seconded by Selectmen Christiansen.
Motion passed 5-0
Budget Review/Discussion
Chairman Yeaton expressed her thanks to all who worked on the budget and to the
voters who she felt clearly understood what was in the budget and the needs of the
Town.

IV.
Old Business:
V.
Tax Deeds
D. Jodoin explained where the Town stood with the properties that are up for deed in
2026 for non-payment of their 2023 property taxes.
New Business:
Energy Committee
Selectmen Miller agreed to discuss this since the Chair was not there yet. Selectmen
Matt explained the high usage at both the safety center and the Library. Selectmen
Miller also spoke about the net metering program. Currently there is a bill at the State
that would give municipalities two years of net metering from the moment that they
start collecting and that would be beneficial to the Town if they moved forward with
the noted projects.
The energy committee is asking the Board to support the Senate Bill and the letter
that Clean Energy has put together.
Chairman Yeaton was concerned that the language in the document stated that the
community supported this bill but that really should be that the Board supports it. The
language was changed to reflect this. Motion by Selectmen Goulet to approve the
letter as amended, seconded by Selectmen Christiansen seconded. Motion passed 5-0.
Election of Officers
Selectmen Goulet motioned to appoint Karen as the Chairman of the Board, seconded
by Selectmen Christiansen. Motion passed 4-0
Selectmen Miller made a motion to appoint Sandy as the Vice Chair, seconded by
Selectmen Christiansen. Motion passed 4-0.

MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
Between the Town of Pembroke Select Board and the Pembroke Town Library Trustees
This Memorandum of Understanding ("MOU"') is entered into as of this
day of
_2026, by and between the Town of Pembroke Select Board ("Select
Board") and the Pembroke Town Library Trustees ("Library Trustees," and together with Select
Board, the "Parties," and each, a "Party").
WHEREAS, the Select Board and the Library Trustees share an interest in ensuring the
continued success and operation of the Pembroke Town Library ("Library"), and
WHEREAS, the Parties seek to define their respective roles and responsibilities in order to
facilitate effective cooperation, communication, and support for the Library's activities,
operations, and long-term goals,
NOW, THEREFORE, the Parties mutually agree as follows:
Purpose
This MOU is a non-legally binding agreement that outlines the intentions and expectations of the
Parties. It is intended to serve as a guideline between the Select Board and Library Trustees. This
MOU establishes a formal agreement that outlines the roles, responsibilities, and collaborative
efforts of the Select Board and the Library Trustees in overseeing, supporting, and sustaining the
Library.
Responsibilities of the Select Board
The Select Board agrees to:
• Provide appropriate municipal support for the Library, including facilities maintenance,
utilities, and other resources as required.
Electrical
• HVAC
• Plumbing
• Water and sewer
• Gas line
• Alarm systems (annual service included)
• Full lighting fixtures and light bulbs
* Doors and locks
Windows replacements
• Heavy internal cleaning which includes annual carpet shampooing

• Interior and exterior painting
• Exterior building issues, including siding, overhangs, roofing, windows,
fencing, and doors
• Landscaping of grounds (excluding gardens)
Snow removal, including walkways, parking lot, and, if necessary, in the
judgment of the Public Works Director, the Library roof
• Parking area and sidewalk
• Road sign
• Ceiling tiles
* Weekly pickup of trash and recycling
• Pest control, and
• Flooring replacement (as needed)
• Appoint alternate members to the Library Trustees in compliance with applicable State
statutes, and Town policies/bylaws.
• Work collaboratively with the Library Trustees to ensure compliance with relevant laws,
regulations, and town policies governing the Library's operation.
• Permit Library participation in the Town's property and liability insurance, health
insurance, employee benefits, and training programs, at no additional cost to the Library,
continuing to insure the Library building and contents against fire and property damage.
• Continue to provide certain administrative support tasks to the Library-in particular
payroll services, processing of accounts payable and receivable, and assistance with
budgeting-consistent with those services being performed at present.
• Provide the Library Board Treasurer monthly or bi-monthly reports of budget status as
distributed to all other Town department heads (or other schedule as agreed upon).
• Send the appropriated and budgeted funds for the Library in four (4) equal installments to
the Library Trustees, to be issued quarterly (January, April, July & October).
• Confirm that the orders placed/contracts for service signed before December 31 and
invoiced in the following year, will be paid with funds appropriated in the year in which
the orders and contracts were placed per RSA 32:7 Lapse of Appropriations, Section I.
Responsibilities of the Library Trustees
The Library Trustees agree to:
• Oversee the management and operation of the Library, ensuring it provides services in
accordance with its mission and community needs.

• Outside garden beds
What is posted on the road sign
Book return bin (repairs and replacement)
Electric, gas, water, and sewer bills
Telephone
Building keys and locks
Furniture/shelving (repair and replacement)
Library computers (repair and replacement)
Daily cleaning, and

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
March 4, 2026, at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen
Absent: Selectman Sandy Goulet, Selectman Rick Frederickson
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
I.
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:02 pm.
Il. Citizen Comment:
None
Ill.
Scheduled Meetings:
Library - Discussion on fencing and the MOU with the Town
Ryan O'Hora, l'embroke Library Director, and Sue Whitbeck, Library Trustee, were present to
discuss the ponding Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), and the request for a fence.
Director O'Hora explained that he is proposing the MOU between the Selectboard and the
Library Trustees. He stated that he would like there to be consistency, especially with changes to
both the Selectboard and the Library Trustees, and for there to be established protocols in
writing. The last MOU that he was aware of was from 2012 and was in the form of an email.
Selectman Miller found the document clear and liked that there would be something in writing.
Selectman Christiansen was also comfortable with the document.
Selectman Yeaton stated that she had sent questions regarding the MOU to David and those had
been answered prior to the meeting. (ATTACHED)
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to approve the Memorandum of Understanding between
the Selectboard and the Library Trustees, Selectman Miller seconded the motion.
Motion passed 3-0.
Director O'Hora spoke about the requested fencing project. He explained that a long-time patron,
Sally Keniston, who has passed away, had left $10,000 to the Pembroke Library. The family was
provided some possible projects and decided that they would be in favor of the fencing project.
Director O'Hora explained that he reached out to American Fences and other libraries with
fencing for more information. He also spoke about children's programming that this may benefit

but noted that adult programming would also benefit. He discussed garden spaces at different
libraries in the area and the overall benefits.
Mrs. Whitbeck added that they are before the Selectboard because the Town owns the property
and they wanted to seek feedback from the Board on the project.
Director O'Hora continued that American Fences has created the design and walked the Board
through the design.
Selectman Miller asked about the height of the fence. He spoke about privacy fences, and he
feels that it creates a feeling that one needs to be invited in. He suggested reviewing possible
alternate locations or different fencing that would not create a complete block of the area.
He added the possible liability for unattended children. Mrs. Whitbeck stated that this would
primarily be for library activities but stated that the Trustees have not discussed the issue at
length and would be considering this.
Selectman Yeaton suggested a vegetative barrier, like shrubs or bushes. Selectman Miller
discussed possibilities and showed a garden area at another local library as an example. He
emphasized that landscaping could create the aesthetic of a barrier.
Selectman Christiansen expressed concern over covering the windows in the front of the library.
David explained that this would be the only possible location for the project. There was also a
discussion on parental responsibility and the liability of such an area.
Selectman Christiansen liked the idea of a picket fence with vegetation accompanying it.
Selectman Yeaton suggested the use of a landscape architect as to not upset the current beauty of
the library. Mrs. Whitbeck suggested a local landscaper for economical purposes.
Selectman Christiansen noted that since this area is essentially the town center, he was not sure
he would be comfortable with installing a privacy fence.
Selectman Miller discussed pricing and exploring the options before putting a limitation on it. He
emphasized making it a useful, but also pleasing and welcoming space.
Selectman Christiansen suggested gathering more public opinion on the project.
Selectman Miller asked Director O'Hora looking at alternate options to fencing. Director O'Hora
felt that a fence would be the priority for safety concerns. Selectman Miller suggested that all
options be explored.
Selectman Miller stated that he believed that a six-foot privacy fence wouldn't be something the
Board would be interested in. He continued that he would like Director O'Hora and the Trustees

to explore alternate options to that. He suggested planning something and then there could be
further discussion on funding.
Selectman Yeaton agreed that she would like to see different ideas and to start a bigger
discussion.
Sclectman Christiansen encouraged more public feedback and suggested a possible library
contest. He thinks people would be excited about it.
The Selectboard asked Director O'Hora and the Trustees to come back with more ideas and to
get the public involved.
IV.
Old Business:
2026 Tax Deeds
David provided an update for the Board. He stated that a decision would need to be made by
May 6, 2026.
V. New Business:
Manifest/Abatements
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to accept the manifest and abatements without Comcast.
Selectman Miller seconded the motion.
Selectman Miller asked about an invoice for compact fluorescent lights for Public Works. He
asked why these are still being purchased when LEDs are cheaper, more reliable, and easier to
dispose of. David stated he would follow-up with VJ Ranfos, Public Works Director.
Selectman Miller asked about the expenses for the 2015 F-550. He asked if this was a big annual
maintenance or a large problem. David stated that it was a starter issue, and there are also issues
with the transmission.
Motion passed 3-0.
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to accept the manifest and abatements with Comcast.
Selectman Miller seconded the motion.
Motion passed 2-0. Selectman Christiansen abstained.
Minutes 2/18/26
Selectman Christiansen made a motion to accept the minutes for 2/18/26 as presented. Selectman
Miller seconded the motion.
