company, to present the December 31, 2024, audit results. An unmodified or clean opinion was
received for the financial statements that were audited.
Ms. Webb provided an explanation of the audit process. She highlighted that it is focused on risk
assessment. They look for fraud and possible areas for misstatement in the financial statements.
They look at controls in place for the current transaction cycle and select a sample size (typically
40) to see if the system is working per the controls that are in place.
The control tests are rotated every three years. This year (2024) focused on Water and Sewer
user fee billings. This is typically done together because Sewer fees are dependent on water
meter readings. Everything was in order and billed correctly.
Material Adjustment Journal Entries were also reviewed, and there was nothing unusual noted
during the audit.
Ms. Webb spoke about the review of the use of credit cards and relevant documentation. There
was nothing unusual found
The company also incorporates "unexpected procedures," which function as a surprise portion of
the audit. For 2024, employee reimbursements were selected and reviewed. There were no
findings of anything unusual.

She reviewed the Required Supplementary Information section, which includes a Budgetary
Statement for the General Fund. Ultimately, the report found that the Town is in a very healthy
financial position.
Ms. Webb noted that the Town updated its Town Fund Policy, which now states that the Town
would like to retain between 10% and 25% of General Funds Budget Expenditures and the
County and School Taxes. As of December 31, 2024, they Town was within that range.
David Jodoin, Town Administrator, asked why the Department of Revenue Administration
(DRA) numbers were different, and Ms. Webb thought that it may be due to them not including
the County and School Taxes.
Ms. Webb mentioned that the Town still had $382,500 in American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA)
funding as of December 31, 2024. She mentioned that if it is not yet spent, it needs to be by
December 31, 2026. David mentioned that there is approximately $95,000, which is contingent
on the Water Department and the interconnection to Concord.
She spoke about GASB Compliance Guidance updates and how they are reflected in the report.
This was done to promote increased transparency. This led to a discussion on compensated
absences, including things like sick leave, vacation and retirement. David discussed the Town
paying out these items when someone leaves employment.
Selectman Yeaton discussed her public company's practices in this space, which include an
unlimited paid time off policy so that the company does not have to carry such debt. Ms. Webb
stated that her company has a "use it or lose it" policy, and paid time off must be used during the
calendar year that it is granted. Both scenarios eliminate that payout of these benefits.
Ms. Webb provided some highlights from the audit. There were no transactions entered for
which there was a lack of authoritative guidance. There were no issues with management.
She covered a separate listing of the Material Audit Adjustments. She explained that this listing
represents that various audit adjustments that were recorded to ensure that financial statements
were fairly stated which included the OPEB reporting which the Town does not record on their
books, it's merely for the financial statements.
Ms. Webb referenced the management letter. She noted that compensated absences are
mentioned in the letter. It was also noted that one of the Sewer Manifests had only two
commissioner signatures, but one of the expenditures was to one of the signing commissioners.
She suggested the third commissioner signing in this situation.
The last items that Ms. Webb noted was the Police Details Fund, which has had a loss the past
few years. She suggested raising the rates since it is not currently covering the payroll and
retirement. David stated that the rate has been adjusted since the audit, but there may need to be
further adjustments.

Selectman Miller asked how they should determine the rate for detail. David responded that he
could get the breakeven number for the Board. He also cautioned ensuring that the rate is still
competitive with other communities.
The Board thanked Ms. Webb and she stated that she would be back in a couple of months to
start the 2025 Audit.
Health Insurance Committee Questions
Selectman Yeaton stated that the Health Insurance Committee has presented questions to the
Board after they held their first meeting. The Committee was seeking guidance.
Selectman Yeaton read the Committee's request for guidance on the following:
• Whether the Board anticipates the Town contributing a fixed dollar amount per
employee towards employee health insurance or staying with the current premium
split.
• Whether the Board consider applying current employer contribution amounts
uniformly across all plan offerings regardless of premium differences.
Whether the Board would consider offering HRA if a lower premium plan was
chosen to cover a portion of deductibles.
Selectman Miller explained that there are different plan types: single, couple or family. When
they discussed in the summer was ensuring that every employee has the same Town contribution.
This would lead to a different percentage of each type of plan that was selected. This is referred
to as a uniform contribution.
Selectman Miller and Selectman Frederickson agreed that this was a desirable option.
David stated that he thought that this year the Board decided that they would only add three
plans and not change the percentages paid by the Town. Selectmen Goulet agreed that was her
understanding also.
Selectman Goulet questioned the fairness based on the salary of the employee. Selectman
Frederickson explained that an employee with a lower salary would be receiving a higher
percentage.
Selectman Miller explained that premiums are generally based on age as well. Traditionally, the
Town has blended all the premiums together independent of age. This aligns with the uniform
contribution model. If this model was not used, it would be complex to factor in things like age
and salary.
Selectman Christiansen stated that he could support a uniform contribution model, but he would
like to see this stay close to the current 85% amount of Town contribution.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 21, 2026, at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman
Sandy Goulet
Absent: Selectman Rick Frederickson
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 pm.
II.
Citizen Comment:
None
IlI.
Scheduled Meetings:
Sue Whitbeck - Library Legislation
Sue Whitbeck was present to discuss library legislation that is currently being presented at the State
House, specifically House Bill 1214. She stated that, if passed, this bill would allow a warrant article
to be voted on at Town Meeting that can make the Board of Selectmen the governing body of the
library as opposed to the trustees. Neither the Pembroke Library Trustees, nor the Library Trustees
Association, are in favor of the bill.
She stated that there have not been issues with the current structure. She added that the bill's
proposer is suggesting that libraries are turning into business and therefore, libraries should be run
by town governments. Ms. Whitbeck emphasized that the library is not a business, but a non-profit.
She also feels that the library is not political. She stated that she does not feel that the Board needs
more duties.
She continued that New Hampshire had the first tax supported library in the world. Also, she
believes there is a conflict with RSA 202-A, which stated that libraries would be governed by a
Board of Trustees.
Selectman Goulet asked if Pembroke would be required to adopt this if the bill passes. Ms. Whitbeck
stated that they would not be required to adopt it, and she expressed that she would prefer if this
would not be adopted.
Selectman Miller suggested the citizens should write to their representatives on the matter. Ms.
Whitbeck stated that both representatives, Rep. Seaworth and Rep. Mehegan, have stated that they
will not be supporting the bill.

Selectman Goulet appreciated Ms. Whitbeck bringing this to the Board's attention. Selectman
Yeaton asked if Ms. Whitbeck would be speaking at the hearings and Ms. Whitbeck stated that she
would if needed. She added that she thinks that the current system works and she does not feel the
need for change.
NH Trail Dawgs - Trail Permission
Gaylen Reardon, Vice President of NH Trail Dawgs, was present to speak to the Board about the
renewal of the trail permission agreement with the Town for the use of trails on the Range Roads. He
stated that they have had some turnover in their organization and asked if there would be the
possibility of a five-year renewal to ease the burden on the volunteers of the organization.
Selectman Goulet stated that usually the Police Chief is present. She added that normally this is done
for one year as opposed to five.
David Jodoin stated that issues in the past have been taken care of, specifically on Thompson Road.
He is unaware of any other issues.
Selectman Goulet added that she does not have a problem with extending the agreement but would
have liked to have heard from the Chief.
Selectman Miller stated that he would prefer a one-year agreement. He understands the burden, but
he thinks the face-to-face contact would be beneficial. He added that over time, this may be the only
contact that people have with the organization. He spoke about the organization's perception and
thinks that it would be beneficial for them to come each year.
Selectman Goulet added that there are new board members over time. Selectman Yeaton felt that it
should be one year as well. Selectman Goulet stated that they may be willing to entertain a longer
trail agreement in the future.
Mr. Reardon noted that on the standardized state form, there are options for either one or five years.
He added that the Town reserves the right to revoke the agreement at any time. There can still be
contact between the Club and the Town.
Selectman Christiansen stated that he was inclined to do one year as well. He thinks it would be
worth meeting yearly.
Selectman Goulet asked Chief Shea if she had any comment on the relationship or the agreement
with the Trail Dawgs. Chief Shea feels that they have had a good working relationship in the past
and was not aware of any issues.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to approve a one-year Landowner Approval and to require the NH
Trail Dawgs to come before the Board before any types of repairs to the roadway or bridges occur
and authorize the Chair to sign the document. Selectman Miller seconded the motion.

Mr. Reardon expressed that Pembroke has an extended mud season that restricts wheeled vehicle
access before there is snow on the ground. The Club would like to be able to access the trails during
this time to maintain trails, repair bridges, cut branches, or putting up signs. In the past, there was an
agreement, but there was some confusion on the point-of-contact for that permission.
Selectman Yeaton asked specifically what the Club is requesting. Mr. Reardon asked for the
agreement of access during mud season for these purposes. He was advised that he could contact
David to be added to the Selectboard agenda to discuss the access when the time comes.
Selectman Yeaton stated that the Conservation Commission would take interest in this as well. She
added that working through a Selectboard meeting would allow key stakeholders to take part in the
conversation.
Motion passed 4-0.
Public Hearing - Bond Proposals
Selectman Yeaton stated that they would be holding the public hearing for the Bond Proposals for
Articles 3 and 4. This would be a discussion on the proposed state bonding for Memorial Park. Each
would be discussed and have a public hearing separately.
Selectman Miller asked if the public hearing would remain open until February 4, 2026, since it
would be continued. Selectman Yeaton stated that it will be continued and reopened at the public
hearing February 4, 2026.
Selectman Goulet stated that the Board is on the record as the meeting, and that it has already been
on the agenda and added to the website. Residents can choose to attend the public hearing on
February 4, as well, if they would like to make comment.
Chairman Yeaton read Article 3 into the record as follows:
ARTICLE 3 - To see if the town will vote to raise and appropriate the sum of $820,000 (Gross
Budget) for the purpose of replacing a drainage pipe at Memorial Park as part of the Towns required
Asset Management program which is part of the Federally required MS 4 permitting process, and to
authorize the issuance of not more than $820,000 of bonds or notes in accordance with the
provisions of the Municipal Finance Act (RSA 33); and, further, to authorize the Board of Selectmen
to issue and negotiate such bonds or notes and to determine the rate of interest thereon, and, to
further authorize the Board of Selectmen to offset a portions of said appropriation by applying for
and expending Clean Water State Revolving Funds (CWSRF) loan funds or any other grants or
funding sources which may become available. Repayment of the loan funds is expected to up to
Fifteen Percent of Principal forgiveness of loan principal in an amount up to $123,000. (3/5 ballot
vote required)
There were no questions or comments from the Board.
The public hearing was opened for Article 3 at 6:16 pm.

Meeting Minutes

Attendance
Members: Kate Castaldo-Rice, Chair; Clint Hanson, Planning Board Rep; Bryan
Christiansen, Selectmen Rep.; Chuck Therrien; Jessica Stevenson
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Excused: Dana Carlucci
Business
1. Discussion with Bridgett Beckwith, Tax Credit Program Manager, NH Dept.
Business and Economic Affairs
B. Beckwith introduced herself. She has been with State of NH in economic development
for twelve years, and has been in her current position for ten years. Before working for the
State, she worked in bookkeeping.
K. Castaldo-Rice reviewed the questions from last meeting for Bridgett. We asked if she
could look at our Economic Revitalization Zone (ERZ) maps and let us know if they met
the criteria. She agreed. We asked whether residential properties could be included in the
ERZ to make it contiguous. She answered, yes. We asked if the Selectboard needs to
adopt the ERZs via a public hearing. She answered that the Board just needs to vote.
K. Castaldo-Rice said that she had talked to Bridgett about the possibility of inviting
businesses to come and speak with her, if the ERZs are adopted. We could have it at a
regularly scheduled EDC meeting and publicize it to businesses.
B. Beckwith offered a template letter that the EDC could send to businesses to invite them.
It would include her contact information.
B. Christiansen asked Bridgett what are some frequently asked questions that the EDC
has not asked yet.
B. Beckwith said that the program applies to renters as well as owners, the business does
not have to own the building. Businesses need capital investment and job creation. It's
prorated so I never know what I am going to get; it depends on the applicants. The more
applicants, the smaller piece of the pie, but they get something. Typically the property has
to be retail, industrial, or commercial, but we can do mixed use. It only applies to the
business though. If a business owner is unsure what a "capital investment" is, they can
check with their tax preparer. It can be certain types of advertising, expensive or specific
T:\Town Planner\EDC\Minutes\12-01-2025 Minutes.docx
Page 1 of 4

equipment (software). The credit is based on calendar year, so all activity has to happen in
the calendar year. They can apply every year if they meet the criteria.
J. Stevenson asked if the business has to apply every year or does it roll over once they
are already in the program.
B. Beckwith said the credit rolls, so you are only allowed to get a maximum amount. The
amount is $240,000 over six years. You are only allowed to claim $40,000 per year. If a
business gets a $60,000 credit, they could claim $40,000 or stretch it out however they
need to over six years. The business has to apply every year with the way the program is
set up. The program is due to sunset in 2027, but every year I've been there, it's been
renewed. I don't expect it to go away. It's the only thing the State really offers. The
program is only $825,000 for the whole state. Going forward, they will probably make sure
all of their credits are used up before they apply for more. If you get a sizeable credit every
year, then you are technically leaving money on the table if you are not collecting the full
amount. An example is the company BAE. They get the maximum every year, but can only
claim $40,000. Say $240,000 was allotted. Now all that money could have gone to
somebody else because they can't claim it. That is the part we need to fix, to make sure all
that money isn't just sitting there. So far there have been no complaints about not getting
the full amount; something is better than nothing. It's not hard to meet the criteria. One
new job will do it; there is no minimum. So any amount of capital investment will work, they
just need both criteria.
B. Christiansen said that the EDC reviewed the program guidelines at the last meeting. He
asked if buildings need to be vacant in order to qualify.
B. Beckwith said no, and explained there is a little leeway in the RSA and how it was
written. She has gone over it with Revenue Administration many times. The intent was
revitalization of vacant buildings or dilapidated buildings. Each town in NH is unique. It's
become adapted to towns that may not have an old mill building, because how are they
supposed to use it. So the program can be used to reduce turnover too. If you invest in the
building, the tenants are more likely to stay longer.
B. Christiansen asked if the town adopts it, and it's successful, does the business apply
every year for six years unless there is some change in the statute.
B. Beckwith clarified the business does not have to apply every year for six years. The
credit lasts for six years. If they want to and can apply every year, and they meet the
criteria, they can just keep applying forever. There is no limit on that. That is how the
program currently stands.
J. Stevenson asked what the application process is for the business.
B. Beckwith explained it's very simple. It's a 3-page application. It asks information about
the business (contact information), a description of the project, they typically submit a
spreadsheet of capital investments, and invoices to show that they made the purchases in
the year. They submit new employee information (salaries). The town needs to be aware
that the business owner needs to reach out to the town and ask for a copy of the ERZ (to
show the zone they are in). We do that so that the town is aware someone is using it, and
the town can begin to form a relationship with that business.

K. Castaldo-Rice asked if the town doesn't get the ERZ approved until after the new year,
would the business still qualify next year for credits.
B. Beckwith said no, she would need it signed off on before December 31st.
B. Christiansen said the Selectboard are aware of the program and meet on the 3rd and
17i this month. He asked what a town approval looks like, if they just send a copy of the
minutes.
B. Beckwith said the town sends her the minutes approving the ERZ, the maps, and a brief
description about why you wanted to create the zones, and what you want to do in the
area economic development-wise. There is an application that needs to be signed by the
town.
B. Christiansen said if the Selectboard approves this on the 17'h, they would not have
approved minutes until the new year. Is that a problem? B. Beckwith will check, but thinks
she can accept draft minutes until the minutes are approved.
K. Castaldo-Rice asked if a letter from the Selectboard could be submitted. B. Beckwith
said a letter is fine, and you can send the meeting minutes later.
The EDC began to review the maps. B. Beckwith said that if there is a change to the maps
after the ERZ is adopted they can amend it (add or remove a parcel) with just an email to
her, as long as the zone remains contiguous.
K. Castaldo-Rice had a question about the Sheep Davis Road map. There was a large
section of land not included.
Members pointed out that that was land owned by the National Guard. B. Beckwith
confirmed that the National Guard would not qualify.
C. Hanson asked if a signature from the Selectboard Chair on the application will be
sufficient since it indicates that a vote was taken. B. Beckwith said a letter is fine as long
as I know the record of the meeting is on the way.
K. Castaldo-Rice had a question about a hole in the zone. There is a lot that appears to be
missing on the other side of the road from the National Guard. There was some discussion
about what it could be. They will follow up with the Town Planner.

• B. Christiansen will ask the Selectboard to vote on adopting the ERZs at their

Business
1. Update on Business Survey Results Analysis & Outreach Plan
C. Therrien reached out again to the owner of the Little Vintage Venue. He does not know
if she is not getting his messages. He may try to visit the coffee shop to catch her. He is
still waiting for a reply.
J. Stevenson talked to Rob Azevedo. She was not on the Economic Development
Committee (EDC) when the surveys went out, but she spoke to him in terms of his
business and what is happening downtown. He is passionate about the Village and
growing his business. He would be open to learning more about the Economic
Revitalization Zones (ERZs). It was a positive conversation. He enjoys the support from
the town. All ages are enjoying the growth and development of the Village. He is excited
about the bank turning into apartments and thinks more residential within walking distance
of the Village will help. He noted that parking has never once been an issue that has
affected his business since he's been open.
The EDC thanked J. Stevenson for the update.
2. Update on ERZs
3. Information on 79-E
C. Cronin gave a recap of the discussion at the last EDC meeting. ERZs and 79-E were
discussed, the differences and pros and cons. They are both essentially tax credit
programs. In the discussion last month, the EDC was more in favor of ERZs because it is a
much simpler process for the Town. She recapped that the 79-E is a tax credit on property
taxes for façade improvements. The ERZ is a business tax credit on State taxes. The ERZ
has a broader range of criteria that can be applied for tax credits. The ERZs are
administered by the State. 79-E is set up and administered by the Town. For tonight, there
are draft ERZ maps from the 2019 EDC and maps of other areas in town that are
commercially zoned. The EDC can workshop what areas might make sense to present as

ERZs with the draft maps.
B. Christiansen said that he watched the video of the last meeting and updated the
Selectboard on the topic. He agreed with K. Castaldo-Rice that the EDC needs to
accomplish something to get momentum going. A packet in advance of their meeting
would be helpful. Bridgett Beckwith presenting would help too. He agreed that the town is
not in a position to work on 79-E yet.
C. Cronin presented the 2019 draft ERZ maps. The maps were put together by Central NH
Regional Planning Commission, who was working with Bridgett Beckwith and the EDC.
There were two proposed areas. One is the location of the Soucook River Development
District, the location of Associated Grocers, at the intersection of Routes 3 and 106.
Associated Grocers own a few parcels and the other parcel has changed hands many
times. The town has been trying to get that parcel commercially developed. The other map
is Silver Hills Drive and the Concord Sand and Gravel pit. Silver Hills Drive has been pretty
much built out since the map was created. Concord Sand and Gravel is an active pit, and
likely will be years before the property is reclaimed for commercial development.
C. Cronin explained that the other two maps she brought to the meeting are zoning maps
of the Village and the C1 (Commercial/Light Industrial) Zoning District. She noted there is
not a lot of undeveloped property on Route 106. A few properties have changed hands.
One lot is undeveloped and was denied a car wash because it overlays the aquifer.
B. Christiansen asked about underdeveloped or underutilized properties in the area of
Route 106. C. Cronin said she does not know. She was talking about undeveloped
properties, meaning the lot is empty, but underdeveloped business, not land, can be
helped by the ERZ if they expand, or create new jobs, or buy new equipment. B.
Christiansen noted that the ERZ could help someone like J. Stevenson because the
building is underdeveloped. He asked if there are any vacant buildings. C. Cronin said not
to her knowledge.
B. Christiansen said he was unsure about going to the State with 4 different areas. K.
Castaldo-Rice said there is no limit to the size of the ERZ. She wants to include existing
businesses and attract new businesses. She suggested giving options of areas to the
Selectboard and ask their opinion. B. Christiansen suggested ranking all 4 areas for the
Selectboard.
K. Castaldo-Rice would like to include the Village. B. Christiansen was not sure about
including Silver Hills Drive because it's an active sand and gravel pit. His two preferences
are the Village and the Route 106 corridor. J. Stevenson thought the Village would be a
good area because many parcels and businesses could take advantage.
B. Christiansen said the Soucook River Development District has land the town would love
to see developed, but there are geographical challenges. D. Carlucci said that Associated
Grocers went in, and suggested local realtors, Craig and Wendy Keeler, come in and talk
to the EDC. K. Castaldo-Rice noted that an ERZ on that parcel might not be enough of an
incentive to develop that land; there is not enough money in the ERZ.
D. Carlucci informed the EDC that Mr. Bibeau, who owns the town clock building, is having
a problem getting a tenant on an upper floor because he does not have the funds for

There was a question about what State tax the credit is for. K. Castaldo-Rice looked it up

Meeting Minutes
October 6, 2025
Attendance
Members: Kate Castaldo-Rice, Chair; Clint Hanson, Planning Board Rep; Jessica
Stevenson
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Excused: Bryan Christiansen, Selectmen Rep.; Dana Carlucci; Chuck Therrien
Business
1. Update on Business Survey Results Analysis & Outreach Plan
K. Castaldo-Rice gave a recap of the business survey process. The Economic
Development Committee (EDC) collected email addresses from as many businesses in
town as they could. They sent the survey and got 18 responses back. One of the survey
questions asked if the respondent would like someone from the EDC to reach out to them
about their survey answers. About 5 businesses answered yes. Those businesses were
assigned to EDC members to reach out to.
She added that she was assigned to Pembroke City Limits, and due to scheduling conflicts
she will not be able to do the interview. The business owner is willing to meet, but she
cannot make it.
J. Stevenson asked what the goal of the survey was. K. Castaldo-Rice explained that they
were looking for feedback from businesses in town about improvements we can make,
what opportunities there are, letting them know we have an EDC, and taking the survey
results to other boards to see what they can improve. In the future, we would like to survey
the residents as well.
2. Update on ERZs
3. Information on 79-E
K. Castaldo-Rice wanted to talk about these two topics together. Information was sent out
in the packet about both Economic Revitalization Zones (ERZs) and 79-E. They are both
tax credit programs.
K. Castaldo-Rice said ERZs seem to be a simpler process and they are State run,
whereas with 79-E we have to be selective about the process. Her concern about 79-E
T: \TownAdmin\LWilliams\My Documents\Recycling Info\Planning and Zoning\WEB PAGE DOCUMENTS TO UPLOAD\10-06-2025 Minutes.docx

was giving town tax credits to large businesses and the implications that could have on the
local tax rate. We would want to have the Selectboard involved in that. She asked if
something similar was in place when Associated Grocers went in.
C. Cronin said the town did a Tax Increment Financing (TIF) District for Associated
Grocers, which was a tax deferment for the purposes of building the road there. A TIF is a
way for a town to get an infrastructure project done, funded by tax deferment, basically.
79-E is a tax break from local property taxes. She described some of the major differences
between ERZs and 79-E:
Economic Revitalization Zones (ERZs)
Tax credit on State business taxes
State administers (reviews applications,
financials, etc.)
Can be created anywhere in town where
there is an economic interest
Only applies to businesses
Helps develop business (purchasing
equipment, creating new jobs,
infrastructure improvements)
RSA 79-E Community Revitalization Tax
Relief Incentive
Tax credit on property taxes to the Town
Town administers (creates application
process, criteria, reviews financials,
Selectboard review)
Limited to downtown areas (with the
exception that residential tax credits can
be outside of downtown areas
Applies to businesses with an option to
apply to residential for creating new
housing
Only applies to physical building (rehab,
renovation, restoration)
K. Castaldo-Rice thinks that a local property tax credit (79-E) may not be feasible right now
considering all the budget cuts the town is looking at. It might not go over well. It might be
more successful in the future.
C. Hanson described some of the budget issues that originate at the state level. Property
taxes will go up due to State changes, and there is little the Budget Committee will be able
to do about it. Issues with school funding, the State losing a lawsuit, and other expenditure
issues will undoubtedly impact local tax rates and budgets.
K. Castaldo-Rice thinks that an ERZ would be more helpful to businesses because you
don't need to be a new business to take advantage, it can be an existing business that is
proactively growing their business. ERZs will require some work from us on the front end,
but once set up the State administers it.
J. Stevenson asked how long the process would take. K. Castaldo-Rice said she could get
more information from Bridget Beckwith at the State. C. Cronin added that ERZs can be
set up at any time, they do not have to wait until Town Meeting. 79-Es must be adopted
through Town Meeting.

K. Castaldo-Rice would like to get a consensus vote from the EDC in November to move
forward with the ERZs. Bryan could bring it to the Selectboard and we could provide
information to them. If needed, Kate could ask Bridget to present to the Selectboard.
J. Stevenson suggested we inform the local businesses about ERZs to see if they would
be interested in them, and include that feedback into the information for the Selectboard.
K. Castaldo-Rice suggested Dana and other members could help spread the word to the
business community. She added that any feedback could be sent to Carolyn. C. Cronin
suggested a blast email to businesses about ERZs since we already have their email
addresses from the survey.
K. Castaldo-Rice added that the town would need to choose the ERZ districts. The
conversation has been about doing it in the Village and the Route 106 area. J. Stevenson
wondered what the average savings for a small business would be with the tax credit.

K. Castaldo-Rice will ask Bridget Beckwith for examples of smaller businesses that

TOWN OF PEMBROKE
Town Hall ~ 311 Pembroke Street, Pembroke, New Hampshire 03275
Tel: 603-485-4747
Economic Development Committee
Meeting Minutes
September 15, 2025
Attendance
Members: Kate Castaldo-Rice, Chair; Dana Carlucci, Chuck Therrien;; Bryan Christiansen,
Selectmen Rep.
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Others: Jessica Stevenson, business owner; Mark Stevenson, business owner; John
Christ, UNH Cooperative Extension
Excused: Clint Hanson, Planning Board Rep.
Business
1. Discussion with John Christ, Community & Economic Development Extension Field
Specialist, UNH Cooperative Extension
J. Christ introduced himself from the UNH Cooperative Extension. He has worked there
since January as a Field Specialist for Merrimack County. He has been in NH for over a
decade, lives in Plymouth, and used to teach at Plymouth State. He has spent time on
local boards, as well. He wanted to contact towns across the county to make connections
and see how they can work together.
He explained that UNH Extension exists all across the country and is funded federally from
the Department of Agriculture, from the state through UNH, and from the county. In
addition to agriculture and health work, UNH Extension also does community and
economic development. His office is at the county facility in Boscawen. He works with
communities on capacity building and community engagement. UNH Extension can
provide help with one-time events facilitating feedback. They also do larger projects that
take 6 months to a year.
He explained that UNH Extension is usually cheaper to engage than a private consultant.
The difference is that UNH Extension's approach is to help communities do the work, not
do the work for them. They help communities build capacity to do the work so they can
keep their process moving forward after the program ends. UNH Extension offers a
Business Engagement Program to figure out needs, opportunities, and barriers for the
business community. They can produce reports and create action plans to implement.
They offer a Downtowns and Trails Programs to connect trail users with downtowns. There
is a First Impressions Program to train two communities to give feedback on each other's
first impressions with fresh eyes. There is also a Housing Academy to give towns
assistance with navigating state housing programs. He would like to answer any questions
T:\ TownAdmin\LWilliams\My Documents\Recycling Info\Planning and Zoning\WEB PAGE DOCUMENTS TO UPLOAD\09-15-2025 Minutes.docx
Page 1 of 7

the EDC has. He read through the town's Master Plan and would like to learn more about
the town.
B. Christiansen asked if there is a cost to the programs. J. Christ said that currently the
cost of a program is $3,000. An outside consultant would cost a magnitude higher. Our
salaries are paid through other funding sources, so the fee is to cover travel and other
overhead costs. There have been lots of big changes with funding lately, so unless
anything changes, the cost is $3,000. B. Christiansen asked about the process of
engaging UNH Extension for a program; is there a scope of work, deliverables? J. Christ
explained that there would be a memorandum of understanding with the town. First, UNH
Extension assesses whether they have the capacity to help with the project at that time
(staffing, etc.) and whether the town has the capacity to take the project on because there
is work on the town's end as well.
B. Christiansen explained to J. Christ that the newest iteration of the EDC has only been
up and running for about 6 months now. We are still getting started and recruiting
members. He feels that the EDC may not be ready to engage the UNH Extension yet, but
he appreciates what they do. He asked for an example of a successful program in another
town of a similar size to Pembroke. J. Christ said that success does not happen overnight,
but it looks like the town having a vision with a clear roadmap to achieve it, and the
community is doing the work and knows how to sustain that work. They can come to us for
further guidance and they know what resources they can access. That is, realistically, what
a success story looks like. We would help a community identify what they want their
project to look like, and we bring in the broader community to give feedback and buy into
the project. It may take a few years or longer to move the process forward at a reasonable
pace.
K. Castaldo-Rice echoed B. Christiansen's comments about the EDC being at the
beginning stages. She does not feel that the EDC has the manpower to commit to a
program yet. She asked if UNH Extension is available as a resource if we have questions
and if we are not participating in a program. J. Christ confirmed the town does not need to
be participating in a program to reach out. He can offer advice and offer to come back to
the EDC and talk, if needed. He spoke about Franklin, NH, which UNH Extension worked
with for years on both formal and informal programs. A lot has happened in Franklin and
we are not responsible for all of it, but we were a partner in quite a bit of it. We worked with
other partners in the town to move things along. Feel free to contact us at any time.
D. Carlucci asked if UNH Extension handles TIF Districts. J. Christ said he read the master
plan and was curious where Pembroke stood in meeting the master plan goals, which
included a potential TIF District and some other work in the Suncook Village area. D.
Carlucci said there is one good business in there and other property for sale. We have a
nice road, but he thinks the topography is a bit of a hindrance. J. Christ asked the purpose
of the TIF. C. Cronin explained that the TIF was to build the road and traffic light to create
access to commercially zoned land. She believes the TIF is now closed since the road is
complete, but it did help attract Associated Grocers, who own some other land there for
potential expansion. There is other land for sale off and on. That piece has been a
challenge. She said the Village is having a resurgence right now with a lot more
investment, new property owners, and new businesses in the last 5 or 6 years. She
explained that there are buildings being renovated into apartments (TD Bank, Village
School). She explained that some of the programs that are goals in the master plan (ERZs,
T:\TownAdmin\LWilliams\My Documents\Recycling Info\Planning and Zoning\WEB PAGE DOCUMENTS TO UPLOAD\09-15-2025 Minutes.docx
Page 2 of 7

79-E) are things the EDC is learning about. They are in an exploratory phase to see what
options there are and to recruit additional members. D. Carlucci suggested UNH Extension
attend a Meet Me in Suncook meeting.
J. Christ asked what has caused the turnover in the Village. C. Cronin wonders the same
and thinks it was a post-COVID push for individuals to start new businesses. J. Stevenson
said they bought their building (3 Glass St.) post-COVID. She said the Rainville building
matriarch passed away so the family sold the building. The brewery bought their building
from someone else who retired. C. Therrien added Lavallee Store closed and is now a
coffee shop.
J. Christ asked about the relationship between Pembroke and Allenstown in their shared
Suncook Village. D. Carlucci said the Meet Me in Suncook group is made up of both
Pembroke and Allenstown people. Most people have lived on both sides of the river at one
time or another. J. Christ said that cooperation from both towns is a good thing. C.
Therrien mentioned that in the 7 years he has lived in town, he has seen a lot of changes
in the Village, from vacant storefronts to new businesses. He said that as a resident and as
a businessman it's good to see. C. Cronin noted that new residential on both sides of the
river has helped. J. Christ asked if there is increased activity in street life. Members noted
that there is a lot of foot traffic in the Village. C. Cronin talked about opportunity to connect
the future rail trail to the downtown. There was a brief discussion of budget cuts and
funding opportunities.
C. Cronin explained that the commercial areas are in the Village and in the Route 106
area. Route 106 does not have too many economic development challenges. She
explained the biggest pressure is requests to build multifamily and other residential
developments in the commercial areas. There is some openness to mixed use in some
areas. There was a brief discussion of the new State statute mandating multifamily in
commercial zones. It is not an issue in the Route 106 area.
2. Update on CEDRs and ERZs
K. Castaldo-Rice said there has been no news at BEA (Bureau of Economic Affairs) on
CEDRs (Collaborative Economic Development Regions). She said the vision is to have
both CEDRs and regional planning commissions even though they share some functions.
The CEDRs program is being revamped at BEA, but there is currently no funding.
K. Castaldo-Rice said she talked to Bridget Beckwith about ERZs (economic revitalization
zones) and she gave her an updated PowerPoint presentation on ERZs. The PowerPoint
is self-explanatory about the program. The EDC should all review the presentation and
revisit it next month. Bridget is open to attending a meeting, but we should all review the
presentation first to see if we have questions. She explained that the program is for tax
credits for businesses that revitalize the area of the ERZ through new jobs and other
metrics. It is free for the town and the businesses apply for the credits. Bridget would also
be available to meet with businesses about how to apply for the credit. The program is
funded through 2028 and renewed based on the State budget. If it does not get renewed,
then the town doesn't lose anything because it doesn't cost anything.

K. Castaldo-Rice gave an update on Collaborative Economic Development Regions
(CEDRs) and Economic Revitalization Zones (ERZs). She works at the NH Department of
Business and Economic Affairs (BEA). This was discussed at the May meeting. Bridgett
Beckwith at BEA is willing to come to a meeting and give a presentation on ERZs if the
Economic Development Committee (EDC) would like.
B. Christiansen asked if the ERZs got any more funding in their budget. K. Castaldo-Rice

thinks it's a good idea for Bridgett to come and share whatever information she has with

2. Old Home Day Discussion
C. Cronin said at the last meeting there was discussion about possible handouts at Old
Home Day. The EDC wanted to continue that brainstorm tonight.
B. Christiansen recapped that the idea started as a booth at Old Home Day. The EDC
wanted to drive awareness of the Committee. We talked about handing out a flyer to
Pembroke residents. The idea is appealing, but we will have a manpower issue. He noted
the business survey results gave us a lot to work on. He asked what we hope to gain from
handing out information.

there was not a lot of discussion about what the message would be.
K. Castaldo-Rice noted that the resident survey was an interesting idea, but unless there is
a big issue, she doesn't know what we would poll residents on and how much response we
would receive. She noted that the EDC has not done a lot yet, so there is not much we
have to tell the residents right now. B. Christiansen noted that the business survey only
had 18 responses out of 170 surveys sent.
C. Therrien would like the EDC to focus on small business owners to get them involved
with the EDC. They may have ideas and be willing to share with the group. Small
businesses get surveys all the time and most are not interested in filling them out. It would
be helpful to meet with them in person to participate.
K. Castaldo-Rice said her feeling on reaching out to residents is that we are not there yet.
We need to build the EDG up a bit more. She agreed that targeting business owners and
having discussions with them should be the focus right now. Maybe next year we will be
better positioned for Old Home Day.
C. Therrien agreed. He noted that the EDC is still new and getting started. If we want to
succeed, we need to get businesses involved. K. Castaldo-Rice agreed and noted that it's
been difficult to retain business owners on the committee because of their busy schedules.
K. Castaldo-Rice concluded by stating that if members go to Old Home Day, they can still
have conversations with businesses there to introduce themselves and tell them about the
EDC. She agreed with the other members that did not think we were ready to have a
formal outreach plan yet. The EDC agreed that that is the best approach.
3. Business Survey Results Analysis & Outreach Plan
C. Cronin provided a PDF of the raw survey results and also a document that was her
attempt to analyze and categorize the written responses. If the EDC has another way they
want to analyze the results, then that is also totally fine. We got 18 responses and the
survey link is still live.
C. Cronin went through the survey result multiple choice answers first and will go through
the written results after.
• The survey results include a mix of industries that responded.
• Most of the respondents were small business, employing 10 or fewer people, but a
couple of the biggest businesses in town also responded.
• The majority of respondents were located in the Village and in the Route 106 area.
Many factors went into the reasons why the business chose the location that they
did.
• More than 50% said Pembroke is a favorable town to do business in.
• Businesses deal with a lot of town departments, boards, and services. The Clerk's
office was the most used office, followed by permitting and land use. More than
50% were satisfied with their municipal experience.
More than 50% do not plan to change their business. 7 businesses plan to expand
in Pembroke. None are moving or closing.

• The biggest challenges in order are employee recruitment and retention, then costs
of doing business, affordable housing, local taxes and government, and last is
parking and traffic issues.
• 56% say the best thing about doing business in Pembroke is the location, followed
by utility availability, recreation and scenic beauty, and lastly labor force availability.
• Several respondents want to be contacted to discuss their survey responses and a
few are interested in learning more about joining the EDC.
C. Cronin discussed how she quantified and analyzed the written responses into a
document highlighting the survey takeaways. She cut and pasted all the written responses
and sorted them into categories that she believed made sense. She broke up the feedback
into positive and negative feedback, then broke up the information further into what she felt
fell into five different categories:
1. Town Hall/Departments - Interface with town employees, town offices, and town
services.
2. Town Boards - Interface with town Boards, made up of elected or appointed
residents.
3. Character/Amenities - The features of the town overall, which may include
geography, facilities, amenities, and descriptive characteristics.
4. Community - The people of the town (residents, business owners, the people who
live and work in Pembroke).
5. Business/Economic Factors - Factors which the Town may or may not have some
control over, but which impact a business' finances and operations in accordance
with their business plan.
Lastly, she broke out the feedback that the Town has some control over as actionable
items, and which Department or Board is it relevant to.
B. Christiansen appreciated the executive summary and its organization. He asked if there
is a regularly scheduled department head meeting. C. Cronin said there is not. B.
Christiansen thinks this is good information to share with department heads. He noted that

share directly with other departments.
C. Cronin suggested that the EDC give the information to the Board of Selectmen to share
with departments. It wasn't the EDC's intent to audit the town departments, but as a result
of the survey, we did get some really good and interesting feedback that should be shared
with departments.
B. Christiansen asked C. Cronin to share the information with David Jodoin to share with

1. Ryan O'Hora, Pembroke Library Director
Ryan O'Hora submitted a letter and packet to the EDC. The packet is from the American
Library Association. The American Library Association had a $2 million grant awarded in
2020 trying to connect libraries with businesses. They connected with libraries across the
US trying to coordinate with towns about business plans and ideas. Different libraries did
different things. Large and small libraries participated in working with their communities to
help support businesses. A lot of it is about providing the space. The library in Lewiston,
Maine, for example, worked with their local career center to host one-on-one meetings at
the library since their own space wasn't as effective.
R. O'Hora said he knows a lot of people in town who are small entrepreneurs and are
looking for ways to build their business. R. O'Hora wanted to introduce himself to the EDC
and offer that the library can be a resource for economic development. For example, the
library could host a networking night for local entrepreneurs. He also suggested an event
with people in the trades who could connect with local teens. There is opportunity for the
EDC to partner with the library, so he wanted to offer that invitation.
B. Christiansen was excited about the idea and admitted that he did not have the library on
his radar as a component of economic development, but after listening to the presentation,
he thinks it would be great.
R. O'Hora suggested that if the members look up "libraries" and "community economics",
there are tons of different reports on how libraries build their communities' economy. One
of the big aspects is the "intangible economy", where you have people who love to live in
their town. Attracting businesses is great, but also being able to think about the intangible
and the community as a place where you want to live. He mentioned that he has made

many friends and connections through the library. The library is a great meeting spot for
people.
B. Christiansen agreed with the "intangibles" and noted that Pembroke is a great location
and a great place to live. Having something at the library would be incredible. We could
have a workshop together to think of ideas.
C. Cronin added that the library really functions more as a community center than just a
place to borrow books. The library and the EDC could collaborate on a networking night.
The library is a great resource and amenity to the town and that should be highlighted.
C. Therrien said that especially in a small town like Pembroke, the library is a part of the
community. It's nice to have that resource.
The EDC thanked Ryan for his time and said they would be in touch.

C. Cronin said the survey went out a couple months ago. It was sent out twice to over 100

B. Christiansen noted that the survey was targeted at 100+ business. 18 responded. There
was some conversation about whether we open the survey up to the public and how that
might skew our survey responses. The question at this point is quality or quantity.
D. Carlucci suggested having a booth at Old Home Day.
Old Home Day is three months away and there was a question as to whether the EDC
wants to hold the survey open that long.
C. Cronin reminded them that the initial plan was to get the survey out prior to Memorial

vacation. Unfortunately, we did not get many responses, but overall the comments have
constructive feedback. We will be able to extract achievable goals and tasks from the
responses. We have a 10% return on the surveys, which is what we expected. I am waiting
for the next meeting when is Kate back to bring the survey results to the EDC for analysis.
But if the EDC wants to extend the survey, then I won't analyze the results yet.
B. Christiansen is satisfied if there is actionable feedback.
C. Cronin said that there is definitely feedback that can be brought to the Selectboard and

to get in touch with them about their answers and some answered yes. There were also

Attendance: Clint Hanson, Planning Board Rep.; Kate Castaldo-Rice, Chair; Bryan

Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
The Economic Development Committee (EDC) received a resignation letter from Member
Matthew Roan, regretfully stepping down from the committee due to business obligations

members. The following suggestions were made:
• Post on Facebook

Business
1. Election of Vice Chair
This agenda item is postponed until the EDC can recruit more members.
2. Final Review of Business Listing
C. Cronin put together a memo, which flagged businesses that were designated as
"Dissolved", "Expired", or had "no data" on the Secretary of State website. The question
posed to the EDC is whether to include these businesses in the survey or not. The
purpose of paring down the list is to find balance between sending out as many surveys as
possible and not wasting money on postage for postcards that may not get a response.
The EDC went through 34 businesses that fell into these three categories. They decided to
keep anything with an email address, delete anything that has a duplicate mailing address,
and delete any business that is known to be defunct.
The EDC estimated that 84 postcards would be mailed at an approximate cost of $47. The
EDC has no budget, but David Jodoin indicated that they could find some money for
mailings.
D. Carlucci said that he had handed out about 30 flyers around the Village asking
businesses to update their contact information, but he got no response.
3. Review Draft Business Survey Questions

C. Cronin put together a first draft of a survey. She tried to capture the essence of the
EDC's questions into a survey format. The parameters were that the survey should be 10-
15 questions and not be all text box (essay) questions. This draft has 14 questions and a
combination of text box and multiple choice questions. Feel free to discuss and make any
changes.
B. Christiansen would like to add a question asking if the survey respondent would like to
join the EDC. All the questions are relevant, but I would like to see this shortened a bit, and
see what questions we can get rid of. He asked if we need to know what industry they are
in. K. Castaldo-Rice explained that it helps with analyzing the data. B. Christiansen
agreed.
The EDC discussed the question asking about the respondent's experience with the Town.
It includes an exhaustive list of Town Boards and Departments that interface with
commercial development. They would like to add EMS to the list. K. Castaldo-Rice asked if
the plan is to present the findings of the survey to the Select board. She wants to know
how this feedback will get back to these departments. B. Christiansen explained the
current Select board is very interested in this and will be interested in any
recommendations. C. Hanson expects that there may be a discussion with all these
departments to go over the feedback. As we grow as a town, this feedback will be
important.
B. Christiansen asked if we can add a catchall text box at the end of the survey, asking if
there is anything else they would like to add, instead of including so many text box
questions throughout. K. Castaldo-Rice said that we will need to analyze all text box
answers manually and they add time to the survey. She agreed that some text boxes could
be combined. B. Christiansen suggested that the text box questions be optional, so the
survey taker could skip them if they wanted.
C. Cronin wanted to circle back to the question on departments and boards. We don't need
to look at the town experience question in a bigger sense than it is. The question is asking
for their experience with all these different departments, but the EDC is looking at that
through the lens of "is it business-friendly." So this committee doesn't need to task itself
with auditing these departments through the survey because we are looking at them
through a very narrow scope. K. Castaldo-Rice agreed and asked if we could pare down
and combine the text box about town experience with another text box. The Committee
agreed to make all text boxes optional.
C. Cronin asked for feedback on the question about future plans. She asked for future
plans "within the next year". We want to be able to address red flag issues because those
will be most relevant to the EDC. She asked about the lists she made of the town's
challenges and benefits to see if the EDC had any changes.
B. Christiansen wants to add "electricity" to the list of utilities. The EDC agreed. C. Hanson
thought changes "over the next year" was too short-sighted. The EDC agreed on "1-3"
years.
C. Cronin asked about the text box questions about the Town's strengths or weaknesses.
She suggested the respondent could add suggestions for improvement there. There is a
question asking if the respondent wants to follow-up on their answers with an EDC
member. We would have a rep from this committee discuss with them and they can get

more information and also make them feel heard. D. Carlucci said that this shows the town

February 3, 2025
Attendance: Clint Hanson, Planning Board Rep.; Kate Castaldo-Rice, Chair; Bryan
Christiansen, Selectmen Rep.

Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Business
1. Meeting Date and Time Alternatives
It was discussed that Dana cannot make the 5pm meeting time and that 6pm is better. B
Christiansen explained the reason for the 5pm start time was to accommodate EDC
members who are business-owners and non-residents, so that they could attend the
meeting directly after work. We ended up not having any members that fit that description,
though.
B. Christiansen made a motion to move the meeting start time to 6pm going forward. C.
Hanson seconded the motion. The Committee unanimously voted to move the meeting
time to 6pm.
The next meeting will be March 3, 2025 at 6pm. K. Castaldo-Rice said that if the EDC gets
more members, they could revisit the meeting time at that time.
2. Election Vice Chair
K. Castaldo-Rice explained they cannot vote on a vice chair tonight. C. Hanson and B.
Christiansen cannot serve because they are appointed representatives of Planning Board
and Select Board, respectively.
K. Castaldo-Rice proposed to leave the vice chair position open for now, and if she cannot
attend a meeting, she will appoint another member to chair in her place for that one
meeting. C. Hanson and B. Christiansen agreed that made sense.
3. Business Inventory and Contact Info
C. Cronin said that since the last meeting, she and Kate have been working on acquiring
contact emails for businesses from the Secretary of State website. The challenge they are
running into is that the website locks you out after a certain number of searches. They can
access the website the following day, but it's slowed our progress.
C:\Users\LWilliams\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\INetCache\Content.Outlook\3FVT66LG\02-03-2025 Minutes.docx

K. Castaldo-Rice said another issue is that many of the businesses are listed as "expired"
or "administratively dissolved",
, so we don't know if they are still active business. B.
Christiansen said that even if it's listed as "expired",
", it may just be that the business has
not filed their renewal yet. C. Hanson added that some may not know they have to renew.
K. Castaldo-Rice asked if ones listed as "administratively dissolved" can be assumed to no
longer be in business. We have to look into those. C. Cronin said that she noted for each
business she looked up if they were expired, dissolved, or if there is no data. We can
compare these to Google searches.
C. Cronin would like the EDC to make decisions tonight on whether to delete or keep
certain items. There are 5 categories to look at: potential duplicates, family farms, home
businesses, businesses where there are questions about whether they are still active or in
town, and businesses that the Secretary of State have marked as "expired", "dissolved", or
"not found".
Home Businesses - The EDC agreed that home businesses should be included in the
survey. They are important and part of the local economy. We want their input, however,
survey questions may have to be added or modified to accommodate home businesses.
Family Farms - C. Cronin explained that there are a couple family farms listed. There are
different categories. Some have a location and customers. Some are purely agricultural. I
don't mean to exclude farms, we just need to decide what makes the most sense with
regard to the parameters of the survey. The EDC agreed to include all family farms and
leave it up to the individuals to respond to the survey or not.
Duplicates - C. Cronin explained that she flagged businesses that are potentially
duplicates of another business. These are additional LLCs or other branches of the same
business. If you Google these business names, they come back to other existing
businesses, addresses, and contact info. The EDC went through each one and decided to
delete all duplicates.
Questionable Items - C. Cronin flagged these businesses because there is a question as
to whether they still exist or not. The EDC went through each one and decided which to
keep or delete based on a combination of Googling and personal knowledge.
Secretary of State Expired, Dissolved, Not Found - The question is whether to include
these businesses. The EDC agreed to keep anything that had an email address
associated with it, regardless of business status.
The EDC agreed that the survey should be web-based. A QR Code and link to the survey
should be included on the mailed postcard. If anyone is more comfortable with a paper
survey, there will be information on the card to contact Carolyn at Town Hall.
K. Castaldo-Rice has experience with Microsoft Forms and will look into it for the next
meeting. It can track responses, make graphs, and has other helpful features for the
survey.
The EDC agreed to ask demographic data. They want to know the industry. They want to
know the size (1-50 employees, 50-100 employees, and 100+ employees).

The EDC discussed the merits of making the survey anonymous or not. C. Cronin added
that a goal of the survey is to include their contact info because we want to ask if they want
someone from the EDC to follow-up with them on their answers. We want to strengthen
the relationship between this town committee and the business community, and it helps if
we know who they are. B. Christiansen pointed out that they are not asking about sales or
profits, so I don't think people will object to including their business name. Otherwise, they
just won't respond.
K. Castaldo-Rice considered the cost of postage and asked whether we send a postcard to
every business, or only to the ones we don't have emails for. The EDC agreed to email the
survey, and any emails that bounce back or any businesses that do not have email
addresses, can be mailed a postcard.
K. Castaldo-Rice asked if the survey should ask a question that ties in the business listing
on the Town website. We don't want to pester people more than once, so we should ask
them when we send the survey if they want to be on the website. C. Hanson agreed and
said that it gives them the option to be included or not.
C. Cronin raised the hypothetical question of whether to continue with the Town website
business listing. It was started before people could use Google to find local businesses. K.
Castaldo-Rice asked if the EDC is responsible for maintaining the list on the website. C.
Cronin said that's a good question, because no one actively maintains it, and that's a
problem. Once we post the information, how do we know when a business closes or
moves, and who updates the website and how often? K. Castaldo-Rice asked if the EDC
has the ability to remove the list. The EDC agreed that people would use Google to find a
local business.
C. Cronin also argued the other side, that the listing gives the businesses a sense of

keep the listing would be if we need to contact them. K. Castaldo-Rice said the EDC would
maintain the business listing internally anyway.
B. Christiansen would support a recommendation to get rid of the listing on the Town

over a decade ago. C. Hanson assumed that the Select Board is responsible for the listing

recommend that the listing is no longer useful, but if the Select Board want to keep it, then

1) Why did you choose to locate your business in Pembroke? Why that specific location or

provide for support?

Business
1. Election Vice Chair
K. Castaldo-Rice opened the meeting at 5:00 PM. C. Cronin said she got a call from Chris
Glenn, who could not attend and felt bad cancelling last minute again. In fairness to the
EDC, he has decided to step down from the Committee because there is too much on his
plate right now. The Committee thanked Chris for his efforts.
The EDC decided to continue the election of a Vice Chair to the next meeting when they
have a full committee. There was discussion that the Vice Chair should be a representative
from the business community since the Chair is not. D. Carlucci pointed out that, being a
business owner, he never knows what his schedule is going to be or what may come up at
the last minute, so felt that he could not serve as Vice Chair. He also noted that the 5pm
start time is difficult.
C. Hanson pointed out that 5pm is an unusual start time. Most boards and committees
meet around 6pm. He also pointed out that he and Bryan technically cannot serve as Vice
Chair because they are appointed by their boards, Selectboard and Planning Board.
K. Castaldo-Rice asked if we want to reconsider the meeting time if 5pm is presenting
challenges for people. She asked why 5pm was picked. C. Cronin said that that was what
Bryan came up with as a starting point when we were establishing the committee. That
was before we had any committee members. The former EDC used to meet at 6pm.
K. Castaldo-Rice suggested sending out an email to all committee members asking if there
was a preferred time they would like to meet. K. Castaldo-Rice skipped ahead to the "Next
Meeting" item on the agenda.
2. Next Meeting

K. Castaldo-Rice said that, while they are talking about scheduling, she will not be
available for the next meeting on February 3r°, as she will be out of town for work. She said
the EDC can still meet, she just won't be present.
C. Cronin pointed out that they won't have a Vice Chair to run the meeting. K. Castaldo-
Rice suggested she could assign someone to run the meeting in her absence. She asked
C. Cronin to send an email to the EDC members about the February meeting and about
the start time in general.
3. Business Inventory and Contact Info
K. Castaldo-Rice thanked C. Cronin for combining their two lists into one. She does not
have a lot of business contacts in Pembroke to fill in the blanks, but she has a solution to
that.
D. Carlucci said he took it upon himself to deliver letters to the 30 businesses in the B1
and B2 Districts. The letter asks that the business owner email him if they have changes to
their contact information for the business directory. He said he hoped it was OK that he did
that.
K. Castaldo-Rice thanked D. Carlucci and said it's good for the EDC members to work with
the business community on a personal level. K. Castaldo-Rice took a copy of the list of
businesses that D. Carlucci approached so that the EDC would not duplicate efforts.
K. Castaldo-Rice said that all businesses have to register with the Secretary of State. The
spreadsheet was procured from the NH Employment Security listing and the Assessing
database of any property coded as commercial. She said the Secretary of State has
contact information for every business, the problem is that you have to search each
business individually, and we have over 200 businesses in our spreadsheet. It's time-
consuming, but useful. The reason we wanted EDC members to reach out and get info, is
because the EDC members may have relationships with these businesses, which may
result in a more accurate contact (ex. a person willing to work with us, not a generic email
address). Using the Secretary of State info is impersonal, but we are looking to survey
businesses and update the directory, so that's a way to do that.
D. Carlucci said that with the directory on the website, it's hard to know which businesses
are still in town. That's why he wanted to reach out. K. Castaldo-Rice agreed that it doesn't
help to have outdated information on the website.
C. Cronin offered some background on how the Town website business directory came to
be. That list was a voluntary list, not meant to be all-inclusive of every business in town.
Businesses that wanted to be listed had to fill out a form and return it to the town. The form
says to please inform the town if your business closes so we can remove it from the list,
but no one ever did that.
C. Cronin said that when the EDC wanted to put together the spreadsheet, she went
through the town business listing and tried to figure out what businesses were still in
operation. She entered that info as notes in the spreadsheet, in hopes that EDC members
might have better knowledge to confirm or deny that those businesses were still operable.

With that, she feels that the business directory on the website is secondary to the purpose
of the spreadsheet. The spreadsheet needs to be accurate so that we can survey the
businesses. We want to survey as many businesses as possible, and we don't want to
send surveys to places that are no longer in business or no longer in town. She explained
that at the last EDC meeting, there was talk about including a survey question asking
whether they would like to be added to the website directory. Once we have all the survey
responses, as part of our data processing, we can make note of who wants to be listed on
the website. She said that is why she is pushing for the accuracy and completeness of
information on the spreadsheet. If we put the effort to put a survey together, it's not worth it
if we only send it to 30 people.
C. Cronin said that at the last meeting, Bryan asked if there was any money to do a mailing
since we have addresses, but not necessarily emails, for these businesses. David said,
yes, there is some money if we want to mail a postcard with a QR Code or link to the
survey.
K. Castaldo-Rice said it doesn't hurt to send both an email and a mailing. The email may
end up in spam or people may be unlikely to click a link that they don't know.
C. Cronin said that what she needs help with, in the spreadsheet, is determining which
home businesses are still in business and also which businesses to delete. (There are
businesses that have multiple LLCs linking back to one business.) Those issues are noted
in the spreadsheet. She reiterated we need to check the list for accuracy and delete
duplicates where appropriate. K. Castaldo-Rice said Secretary of State may list which
businesses are associated with others, so we can delete as necessary.
K. Castaldo-Rice said she would like to continue with the charge to make sure that the list
is as accurate as possible, and she would like to start to venture into the Secretary of State
website to fill in the missing contact information. K. Castaldo-Rice will work on the first 100
businesses in the spreadsheet and C. Cronin will take the rest.

Carlucci seconded the motion. The Committee unanimously voted to approve the minutes.

Meeting Minutes
January 6, 2025
Attendance: Bryan Christiansen, Selectmen Rep.; Matt Roan, Clint Hanson, Planning
Board Rep.
Excused: Kate Castaldo-Rice, Chris Glenn, Dana Carlucci
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Business
1. Election of Chair and Vice Chair
B. Christiansen opened the meeting at 5:00 PM. C. Hanson noted that Kate has done a
great job in just a short amount of time and thinks she would make a good Chair. He said
that Kate is comfortable with him nominating her as Chair.
C. Hanson suggested that someone from the business community be Vice Chair. C.
Hanson and B. Christiansen agreed that the Chair and Vice Chair should not be
representatives to Selectboard and Planning Board since the Committee's job is to advise
those boards.
C. Hanson made a motion to nominate Kate Castaldo-Rice as Chair. M. Roan seconded
the motion. The Committee unanimously voted to elect Kate Castaldo-Rice as Chair.
The members decided to wait for a full Committee to nominate a Vice Chair postpone to
the next meeting.
B. Christiansen volunteered to run the rest of the meeting in Kate's absence.
2. Business Inventory and Contact Info
B. Christiansen noted that Kate and Carolyn did a good job putting together the business
list.
C. Cronin explained how the list was populated and what the next steps would be. She
believes that Kate pulled the Excel database from the Secretary of State's office, which is
a list of all registered businesses. It had several hundred businesses. The Assessing
Department provided a list of properties assessed as commercial. C. Cronin took the two
lists and tried to reconcile them, removing duplicates, removing properties that were
utilities or cell towers, etc. Since the goal is to send a link to a survey, the Committee
C:\Users\LWilliams\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\INetCache\Content.Outlook\3FVT66LG\01-06-2025 Minutes.docx
Page 1 of 4

needs to help fill in the blanks of the business contact information. The list was sent to the
Economic Development Committee (EDC) to review and make sure it is current and
accurate. C. Cronin admitted that this is tedious work, but it is very important to the
process.
B. Christiansen guessed that they had email addresses for about 30% of the 230
businesses listed. He noted that there is no budget for the EDC, but would like to see if the
Town could find funds to do to a mailing since we have the mailing addresses of all the
businesses. C. Cronin suggested a postcard could be printed and mailed with a link to the
survey.
3. Business Retention Survey
C. Cronin suggested there should be a bigger discussion with the whole EDC about the
purpose and the outcome of the survey: what information is the EDC looking for, what type
of questions to ask, etc.
B. Christiansen Googled other town's business retention surveys from around the country.
The surveys asked about demographics and sales, but his idea is how to catalog
businesses, retain them, and what we can do as a town. He suggested a simple survey, no
more than 10 questions.
M. Roan said that, as a business owner, he does not like surveys that ask for sales data
because it's not relevant. He said he would want to know why a business chose to locate
to Pembroke and why their specific location. He agreed we need to pare down the list and
make sure it's accurate.
B. Christiansen suggested there be an original master list of the businesses and that
members could edit their own copy of the list on their own time.
C. Cronin hoped that the EDC would have a discussion about the parameters of the survey
and who they intend to reach. The members' local knowledge of who is still in business or
not would be helpful. There were items she added that she thought were important
(properties actively soliciting tenants), but wanted to discuss with the full Committee. For
example, does the EDC want to reach home businesses, family farms, national
corporations? The EDC needs to discuss. She thinks that to answer those questions, the
EDC needs to have a larger discussion about the intention and the goal if the survey.
C. Cronin wanted to give her opinion as a discussion starter. Her suggested goals of the
survey are:
• To understand what businesses need from the community in order to be successful.
• To be able to help businesses with issues, where the Town is able.
• To make the businesses feel supported and heard by the Town.
She explained that the Town can't offer businesses big dollar incentives, but that we can
listen to issues and concerns, and help where we can. This Committee can have those
conversations with the businesses.

C. Hanson recalled the last EDC came up with the "Prosper in Pembroke" slogan on the
town signage. One question that frequently came up was what is holding small businesses
back when they would like to expand. What can the town provide for support? We have
lots of land in town. Housing is important, but other things can be looked at. There is
opportunity for businesses who might want to locate or expand close to Concord, but not
necessarily be in Concord.
B. Christiansen agreed with the goals of the survey, but there is only half the EDC present.
M. Roan added that the list is daunting. All agreed that the full EDC should work on the list
on their own time and note any changes. C. Cronin can combine any edits from individual
work into one list.
M. Roan suggested that the business list can be added to the town website for people to
review. B. Christiansen confirmed that all the information is public information, except for
the email addresses. C. Cronin suggested a survey question to ask if they would like to be
listed on the town website. B. Christiansen agreed and is in favor of asking that question in
the survey.
B. Christiansen suggested the full EDC meet again before February for the purposes of:
1. Electing a Vice Chair
2. Going over the business list
No other business to be conducted at that meeting.
Tuesday, January 21st was suggested as a tentative date. C. Cronin would send an email
to the full EDC to check availability.
B. Christiansen asked if anyone had any thoughts on survey questions.
M. Roan wants to know why choose Pembroke and why the specific part of town (ex. the
Village, Route 106, etc.) They may have a different perspective that we may never have
considered
B. Christiansen wants to know about permitting, utilities, traffic, and specifically things that
the town has some control over. He also wants to know what challenges they face.
C. Hanson said it's not just retention, but also expansion, and wants to know under what
conditions a business would need to expand and how the town could help.
C. Cronin shared the questions she brought to the meeting:
• What has been your experience doing business in Pembroke?
What are your plans for the future (ex. expand, downsize, relocate)?
What would help you succeed in your goals?
What do they think are the town's strengths and weaknesses?
• Are there any town processes that you've experienced that can be improved?
• Would it be OK for someone from this Committee to follow up with you on your
survey answers?
C. Cronin believes that last question is important because depending how questions or
answers are worded, you may not get the full picture. An in-person or phone conversation
can add a lot more context. That would be a great role for EDC members, to be that liaison
between the business and the town.

Rep.; Clint Hanson, Planning Board Rep; Chuck Schmidt; Brendan Williams
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Excused: Chuck Therrien
Business
1. EDC Facebook Page Business Spotlight Posts
The Committee reviewed responses to its Facebook outreach inviting local businesses to
participate in a business spotlight feature. Businesses identified for possible inclusion were
Monroe Plumbing and Heating, Majestic Moonbeam Farm, The Creative Duckling,
Kinstruct Tiny Homes, and Shirley's Kitchen. Members discussed using a short, consistent
question set for each spotlight and favored a brief written post with a business photo rather
than video. The Committee also discussed whether featured businesses should have a tax
ID. Majestic Moonbeam Farm was noted as not yet having one, and members supported
allowing time for that to be resolved while moving ahead with other businesses. By
consensus, the Committee chose to begin with Monroe Plumbing and Heating and to
prepare a standard list of questions that can be reused for future spotlights.
The set of questions that the EDC agreed upon were:

2) Where do your customers come from?
