MINUTES OF THE JULY 31, 2025
PEMBROKE CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT (CIP) COMMITTEE MEETING
PEMBROKE RECREATION WORKS REQUESTS
The CIP Committee held a meeting on July 31, 2025, at 6:00 p.m., at the Memorial Park Pavillion, Pembroke,
New Hampshire.
The meeting was called to order by Gerry Fleury at 6:07 p.m. Those present and absent were as follows:
PRESENT:
Gerry Fleury
David Jodoin
CIP, Budget Committee
Town Administrator
Matt Miller
Rosemarie Michaud
CIP, Selectman Representative
CIP, Resident
Gene Gauss
Bethany Chase-Reynolds

ALSO PRESENT:

Pembroke Recreation

CIP, Selectmen Rep

Matt Miller made a motion to approve the meeting minutes of July 24, 2025. Rosemarie Michaud seconded the
motion.
The minutes were approved on a 4-0 vote. Bethany Chase-Reynolds and Kathy Cruson abstained.
Pembroke Recreation - 2026 CIP Requests
Requests:
Stage and Roof Project
Pavillion Roof
Bathroom Renovation
$15,000
$10,000
$5,000
$30,000
Steve Fowler of the Pembroke Recreation Commission was present to discuss the CIP requests for 2026.
Gerry Fleury stated that Recreation is looking for a total of $30,000 for three projects. The bathrooms are
planned for 2030 at a cost of approximately $50,000.
Gerry Fleury spoke about attending meetings regarding the stage project. He stated that he has not been
impressed with the record keeping on how the project will be paid for. He mentioned two projects that had been
completed this year which were the gazebo roof and bathroom doors at Memorial Field. This had a total cost of
$11,000. The balance in the reserve is approximately $21,000 currently (after the $11,000 from this year's
projects is subtracted), plus a donation from Brady Sullivan in the amount of $20,000. They currently have
enough for the stage project.
Gerry Fleury added that the money in the reserve cannot be spent until March when there is approval at Town
Meeting. He also mentioned that the Selectboard may become agents to expend of this account through a
warrant article.
Gerry Fleury stated that it has been deemed that the stage is beyond repair. The new stage will be enclosed on
three sides and built on a slab. It will also be facing in a different direction. If approved, the project will
tentatively happen in a year's time.
Steve Fowler added that he was confused by the request of $15,000 when they are awaiting a revised estimate.
Steve Fowler also asked about assembly. He was unsure if this was part of the bid. Gerry Fleury added that
there were different kits discussed. It was agreed that the cedar model was selected and there was no assembly
included. Volunteers would need to build the current model under discussion.
Gerry Fleury stated that the turnkey option (which included assembly) was rejected because the company
wanted to do the project right away.
Rosemarie Michaud asked about volunteers putting the stage together and asked if it would be insured. David
Jodoin confirmed that it could be insured.
Steve Fowler asked if it there was a definite number for the cost of the stage. Gerry Fleury noted that the cost of
the slab came in at $9,800. David Jodoin recalls it being $35,000 total, and possibly $40,000 with inflation
considered for next year.

Bethany Chase-Reynolds expressed concern over not using insured contractors for the project.
Steve Fowler asked about potential inflation costs. Gerry Fleury explained that money can be shifted from other
projects if necessary.
Kathy Cruson asked about the bathroom renovations. Steve Fowler stated that this project is mostly to bring the
bathrooms into ADA compliance.
Gene Gauss spoke about the cost of the pavilion roof ($30,000). This is planned for 2028. Gene Gauss thinks
this is an extremely high estimate based on the replacement of the roof at his residence. There was some
discussion about different approaches to the project.
Matt Miller suggested a metal roof because it would last forever. There was some discussion of this as an
option.
Rosemarie asked how often the stage is used. David Jodoin stated that it is used by the Recreation Department
for children in the summer and it is used for Old Home Day. Steve Fowler added that it is also used for concerts
in the park during the summer.
Steve Fowler made a comment about the delay of the stage replacement with a roof over many years. He stated
that the Pembroke Recreation Commission would be extremely happy if this project could be completed.
Gerry provided some insight regarding putting a roof on the existing stage and how that is problematic because
it is a hexagon. The recommendation has been for the stage to be replaced due to its current condition. Also,
spinning it in a different direction will improve the experience for both performers and the audience.
Moving on to a different subject, Matt Miller spoke about the Energy Committee looking at ways to save
money. The Safety Center is the largest energy consumer, with the transfer station next. They have asked two
solar companies to visit the Safety Center and to provide proposals. He will be providing an update next week.
Gerry Fleury mentioned that there is approximately $30,000 in the Energy Capital Receive. Matt Miller stated
that the proposals ranged from $142,000 to $250,000. This does not include potential credits.
There was also discussion about the Safety Center roof being approximately 22 years old. One proposal
suggested replacing part of the roof. The recommendation for the roof placement stems from the solar panels
lasting approximately 30 years. It would be an additional cost to remove and reinstall the panels when it came
time to replace the roof.
Gerry Fleury stated that there would need to be a cost/benefit breakeven analysis for a project of this size. Matt
Miller agreed that an analysis could be prepared.
The next meeting will take place at Pembroke Academy to discuss the School District's 2026 CIP Requests and
to further discuss the installation of solar panels at the Safety Center.
There being no further business to come before the Committee, Gene Gauss made a motion to adjourn, the
motion was seconded by Matt Miller, and the meeting was adjourned at 6:43 p.m.

MINUTES OF THE JULY 24, 2025
PEMBROKE CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT (CIP) COMMITTEE MEETING
ROADS AND PUBLIC WORKS REQUESTS
The CIP Committee held a meeting on July 24, 2025, at 6:00 p.m., at Pembroke Public Works, Pembroke, New
Hampshire.
The meeting was called to order by Gerry Fleury at 6:04 p.m. Those present and absent were as follows:
PRESENT:
Gerry Fleury
CIP, Budget Committee
Matt Miller
CIP, Selectman Alternate
Gene Gauss
CIP, School Board
Stephanie Cravotta
CIP, Planning Board Rep
ALSO PRESENT:
VJ Ranfos
Director, Pembroke Public Works
EXCUSED:
Bethany Chase-Reynolds
CIP, Resident
David Jodoin
Town Administrator
Rosemarie Michaud
CIP, Resident
Andrew Yonchak
CIP, Resident
Kate Castaldo-Rice
Recording Secretary
Adam Mendozza
Pembroke Public Works
Karen Yeaton
CIP, Selectmen Rep

Gene Gauss made a motion to approve the meeting minutes of August 22, 2024. Rosemarie Michaud seconded
the motion.
There was one correction to the minutes. There was a typo calling it a "pubic hearing" instead of a "public
hearing." There were no other changes or amendments.
The minutes were approved on a 4-0 vote. Stephanie Cravotta abstained.
Gene Gauss made a motion to approve the meeting minutes of July 17, 2025. Rosemarie Michaud seconded the
motion.
There was one correction to the minutes. There was a typo where "they" needed to be changed to "the."
The minutes were approved on a 3-0 vote with Stephanie Cravotta and Andrew Yonchak abstaining.
Roads - 2026 CIP Requests
Gerry Fleury stated that the first item is the Roads Budget, which is in the Operating Budget and not a Capital
Improvements item.
David Jodoin noted that they are looking for three items in the operating budget, sidewalk maintenance, paving
project and normal paving. They are looking for $850,000 for the Roads Operating Budget.
There was discussion about the CIP item requests, which are listed below.
Requests:
Deerpath Lane Road Improvement
Fairview Avenue and Renarl Avenue Improvement
Memorial Park Shoreline Restoration
Memorial Park Drainage Project
$1,100,000
$760,000
$810,000
$820,000
$3,490,000
Gerry Fleury asked VJ Ranfos to discuss the proposed projects. He also inquired about the loans and loan
forgiveness associated with some of the projects.
VJ Ranfos explained that there was a loan applied for and loan forgiveness for the Memorial Park Shoreline
Restoration Project and the Memorial Park Drainage Project. They applied for a loan through the Clean Water
State Revolving Fund through the Department of Environmental Services (DES). DES had advised to split the
application into two projects. The Memorial Park Drainage Project was ranked second of nine proposed
projects. Memorial Park Shoreline Stabilization Project ranked third.
VJ Ranfos continued to explain the loan forgiveness portion of the loans, which is equal to 15% of the principal
of the loan. This is a total loan forgiveness of $244,500.
Gerry Fleury noted that this is contingent upon approval at Town Meeting. VJ Ranfos noted that this requires
the residents to approve the total of the projects.

Gene Gauss asked what happens if this does not get approved at Town Meeting. He asked what penalization
would apply from the state or federal government if these projects were not approved. VJ Ranfos stated that he
could not answer that question. Gene Gauss is concerned as to how to sell these projects to residents.
Andrew asked if there are examples of towns being penalized. VJ Ranfos has heard of towns being fined for not
meeting MS-4 requirements. The drainage project is more related to the MS-4 requirements.
Gerry spoke about the erosion of the Suncook River. He noted that he has seen and documented the shoreline
moving back over time. He mentioned that someone has done some survey work down there. VJ Ranfos stated
that this is current work that is being done. Gerry asked to see the plans once they are prepared.
VJ added that DES feels that both projects are important given their rankings.
Gerry Fleury moved the discussion to the $850,000 for Road Construction. He noted that this is an increase of
$50,000 over last year.
VJ Ranfos stated that there were two roads that they ran out of money for this year. He added that the Roads
Committee had suggested a budget of $1.5 million, but Public Works is trying to increase the budget in small
manageable increments.
Gerry Fleury listed the roads that are planned as part of the budget request. VJ Ranfos spoke about their work
with Central New Hampshire Regional Planning Commission (CHRPC) on the prioritization of projects.
Gene Gauss spoke about letting some of the roads going back to dirt and asked about the impacts on
maintenance. VJ Ranfos stated that dirt roads are harder to maintain. The only dirt roads left in town are Nixon
Road and Sand Road.
Rosemarie Michaud asked about paving on Fourth Range Road up near Brickett Hill Road. VJ Ranfos noted
that because of the construction in the San Ken Homes Development, they will be waiting to do paving in this
area.
Gerry Fleury questioned the customary $10,000 request for the cemetery. David Jodoin stated that this has been
retracted and there is no current request for funding. VJ Ranfos confirmed this.
Gerry Fleury asked if the work had been completed at the entrances of Evergreen cemetery. VJ Ranfos
confirmed that one entrance had been completed.
Gene Gauss suggested that they need to spend the money to expand and generate revenue. VJ Ranfos noted that
there has been an interest in an ash garden to spread ashes.
Rosemarie Michaud asked about Perpetual Care. Gerry Fleury noted that Perpetual Care lots are no longer sold,
but maintenance on existing lots is grandfathered. This is used to repair tombstones, etc. The town can ask for a
percentage of maintenance for those Perpetual Care Graves. He noted that the trust has more money in accrued
interest than in principle.
Andrew Yonchak circled back to the Deerpath Lane and Fairview and Renarl Projects. He asked if these were
scheduled projects. VJ Ranfos explained that they are larger than just maintenance or re-pavement. There are
drainage concerns that need to be addressed. The plan is to bond both projects together.

MINUTES OF THE JULY 17, 2025
PEMBROKE CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT (CIP) COMMITTEE MEETING
AMBULANCE, POLICE, AND FIRE REQUESTS
The CIP Committee held a meeting on July 17, 2025, at 6:00 p.m., at Pembroke Safety Center, Pembroke, New
Hampshire.
The meeting was called to order by Gerry Fleury at 6:00 p.m. Those present and absent were as follows:
PRESENT:
Gerry Fleury
CIP, Budget Committee
Matt Miller
CIP, Selectman Alternate
Gene Gauss
CIP, School Board
ALSO PRESENT:
Chris Gamache
Director, Pembroke EMS
Erik Paulsen
Chief, Pembroke Fire Department
EXCUSED:
Andrew Yonchak
CIP, Resident
Stephanie Cravotta
CIP, Planning Board Rep
Kate Castaldo-Rice
Recording Secretary
David Jodoin
Town Administrator
Rosemarie Michaud
CIP, Resident
Gary Gaskell
Chief, Pembroke Police Department
Robert Farley
Assistant Chief, Pembroke Fire Department
CIr, Resiase Reynolds
Karen Yeaton
CIP, Selectmen Rep

First on the agenda was the election of Chairman and Vice Chairman of the CIP Committee.
Rosemarie Michaud nominated Gerry Fleury as Chairman, Matt Miller seconded the motion. It was approved
unanimously.
Gerry Fleury nominated Rosemarie Michaud as Vice Chairman, Gene Gauss seconded the motion. It was
approved unanimously.
Gerry Fleury stated that Pembroke EMS would present first.
Ambulance - 2026 CIP Requests
Requests:
Annual Capital Reserve Funding Request
$130,000
$130,000
Chris Gamache, Director of Pembroke EMS, explained that they had just finished their replacement cycle for
equipment and that the new ambulance is in service. They are now preparing for the next cycle and maintaining
the old truck. Unless something unforeseen happens, this will be the plan for the next couple of years.
Gerry Fleury mentioned that the cardiac monitor, which was a big-ticket item, had already been purchased.
Director Gamache confirmed the purchase and operation of the cardiac monitor.
Rosemarie Michaud asked what the next big-ticket item would be for Pembroke EMS and in what year they
would be looking to make the purchase. Director Gamache stated that in three to four years, they would be
looking to purchase a new ambulance, which has a lead time of approximately 36 months. The new ambulance,
that is currently in service, was ordered in 2022.
There was some discussion about the payment schedule for a new ambulance, and the deposit would be
approximately 15% of the total cost, but this does not lock in the price. Director Gamache explained that they
paid approximately $20,000 over the initial quoted cost for the current ambulance.
Gerry Fleury spoke about some research that he has done on the market for emergency vehicles and the large
margins being made on these vehicles. Director Gamache added that large departments are ordering vehicles
early in anticipation of their replacement cycles and this is creating artificial demand.
David Jodoin suggested possibly purchasing a chassis and putting the current box on it to save money. Director
Gamache stated that this could be an option, but he was unsure of refurbishment costs.
Gerry Fleury spoke about the current process for emergency vehicle purchases. Currently, deposits are made
into the capital reserve to fund such purchases. He questioned at what point the Town should consider bonding
some of these purchases. Matt Miller added that if the life span of the vehicle is similar to the bond terms, this
may make sense.
Pembroke Police Department - 2026 CIP Requests
Requests:
Police Cruiser
Portable Radios
Camera Security and Access Control
$48,000
$75,000
$175,000
$298,000

Gerry Fleury spoke about the request for a new cruiser. He spoke about CIP reviewing items that are funded
through Capital Reserve Accounts. He questioned whether the cruiser would need to be subject to the CIP
process since it would be a budget line item in the operating budget. There was some discussion about the
possibility of a year where the Department needed more than one cruiser, and in this case, Chief Gaskell stated
that he would bring that forward to CIP.
Chief Gaskell explained the status of the Department's cruisers. There are currently five without warranty. The
cruiser that they are seeking to replace is the oldest and has the most mileage and engine hours.
Gerry Fleury mentioned the high cost of portable radios and cameras. He asked if they were manufactured in
China. Chief Gaskell stated that he would get this information for him. There may be compliance related
reasons for the cost due to the products needing to be made domestically for this purpose.
Matt Miller spoke about assets being tracked outside of CIP. David Jodoin confirmed that the cruiser would still
be tracked as an asset outside of the CIP process. He noted that anything that has a value greater than $10,000 is
considered an asset and tracked regardless of CIP status.
Matt Miller does not feel that hearing about the cruisers in CIP is a bad thing, even if it does not need to be
approved by the Committee. It would not be voted on, but CIP could be made aware. Gerry Fleury noted that
nothing is approved at CIP, it is only ranked. Matt Miller added that this does still hold weight. The Committee
agreed that cruisers, even when in the operating budget, would be reported to CIP, but not ranked.
Gerry Fleury shifted the conversation to the portable radio request. Chief Gaskell stated that the current radios
were purchased approximately 11 years prior. He explained that there are no more spare radios if they are fully
staffed. He continued that the current radios are obsolete and cannot be repaired at this point.
Gerry Fleury asked Rob Farley about the radios and why they have such a high cost since he is a ham (amateur)
radio operator. Rob Farley stated that these radios are specifically made for public safety. They have a higher
degree of sensitivity and are more durable than a typical radio. They are software controlled.
Gerry Fleury stated that the manufacturer should not make a difference and asked if it is a matter of choice.
Chief Gaskell explained that both brands in question have a three-year warranty and they are both used by
surrounding towns.
Matt Miller asked about the lifespan of new radios and how long the manufacturer will support the devices.
Chief Gaskell reiterated that the warranty is for a three-year period, but that the manufacturer will probably
make parts for approximately five to seven years.
Matt Miller asked if all hospitals, schools, etc. use this type of device. Rob Farley explained that these are
standard, and the technology is used by these facilities.
There was discussion about the schools purchasing different radios a few years back, and now public safety
must carry two radios in order to communicate with the schools. There was further discussion about different
entities that should coordinate radios in the case of an emergency.
Chief Gaskell spoke about wanting to go with the Viking radios as this is what County Dispatch uses. Matt
Miller asked if these radios will be compatible with the school's radios. Chief Gaskell stated that he would be
requesting some dual band radios for this purpose, but not all the radios would be dual band and able to talk to
the schools.

Re:
2027 CIP Request for the Purchase of Two Police Patrol Electronic Bikes (E-Bikes)
2027 CIP Request Explanation: Police Patrol Electronic Bikes (E-Bikes)
The Pembroke Police Department respectfully requests approval to utilize Capital
Improvement Plan (CIP) funds from the Police Small Equipment Fund to purchase two
electric patrol bicycles (e-bikes) and associated police equipment for deployment as part of
the Department's community policing and patrol operations.
The Department currently maintains a bicycle patrol program utilizing traditional
mountain bikes. However, three of the Department's four patrol bicycles are at or
approaching 20 years of service, having been purchased in 2005, 2006, and 2007. As these
bicycles continue to age, obtaining replacement parts and performing necessary repairs
have become increasingly difficult, resulting in higher maintenance challenges and
concerns regarding long-term reliability. The Department's fourth patrol bicycle,
purchased in 2019, is also approaching eight years of service. Replacing a portion of the
bicycle fleet with modern police e-bikes will ensure officers have reliable equipment while
significantly enhancing patrol capabilities.
Recognizing the benefits of electric patrol bicycles, the Department previously applied for
grant funding in the fall of 2025 to purchase this equipment. Although the application was
not selected for funding, the Department remains committed to pursuing grant
opportunities and will continue to seek available funding that could offset or potentially
cover the cost of this purchase. However, rather than delaying the project indefinitely
while awaiting uncertain grant opportunities, the Department requests authorization to
utilize available CIP Small Equipment funds for the full purchase amount after a vendor is
selected if grant funding is unavailable or the Department is again unsuccessful in securing
an award
The addition of e-bikes will enhance the Department's ability to provide proactive, visible
policing while improving mobility and response capabilities in areas where traditional
patrol vehicles may be less effective. While conventional mountain bikes have long been
recognized as valuable tools for community policing, modern police e-bikes offer several
significant operational advantages.
1

Key benefits of police e-bikes include:
• Expanded Patrol Coverage: Electric pedal assistance allows officers to cover
substantially greater distances during a shift without excessive physical fatigue.
This enables more consistent patrol coverage throughout the Village area and other
high-traffic locations.
• Improved Response Times: Officers can respond more quickly to calls for
service, suspicious activity, or citizen requests in areas where patrol vehicles may
be delayed by traffic, pedestrians, or limited vehicle access.
• Enhanced Terrain Capability: The electric assist motor enables officers to
navigate hills and uneven terrain with greater ease than traditional bicycles, making
patrols practical in neighborhoods with challenging topography.
• Greater Operational Flexibility: With increased range and reduced officer
fatigue, e-bikes can be effectively deployed beyond the Village area into more
congested residential neighborhoods, parks, trails, and other locations where
vehicle access is limited or inefficient.
• Increased Community Engagement: Bicycle patrols allow officers to interact
more naturally with residents, business owners, and visitors, strengthening
community relationships while maintaining a highly visible law enforcement
presence.
Reduced Vehicle Use: Utilizing e-bikes for appropriate patrol assignments reduces
reliance on marked cruisers for short-distance patrols, contributing to lower fuel
consumption and reduced vehicle wear and maintenance costs.
The primary deployment area for the e-bikes will be the Village area, where bicycle
patrols provide an effective and approachable law enforcement presence. However, the
enhanced range and hill-climbing capability of e-bikes will also allow officers to patrol
more congested residential neighborhoods, parks, and other areas where vehicle patrols are
less practical while maintaining the ability to respond efficiently throughout Town.
The e-bikes will also serve as valuable assets during community events and large public
gatherings where vehicle access is restricted or pedestrian traffic is significant. These
include, but are not limited to:
• Old Home Day
• Halloween Trick-or-Treat activities
• The annual Regatta
• Other community events requiring increased police visibility and rapid mobility
These events often require officers to navigate crowded streets, parks, and pedestrian areas
where e-bikes provide a distinct operational advantage over both patrol cruisers and
traditional bicycles.
Funding for this purchase is available within the Police Small Equipment Fund established
through the Capital Improvement Plan. No additional appropriation is requested. Utilizing
existing CIP funds allows the Department to move forward with replacing aging

PEMBROKE CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT (CIP) COMMITTEE MEETING
PEMBROKE TOWN HALL
The CIP Committee held a meeting on August 13, 2026, at 6:00 PM., at Pembroke Town Hall.
The meeting was called to order by Rosemarie Michaud at 6:02 PM. Those present and absent were as follows:
PRESENT:
Rosemarie Michaud
CIP, Resident
Matt Miller
CIP, Selectboard Rep.
Kathy Cruson
CIP, Planning Board Rep.
David Jodoin
Town Administrator
Michael Rodney
CIP, Resident
Gene Gauss
CIP, School Board Rep.
ALSO PRESENT:
Richard Wengenroth
Energy Committee Chair
Chief Dawn Shea
Pembroke Police
Lt. Chris Cunha
Pembroke Police
EXCUSED:
Karen Yeaton
CIP, Selectboard Alt. Rep.
Approval of Minutes
Motion by Michael Rodney to accept the minutes of August 6th, seconded by Kathy Cruson. Motion passed 5-0.
Police Department - 2027 CIP Requests
Chief Shea and Lieutenant Cunha were in to present their 2027 CIP.
Chief Shea stated you're all aware we have a mountain bike program that we've had since I was the first
mountain bike officer in the town of Pembroke 20+ years ago. All of our bikes are aging past the point of being
repaired
With the development of technology and also what we're dealing with out there now, I know E-bikes are a hot
topic in this community and we are trying to wrap our head around how to enforce.

To replace out current mountain bikes with e-bikes is a more prudent way to go at this point. Pricing isn't
frankly that much different between the traditional mountain bikes that are built for police patrol and this gives
us the expanded capacity to go further during our patrols. We struggle right now if we have only one officer on
duty it's hard to deploy a mountain bike because of the delay in the response time.
Purchasing these bikes kind of gives us the ability to go further, do more things, while still being out of the
cruisers. It is proven in community policing that when you are out in public making contact with residents it's
much better than through the window of a cruiser.
The officer will stop to talk to people and have a little bit more face to face interaction, a little friendlier
presence and kind of gives us that ability to have those interactions with the public.
Kathy Cruson stated that a person saw the CIP request and said to me "why can't they just ride bikes like
everybody else." Kathy said that she told the person that the Police are dealing with a lot of e-bike issues now in
the community.
Chief Shea agreed that it's a challenge that's not unique to Pembroke unfortunately right now every community
in the state of New Hampshire is kind of grappling with this problem of how to educate, regulate, and enforce
the uptick of motorized scooters, motorized bicycles, e-bikes, what is permitted and what's not and where they
can ride. Right now under our town ordinance we restrict to some degree but that is something that we're going
to need to look at and probably expand.
Selectman Miller commented that he thought it's good if the police have e-bikes because that'll give you more
credibility especially if you're starting to do more of the public outreach and education if you have e-bikes. It's
going to be hard to hear a message about e-bike safety if you don't have any e-bikes.
Selectman Millers questions for the Chief were kind of related to the ancillary stuff that you might need to
support e-bikes. He commented that you may need to haul the e-bike somewhere where you're going to patrol
and some of the places are really close to the police station like Memorial Park and Donna Drive and all that but
there might be other places where you go and it's remote and you have to get your bikes out there. So I'm just
curious if you could say a couple of things about hauling the bikes or any other things that you need to support
the full use of the e-bikes.
Chief Shea commented that it's a little bit of an unknown on that right now because of the weight and the
capacity of the bikes. We do have bike racks for our standard bikes now that they have the capacity of like 3
bikes. We need to explore if these racks will work with the proposed E-bikes.
We also, as you know, our next vehicle is going to be a pickup truck which gives us a little bit more options to
haul them. Right now we'd be looking at deploying these primarily in the village area, Tina, Smith, maybe
Donna Drive and none of those are too far from centralized if they start from the PD.
Selectman Miller commented that he had hoped that the request includes whatever else you'll need to support
the bikes.
Michael Rodney stated that he felt that community policing is great idea and are we looking at increasing
patrols

Chief Shea stated that we would like to ideally use them all summer long if we can structure our schedule that
we have extra coverage it will make it a no-brainer but we've been running low on personnel. We are currently
down two positions that we're trying to fill.
Lieutenant Cunha stated that the top speed is 28 mph on these bikes.
Chief Shea stated that the range that they are looking at on the two is about 50 to 60 miles on a full charge at
full speed.
Lieutenant Cunha added right now our bike officers are the Chief, myself, our Detective Sergeant, our SRO, and
then 1 patrol officer. So we're looking to put at least 1 maybe 2 more officers through that school next year to
get them certified to be able to do this.
Selectman Miller commented that he looked up the weight and they are 80 pounds.
Chief Shea commented that the motor portion of the bikes is easier to service through local bike shops so you
don't necessarily need a specialized dealer to service them.
Gene Gauss asked about the lifespan of the batteries.
Michael Rodney commented that he had looked it up and it's just 3 to 5 years depending upon a lot of factors
whether you drain it all the way down which would reduce your effective range and then storage obviously if
it's over 90 degrees it's going to go bad an if it's really cold it's going to go bad quicker also. I looked up the
costs which is a very close tight range actually its $300 to $1200 so you can really just throw a number out
there, $300 to $1200 but you could expect in 3 years that for two bikes it's going to be upwards of $2400 to
replace the batteries.
Rosemarie Michaud commented that the plan is to get 2 electric bikes. Now is there a plan down the road to get
more or are you going to just have two.
Chief Shea stated that ideally I would like to probably add maybe 2 more down the road. If we are able to get
more of our officers trained we would deploy during Halloween, some in the village, and some in the Donna
Drive area.
Rosemarie Michaud what months would they be used?
Chief Shea stated that they would use them as much as they could but it depended on available officers.
Michael Rodney asked one last question, and that was the companies offering these E-bikes.
Chief Shea stated that she had two companies that they were looking at Recon and Transcor which carried the
Police package.
Energy Committee
Richard Wengenroth introduced himself as the Chair of the Energy Committee.
The first discussion was about the Library request for Solar.

MINUTES OF THE AUGUST 6, 2026
PEMBROKE CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT (CIP) COMMITTEE MEETING
PEMBROKE SCHOOL DISTRICT REQUESTS
The CIP Committee held a meeting on August 6, 2026, at 6:00 p.m., at Pembroke Academy Cafeteria.
The meeting was called to order by Rosemarie Michaud at 6:08 p.m. Those present and absent were as follows:
PRESENT:
Rosemarie Michaud
CIP, Resident
Matt Miller
CIP, Selectboard Rep.
Kathy Cruson
CIP, Planning Board Rep.
David Jodoin
Town Administrator
Michael Rodney
CIP, Resident
Gene Gauss
CIP, School Board Rep.
ALSO PRESENT:
Josh Coughlin
Facilities Director, Pembroke Schools
EXCUSED:
Karen Yeaton
CIP, Selectboard Alt. Rep.
Matt Miller made a motion to approve the meeting minutes of July 30, 2026 as presented. Kathy Cruson
seconded the motion.
Minutes were approved by a 4-0 vote. Gene Gauss abstained.
Josh Coughlin Facilities Director presented the 2027/28 Pembroke School District proposals.
Pembroke School District - 2027/28 CIP Requests
Josh Coughlin commented that he had historically over the years he explained to the CIP Committee the
requested funds that they were looking at as well as the expenses.
The first account discussed was the Vehicle Replacement Capital Reserve Fund. Josh Coughlin explained that
they were looking for a $12,000 deposit for the 2027/28 school year from year end surplus funds if they were
available.
Rosemarie Michaud asked what years the trucks were purchased. Josh Coughlin apologized for not having that
information but he could get it if needed.

Josh Coughlin explained that the next fund would be the School Building Capital Reserve Funds and they
would be looking at depositing $200,000 into this fund if there are surplus funds remaining. Josh Coughlin
commented that for years the amount had been at $155,000 and he always commented that the funding was too
low due to increased costs for supplies.
Josh Coughlin stated that they would draw $20,000 out of the Fund for replacement flooring and $300,000 for
roof replacement at the Academic Wing at Pembroke Academy.
Rosemarie Michaud asked where the flooring would be replaced. Josh Coughlin explained that it would be
district wide wherever the need was the greatest.
Kathy Cruson asked what the age of the Academic roof was. Josh Coughlin commented that it was the original
roof circa 1999/2000 and they are starting to chase water leaks
Rosemarie Michaud asked if the projects would go out to bid.
Josh Coughlin confirmed that they would and they try and always get three bids but there have been times when
they have only received one.
Josh Coughlin explained that the next item would be the School Technology Capital Reserve Fund and the
district would be looking at depositing $10,000 in this fund with no withdrawals.
Josh Coughlin commented that the next item would be the School Site Improvement Capital Reserve Fund
where they would be looking at depositing $75,000 into this fund if there are any surplus funds remaining and
the following year we would look to increase it to $100,000. This fund is specifically for paving. Over the last
20 years the Pembroke School District has not done much paving but we are setting up a plan to be more
consistent with paving something each year.
Kathy Cruson asked if this fund also covered possible work on the fields. Josh Coughlin confirmed this it was.
Rosemarie Michaud questioned whether there would be an opportunity for the Town and School to work
together on potential bidding.
Josh Coughlin stated that he regularly speaks with the Public Works Director but because of timing and
different year ends it is very difficult.
Matt Miller asked if there were more extensive projects that were on the horizon. Josh Coughlin stated that
there were some small projects and he should probably have listed some future field work which he will add but
it's nothing major, the major item here is paving.
Rosemarie Michaud asked about the line Old Entrance Design /PA. Josh Coughlin explained there is an area on
site that is blocked off that will need to be addressed at some point.
Josh Coughlin then went over the next fund the School Equipment Capital Reserve Fund and the request to
deposit $25,000 into that fund if surplus funds remained at the yearend while also removing $10,000 for
cameras and maintenance. Josh stated that overall that is the schools CIP request for this year.

Rosemarie Michaud questioned the future purchases of the scrubbers and how many the district had. Josh
Coughlin explained that depending on funding there may be a purchase this year and the school has three
machines one for each building.
Kathy Cruson asked who repairs the trucks. Josh Coughlin commented that they are serviced in Town at
Pellerin Motorsports. Anything factory warranty they are brought to the dealership.
Rosemarie Michaud questioned the future tractor purchases. Josh Coughlin explained what equipment the
Pembroke School District currently had.
There being no further business to come before the Committee, Matt Miller made a motion to adjourn, the
motion was seconded by Gene Gauss, and the meeting was adjourned at 6:38 p.m.

Adult Softball Field - The commission has run weekend tournaments that have been very profitable to
the commission. Over time, sediment builds up on the edge creating a raised edge. We are asking to
laser grade the adult infield and re-cut the diamond to ensure player safety and to be able to hold
weekend tournaments. This spring we brought approximately close to $3,000. Tournaments are being
planned now for the fall which will add more revenue to recreation.
Point Field -
Last fall, the Suncook Little League advised the Pembroke Recreation Commission that they would again
be offering softball programming for young female athletes in the Suncook area. This notification also
served to inform the Recreation Commission that they would need to improve a field for softball access a
Memorial Park. With the growth of the girl's program, and the adult field being used by the Co-Ed
leagues and for weekend tournaments, we need to find a field dedicated to the softball as the same
standard as the boys' fields.
One of the recommendations made by the commission involved modifying the "Point Field," to be the
girls' primary softball field. The Point Field is currently being utilized for Little League Farm and T-Ball
divisions. The commission felt this option is the most fiscally responsible and offers the most equitable
option for a quality field, whereas it has enclosed dugouts and a permanent fence.
Modifications would be an all-dirt infield leveled with ball field/infield mix.
Little League did submit a comprehensive plan to restore the "Middle Field," and utilize that as the primary
softball field. The plans also included a detailed list of expenses, which estimate the completed cost of the
restoration at approximately $20,000.00. The commission is less favorable to this idea due to the
uncertainty involving the landfill that is located in the area of the Middle Field and the effects it may have
on the restored field. It is also worth noting that a sizable section of the Middle Field outfield doubles as a
parking area for the Regatta, Old Home Day, and special events. This would restrict the installation of any
type of home run fence.
The commission is asking to put $6,500 towards this project.

the recreation roof which is rotting. There were two estimates that came in and the Building Committee
recommended the vendor who will be removing the entire existing roof and replacing it with new shingles.
Matt Miller questioned the roofing quotes and how the work would be completed.
Rose Galligan explained that the Building Committee said that the quote to remove everything was the better of
the two and recommended proceeding with that one.
The second request for $13,000 that was discussed was the softball fields. Sandy Goulet explained that the
Recreation Commission had run weekend tournaments on the Adult Field and those have been very profitable.
The commission is asking for funding to laser grade the infield and re-cut the diamond to insure player safety.
One of the recommendations made by the Recreation Commission was to modify the Point Field to be the girl's
primary softball field. The Point Field is currently being used for the Little League Farm Team and T-Ball. The
Recreation Commission felt this option was the most fiscally responsible and offers the most equitable option
for a quality field, whereas it has enclosed dugouts and a permanent fence.
For the Point Field, Suncook Little League advised the Recreation Commission that they would be running a
girls softball program and that field improvements would need to be done.
Suncook Little League submitted a comprehensive plan to restore the Point Field at a cost of approximately
$22,000.
Matt Miller questioned the costs of $13,000 for the fields.
Sandy Goulet explained that the Recreation Commission didn't want to ask for more than $30,000 in total and
that they would prioritize the work on the fields.
Dale Arnt Suncook Little League explained that the League was looking at making upgrades to the field that
wouldn't require water by installing stone dust.

Matt Petersons commented that the material to be used on the field would ultimately be discussed with the
Recreation Commission before anything was done.
Matt Miller asked how this project would be managed and supervised if it were to be approved considering the
issues in the past with the previous dugout build.
Matt Petersons Suncook Little league stated that they have a group of volunteers now who take care of field
maintenance.
Sandy Goulet explained that not all of the numbers have been finalized so far and that she would be managing
the program when it came to the upgrades.
Michael Rodney brought up the $13,000 costs for the field repairs and that could theoretically be zero if we
were able to have sponsored advertisement and that would keep the costs off of the taxpayers.
Michael Rodney commented that he felt that the $13,000 request this year would continue for needed repairs
and upgrades.
Sandy Goulet explained that she has brought the idea of banners to the Selectboard and they were not in favor
of this.
Matt Petersons Suncook Little League commented that he felt that there were ways of having signage that is
done right and would not be an eyesore.
Matt Miller suggested coming up with a comprehensive plan of what would be done and the costs because he
was afraid that there may be issues that come up and the project does not get completed in its entirety.
Dale Arnt Suncook Little League commented that the Little League Board had been focusing on the Point Field
and the necessary repairs needed.
David Jodoin explained that the next meeting will take place at Pembroke Academy in the Cafeteria to discuss
the School District's 2027 28 CIP Requests.

Discrepancies In Location of Heiser Conservation Area Northwestern Boundary
The Pembroke Conservation Commission has conducted GPS surveys of all boundaries and corner
points of Town conservation properties. Results from these surveys are used to quickly find boundaries
during field monitoring visits to the properties. GPS points are always checked against corresponding
points on the Town's assessment map, maintained by AxisGIS. In most instances GPS points collected
by the PCC are within reasonable distances (<20 feet) from corners identified on the assessment maps,
considering the accuracy limitations of hand-held GPS receivers. However, in the case of the
northwestern boundary of the Heiser parcel (941-0042), we have found a discrepancy whereby AxisGIS
points are consistently shifted to the southeast of GIS locations. The distance of the shift varies from 18
to 93 feet. We are confident of the GIS locations because the boundary follows stone walls which are
readily identified in the field and on arial imagery. We have also repeatedly surveyed these points with
little variation between GIS surveys. We recognize that AxisGIS (and the Town) must deal with maps
and deed descriptions which vary in accuracy and can change over time such that parcel boundaries are
not totally consistent. We also recognize that the differences we have identified may have no
consequences for Town administration. However, because these differences are significantly larger than
we normally experience, we felt it important to bring it to your attention. Listed below is a series of

PEMBROKE CONSERVATION COMMISSION
MEETING MINUTES
October 13, 2025
In attendance: Ammy Heiser (Co-Chair), Erin Insley (Co-Chair), Carol Bertsimas (Vice Chair), Brian
Mrazik (Secretary), Ayn Whytemare, Robert Bourque (PB Rep)
Absent: Wendy Weisiger, Karen Yeaton (BOS Rep)
Guests: Jeff Evans, Five Rivers Conservation Trust; Elaina Enzien and Adam Taschereau, Gelinas Farm
Call to Order: Meeting called to order at 7:08 PM.
Planning Board Applications: None
NHDES Letters and Applications: None
Zoning Board Applications: None
Potential Acquisitions:
1. Lariviere: Ammy reported that the deed language has been finalized and that it included additional
protections to ensure that the property will not be used for purposes other than conservation in the
future. Capital Appraisal Associates will begin work on the appraisal of the property in early December
and it should be complete before the end of the year.
2. Phipps: No change in status. Ammy will contact Jim Powers, the real estate broker for the Plourde
property, to determine its status relative to potential procurement by the CC.
3. Gelinas Farm: Jeff Evans, Director of Conservation for the Five Rivers Conservation Trust, stated
that FRCT was working with the farm owners, Elaina Enzien and Adam Taschereau, to place the ~ 60-
acre farm under a conservation easement. The farm has been used for equestrian lessons, events and
boarding, as well as beef cattle grazing, for many decades. The owners wish to continue farm operations,
as in the past, but are concerned that increasing development pressure in the 4" Range Road area will
eventually lead to the loss of the farm and the rural/agricultural character of the landscape. They would
be seeking payment for the easement to recover their land purchase costs. Jeff stated that FRCT has
evaluated the conservation values of the property, which contains prime wildlife habitat and prime
farmland soils, and determined that there is sufficiently high valuation to qualify for funding grants from
the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service's Agricultural Conservation Easement Program
(ACEP-ALE) and the New Hampshire Land and Community Heritage Investment Program (LCHIP).
However, since the Gelinas Farm would, of necessity, be off limits to hunting, LCHIP funding would
not be available. A NRCS grant, if awarded, would pay 50 percent of the fair market value of the land
toward an agricultural easement. Jeff stated that the process would begin by obtaining an appraisal of the
land's fair market value and development of a budget and funding plan. Then the Federal grant
application would take place. Once funding was secured, the actual acquisition process would begin.
The process would essentially be the same as that followed for acquisition of the Hillman Farm. Jeff
requested that the CC pay for the appraisal to initiate the grant application process. If FRCT is awarded
a grant, he would then be looking to the CC to contribute substantial funding toward meeting the ACEP-
ALE local matching requirement.

The CC then discussed whether to fund the appraisal which would likely cost around $6,000. The CC
discussed the public value of having the easement in place. The owners were questioned about public
access considering that large farm animals would be on the site. They stated that the pasture would be
fenced off but that they were willing to create a public walking and viewing corridor along the property
that would likely extend from 4" to 5'' Range Roads. This corridor would be defined in the easement.
The CC identified additional benefits of keeping the land in agricultural use, including: open space
conservation; the protection of natural and scenic attributes of the land and its cultural amenities; the
protection of the high quality scenic vista that characterizes the site; maintenance of the open,
undeveloped character of the community; maintenance of wildlife corridors and high value wildlife
habitat; and the protection of agricultural soils and promotion of agricultural uses on the site. All of the
above contribute to the overall quality of life in the Town of Pembroke. The CC concluded that it to
provide funding for the appraisal necessary to begin the process. Bob requested that a limit on the
amount of funding be stated.
Ayn moved that the CC provide funds, not to exceed $ 10,000, tor FRUI to obtain an appraisal of the
fair market value of the land only. Bob seconded. All voted in favor.
Conservation Lands:
1. Beck: Ammy is still awaiting a return call from Jacques Belanger regarding verification of the
boundary marker at 445 Micol Rd.
2. Adopt-a-Conservation Area: The Volunteer Agreement and Release and Waiver of Liability and
Indemnity Agreement have been finalized. Ammy and Brian will meet with Stetson Heiser on the Ames
Brook parcel to determine the extent of mowing that will be undertaken this fall.
3. Monitoring: Ammy and Brian completed monitoring of the Heiser parcel on October 2. Boundaries
were reviewed to try to resolve a discrepancy between the Town tax map and the CC's GPS survey on
the northwestern line of the property. Brian will prepare a statement summarizing the problem for
possible consideration by AxisGIS.
New signs need to be made for the Heiser parcel to replace the one that is missing on Academy Rd. and
for the Whittemore parcel on the corner of 5'h Range and Kimball roads.
The remaining assignments for fall monitoring are as follows: Ammy & Erin: Brittany, Gamlin and
Whittemore; Ammy & Sarah Pillsbury: Hillman Farm; Ayn: Merrimack River and White Sands; Brian
and Carol: Center Hill.
Ammy circulated an email from Charlotte Harding of the Conservation Land Stewardship Program
regarding submittal of the annual monitoring report for the Bragfield Parcel. Carol will respond.
Review and Approve Minutes of June 9, and September 8, 2025 Meetings:
1. June 9: This will take place at the next meeting where all members are present.
2. September 8: Carol moved to accept the minutes, as amended. Ammy seconded. All voted in favor.

Other Business:
1. NHACC 2025 Conference: Ammy, Erin, Wendy, Ayn and Brian plan to attend the conference on
November 1. Field trips will be held at Memorial Field, the Heiser Conservation Area, and Bear Brook
Park.
2. Joint Workshop with Planning Board, Zoning and CC: Ammy, Erin, Wendy and Bob attended
this meeting on September 16' to discuss zoning amendments for the 2026 Town Meeting. The CC
members provided recommendations regarding zoning changes affecting PFAS producers, and wetlands.
Bob circulated copies of the minutes to all members. The CC greatly appreciated the opportunity to meet
and discuss these issues with the Town's two major land-use management Boards.
Mail and Correspondence: None of significance.
Adjournment: By consensus, the meeting was adjourned at 9:15 PM.

PEMBROKE CONSERVATION COMMISSION
MEETING MINUTES
August 11, 2025
In attendance: Ammy Heiser (Co-Chair), Erin Insley (Co-Chair), Carol Bertsimas (Vice Chair), Brian
Mrazik (Secretary), Ayn Whytemare
Absent: Wendy Weisiger
Guest: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Call to Order: Meeting called to order at 7:07 PM.
Planning Board Proposed 2026 Zoning Amendments: Carolyn Cronin briefed the CC on zoning
amendments that the Planning Board is considering for the 2026 Town Meeting. The PB is requesting
the CC's input on the following items:
1. Aquifer Protection Ordinance: This amendment would define if and how PFAS-
producing/utilizing facilities would be permitted to operate in the aquifer district. Carolyn provided a
draft ordinance, based on a model developed by NHDES, whereby the PB could issue a Special Use
Permit (SUP) allowing new facilities, or the expansion of existing facilities, that have a potential to
release PFAS compounds. The basis for issuance of a SUP would be the submission of plans and other
information by the applicant demonstrating that operations and source controls effectively limit releases
and thereby present no significant risk to public health, water resources and the environment. The CC
discussed the increasingly widespread contamination of water supplies with PFAS, including several
communities in New Hampshire (Merrimack, Litchfield, Portsmouth and Pembroke). The national
drinking water standard recently revised by EPA specifies Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for
many PFAS compounds of 10 ppt (parts per trillion) or less. Pembroke is currently mixing PFAS-
contaminated water from one of its wells along the Soucook River with water from non-contaminated
sources to comply with the MCL. Exposure to PFAS in drinking water has been linked to a wide variety
of cancers, thyroid and liver disease, and other serious health effects. Of additional concern is that PFAS
are persistent in the environment ("forever chemicals") and accumulate in water, soil, and body tissues
over time. Based on the severity of health risks and the persistence of these chemicals in the
environment, the CC considers an amendment to the aquiter protection ordinance to be of the highest
priority and recommends that any new facility or expansion of existing facilities, which would generate
or utilize PFAS in other than incidental applications and quantities, be prohibited entirely in the aquifer
district.
2. Wetlands Protection Ordinance: Carolyn explained that the existing Wetland Ordinance is
contradictory in that it allows the issuance of a SUP in a wetland if impacts are minimized, but prohibits
any disturbance in the 50-foot buffer. The CC agrees that this needs to be corrected on a priority basis.
The CC discussed three alternatives: 1. Making the prohibition in both the buffer and the wetland; 2.
Allowing disturbance in both the wetland and buffer with a SUP; and 3. Applying the prohibition to the
wetland but allowing a SUP in the buffer. Carolyn advised that if SUPs are precluded, then the only
relief available would be a variance by the Zoning Board on the basis of hardship. Currently, there is no
formal procedure for CC review of a variance. The CC concluded that option 3 made the most sense and
will probably recommend that option to the PB.
3. Open Space Development Ordinance: Carolyn reviewed the history of the previous ordinance, its
repeal in 2020, and the results of a property owner survey in 2021. She stated that the PB would like the
CC's opinion on where to go from here. After considerable discussion, the CC concluded that an open

space development option can be an effective conservation tool only if it can achieve natural resources
objectives important to the Town, such as preserving important natural and/or cultural features, water
resources, agricultural land, wildlife habitat, scenic vistas, and historic sites and structures. Additional
potential benefits of open space development include: 1. More efficient use of land, shorter networks of
streets and utilities, and reduced development costs. It can also provide incentives to avoid the
development of portions of sites that are ill-suited for development such as areas with poor soil
conditions, a high-water table, subject to flooding, or steep slopes.
A major problem with the previous ordinance was that the developer could elect to use the higher
density provisions, as a cost saving measure, without any requirement to preserve those portions of the
property that the Town considers to be the most important natural and/or cultural features. The CC
would like to work with the PB to craft a more structured ordinance that gives the PB the sole discretion
as to whether the open space option can be utilized. State statutes allow for town discretion, in the use of
open space development, to encourage towns and developers to work jointly on developing and
negotiating a plan that best meets the objectives of both parties. The CC suggests that, instead of starting
from scratch, the CC and PB review existing well-structured ordinances developed by other Towns, such
as Bedford, Hopkinton, Dover and Greenland, and then select those provisions that best meet
Pembroke's setting and objectives. The CC suggested that Carolyn set up a joint meeting with the PB
and Zoning Board to discuss these matters in September or October.
Planning Board Applications:
1. Minor Site Plan Application #25-105 and Special Use Permit Application SUP-AC #25-311,
Main Street 141 Realty Company, LLC, owner of Tax Map VE, Lot 168 located at 141 Village
Lane. The Applicant proposes a change in use from an office to a driving school and requests a Special
Use Permit for education use over the aquifer. Since the proposed change in use involves no alteration of
the site which might adversely impact the aquifer, the CC has no comment on the proposal.
2. Major Site Plan Application #25-104 and Special Use Permit Application SUP-AC #25-310, MJ
Properties NH, LLC, owner of Tax Map 266, Lot 117 located at 109 Wilkins Ave. The Applicant
proposes to construct a multifamily development consisting of two 6-unit buildings, with associated
parking and stormwater management, to be served by town water and sewer.
With the new application, the applicant has submitted a engineering report dated July 1, 2025 and titled
"Stormwater Management Report, Wilkins Ave. Multi-Family Housing" prepared by Fieldstone Land
Consultants. This report includes modeling details of the storm-water hydrology under existing
conditions and under the proposed system of subcatchments, filtration basins, sump catches and swales.
The CC has reviewed this report, in conjunction with recommendations made by the Town Engineer
(KV Partners, LLC) in a letter of July 16, 2025 to the Town Planner, and believes that the proposed
stormwater management system, with modifications recommended by the Town Engineer, will satisfy
our previously stated concerns about stormwater.
The CC remains concerned about provisions for the long-term inspection and maintenance of privately
owned stormwater management systems, as discussed in the minutes of our July 14 meeting.
NDES Letters and Applications: The CC received a copy of the approved NHDES Wetland Permit
by notification for the Eversource work along its right-of-way at Tax Map 634, Lots 2 & 23-1.
Zoning Board Applications: None

Potential Acquisitions:
1. Lariviere: Ammy reported that Lisetta Sylvestri, with Ransmeier & Spellman P.C., will serve as
attorney for this acquisition. Because John Lariviere will be the client, a Conflict-of-Interest Waiver was
executed between the firm and the Town. The Town Attorney will review and approve the draft deed
and other acquisition documents. Approval of the acquisition will go before the BOS at their August 20th
meeting. There is a 60-day limit on the use of the appraisal. Ammy will be working with Lisetta to
secure the appraisal as soon as possible so that the acquisition can be completed before the end of the
year.
2. Phipps: The Plourde parcel along the Soucook River, that the CC has been interested in acquiring, is
apparently in foreclosure. The CC has identified this parcel as a good candidate for the Phipps
acquisition and will pursue its procurement.
Conservation Lands:
1. Beck: Ayn organized an onsite meeting with representatives of the CC, the Town Code Enforcement
Officer, and Brandon Fish, the property owner at 445 Micol Rd, regarding his continuing encroachment
on the conservation area. Property boundaries were located, as there was some confusion because older
boundary markers were not removed after the recent Belanger survey. Mr. Fish agreed to cease mowing
beyond the established property line.
Ayn is sent a certified letter to the abutter at 431 Terrie Dr. requesting that two structures placed on the
conservation area be removed. The property owner, Jonathan Procopio, requested to meet with the CC to
discuss the issue at our August 11 meeting, but did not attend. Ayn will contact him to determine his
plan regarding the removal of the structures.
2. Adopt-a-Conservation Area: David Jodoin advised Erin that the draft documents for this program
have been sent to the Town's insurer for review, but no reply has been received.
3. Monitoring: No action taken since the previous meeting. Ayn stated that she will conduct a
community hike on Ames Brook this fall and she can probably do the monitoring at the same time.
Review and Approve Minutes of June 9, and July 14, 2025 Meetings: Carol motioned to approve the
minutes of the July 14 meeting, as drafted. Erin seconded. All voted in favor. Approval of the June
meeting minutes was postponed again because there was not a quorum of those who attended. Aside
from Josh Bursey, who participated as the PB representative for that meeting, only 3 regular CC
members were present. It is now unclear how a quorum can be obtained. Ammy will look into this.
Other Business:
1. Pembroke Natural Resources Inventory: Brian provided copies of the files to David Jodoin on a
flash drive, as requested
2. Conference Room Maps: The CC has received full scale maps from the 2020 Town Master Plan
from the CNHRPC including: 1. Unfragmented Lands; 2. Water Resources; 3. Prime Agricultural Land;
4. Conservation Land; and 5. Wetlands. The CC will decide which ones to display in the conference
room.

PEMBROKE CONSERVATION COMMISSION
MEETING MINUTES
May 12, 2025
In attendance: Ammy Heiser (Co-Chair), Erin Insley (Co-Chair), Carol Bertsimas (Vice Chair), Brian
Mrazik (Secretary), Wendy Weisiger, Ayn Whytemare, Kathy Cruson (PB), Karen Yeaton (BOS Rep)
Absent: None
Guests: Andrew Seraikas & F. Webster Stout, Beaver Brook Planning and Design, LLC
Tom Berkeley Riveredge Properties, LLC
Call to Order: Meeting called to order at 7:02 PM.
Planning Board Applications:
1. Major Subdivision Application #25-04, Riveredge Properties, LLC, owner of Tax Map 563, Lot 101
located at 338-356 Brickett Hill Rd. The Applicant presented plans for Phase II of the project which
includes 2 lots (5&6) on 4' Range Road. These lots will each have a 12-foot wide driveway that will
cross the drainage ditch on the southwest side of the road. The Applicant is seeking an expedited
wetlands permit for placing an 18" culvert at each driveway crossing. An upgraded 18" culvert is also
proposed for the driveway to Lot 4. Carol questioned the Applicant regarding the high-water table in the
area and whether it would require specialized septic and drainage system designs. The Applicant stated
that raised septic systems will be employed if necessary, but he did not have any special plans for
drainage. The CC concluded that it would sign off on the expedited wetlands application.
2. Conceptual Plan, MJ Properties NH, LLC, owner of Tax Map 266, Lot 117 located at 109
Wilkins Ave. The Applicant seeks feedback on a conceptual plan to construct a 4-building, 21-unit
multifamily development in the Wetland Protection (WP) Overlay, the Municipal Separate Storm Sewer
System (MS4) Overlay, and the Aquifer Conservation (AC) Overlay. This plan is an expansion of that
which came before the CC for comment in January 2025. Reference is made to the January 13, 2025
Minutes of the CC meeting, where the CC expressed numerous concerns about stormwater impacts from
the development, including:
• The need to assess the likely quantities and concentrations of pollutants in stormwater and the
capabilities of the planned stormwater drainage system to mitigate pollution of both infiltrated and
discharged waters. This information is necessary for the Town to meet its MS4 management and
reporting requirements.
• The need to assess the amount of stormwater to be infiltrated on a seasonal basis to verify that no
adverse impacts to the local groundwater levels will be imposed on downhill abutters.
• The need to assess the amount of stormwater discharged to the 6" culvert along Buck Street and the
capacity of this culvert to carry its existing load as well as any increased load from stormwater
originating in the development. To avoid cost to the Town to upsize this culvert an upgrade, funded
by the developer, should be considered as a condition for approval of the plan.
• The need for assurance that a long-term inspection and maintenance program for the stormwater
drainage system is in place after approval of the project to avoid potential future adverse impacts on
downstream infrastructure and water quality.

The revised and expanded project plan has not addressed these issues. The CC is further concerned that
the project, (which has expanded from 2 buildings with 12 units to 4 buildings with 21 units, and will
likely have a total impervious area (including buildings, roads and parking areas) in excess of 40,000
sq.ft.) will further exacerbate the water quantity and quality issues associated with this plan. The
expanded plan also calls for a second separate stormwater management system, raising concerns as
described previously. The CC also notes that the plan relies on off-site disposal, for snow amounts that
exceed the minimal provided on-site.
3. Major Site Plan Application #25-103 and Special Use Permit Application SUP-AC #25-305,
Cornerstone Realty Holdings, LLC, owner of Tax Map VW, Lot 187 located at 30 High St. The lot
is in the Aquifer Conservation (AC) Overlay, and the Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4)
Overlay. The Applicant proposes an amended site plan to demolish the Block C building and replace it
with new construction for the remaining 16 units of the approved 32-unit site plan.
The CC notes that the proposed demolition and replacement of the Block C building is a major deviation
from the original plan which called residential conversion of only the existing buildings. The Block C
building is, by far, the largest of the buildings, comprising 16 out of the proposed total of 32 units. Thus,
the project has changed from one of 'conversion' to one with major new construction. The implications
of this change for any 'grandfathering' provisions, such as those which may be associated with the MS4
program, are not clear. The Applicant states that: "Stormwater runoff from the property is collected in
existing closed drainage systems in the previously developed area of the site. The development includes
new catch basins connected to these systems, as well as an open infiltration basin west of the covered
parking to provide mitigation and treatment of stormwater." Some of the existing drainage systems,
shown in the Grading and Drainage Plan, appear to remain directly connected to the Town's stormwater
sewer on High St. It is suggested that the Planning Board determine whether the proposed drainage plan
for the entire project will meet the current MS4 requirements, and whether it is feasible to direct all
stormwater from the entire parcel to the proposed infiltration basin.
We also note that the plan calls for filling and steepening of site slopes to accommodate the new
buildings. The proposed 2:1 slope is greater than existing slope conditions. Will this require an alteration
of terrain permit?
Finally, how the Applicant identifies, contains and disposes of hazardous materials during the
demolition process should be addressed.
DES Letters and Applications: None
Zoning Board Applications: None
Potential Acquisitions:
1. Lariviere: Ammy reported that Lisetta Sylvestri, with Ransmeier & Spellman P.C., will serve as
attorney for this acquisition. John Lariviere will be the client. The Town Attorney will review the draft
deed and other acquisition documents. The CC will pay for the legal fees and the appraisal. Lisetta will
identify some qualified appraisers.

2. Pembroke Pines: The CC is waiting on Pembroke Pines to have the deed drawn up. Ammy has not
received a response from Tim Peloquin regarding the status. She will contact Bob MacCormack if
necessary.
3. Phipps: The BOS has accepted the additional $16,000 from the Phipps trust. Ammy drafted a letter to
the Phipps family to provide them with an update on this acquisition and thank them for their patience
while we continue to identify and evaluate suitable properties. The draft has been forwarded to David
Jodoin for review. Ammy will talk to Lee Grimes about the possibility of acquiring one of his forested
lots.
Conservation Lands:
1. Beck: During the annual monitoring visit, the CC could not find the granite marker identified as 'E'
on the new map. Ammy contacted Jacques Belanger who stated that it was installed as described. Ammy
and Jacques will visit the site again this week to determine the status. With regard to identified
encroachments, Erin will provide Ayn with the name and address of the abutter on Terrie Drive and Ayn
will send a letter requesting that two structures (chicken coup and shed) be removed from the property
within 90 days.
2. Adopt-a-Conservation Area: David Jodoin is having the draft forms and documents reviewed by the
Town Attorney and the Town insurance provider.
3. Conservation Lands Deeds: Ammy is compiling a comprehensive collection of the deed documents
for each property and preparing a summary chart.
4. Monitoring: Brian completed the monitoring for Ames Brook during the community hike and
submitted the report. Assignments for monitoring additional areas are as follows: Carol - Dougherty,
Wendy - Butterfield, Ammy and Erin - Whittemore, Brittany and Gamlin, Ammy and Brian - Heiser,
Carol & Brian - Bragfield and Beacon Hill.
Review and Approve Minutes of April 14, 2025 Meeting: Ammy motioned to approve the minutes of
the April 14 meeting, as drafted. Carol seconded. All voted in favor.
Other Business:
1. Pembroke Natural Resources Inventory: Erin is working with David Jodoin to get this on the Town
website.
2. Conference Room Maps: Ammy will review existing large-scale maps from the NRI and determine

3. Source Water Protection Conference: The New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services
will be holding this conference on Thursday, June 12" at the Edward Cross Training Complex (National
Guard facility) located at 722 Riverwood Drive in Pembroke, NH. The conference will focus on how to
ensure the long-term protection of drinking water resources. To register, see the American Ground

PEMBROKE CONSERVATION COMMISSION
MEETING MINUTES
April 14, 2025
In attendance: Ammy Heiser (Co-Chair), Erin Insley (Co-Chair), Carol Bertsimas (Vice Chair), Brian
Mrazik (Secretary), Wendy Weisiger, Brent Edmonds (PB Rep), Rick Frederickson representing Karen
Yeaton (BOS Rep)
Absent: Ayn Whytemare
Guests: Conor Madison, GZA Environmental, Donald Stokes, Eversource
Call to Order: Meeting called to order at 7:09 PM.
Planning Board Applications:
1. Special Use Permit Applications SUP-WP #25-303 and SUP-AC #25-304,
Eversource Energy, owner of a utility easement on Tax Map 634, Lots 2 and 23-1.
The Applicant requests Special Use Permits for utility construction in wetlands, wetland buffers, and the
Aquifer Conservation District.
Mr. Madison presented Eversource's plan for upcoming maintenance work on their 334G distribution
line. They are replacing 9 wooden utility poles in Pembroke with steel structures. Other poles are being
replaced along the same line in Concord and Bow. There will be no widening of the right-of-way or
change in alignment. In Pembroke, the project requires approximately 4,225 square feet of temporary
wetland impact and 51,597 sq.ft. of buffer impact for construction access and work pad placement.
Some 37,436 sq.ft. of permanent impact to buffers will remain within the existing ROW as new access
roads and work pads. Work will be conducted in accordance with the NHDES 2019 Best
Management Practices Manual for Utilities in and Adjacent to Wetlands and Waterbodies.
Timber matting and erosion controls will be installed to span the wetlands and stream channel.
Upon completion of work, timber matting will be removed, and temporarily impacted wetlands will be
stabilized with straw waddles and will be restored using a native herbaceous grass seed mix. On-
site chemicals are limited to vehicle and equipment fuel and lubricants which will be managed in
accordance with the Utility BMP manual. Fueling will conducted at least 100 feet away from wetlands
and waterbodies. Spill prevention and control plans are required in addition to daily inspections of
equipment for leaks. Construction has been scheduled from October 15, 2025 to March 31, 2026 to
avoid working during the growing season.
The planned work area is in the Old Suncook Oxbows Wetland Evaluation Unit which is one of the
highest-ranking wetland areas in the Town of Pembroke, as identified in the Town's Natural Resources
Inventory. The CC is concerned that the project will involve 37,436 sq. feet of permanent impact to
wetland buffers, including new gravel roads and work pads. The CC recognizes the need for
maintenance of our public utility infrastructure and the efforts which are being undertaken by
Eversource to minimize the environmental footprint of this project. A question remains as to whether all
the proposed gravel roadways are necessary given the secondary access routes shown on the project
maps.
2. Major Subdivision Application #25-04, Riveredge Properties, LLC, owner of Tax Map 563, Lot 101
located at 338-356 Brickett Hill Rd. The Applicant proposes a phased subdivision of the parcel into 6
lots to be served by onsite well and septic. Phase I will include 4 lots and Phase II include 2 lots. The CC
is aware of high-water tables and potentially shallow depths to bedrock in the area which may

complicate the installation of septic systems and the handling of stormwater drainage. Since this is only
a subdivision plan, the CC recommends that any approved layout will ensure that each lot can be
developed without impact to the wetlands buffer.
3. Minor Subdivision Application #25-03, Lavallee Family 2017 Trust, owners of Tax Map 941, Lots
45-1 and 46 located at 310 & 314 Buck St. The Applicant proposes a lot line adjustment to convey
21,894 SF from Lot 45-1 to Lot 46. Since this involves only a lot line adjustment and was previously
submitted, the CC has no new comment.
4. Conditional Approval Extension Request, Site Plan #23-103 and Special Use Permit SUP-AC
#23-309. The Applicant requests a one-year extension of the conditional approval granted on June 25,
2024 (valid until June 25, 2025) to construct worker housing buildings for seasonal agricultural workers.
Since this is an extension request for time limits of conditional approval and the CC has previously
reviewed, no additional comments are offered.
5. Major site plan application to the City of Concord for a new 11,550-square-foot, 10-bay,
aircraft hangar at 65 Airport Rd. Wendy discussed this plan with NH Fish and Game who advised
that the plan is part of a development zone established when the Karner Blue butterfly habitat
management plan was negotiated. Since it is consistent with the established habitat plan, the CC has no
comment on the site plan application.
DES Letters and Applications: The CC received a copy of a Forestry Statutory Permit-by-Notification
for Tax Map 264, Lot 64 on 3rd Range Road.
Zoning Board Applications: None
Potential Acquisitions:
1. Lariviere: Ammy talked to John Lariviere about the status of this acquisition and advised him that
the process should be completed this year. Wendy identified Paul MacDonald, with Ransmeier &
Spellman P.C., as a well-qualified land-use attorney for this action and Ammy will contact him to
discuss the plan. Once the deed and tax work are complete, we will have an appraisal done and hold a
public hearing.
2. Pembroke Pines: The CC is waiting on Pembroke Pines to have the deed drawn up.
3. Phipps: The Town was notified by the Phipps Trust that an additional $16,000 would be added to the
donation for the acquisition of a forested conservation area, bringing the total to $86,000. Ammy will
draft a letter to the Phipps family to provide them with an update on this acquisition and thank them for
their patience while we continue to identify and evaluate suitable properties.
Conservation Lands:
1. Beck: The CC conducted the annual monitoring visit for this property on April 9. The visit included
an examination of the boundary markers and blazing, and encroachments identified during the recent
survey of the property. Two action items were identified: 1. The CC could not find the granite marker
identified as 'E' on the new map. Ammy will contact Jacques Belanger to determine the status. She will
also ask him about removal of the temporary stakes placed along the roadways. 2. The CC will send a

letter to the abutter at 431 Terrie Dr. requesting that two structures (chicken coup and shed) be removed
from the property within 90 days. Erin will ask Ayn to do this.
2. Adopt-a-Conservation Area/Ames Brook: We are waiting on David Jodoin to get the draft Adopt-
a-Conservation Area forms and documents reviewed by the Town Attorney and the Town insurance
provider.
4. Legal requirements to protect conservation lands in perpetuity: No new action. Ammy agreed to
compile a comprehensive collection of the deed documents for each property,
5. Annual Monitoring Day: This was canceled due to bad weather. Erin will ask Ayn to circulate an
updated list of the properties needing monitoring. Some of these areas can be done during the upcoming
community hikes. Others can be done by CC members as schedules permit over the spring and summer
months.
Review and Approve Minutes of March 10, 2025 Meeting: Wendy motioned to approve the minutes
of the March 10 meeting, as drafted. Carol seconded. All voted in favor.
Other Business:
1. Pembroke Natural Resources Inventory: Erin is working with David Jodoin to determine the best
approach to get this on the Town website.
2. Conservation Land Community Hikes: Erin put the hike schedule on the CC Facebook page.
3. Range Road Subcommittee: Carol has been appointed as the CC representative on this 5-member

The CC recommends that a Special Use Permit not be granted for placement of any part of the
barn within the wetland buffer. Cattle farming has historically been a major contributor to the
pollution of both surface and ground water due to high levels of nutrients and bacteria in manure
and sediment runoff from barnyards and pastures. To prevent pollution, the Town's zoning
ordinance prohibits the placement of a septic system within 75 feet of a wetland, but potential
contamination from barn yard areas is significantly greater, even with a proposed herd of less
than 20 animals. A Special Use Permit is also not warranted in this case because the applicant

has alternative locations that do not encroach upon the wetland protection zone. Based on maps
submitted by the applicant, moving the proposed location of the barn approximately 40 feet north
along the stonewall appears to be sufficient to clear the wetland buffer. The applicant needs to
work closely with the NH Department of Agriculture and the USDA Natural Resources
Conservation Service to develop and apply site-specific best-management practices (BMPs), to
the operation of this farm. The prescribed BMPs should be incorporated as a condition for
approval of any Town permitting for livestock operations on the property.

Pembroke Pines regarding acquisition of 12.5+/- forested acres of land with 1500 feet +/- of
