FINAL
BUDGET COMMITTEE
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
February 13, 2025
Video recordings of Budget Committee meetings can be found at:
https://townhallstreams.com/towns/pembroke_nh
The relative start time of each agenda section is noted below.
NOTE: No video recording of this meeting is available as it was held at Pembroke Academy following the public hearing.
Mark LePage, Chairman, called the meeting to order at 9:17 pm.
I.
Attendance
Budget Committee Present: Mark LePage, Gerry Fleury, Clint Hanson, Brian Seaworth, Louis Caron, Matt Miller,
Sue Whitbeck, Kristopher DeLorme, Jason Mayeu, Gene Gauss
Budget Committee Excused: None
Budget Committee Not Present: None
II. Approval of Minutes: January 30, 2025
Clint Hanson made a motion to approve the minutes of January 30, 2025. Louis Caron seconded the motion.
Motion passed 9-0.
Mark explained that both Town and School Budgets needed to be revoted this evening. He stated that they can change the
recommendation or vote to leave the recommended cuts in place.
Ill.
Final Deliberation and Voting - School Budget
Gene Gauss made a motion to approve the School Budget as proposed by the School Board in the amount of $33,429,347.
Kris DeLorme seconded the motion.
Gene added that based on the feedback heard at the meeting, there is a willingness from the community to proceed with
this budget. He feels that the School Board and Selectboard made an extreme effort to minimize the impact. He believes
that it is beyond affordability at this point. He emphasized that the Selectboard and School Board tried to minimize the
impact as much as possible. He would like to see the Budget Committee recommend the original budget that the School
Board proposed.
Brian Seaworth added that he doesn't think the approach worked. His hope was that by setting a number and analyzing the
impact, it would generate a point of discussion. He doesn't feel that the effects of a $400,000 cut were articulated. He
feels that a lot of people were confused about where the cuts were coming from. He wonders if there is a point in having a
cut when the residents can decide the cut themselves.
Gene agreed with Brian. He stated that he plans to do the same type of motion with the Town Budget. He stated that
nothing matters until March 8th and March 15th. It is ultimately in the hands of the taxpayers. Mark added that has always
been the case. Gene stated that the job of the Committee is to look past affordability and to look at what the Selectboard

and School Board put together to ensure it is on the up and up. He feels that questions can be answered at the town
meetings.
Matt Miller stated that it is difficult situation for the Committee. The point of the Budget Committee is to ensure clean
budgets. There would be some excess without the Budget Committee. The Committee has an important role to create
momentum to come to the best most modest budget. He sees value in the Budget Committee recommending what it did,
even though the boards will be defending their proposed budgets at the respective meetings.
Sue Whitbeck stated that she gets concerned if Pembroke gets a reputation for being an inferior school district. She feels
that Pembroke has a safe high school now. She commented on the quality of the people in the building. She feels that the
people taking care of the children are important too. She brought up Dr. Dan Morris leaving Pembroke Academy. She
feels that he cares about the kids, but also the teachers and taking care of them. She doesn't feel that he can be replaced.
She also feels as though Pembroke would not have lost him if it wasn't for last year's cut.
Gerry Fleury commented that there is too much emphasis being placed on the things that will get cut if the budget does
not pass as recommended by the School Board. He does not want to create the perception that the Budget Committee
rubber stamps the budgets presented by the Selectboard and the School Board. He added that the same people might come
back that came last year to cut the budget. He feels that the recommendation of cuts is a good idea and then the voters can
vote to put it back in if they feel that is what needs to be done. The voters are the ones that will pay the bill. If every parent
in the school shows up at the School District Meeting, the School Board could have all the money they asked for. He
emphasized that the decision belongs with the voters.
Mark spoke about irrelevancy. He added that the Budget Committee may be seen as not doing its job. He spoke about the
credibility of the Budget Committee, which is hard to build and can be lost in a second. They have put a lot of time and
effort into these budgets; however, he doesn't think that this makes the decision any easier. He feels that there is
something to be said for the Budget Committee having taken a hard look at the bottom line and coming back against it. He
inquired what are people would say about a $1000 or $1200 tax increase after last year.
Kris added that he hears a number, and he doesn't hear anyone explaining it one way or the other. He stated that as a
taxpayer he would want to hear why the members of the Budget Committee voted the way they did individually. The
populus is not getting that discussion. These discussions need to be had in front of the populus so they can see where the
disagreement is. He has voted both ways on the School Budget since he has lived in Pembroke. He feels that people left
the meeting thinking that the $400,000 proposed cut had to do with the track. He also would disagree on the aspect of
rubber stamping. Most of the audience were in favor of the budget. He is listening to what people said at the meeting and
voting in favor. That is not rubber stamping.
Gerry stated that the situation last year wasn't much different. They were blindsided at the School District Meeting. He
didn't think the school would be able to operate, but he has since seen them make it work. He disagrees and feels that
there is a danger in the Budget Committee rubber stamping budgets. He feels that they would run the risk of another large
cut like they saw in the previous year.
Kris added that he shares the same fear. Sue stated that there are no guarantees either way. Mark reminded the Committee
that their charter is to bring forth a set of number that best serves the town. This is in terms of the wellbeing of the school
and town, but also the taxpayers.
Jason Mayeu stated that he feels that the Budget Committee having reduced the budget opens the discussion in some
ways. He saw a mixed crowd at the hearing, but they favored the originally proposed budgets. He agrees that the
Committee doesn't want to feel like they are rubber stamping. He added that he is one of the biggest school supporters
and it pains him to think about needing to ask them to cut this year's budget again, but he knows there are people in the
community that need the cut in terms of affordability. He is confident that there is not a lot of fat in either of the budgets
based on the hard work done on the budgets. He feels that part of the Committees charge is affordability. They need to
find common ground between those for and those against. He feels that this begs the question on whether the Committee
should be provoking the conversation by not agreeing with the originally proposed budgets.

Jason added that he is not sure that he agrees with Gerry that the cuts at the Town Meeting last year were a reaction to
What happened at the School Budget meeting. He feels that people that were at the meeting wanted to see cuts regardless.
He noted that he is struggling with the decision. He knows where his votes will land on those respective Saturdays but
struggles with whether it is better for the Committee to not just agree with the proposed budgets in the hopes of furthering
the conversation.
Mark added that the Budget Committee has gone along with budgets in the past. The difference is the size of the increase.
It is the magnitude of these increases. Sue stated that the tone at every meeting is set by the first couple of people on the
microphone. If they get up and are very negative, it generates more negativity and vice versa.
Matt stated that as a committee, the Committee's role is to create a contrast. The Committee members are not residents
when they are on the Committee. He thinks that the feedback at the meeting from both sides was a good sign. He feels that
the Committee should recommend the same budgets they came into meeting with because it created a good discussion.
Gene stated that he decided that it would be better to have two different numbers going into the meeting because it will be
countered by the School Board and spark the discussion. This will minimize the risk of someone coming up with a large
cut. He emphasized that he does not believe that the proposed budgets have any fat. He added that if they were to see a cut
and somehow did not lose personnel, there could be maintenance issues at the schools from putting things off. He used the
example of the Village School and the $3 million it would have cost to bring up to code. He believes both budgets were
done in good conscience while trying to minimize the impact on the residents.
The vote was taken on Gene's original motion. The motion failed on a 4-5 vote. This brought the Committee back to their
original proposed cut of $400,000.
Mark noted that all the other articles must also be voted on as well. This can be done in one motion or separate motions.
He explained that there can be a motion to reaffirm.
Gerry stated that he could support reaffirming what they had already voted on all the articles. He pointed out that all the
articles are not adequately funded. For example, if Article 7 passes, there is no guarantee that Article 6 will pass to fund it.
Clint agreed and stated that if the money is not there, you can't spend it.
Gerry inquired whether language could be crafted as to ensure that the authorization doesn't expire. Clint did not believe
this was possible and suggested that legal be consulted. Gerry mentioned that the School Board could possibly amend this,
if possible, at School District Meeting. Mark stated that Gene had taken a note on that and would follow up.
Gerry made a motion to reaffirm all warrant articles. Clint seconded the motion.
The motion passed on an 8-1 vote.
IV.
Final Deliberation and Voting - Town Budget
Gene made a motion to return the Budget Committee's recommendation to the Board of Selectmen's original proposed
budget amount of $11,588,075. Clint seconded the motion.
The motion failed on a 3-6 vote.
Jason made a motion to reaffirm all warrant articles. Gerry seconded the motion.
Brian inquired if there had been any discussion by the Selectboard on where the $150,000 cut, recommended by the
Budget Committee, would be allocated. Matt stated that there had been discussions, but it had not been settled. Brian
shared concerns that residents may think that this cut will come from roads instead of other possible areas. He just wanted

BUDGET COMMITTEE
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 16, 2025 at 6:30 PM
FINAL
Video recordings of Budget Committee meetings can be found at:
https://townhallstreams.com/towns/pembroke_nh
The relative start time of each agenda section is noted below.
Mark LePage, Chairman, called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
I.
Attendance
Budget Committee Present: Mark LePage, Gerry Fleury, Clint Hanson, Brian Seaworth, Louis Caron, Matt Miller,
Sue Whitbeck, Kristopher DeLorme, Jason Mayeu, Kerri Dean
Budget Committee Excused: Gene Gauss
Budget Committee Not Present: None
Mark started by stating that Kerri Dean would be present as Alternate School Board Representative in place of Gene
Gauss.
II.
Approval of Minutes: January 9, 2025 [00:00:08]
Clint Hanson made a motion to approve the minutes of January 9, 2025. Louis Caron seconded the motion.
Kerri Dean abstained. Motion passed 8-0.
III. School Budget Review - Review [00:01:30]
**NOTE: For all budget review, highlights are provided. For full details, please review the video recording, available on
the Town website.
Mark stated that this would be the last session on the School Budget. Patty Sherman, School District Superintendent, was
in attendance to answer questions regarding the budget. Patty shared that she had emailed all budget updates to the Budget
Committee during the week.
Matt Miller asked the status of getting the meeting minutes from the Concord Regional Technical Center (CRTC) Board
Meeting. Patty stated that they have not received the minutes from the Committee meeting that took place, and they are
unaware if there has been a Board meeting. There is a new CRTC agreement so there is a regulation change that does not
require it. This has not been approved by the Department of Education (DOE) yet. She will follow-up on receiving any
minutes available. Matt would also like the last three-year review that was completed.
Mark stated that he received an email response from Amber Wheeler, School District Business Administrator, regarding
the numbers on the School's Tax Rate Forecast Sheet and whether it was a $2.2 million or $2.6 million increase being
presented. There is an operational budget warrant article that is set at a certain amount. If the warrant articles are added
into the budget, it is an invalid amount. By increasing the operating budget and going above what has been approved, it
gives a false comparison to the next year's operating budget. On the Tax Rate Forecast Sheet it shows operating budget
prior to warrant articles. He has reviewed multiple years, and it has not been done this way previously. He cannot
understand why anything is being added in with the operating budget. There is no way to tie anything out if it is done this
way. Patty asked for clarification that Mark wanted to see the amount of the warrant article pertaining to operating budget
only. He confirmed. Patty stated that it did. Amber had said it had to do with the finance system that they use. Mark would
like the School Budget Overview document updated to reflect the correct number.

Gerry Fleury spoke about an article in the Union Leader relative to funding for Catastrophic Aid. The State generally
budgets about $33 million for Catastrophic Aid. The requests from School Districts last year were over $50 million. His
understanding is that the School District gets a prorated amount of the actual Catastrophic Aid expenses. He is concerned
that when the Budget Committee looks at affordability of a tax rate, they must look at certain revenues. They are looking
at estimated revenues for Catastrophic Aid. He wanted to know if the estimate the Budget Committee is looking at is valid
or if there will be a lower percentage reimbursement than what is expected. This will have an impact on the tax rate.
Patty stated that this should not impact Pembroke. Amber underestimates the revenue to ensure that this is not an issue.
The town is supposed get 80%, but she budgets lower to ensure that if there is a shortfall, there is not an unexpected loss
of revenue.
Gerry continued that he had concerns about how much was being budgeted for equipment. At a past meeting, he brought
up a laminator and the cost. He sent Patty a link to a less expensive model. He went on to read the response he got from
the district. The reasoning for the more expensive laminator included reliable service provided by the current company
they work with and previously purchased film not being interchangeable with the model that Gerry had sent. Gerry
provided feedback that there is technical support and a warranty on his model. He feels the message is that they are saying
that they are going to order what they want, and the taxpayers need to pay the bill. The laminator costs approximately
$2400.
He then spoke about a television set for Special Education (SPED). He sees 60" televisions at Walmart for $350. Patty
added that these are not just television sets, they are touchscreens, much like others the district owns that were purchased
with Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) funds. They will be used to project Individualized
Education Plans (IEPs) instead of using paper. Recently, there was a regulatory change that allow them to review and
share IEPs electronically.
Gerry feels that this is a want and not a need. Generally, in the equipment line, he sees a large increase. He is willing to
give the district more money than last year, but he is not willing to see the tax rate exceed and increase of $2.00 per
thousand. This will mean cuts for the School District and the Town.
He spoke about the Budget Committee having to dig into budgets to figure out if they can trust the numbers they are being
given.
Patty clarified that there was no disrespect meant regarding the response about the laminator. She asked them to provide
feedback on why they were purchasing the model that they had chosen. Gerry added that anyone providing an answer
should be aware that he will question it and come back with details. He does not just trust what he is told.
Sue Whitbeck asked about the television for the conference room for IEPs and the potential cost savings from
electronically sharing this information as opposed to using paper. Patty explained that they budgeted $40,000 for the year
and received a bill in July for $17,000. They started the year off with half of their budget already used. There is now a
code on the Pembroke Academy (PA) copier because of the overages. Every department has an allotment for copying. She
continued explaining that there will be a large reduction in copying paper used for IEPs. Mark added that if the sole
purpose is to display documents then a regular television will do this. Patty will get more information from the SPED
department.
Gerry circled back to laminators. He spoke about the laminator being at the end of life. He said the life expectancy of a
laminator is 30 to 40 years. He also asked how many laminators they have. Patty believes that this one came from Village
School, and it is very old.
Sue asked Gerry if Catastrophic Aid was coming out of State funds and what they were budgeting. Gerry replied that he
believed it was $33 million. Sue believed that she had been told at a prior meeting that these were federal funds. Gerry
clarified that it is federal money that is passed through the State. From the Article, the State has placed that limit. He
added that there may be a large education fund that can be tapped, but the State is reluctant to tap into it because of the
lawsuits surrounding defining adequacy and tuition per student.

Patty said there is also a federal requirement stating that SPED should be funding 40% This is not happening currently.
Sue was unaware that the State was putting any type of number on it.
Mark asked for Brian Seaworth's perspective. Brian added that the State runs on a two-year budget cycle, therefore the
number is based on what they knew two and a half years ago. He asked about the SPED concern at that time and the
prospects for increasing SPED allocations and he was told that they were not increasing. He is unsure how the information
that municipalities were seeing did not make it to the person who set the budget. He commented that newspaper articles
are sometimes political as well. He added that Pembroke is lucky that Amber anticipated this when budgeting.
Kerri provided an answer to Sue's question regarding the number of students participating in the Spring Track Program
from the last meeting. Fred Vezina, PA Athletic Director, provided the numbers to be shared with the Committee. There
were 35 in 2021, 32 in 2022, 49 in 2023 and 46 in 2024. Sue gave commentary on these types of programs keeping
children in school. Not everyone is a dedicated student to the other subjects.
Louis asked if these numbers were the total number whose events use the track, or the total involved in track all together.
Jason Mayeu replied that this would be likely all athletes, but that it could be assumed that most would use the track for at
least one event.
Brian asked about the projected number of students decreasing. This also feeds into the State's projection. It was down 66
students. He said that it looks like most is at Pembroke Academy and most students were from Pembroke. They then go up
subsequently. Brian asked how this projection has been calculated. Patty answered that Amber tracks this. It has been a
combination of things which could include movement and homeschooling. Brian said that if it was something systematic,
one would think that it would not just be Pembroke's students but also the other sending districts.
Gerry asked a question about the warrants. This included School and Town. There are warrants for both the Selectboard
and School Board to be agents to expend of certain capital reserves and trusts. If these pass, there is no reason for the
other warrants that are being presented. This would allow money to be expended without presenting warrants for those
reserves and trusts at Town and School District meetings. He was wondering how this would be presented.
Kerri added that there had been no meeting since the previous week. She and Gene have spoken about removing the
warrant article regarding the School Board being agents to expend for Site Improvement. They will discuss how they will
proceed.
Gerry added that School Technology and SPED Capital Reserves being excellent examples of good candidates for the
School Board to be the agents to expend. These are emergency funds. He does not agree that things like replacing roofs or
vehicles should have the Selectboard or School Board being agents to expend. These are high dollar purchases. There is
no audit trail. If it is not explained at the Town or School District Meeting, how will the taxpayers know? He spoke about
the CIP process and how they are not charged with following up on expenditures. He believes that the voters should have
the say, especially for larger expenditures. This creates transparency. This is not present when a group of five or six people
are in a meeting and the public does not attend public hearings.
Kristopher DeLorme asked if there is a legal distinction between "agents to expend," "vote to raise and appropriate," and
"authorize to withdraw an expenditure." He asked if the School Board is given the power to be agents to expend, will they
have the authority to raise and appropriate and expend funds?
Gerry explained that this language is written this way because of the Department of Revenue Administration (DRA). He
added that it is authorization for the School Board to spend money that is there in cash for a specific purpose. Kris
inquired further as he was trying to find the legal distinction.
Mark clarified that agents to expend classifies who gives the okay for funds to be expended. This can be either the voters
or in this case, the School Board. The authorization to withdrawal and expend is the right that is granted to the agent to
expend.
Gerry added that Library and Sewer Commission are agents to expend for their accounts. This is not case for the Town

The relative start time of each agenda section is noted below.
Mark LePage, Chairman, called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
I.
Attendance
Budget Committee Present: Mark LePage, Gerry Fleury, Clint Hanson, Gene Gauss, Brian Seaworth, Louis Caron,
Matt Miller, Sue Whitbeck, Kristopher DeLorme, Jason Mayeu
Budget Committee Excused: None
Budget Committee Not Present: None
II.
Approval of Minutes: January 2, 2025 [00:00:55]
Clint Hanson made a motion to approve the minutes of January 2, 2025. Sue Whitbeck seconded the motion.
Motion passed 9-0.
III. School Budget Review - Special Education [00:01:28]
**NOTE: For all budget review, highlights are provided. For full details, please review the video recording, available on
the Town website.
Jess Bickford and Amber Wheeler were in attendance to present the Special Education (SPED) Budget for 2025.
First, Jess presented a summary of out-of-district placements in Lakes Region schools for comparison purposes. Pembroke
is in the middle of the pack. In Pembroke, 1% of students are in an out-of-district placement. The SPED population is
around 20%. Out-of-district placements may have also been placed by a court order and not by the district. This can also
happen with a Division for Children, Youth and Families (DCYF) order. Mark LePage clarified that the district has no
control over these placements. Jess confirmed that this is the case.
Sue brought up the cost. Jess stated that if the court orders an out-of-district placement, the district pays only a portion
which is capped out, and the rest is reimbursed by the State. She also emphasized that taxpayers are still impacted by this
in the form of State taxes.
Also, each year, the State sets a cap for total SPED expenses. The reimbursements come in around the end of December.
Mark asked if this is catastrophic aid. Jess confirmed that it is. She explained that the school receives 80% of covered
costs for SPED, for costs over $71,130 for last school year, and over $75,319 for this school year. After that, the school
district will receive 100% reimbursement for costs over $215,000 for this year. This year, Pembroke received 66%
reimbursements. The portion the State pays is based on the number of school districts that apply as there is a set amount of
federal funding. The more school districts that apply, the less each school district receives.
Gerry Fleury brought up the chart that SAU 53 has a 24% SPED population. He noticed that none of the component towns
have a number as high as 24%. He wondered how this would be possible when none of the component towns are over the
24% Jess added that she would review the numbers.
Matt Miller asked for clarification on the reimbursement process. He gave an example of a school district hitting $75,000

and getting 80% of costs beyond that about a year later. After that, they would have to hit over $200,000 for 100%
reimbursement. He asked if the $200,000 number is only cumulative based on what the school spends after
reimbursement. Would the school have to have a $1,000,000 expense for the reimbursement? Jess explained that there is
a state formula for the calculation. There are 10 steps to the formula. When budgeting is completed, the full 80% number
is never included. Amber stated that they budget estimated revenues based on 60-64%. If they get the 80%, there are extra
funds, but at least there is not a shortfall. There is one school in the district that did not spend enough for any type of
reimbursement from the State.
Sue asked if the funding is exclusively federal. Jess replied that they come from a pool of federal money and there is no
direct state funding provided for SPED. The funds are only dispersed through the state.
Jess confirmed that the 24% SPED population for the district is correct based on Gerry's previous question and that the
total does not correlate to the cumulative sum of the individual districts.
Jess continued explaining the reimbursements. The State comes up with a number each year for court ordered out-of-
district placements needed in order to "cap out". This year, a district must place approximately $59,000 of court ordered
out-of-district placement. The State covers 100% after this amount.
Mark asked what LEA stands for. Jess answered that is stands for Local Education Agency. The School District is an LEA.
Jess is also an LEA. She has been given the financial decision-making power in an Individualized Education Program
(IEP) meeting. There is always a representative that attends these meetings. They make the determination and allocate
funds during the meeting.
She continued by addressing the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) and the 504 Act. She provided a
summary and links to the Committee for further information. These acts govern the funding required for SPED. There was
also a link to the New Hampshire Department of Education provided.
This is Jess' second year in the position. The first year, she was shadowing Karen and was not a decision maker. She feels
that there are pockets that need to be improved. She listed some things that she has been working on. Unfortunately, she
feels that there is not a quick turnaround as these are systemic practices.
The BRIDGE Program in the SAU is being reviewed. She is currently evaluating if it is financially responsible and
looking at cost versus benefit. She also is in the process of determining if the funds should be used for something else.
Brian Seaworth asked for an overview of the BRIDGE program. This is an alternative program for children with severe
behavior issues. Traditionally for middle school students but has been shifted to elementary based on need. She is looking
at whether there are enough students utilizing the program and if they would be better served in the district with the help
of specialty personnel. Her philosophy is that they belong in the classroom. This is not everyone's philosophy. She wants
Sue asked if the BRIDGE Program is an SAU-wide program. Jess confirmed that it is and that it is based in Epsom.
Jess and her administrative assistant have been working on negotiating SPED transportation costs. There are more
companies now and they have been encouraging them to bid against each other. This may save a couple hundred dollars a
day. Competition is driving cost reduction. She also spoke about ride sharing being utilized if it is not a safety issue for
students or the driver.
She has been reviewing service delivery models. This is for purposes like speech, occupational therapy and other SPED
programs. Mostly, it is currently pulling the students out of the classroom and doing one-on-one work. There may be
options to do small groups (2-3 students) or assigning a speech pathologist into the classroom to work with a group of
students.
Pembroke Hill School (PHS) has been a model of how SPED should be done. She is trying to push this model into other
schools.

Longer term goals include shifting the SPED practices and encouraging co-teaching versus pulling students out of the
classroom to reduce Para education costs. She is reviewing the para program versus certified SPED teachers. She is
looking to increase interventions in K-3. If there were more services at this age, there would be far less services needed
when they are older. They are overhauling how this is done currently.
She has been tracking how many IEPs contain what types of services. She took a snapshot last year to identify trends. Last
year in Pembroke there were 162 para educators required in IEPs. Because of this analysis, there are currently 118 IEPs
with paras included. It does take some years for these goals to be achieved because they want to make sure they are doing
what is right for the students.
The next focus is bringing children back from out-of-district placements. She is not in favor of out-of-district placements
and feels that it institutionalizes the child. She feels that this would be a benefit to all children, not just one or two.
Mark asked the percentage of students in Pembroke that are district placed versus court/DCYF placed. She believes that it
would be 75% district placed and 25% court or DCYF placed.
Matt asked about the law that changed the Medicaid reimbursement process. In the past, students had to self-identify. He
inquired about the process for Medicaid reimbursements currently. Jess explained that it has decreased due in part to
stricter rules. She also believes that this is due to the vendor that they are using as well. There is a Request for
Qualifications (RFQ) in place as the contract is up in one year. They have heard from two vendors. The selection
committee has identified who they would like to target for the Requests for Proposal (RFP). Decisions will be made in
the fall. She feels that the number of reimbursements should increase with a change of vendor.
Matt asked about upcoming legislation. He asked if there is a public comment process. Jess asked if Pembroke would like
an update on legislative update quarterly from her. She focuses on SPED, Services and Civil Rights bills. The titles for the
bills have all been submitted. The Legislative Service Request (LSR) blurbs were due last week. This is a one liner about
what the bill will be about. She has 100 or so bills that she is tracking. She is also part of a committee for SPED directors
in the state that also tracks legislation. Matt thinks that it would be great if she would share legislative updates with
potential impact and she can then facilitate feedback from town board and committees. She is more than happy to testify
on behalf of the town boards or committees.
SPED transportation costs are going down. PHS is down about $130,000 for the year. Three Rivers School (TRS) and
Pembroke Academy (PA) are up which offsets the PHS reduction. Overall, transport is up $360,000. She is trying to
control the inflation of that over time. She feels that this is a minimal increase compared to those in the past. She is
pushing back on transportation in meetings where necessary.
Matt asked about SPED transportation and transportation to public, charter and private school. If a parent decides to send
their child somewhere other than public school and if there is any point where the taxpayer obligation ends. Jess said that
Green Valley is a non-profit school in the Pembroke School District. The SAU, as an LEA, must provide services to
students at that school. They can use IDEA grant funding. A portion must be set aside for these types of schools. Matt
asked if this includes transportation from other towns. Jess stated that this does not include transportation from other
towns, only services. Transportation only applies when it is a district placement and not when it is parent choice. For any
private schools that are for-profit, there is no obligation to provide services. If a parent decides to send them to a charter
school, it is technically public, and therefore services and transportation must be provided. This applies to all public
schools.
Mark asked if this always applies for any school regardless of district when it is the parent's choice. Jess said that it
applies for public schools (including charter schools), and they must have been determined to require SPED by the
district. The SAU is also required to provide evaluation for these students and is responsible to ensure that services are

TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 2, 2025 at 6:30 PM
FINAL
Video recordings of Budget Committee meetings can be found at:
https://townhallstreams.com/towns/pembroke_nh
The relative start time of each agenda section is noted below.
Mark LePage, Chairman, called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
I.
Attendance
Budget Committee Present: Mark LePage, Gerry Fleury, Clint Hanson, Gene Gauss, Brian Seaworth, Louis Caron,
Jason Mayeu, Matt Miller, Sue Whitbeck, Kristopher DeLorme
Budget Committee Excused: None
Budget Committee Not Present: None
Mark LePage informed the Committee that Jenn Miscovic has stepped down from the Budget Committee. She is
accepting a full-time position with the Town Hall, which by RSA prohibits her continued role on the Budget Committee.
He thanked her for her years of service and wished her the best.
Il.
Approval of Minutes: December 19, 2024 [00:02:00]
Clint Hanson made a motion to approve the minutes of December 19, 2024. Louis Caron seconded the motion.
Motion passed 9-0.
Ill.
School Budget Review [00:02:28]
**NOTE: For all budget review, highlights are provided. For full details, please review the video recording, available on
the Town website.
Mark started by stating that there would be an overview of the School Budget.
Amber Wheeler, SAU 53 Business Administrator, and Patty Sherman, SAU 53 Superintendent, were in attendance to
present the School Budget. Amber went over the structure of the summary packet. She then explained the account line
numbering in the Proposed Budget.
Amber started with the 1100 lines (Regular Education). The 1100 lines propose an increase of $543,620 to $7,529,423.
The teacher salaries increase includes 10 additional days for the Digital Learning Specialist. There were also track
changes, which are salary increases caused by furthering education that triggers reclassification. There is also a proposal
to add four Kindergarten regular education aids. These were in the proposed budget last year but were ultimately cut from
the budget.
There was a decrease in English Language Learner (ELL) salaries due to decreased need for services. Sue Whitbeck asked
if there is any ELL staff left. Patty explained that all ELL staff members are now employed by the SAU, and they are then
charged to the school based on need.
Maintenance Contracts increased as well, with $9,300 of the increase being attributed to copier cost. This was done to
avoid overages caused by increased costs for going over the contracted amount. Gerry Fleury inquired about the potential
for future overages, and Amber stated that she cannot guarantee no overage, but that there are measures in place and

believes that this is being monitored appropriately.
Supplies and books have a proposed increase of $52,061. The is due to the cost of supplies increasing. Physical Education
is looking for some additional materials as well. Art supplies is also an increase in costs and curriculum changes. Science
supplies are decreasing.
Matt Miller inquired about the supply line for the Green House at Pembroke Academy. He asked if there were new
programs that attributed to the $6,000 proposed where no budget existed last year. Patty explained that there is a science
teacher currently using the green house, as well as a new program for Animal/Plant Science. This was started last year
through grant funding.
There is a large, proposed increase for the replacement cycle for computers. This was funded by the Elementary and
Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) Fund this year after the cut. To keep the replacement cycle going, this
request is being made to the budget.
Amber listed miscellaneous supplies needed for all three schools. For example, chairs, cabinets, white boards, tables, and
a kiln.
Matt asked about the server replacement and Network-attached Storage (NAS) backup. He asked what considerations
were being considered to doing server replacement out of the capital reserve account versus the budget. Patty answered
that the Technology Reserve Fund was initially set up for emergencies with a contingency amount of $60,000 ($20,000
per school). This Reserve account was tapped into last year for budget items and is now down to around $39,000. The
School Board can choose to use this for the server replacement this year if they deem necessary.
Next, Amber spoke about the 1200 lines (Special Education). She informed the Committee that Jess Bickford, Director of
Student Services, would be going into more detail on at the meeting on January 9, 2025. These lines propose an increase
of $635,482 for a total budget of $6,213,329.
Contracted services increased by $20,053. This is due to the rate for the provider increasing. There are also speech
pathology services, which are required.
Summer and Special Placement are based on student needs. This will be explained by Jess Bickford.
Sue asked whether a teacher had left at Three Rivers (SPED). Patty explained that a teacher did leave and they have
chosen not to fill the position. Sue followed-up and asked if the case loads are still reasonable. The response was that the
person serving as the Local Educational Agency (LEA) Representative has been assigned as a case manager. The Assistant
Principal will be covering both SPED and Assistant Principal duties.
Amber continued by speaking about the 1300 lines (Vocational Programs). There is a decrease of $3,487 in the proposed
budget for a total request of $842,437.
Gerry asked about the Vocational Program including 110 students and if that has changed year over year. Patty and Amber
stated that it is close to the same. Gerry asked if there is a direct correlation between tuition cost and the number of
students enrolled. Patty added that the tuition varies based on reimbursement from the State each year. Gerry asked if
students would be turned away and Patty said that this would only happen if the program was full.
Next, Amber spoke about the 1400 lines (Co-Curriculars). There is an increase of $14,811 with a total proposed budget
request of $500,712.
The increase includes an assistant coach for the Cross-Country program which serves approximately 35-40 students. They
are also looking to purchase new hurdles, which have not been purchased due to a budget freeze.
There is also an increase in dues for the New Hampshire Interscholastic Athletic Association (NHIAA) and increase rents
for fields being used by various programs.

Mark asked about which fields are being used that incur rental fees. Patty answered that the Buck Street fields are used
for soccer roughly two times per week. There are four teams that need to practice, and the main field is for games only.
There is also another field needed as darkness increases as the fall goes on.
Amber, then, spoke about the 2100 lines (Other Support Services). This is a proposed increase of $10,480 for a total
request of $783,888. This includes the guidance department and school nurse, as well as other expenses for enrichment
and assemblies.
PSAT expenses will be offset by revenue as parents are now required to reimburse Pembroke Academy for testing. This
is a change from the tests previously being covered by the district.
Matt asked where diagnostic services has moved. It is now in the 1200 lines.
Mark asked about lines being zeroed out and how long they remain in the budget. Amber stated that they must be zeroed
out for three years before they fall off. (Note: This is because the software reports draw on three years of data when they
are generated so zeroing out data ahead of that time would incapacitate those reports).
There is an increase of $7,199 for 24 days for a Summer Nurse for the Pushing Your Limits Summer Program. This was
previously paid for through the ESSER grant. There is also a request for 30 hours for a nurse to do Kindergarten
screenings during the summer.
Amber then spoke about the 2200 line (Instructional Services). There is a total request of $107,418 with an increase of
$24,956. This grouping is for workshops/professional development, professional dues, librarian and aide's salaries and
library equipment and software.
There are requests for books for the libraries at both Pembroke Academy and Three Rivers. The total request amount for
both is $12,800. This is an increase of $6,300. These requests were cut last year.
Gerry questioned the proposed cost of the replacement laminator. He found a top-of-the-line laminator with the highest
capacity designed specifically for schools for $700 cheaper. He stated that this introduces an element of doubt because it
feels like this is an arbitrary number. Patty said if he would share the link, she would be happy to find out why there is a
discrepancy in pricing
Sue asked about the Media Generalist. She can see Hill School and PA but wanted to know what is happening at Three
Rivers. Patty answered that there has been a change in structure at both schools. There is someone serving both Media
Generalist and Librarian. This is a shared position at Three Rivers.
Matt asked why there are so many requests for extra days during the summer and what is triggering these requests. Patty
explained that these were previously funded by ESSER funds. She used Pembroke Academy as an example. With students
coming from multiple sending schools, records need to be transferred and organized. There are also increasing medical
needs of students entering PA. Also, the technology integrators are busy reimaging computers, etc. during the summer
month. This must be done before school starts.
Next Amber spoke about the 2300 lines (Board Services). The total request for this budget cycle is $994,852 with a
requested increase of $41,856. This includes School Board Member salaries, Clerk, Secretary, Treasurer, moderator,
Supervisor of the Checklist stipend, advertising, attorney fees, auditing and actuary services, and district assessments.
There are requested increases in legal services.
The district share is 38.8% This is the SAU budget broken out by percentage for the districts. Pembroke's portion
increased by $26,836.
Mark asked about Board Expenses. He noted there are separate line items for things like workshops, advertising, supplies

BUDGET COMMITTEE
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
February 5, 2026
FINAL
PUBLIC HEARING
The meeting started at approximately 7:00 pm.
Mark LePage, Budget Committee Chair, opened the public hearing to discuss the proposed 2026
municipal and 2026-27 school district budgets and warrant articles.
Pre-Hearing Presentations
Budget Committee Introduction & Process
Mark LePage introduced the committee members and explained that all Budget Committee meetings
are public, live-streamed, and recorded. LePage emphasized that the Committee conducts thorough
deliberations and does not simply rubber-stamp proposals, with detailed discussions available in
videos from January 22nd and 29th.
Budget Pressures and Challenges
Key budget pressures identified include contractual salary increases, health insurance premium
increases, general inflation, and workers' compensation insurance increases. The school district faces
an $804,000 health insurance increase due to a record 30.3% rate increase, along with increases in
liability insurance, transportation, tuition obligations, and reduced state revenue. The town faces
increases in equipment costs, workers' compensation insurance, and ambulance services. He noted
that these impacts are not unique to Pembroke and are being face by other communities in New
Hampshire.
Town Budget Presentation
Selectman Matt Miller presented the town budget structure, explaining that the general fund operating
budget is increasing 3.9% to $9.38 million, slightly above the regional inflation rate of 3.3%. Water
and Sewer transfers are up 8.9%, though these represent user fees and do not affect property taxes.
Capital reserve funds are requested at $1.043 million, representing an 8.9% increase needed to address
prior underfunding and maintain the capital improvements plan. Two bonds totaling $1.6 million are
proposed for Memorial Park projects, which represents an 85% decrease from the prior year's $10.4
million bond. Town revenues are conservatively estimated to decrease 13.1%, which will impact
property taxes. Warrant Article 12 proposes a total budget of $12,195,101, representing a 5% increase
over 2025.
VJ Ranfos, the Public Works Director, explained that Memorial Park drainage and shoreline
stabilization projects ranked #2 and #3 in a competitive state funding process with 25-30 applications,
with the State selecting 10 projects. The projects will receive 15% loan forgiveness from the Clean
Water State Revolving Fund. Ranfos noted that emergency drainage work was necessary due to a 50-
100-year-old failing pipe that required an emergency permit from the Department of Environmental
Services five years ago to stop erosion along the Merrimack River.
David Jodoin, the Town Administrator, covered the warrant articles related to tax exemptions and
capital spending. Articles 5 through 8 address Veteran and Elderly Tax Exemptions, adjusted for state
changes and cost-of-living increases. The Disabled Veteran Exemption is increasing from $2,000 to
$4,000 annually due to state rule changes eliminating the ability to stack exemptions. The Veteran
Exemption is increasing from $500 to $750 annually. Articles 9 through 10 authorize the Select Board

as agents to expend capital reserve funds without returning to Town Meeting. Article 11 proposes
renaming the "Town Buildings Municipal Facilities Capital Reserve" to "Municipal Town Facilities
and Grounds Capital Reserve" to clarify coverage of landfill pavement and Public Works Garage
improvements. Article 14 presents a collective bargaining agreement with the Public Works
Department for voter approval. Articles 15 and 16 address funding for sidewalk repairs on Pembroke
Street and Pembroke Hill Road, and a new stage with roof at Memorial Park.
School Budget Presentation
Melanie Camelo, School Board Chair, presented the 2026-2027 school budget totaling $34.9 million,
representing a 4.23% increase of $1,498,226. The primary budget drivers are health insurance costs
($804,000 increase), vocational programs, transportation, and salaries. Benefits represent 48% of the
total budget increase, while special education and transportation together comprise 21% of the budget.
Vocational programs represent an 11% increase due to staffing adjustments related to collective
bargaining agreements and anticipated growth in Concord Regional Technical Center (CRTC
participation. Salaries, excluding special education, represent 16% of the budget increase.
Camelo highlighted the District's strategic goals and achievements, noting that Pembroke has been
recognized as a district of choice. Pembroke Academy was named High School of the Year in 2023,
and in 2024 the District had both the New Hampshire Teacher of the Year and Special Educator of the
Year. The District faces significant challenges including New Hampshire's 50th national ranking for
state education funding, adequacy aid decreasing from 40.29% to 37.97%, and state base aid of
$4,265.64 per student falling well below the $7,356.01 per-student threshold set by the New
Hampshire Supreme Court. Enrollment is declining due to educational alternatives and declining birth
rates, and a housing affordability crisis is limiting new residents. Grant funding has been reduced
following the end of Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) funding.
To manage costs, the school has implemented a new bus contract effective July 1, 2026, which
includes enhanced service and built-in fuel cost stabilization to provide consistency in budgeting.
Warrant Article 3 proposes a Benefits Expandable Trust to cover unexpected health care costs such as
those experienced with SchoolCare this year. Warrant Article 5 proposes a Tuition Expandable Trust
fund to support the development of the open enrollment program. Warrant Article 14 proposes a
Retainer Fund allowing up to 5% of unassigned general funds for unexpected expenses, aligning
Pembroke with other districts in SAU 53. Camelo emphasized that the District's local open enrollment
policy, adopted January 27', is distinct from the pending state universal open enrollment legislation.
Budget Committee Recommendations
Mark LePage reported that the Budget Committee unanimously supports both the Town and School
budgets as necessary and reasonable, with budgets backed by detailed, comprehensive supporting
information. He stressed that cutting either budget meaningfully would result in service reductions or
losses. The property tax impact shows an 11.7% net tax increase leading to a 10.6% total tax rate rise.
The school tax rate increase is $1.49, which includes a $0.76 town increase and a 10% county
increase. School revenues are down approximately $1 million, and town revenues are down $200.000
with the net amount to be raised by taxes representing a school increase of $1.9 million (11.2%) and a
town increase of $991,000 (14.6%).
Public Comments & Discussion
The public hearing was opened at 7:55 pm.
Penti Alto - Batchelder Road

Mr. Alto asked about alternative tax payment methods, such as allowing residents to contribute labor
or skills in exchange for tax reductions, referencing historical town practices.
Mark LePage responded that while volunteer contributions could be helpful, any compensation would
create insurance and liability issues that would be difficult to manage.
Susan Seidner - 439 Deer Path Lane
Ms. Seidner praised the town and school presentations for clarity and emphasized the importance of
distinguishing Pembroke's local open enrollment, which voters approved, from the pending state
universal open enrollment legislation that could significantly impact taxes.
Melanie Camelo explained that universal open enrollment would make every public school an open
enrollment school, giving parental choice. While parental choice has merit, she expressed concern
about the speed of implementation without working out important details such as the application
brocess, frequency of transfers, and waiting lists. The state bill allows up to 100% capacity withou
restrictions, meaning that theoretically 50 or more students from one school could leave for another
simultaneously. In such a scenario, the sending town would have to pay 100% of tuition to the
Camelo raised equity concerns, noting that Pembroke's per-pupil cost is $20,241 compared to the state
average of $27,000, meaning students leaving for more expensive districts would require parents to
cover the $7,000 difference, which not all families can afford. Transportation would be the parents'
responsibility, making true universal open enrollment inaccessible to some families. She emphasized
that school boards are calling for details to be worked out before implementation, as budgeting 18
months in advance becomes impossible with unpredictable student enrollment.
Jim Parker - 240 Pembroke Hill Road
Mr. Parker questioned the cost of the veteran exemption increase from $500 to $750, noting the
$90,000 annual burden on other taxpayers and expressing concern about fairness given his military
service includes a pension and annuity.
Mark LePage acknowledged the cost impact but noted that veteran support is a community value.
Sally Highland - Batchelder Road
Ms. Highland asked why the operating budget shows a 5% increase while the property tax impact
appears higher on the tax sheet.
Mark LePage clarified the distinction between the operating budget (a single warrant article) and
appropriations (the sum of all warrant articles combined). He explained that appropriations include
the operating budget plus capital reserves ($1.043 million) and bonds ($1.6 million), and the tax rate
is calculated on total appropriations, which explains the difference in percentages.
Peter Mehegan - 145 Pembroke Street
Mr. Mehegan, a State Representative, requested detailed breakdown of special education placements
and praised the transparency showing individual out-of-district placement costs exceeding $100,000
each. School officials confirmed that special placements are listed by school with account codes
provided for transparency, noting that single placements can cost $250,000 or more, which impacts
other programs like music that serve 150 students at Pembroke Academy. Mehegan expressed
concern about the need to cap unsustainable special education costs.

BUDGET COMMITTEE
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 29, 2026
FINAL
Video recordings of Budget Committee meetings can be found at:
https://townhallstreams.com/towns/pembroke_nh
Mark LePage, Chairman, called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
I.
Attendance
Budget Committee Present: Mark LePage, Gerry Fleury, Clint Hanson, Matt Miller, Louis Caron,
Brian Seaworth, Jason Mayeu, Sue Whitbeck, Gene Gauss, Mariana Beer, Kristopher DeLorme
Budget Committee Excused: None
Budget Committee Not Present: None
Chair Mark LePage outlined the evening's agenda, noting that the committee would review the entire
town warrant with easier items first and the operating budget (Article 12) discussed last, followed by
the school operating budget (Article 2), and concluding with discussion of the public hearing
scheduled for the following week. He noted that minutes from January 15" had just been received and
would be addressed next week. All warrant articles would be subject to roll call votes.
II. Deliberations for Public Hearing
a. Town Warrant Articles and Operating Budget
ARTICLE 3 - To see if the town will vote to raise and appropriate the sum of $820,000 (Gross
Budget) for the purpose of replacing a drainage pipe at Memorial Park as part of the Town's
required Asset Management program which is part of the Federally required MS 4 permitting
process, and to authorize the issuance of not more than $820,000 of bonds or notes in
accordance with the provisions of the Municipal Finance Act (RSA 33); and, further, to
authorize the Board of Selectmen to issue and negotiate such bonds or notes and to determine
the rate of interest thereon, and, to further authorize the Board of Selectmen to offset a portion
of said appropriation by applying for and expending Clean Water State Revolving Funds
(CWSRF) loan funds or any other grants or funding sources which may become available.
Repayment of the loan funds is expected to include up to Fifteen Percent of loan principal
forgiveness in an amount up to $123,000 (3/5 ballot vote required)
Gerry Fleury made a motion to consider Article 3. Clint Hanson seconded the motion.
Gerry Fleury provided essential context. He explained that the existing clay pipe drains water from
the Hillcrest-Broadway area through the Village to the Merrimack River. The pipe is in poor
condition, and its failure could cause significant flooding damage during heavy rain or snowmelt. He
noted the project's complexity due to the gas line running beneath it, though test pits had been
conducted to locate it.
Mark LePage raised a technical question about wording in the article, and David Jodoin clarified that
the lawyer had corrected it to read "is expected to include up to 15% of loan principal forgiveness in
an amount up to $123,000."
Mariana Beer asked about the principal uses of Memorial Park, and VJ Ranfos provided a
comprehensive list: basketball courts, baseball, softball, soccer, boat launch, old home day, gazebo,

picnics, concerts, regattas, and summer recreation programs. Gerry Fleury clarified that the drainage
project involves an underground pipe that won't be visible to park users.
Louis Caron asked whether the project would address pollution reduction, and VJ Ranfos confirmed
that a detention pond would be constructed near Exchange Street to help reduce sediment flow.
Mariana Beer inquired about the project timeline, and VJ Ranfos responded that construction is
targeted for summer 2026 with real numbers expected by the March meeting.
The article was recommended on a 10-0 vote.
ARTICLE 4 - To see if the town will vote to raise and appropriate the sum of $790,000 (Gross
eroding of the banks which are a safety and environmental issue, and to authorize the issuance
of not more than $790,000 of bonds or notes in accordance with the provisions of the Municipal
Finance Act (RSA 33); and, further, to authorize the Board of Selectmen to issue and negotiate
Board of Selectmen to offset a portion of said appropriation by applying for and expending
Clean Water State Revolving Funds (CWSRF) loan funds or any other grants or funding
Fifteen Percent forgiveness of loan principal in an amount up to $118,500 (3/5 ballot vote
required)
Gene Gauss made a motion to consider Article 4. Clint Hanson seconded the motion.
Mark LePage provided detailed information about Memorial Park's amenities and recreational uses.
Louis Caron shared a personal anecdote about walking in a conservation area in Concord where
similar erosion had occurred, pushing back the shoreline and making paths inaccessible, raising the
question of whether the project would truly preserve the park's footprint.
Gerry Fleury provided extensive context about the erosion problem, explaining that dams in Epsom
had been removed, causing the Suncook River to carry significant sand downstream, creating a "hydro
sandblast effect" on everything downstream. He described how gravel had filled the riverbed and
noted that removal of a dam on Buck Street had been necessary because water would overrun the
banks. Fleury explained that he had personally observed the damage over time and documented
significant loss of the park's embankment. He referenced recommendations from the Corps of
Engineers in the 1990s to cut tall trees along the Merrimack riverside to prevent root systems from
ringing soil down when trees fell. He noted that 30 years later, trees are beginning to fall again, anc
varned that the Suncook River is heading in a northerly path toward the Merrimack, threatening th
boat ramp and point. He emphasized that without intervention, the town will continue to lose sections
of the field.
Louis Caron summarized that preservation of the park's footprint appears to be a priority, and Gerry
Fleury confirmed this, with VJ Ranfos nodding in agreement. VJ Ranfos clarified that most erosion
(approximately 75%) is on the Suncook River, with smaller sections on the Merrimack.
The article was recommended on a 10-0 vote.
ARTICLE 5 - Shall the Town vote to modify Chapter 138, Article V of the Pembroke Town
Code titled Total Service Connected Disability Exemption to increase the tax credit from $2,000

per year to $4,000 in light of a new law that was adopted in 2025 which prohibits these veterans
from also claiming other veterans tax credits and exemptions.
Gene Gauss made a motion to consider Article 5. Clint Hanson seconded the motion.
Brian Seaworth asked whether an estimate of the total revenue impact should be included, and David
Jodoin responded that they could provide a best guess estimate based on current applicants but
couldn't predict new applications.
Gerry Fleury asked for clarification about whether these articles were needed to ratify state law
changes. David Jodoin confirmed that the state had made changes previously requiring town
ratification. He explained that the $2,000 to $4,000 increase was because disabled veterans could no
longer stack exemptions, so the Select Board decided to increase both the disabled exemption and the
general veteran's credit (from $500 to $750) to compensate for those who previously benefited from
stacking.
Louis Caron asked how many applicants currently qualify. David Jodoin provided numbers: 14
currently qualify for the disabled exemption at a cost of $28,000, which would increase to $56,000.
The overall revenue impact of Articles 5 and 6 combined is estimated at $90,000, which Mark LePage
had already reduced from the tax sheet.
Brian Seaworth sought clarification about whether these were law changes or adjustments. David
Jodoin explained that Articles 7 and 8 are adjustments based on inflation factors, while Article 5
involves both a state law change (prohibiting stacking) and a town increase to compensate.
The article was recommended on a 9-0 vote with Kristopher DeLorme abstaining.
ARTICLE 6 - Shall the town vote to modify Chapter 138, Article VI under the provisions of
RSA 72:28, and 72:28-b (Veterans Tax Credits) to increase the current credits from $500 per
year to $750 per year.
Clint Hanson made a motion to consider Article 6. Louis Caron seconded the motion.
Mark LePage explained that this article simply increases the credit amount and, combined with
Article 5, represents a $90,000 revenue impact.
Mariana Beer asked whether the $90,000 was an estimate or based on previous applicants. Mark
LePage clarified that it was based on current applicants as of that date, though new applicants could
increase the impact.
The article was recommended on a 9-0 vote with Kristopher DeLorme abstaining.
ARTICLE 7 - Shall the town vote to modify Chapter 138, Article IV of the Pembroke Town
Code, entitled Elderly Exemptions under the provisions of RSA 72:39-a for elderly exemption
from property tax in Pembroke, based on assessed value, for qualified taxpayers, to be as
follows: for a person 65 years of age up to 74 years, $48,673 (from $47,250); for a person 75
years of age up to 79 years, $89,658 (from $87,750); for a person 80 years of age or older
$170,743 (from $168,750). To qualify, the person must have been a New Hampshire resident for
at least the last 3 consecutive years, own the real estate individually or jointly, or if the real
estate is owned by such person's spouse, they must have been married to each other for at least
the last 5 consecutive years. In addition, the taxpayer must have a net income of not more than
$29,827 or, if married, a combined net income of less than $42,700; and own net assets not in
excess of $45,000 excluding the value of the person's residence.

BUDGET COMMITTEE
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 22, 2026
FINAL
Video recordings of Budget Committee meetings can be found at:
https://townhallstreams.com/towns/pembroke_nh
The relative start time of each agenda section is noted below.
Mark LePage, Chairman, called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
I.
Attendance
Budget Committee Present: Mark LePage, Gerry Fleury, Clint Hanson, Matt Miller, Louis Caron,
Brian Seaworth, Jason Mayeu, Sue Whitbeck, Gene Gauss, Mariana Beer, Kristopher DeLorme
Budget Committee Excused: None
Budget Committee Not Present: None
Il.
School Budget Review
Mark LePage opened by noting that the budget committee had received updated school budget
warrant materials with minor corrections. Jess Bickford added that Warrant Article #15 was newly
added, which addresses the adoption and request to reuse retainage funds at the end of the year. Mark
LePage also noted that a tweaked tax revenue sheet had been distributed and a draft MS-27 Form was
Gerry Fleury addressed the committee regarding two underutilized trust funds: the Promotion of
Literacy Fund with a balance of $10,139.41 (K-8 eligible) and the Educational Opportunities Fund
with a balance of $12,104.84 (K-12 eligible). These funds require formal project proposals and can be
accessed through the Trustees of Trust Funds. Fleury noted that administrators may be unaware these
funds exist and recommended reviewing the trust fund documentation available on the town website
under the Budget Committee tab.
Amber Wheeler explained Warrant Article 15, which seeks authorization to retain up to 5% of net
assessment for emergency or unexpected expenses such as HVAC failures or Special Education costs.
use and required commissioner approval. Under current policy, funds can be used for any budgeted
need without prior approval. The retainage fund operates on a non-rolling basis, meaning retained
funds only offset taxes if the same amount is retained annually; otherwise, unused funds revert to
offset taxes. The dollar amount is discretionary, with the school board determining how much to
retain up to the 5% maximum. Committee members clarified the mechanics and confirmed that first-
year retention reduces tax offset as a one-time impact, while subsequent years stabilize if amounts
remain consistent.
Regarding Warrant Articles 4, 5, 6, and 7, Amber Wheeler explained that a Benefits Trust Fund
would be created to address situations like the SchoolCare assessment situation discovered in late
September/October, which was a dramatic hit to the budget. Creating a trust fund ensures that if
something similar happens in the future, it will not have as dramatic an effect on the current operating
budget. The Tuition Trust Fund came about from discussions regarding open enrollment, as Pembroke
has already felt the impact of students leaving to attend Prospect Mountain, causing the tuition rate to
increase significantly. The Committee confirmed that if articles 4 and 6 do not pass, articles 5 and 7
would have to be tabled because you cannot appropriate funds to a trust that voters disapprove.

The Committee discussed that the statute specifically requires a public hearing by the School Board
prior to spending money from an established trust. Jess Bickford confirmed that when the School
Board becomes agents to expend, they still must hold a public hearing to let the public know they are
utilizing the trust. The Trustees of Trust Funds check the records of school board meetings to ensure
the hearing was held; otherwise, the funds will not be dispersed.
Regarding the school warrant articles overview, Article 11 is from a reserve fund, and Articles 13 and
14 are from surplus. The articles are funded in order, so if there is $100,000 left at the end of the year
and the first item is $100,000, that is the only one that gets funded. This is considered a prioritization
order. The capital reserve fund has a separate line item for school-related expenses versus town-
related expenses, and they are completely distinct entities.
The Committee discussed various budget items, including enrollment projections where Jason Mayeu
requested that enrollment numbers be moved outside of graphs to avoid blocking other data. Sue
Whitbeck raised concerns about future infrastructure costs related to the Pembroke Academy addition
and the potential for dramatic enrollment downturns. Clint Hanson noted that the tuition structure is
problematic because it includes all operational costs, including building maintenance, which the
district could be stuck with if enrollment declines.
Regarding open enrollment and tuition details, Jess Bickford explained that when a Pembroke family
sends their student to Prospect Mountain, Pembroke does not pay Prospect Mountain's tuition rate;
they pay Pembroke's tuition rate. Pembroke is in a fortunate situation where the tuition rate is one of
the lowest in the state. If they take in students from other towns, they will charge those students their
tuition rate, which in many circumstances would be greater than Pembroke's tuition rate.
For the SchoolCare assessment, $400,000 came out of surplus from the prior year, and $200,000 came
out of this year's Operating Budget. Jess Bickford explained that there are many new things in the
budget but not new lines. Supplies change based on whatever needs arise. There are some changes in
Special Education, which happen every year based on student need. They have a technology
replacement plan that is followed, and she does not anticipate a huge shift in any kind of digital
platform soon.
Jason Mayeu identified significant budget line changes in teacher salaries, contracted services
(specifically special education), liability insurance, and bus contracts. For maintenance projects, the
district is planning cabinet replacements, sound barriers, exterior doors, camera servers, bleachers,
countertops, masonry, and heating controls. These projects were deferred from the prior year and are
being reintroduced based on facility needs. For vocational tuition, the CRTC Tuition increased
approximately 10% due to declining state funding, which means Pembroke's costs rise as the State
contribution decreases.
Gerry Fleury asked a question about what would happen if someone moved to cut $3 million from the
budget. Jess Bickford responded they would be looking at doomsday. Their last $3 million dollar cut
around 27 staff members, and they could not function with 27 additional staff members gone. They
would be forced to combine Hill School and would have to do renovations. Gene Gauss noted that
open enrollment would go away, and they would essentially have no school because everyone would
leave to go to open enrollment schools. Jess Bickford explained that they would have no control over
the cost that they send out for students to attend other schools that are not in Pembroke and would be
forced to pay that tuition.
Louis Caron emphasized the need to communicate both revenue declines and cost increases to the
public. He noted that State Adequacy Aid is declining while costs are increasing in areas including
salaries, contracted services, maintenance, and vocational tuition. He stressed that tax rate increases
are driven by both spending increases and revenue decreases, not just one factor. Mark LePage
acknowledged that this dual message would be emphasized during the public hearing presentation.

Ill.
Begin Deliberations for Public Hearing
Mark LePage explained the deliberation process for the remainder of the budget season. The
Committee is transitioning into the deliberation process, which means deciding what to bring forward
to recommend for the public hearing, and then taking another pass to make a final recommendation
for School District and Town Meetings in March. By the end of Thursday evening, the committee
must have recommendations for every warrant article, including the operating budget with a specific
dollar amount. All warrant recommendations will be done as roll call votes.
The public hearing is scheduled for February 5'h at 7:00 PM at the PA Auditorium, where the School
and Town will present their budgets, the Budget Committee will present the tax sheet, and the public
will have the opportunity to ask questions. Immediately following the public hearing, the Budget
Committee will hold a meeting to revote on warrant articles if needed based on public input. February
12'h is designated as a contingency meeting in case weather postpones the February 5* hearing. Final
recommendations must be submitted to the Selectboard by February 18th
Mark LePage reminded the committee that their charter requires balancing both need and
affordability. Clint Hanson stated that cutting the budget likely means layoffs. Mark LePage noted
they should remember what happened last year when taxpayers decided to restore recommended
reductions, and that outcome is acceptable too.
Matt Miller noted that this will be the fourth year in a row where they are proposing a 10% increase in
the amount to be raised by taxes, which is tough and very visible. Mark LePage noted that since he
just got the warrant from David Jodoin tonight, he needs to make another pass through the tax sheet to
ensure the numbers are correct. The Public Works Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) number is
not in the tax sheet because he did not know what it was, so there will be a new iteration of the tax
sheet.
Gene Gauss made a request that the Committee try to finalize their deliberations on the operating
budgets next week so there are no surprises at the public hearing. He noted that in the past, the
Committee came to a number during deliberations and then came back to the public hearing with
another number, which was difficult. Mark LePage agreed that in the spirit of the public hearing, he
agrees with this request.
The committee proceeded with roll call votes on school warrant articles. Mark LePage would not be
voting as is customary for the role of Chair of the Budget Committee.
Article 5 - To see if the Pembroke School District will, contingent upon the passage of Article 4,
vote to raise and appropriate the sum of up to One Hundred Thousand Dollars ($100,000), to be
added to the Benefits Expendable Trust Fund previously established. This sum to come from
the June 30, 2026, unassigned fund balance available for transfer on July 1, 2026. No amount to
be raised from additional taxation.
Clint Hanson made a motion to recommend the warrant article. Louis Caron seconded the motion.
The committee confirmed the fund is designed to buffer unexpected health insurance or benefits costs.
The article was recommended on a 10-0 vote.
Article 7- To see if the Pembroke School District will, contingent upon the passage of Article 6,
vote to raise and appropriate the sum of up to One Hundred Thousand Dollars ($100,000), to be
added to the Tuition Expendable Trust Fund previously established. This sum to come from the
June 30, 2026, unassigned fund balance available for transfer on July 1, 2026. No amount to be
raised from additional taxation.
