BUDGET COMMITTEE
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 15, 2026
FINAL
Video recordings of Budget Committee meetings can be found at:
https://townhallstreams.com/towns/pembroke_nh
The relative start time of each agenda section is noted below.
Mark LePage, Chairman, called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
Attendance
Budget Committee Present: Mark LePage, Gerry Fleury, Clint Hanson, Matt Miller, Louis Caron, Brian Seaworth,
Jason Mayeu, Sue Whitbeck, Gene Gauss, Mariana Beer, Kristopher DeLorme
Budget Committee Excused: None
Budget Committee Not Present: None
II. Approval of Minutes - January 15
Clint Hanson made a motion to approve the minutes of January 8, 2026. Jason Mayeu seconded the motion.
Louis Caron asked that a correction be made to the percentage of payroll/personnel costs that can be attributed to the
School Budget from last meeting.
The motion passed on an 10-0 vote as amended.
Ill.
School Budget Review - Overview
The Special School District Meeting that is being held on January 27, 2025, at Pembroke Academy will be held in the
auditorium, as opposed to the library.
Mark stated that there is a total of $575,000 in School warrant articles. These are all planned to be funded from surplus.
Jess Bickford, Superintendent, and Dr. Andra Hall, Assistant Superintendent of Student Services, were in attendance to
discuss the Special Education portion of the budget.
Dr. Hall covered a summary of Special Education costs that was provided to the Committee. She explained some of the
changes that the district has made in providing Special Education services. She stated that generally, it is more cost
effective to provide these services within the district, as opposed to using outside services. The decision whether to
provide services in or out-of-district are based on cost effectiveness and the availability of staff to provide the required
services.
She explained that even if a parent chooses to enroll their student in a charter school, the district is still responsible for
covering the costs of their Special Education services. She added that the State funds education in two buckets, Adequacy
Aid and Differential Aid, and while the district would still receive Adequacy Aid for the student, the charter school would
receive the Differential Aid, and the district would still be responsible for covering the student's special education costs.
Dr. Hall spoke about Special Education transportation costs. Superintendent Bickford added that the district will be going
out to bid next year on Special Education transportation services. Dr. Hall stated that, in some cases, transportation for
Special Education is more expensive than educational costs. She is hopeful that with more competition, there will be more
competitive pricing.

Mariana Beer asked about the difference in costs for Summer Special Placements between the three schools. Dr. Hall
explained that this differs between schools due to the needs at each school. She continued that this includes out-of-district
placements for Pembroke Academy, where Pembroke Hill School has no out-of-district placements. Superintendent
Bickford added that transition services also account for a large portion of these costs. There are different needs based on
the student that also account for some of the differences.
Dr. Hall provided the Committee with information on the total number of students identified with Special Education needs
across the Pembroke School District.
There was some discussion about Episodes of Treatment, which generally involve mental health services. This has
generally been requested by parents through the State. Currently, the State pays most of these services. These are
generally meant to be short-term placements, but the district is seeing some placements becoming more long-term.
Dr. Hall explained the State's Special Education funding and the associated formulas for those calculations. The threshold
for reimbursement continues to go up on an annual basis.
Sue Whitbeck asked when the reimbursements are received from the State. Superintendent Bickford stated that
reimbursements for the prior year are paid to the district in December of the following year. Dr. Hall explained that there
is a different reimbursement formula for students that are placed by the court system.
Dr. Hall reviewed some of the cost cutting measures that are currently in progress. She discussed negotiating
transportation costs, as well as working with parents/families to provide transportation, which is more cost effective for
the district.
Dr. Hall is also completing a deep dive of current caseloads and services offered. Superintendent Bickford explained that
they want to make sure there is even distribution of cases and effective use of staff.
She explained that special education practices are also shifting, and this is being reflected specifically at the Hill School.
She spoke about more co-teaching and pulling students who receive services into the classroom as opposed to providing
services that remove these students from the classroom. She also spoke about reintegration efforts.
Superintendent Bickford stated that she chose to close the Bridge Program due to the data not supporting its continuation.
Hill School has now created the Star Program. She added that the trajectory of out-of-district placements has been
decreasing.
Dr. Hall also stated that they are working on promoting collaboration between Special Education and General Education.
This model puts focus on Pre-K through Third Grade. She spoke about the importance of early intervention and its long-
term cost saving effects.
Superintendent Bickford stated that last year Special Education Coordinators attended training on reducing the reliance on
one-to-one paraprofessional support.
Dr. Hall spoke about the district's efforts to bring back students that are in out-of-district placements. She stated that it is
meant to be a slow process of reintegration. She spoke about their data driven approach to Special Education.
Kris DeLorme asked what drives out-of-district placements. Superintendent Bickford explained that this is usually
decided when it becomes too restrictive for the student or too costly for the district to provide these services.
Kris asked what drives Individualized Education Programs (IEPs). Superintendent Bickford explained the assessment
process and the guidance from the Department of Education that dictates the services that they receive.
Mark asked if there were any new positions added to this year's budget for Special Education. Superintendent Bickford
stated that there is a part-time need for an Occupational Therapist. There is also an opening at Three Rivers School, which
is currently being filled by a contractor.

He asked if they were seeing any new trends emerging in the Special Education space. Dr. Hall stated that trauma is
affecting the work that they do. She also noted that there is an impact from COVID, as well. There was some further
discussion on the lasting effects of COVID on all students, including the physical effects.
Matt Miller asked about the statewide phone ban and its effects. Dr. Hall and Superintendent Bickford gave extremely
positive feedback. Superintendent Bickford provided comments on technology outside of school and its effects in school.
Mark asked if there are any big changes coming in the Special Education space, including in legislation. Dr. Hall
mentioned that the district is paying for Special Education in Charter Schools due to current legislation. She hopes that
this is given thought when Open Enrollment is considered
Mark asked what keeps the Superintendent and Dr. Hall up at night. Dr. Hall stated that her biggest concern is children
getting lost in the Open Enrollment process.
Sue Whitbeck spoke about the shift in parent's thoughts on Special Education. She spoke about the district always saying
yes to Special Education requests in the past. Superintendent Bickford mentioned concerns about the appeal process
through the State, which often sides with parental requests, despite district recommendations.
There was a larger discussion about unfunded mandates for Special Education, both at the State and Federal level.
Gene Gauss stated that this is the first year that the School Board has not had to have a warrant article to add to the
Special Education Expendable Trust. He feels that there has been improvement.
Louis asked about how Open Enrollment will impact Special Education expenses. Superintendent Bickford explained that
there will need to be some decisions made at the State level on this. Currently, the sending district would be responsible.
Jason recognized the decreases in Special Education spending. He inquired about the 14.5% increase in teacher salaries at
Hill School for Special Education. Superintendent Bickford explained that this includes some turnover and Collective
Bargaining Agreement increases.
Kris asked if a school district can refuse a student for Open Enrollment because they have a disability. Superintendent
Bickford stated that they cannot. She added that they can set certain criteria, such as limiting enrollment for certain
programs.
Superintendent Bickford explained the district's proposal of a warrant article to make Pembroke Open Enrollment. She
explained that at the beginning of the discussion, this was a proposal to generate revenue. As the discussion progressed,
there was an embrace in the philosophy of Open Enrollment. There is a want for the Pembroke School District to be a
district of choice.
She added that setting the exit criteria at zero to start to allow the district to learn the impacts. Eventually, the goal is to
make it, so students do not want to leave the district.
Jason added that he has heard the concerns about this exit rate proposal but encouraged the district to be able to explain
clearly why they are proposing this and the timelines involved. He is not sure that it is currently clear to the public.
Superintendent Bickford expressed that the district would like to get ahead of proposed legislation.
Louis asked if the exit rate can be amended. Gene explained the discussions on the exit rate and the financial impacts to
taxpayers. He expressed that this has a significant impact on the decision to set the exit rate at 0%. He emphasized the
importance of being able to forecast the budget.
Mark added that criteria would need to be developed if students were allowed to leave which could become difficult.

BUDGET COMMITTEE
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 8, 2026
FINAL
Video recordings of Budget Committee meetings can be found at:
https://townhallstreams.com/towns/pembroke_nh
The relative start time of each agenda section is noted below.
Mark LePage, Chairman, called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.
I.
Attendance
Budget Committee Present: Mark LePage, Gerry Fleury, Clint Hanson, Matt Miller, Kristopher DeLorme, Louis
Caron, Brian Seaworth, Jason Mayeu, Sue Whitbeck, Kerri Dean (for Gene Gauss)
Budget Committee Excused: Gene Gauss, Mariana Beer
Budget Committee Not Present: None
II. Approval of Minutes - December 11 & December 18
Clint Hanson made a motion to approve the minutes of December 11, 2025. Gerry Fleury seconded the motion. The
motion passed on an 8-0 vote. Kerri Dean and Brian Seaworth abstained.
Clint Hanson made a motion to approve the minutes of December 18, 2025. Louis Caron seconded the motion. The
motion passed on an 8-0 vote. Kerri Dean and Sue Whitbeck abstained.
III. Town Budget - Update
Mark stated that new numbers for the Town Budget were received from David Jodoin, Town Administrator. The
Department of Public Works (DPW) contract is still outstanding.
Gerry Fleury mentioned that the impact of $100,000 in spending remains at $0.08 on the tax rate. Mark stated that the
valuation for property in the town increased by $4 million. The current budget, short of the DPW contract, is an increase
of $300,000 with $100,000 increase in expenditure and $200,000 decrease in revenue.
IV.
School Budget Review - Overview
Jess Bickford, Superintendent, and Amber Wheeler, Business Administrator, were in attendance to present an overview of
the 2026-2027 School District Budget.
Mark complimented Superintendent Bickford and Ms. Wheeler on the summary provided, and level of detail provided to
the Committee.
Ms. Wheeler stated that overall, they wanted to maintain current programs for both regular and special education. She
noted that there are some instructional supplies needed that have not been purchased in the last couple of years. She also
added that trust funds have been used to cover some expenses over that period, and the School Board plans to continue
this practice.
She stated that the Special Education budget is based on student need for students that are currently enrolled.

Ms. Wheeler spoke about a dramatic increase in Personnel Costs due to health insurance increases. There was traditionally
a 3% to 9% increase in the SAU year over year, and this year, they budgeted for a 15% increase. The actual increase was
30.3%. She spoke about the difference between SchoolCare and HealthTrust in how each fund their risk pool.
Gerry Fleury asked about Ms. Wheeler's confidence level in SchoolCare's obligation to provide service. Ms. Wheeler
could not confirm her confidence level. Gerry expressed his concern with their status and their ability to meet their
obligation.
Superintendent Bickford explained that this year they did a thorough analysis of available options for health insurance.
Anthem has refused to provide a quote due to the current risk, and HealthTrust will be providing a quote in April. They
will continue to explore this option.
Ms. Wheeler stated that liability insurance has gone up drastically due to claims. She added that their provider, Primex, is
also providing cybersecurity training, which will be available to staff members. In addition, they will also be assisting the
district with a cybersecurity emergency plan.
Mark asked about the claims filed and if there are actions that can be taken proactively to prevent future claims.
Superintendent Bickford spoke about the meeting schedule and safety review process that is in place.
Ms. Wheeler spoke about the new regular education transportation vendor that was selected. Superintendent Bickford
added that special education transportation will be put out to bid next year. Ms. Wheeler added that, this year, they broke
out the RFP by town, as opposed to putting the whole SAU out to bid as one contract, which appears to have generated
more interest from vendors.
Kerri Dean stated that some of the current bus drivers from Dale Transportation have reached out to the new vendor to
express interest in switching over, mostly for the reason of staying with their students.
Mark asked about the warrant articles that the School District will propose and if they will be funded from surplus or
additional taxation. Superintendent Bickford stated that they will be funded from surplus.
Ms. Wheeler spoke about the Regular Instruction lines. There was an increase of approximately $219,000 in regular
education with the majority being due to salary increases required by the Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA).
Ms. Wheeler spoke about the Special Education lines, which show an increase of approximately $253,000. The majority
is due to salary and contracted service increases. She highlighted that there was a reduction in out-of-district placements
and summer placements of approximately $150,000 and $27,000 respectively. These services are now provided in-district,
which offers a cost savings to the SAU. Special Education specifics will be discussed at the next meeting.
She spoke about the Concord Regional Technical Center (CRTC) program and the anticipated growth of the program.
Mark asked about the tuition per student and Superintendent Bickford explained that it depends on the amount of state
funding that CRTC receives. Mark followed up by asking about enrollment in the program and the numbers were not
readily available, but Ms. Wheeler stated that she would get that information to the Committee.
Ms. Wheeler spoke about the new Open Enrollment Tuition lines, which requires at least $1 in them maintain the lines in
the budget. This is a standard procedure for lines that are currently unused. Currently, they have $O, so the Committee was
asked to vote to place a total of $3 in the lines, with $1 from each school to support each line.
Clint Hanson made a motion to add $1 to each Open Enrollment Tuition line by removing it from another line as required
by State Law. Gerry seconded the motion. The motion passed 9-0.
Ms. Wheeler mentioned that they are proposing approximately $65,000 in maintenance projects at the three schools. At
Hill School, they are proposing cabinets, sound barrier systems and exterior doors. At Three Rivers, they are proposing a

camera server, sound barrier system, bleachers and countertops. At Pembroke Academy, they propose abatements,
countertops, masonry and heating control updates.
Ms. Wheeler spoke about the increases in the Benefits Services lines due to health care increases, as previously discussed.
This increase reflects a $746,231 increase for a total budget of $9,547,137. She listed some decreases within the lines as
well including district retirements and adjustments for non-certified staff and administrators.
Matt Miller asked about the status of the track. Superintendent Bickford stated that she would get a formal update, but she
believes they are trying to get the project done as soon as possible for the spring season.
Ms. Wheeler spoke about the Leases line. It was explained that this is comparable to a bond. She noted that there is a
$240,217 decrease because a portion of one of the leases being paid in full as of July 2025.
Ms. Wheeler explained the food service program and its accounting procedures. Unpaid student debt cannot be paid by
revenues from the program but instead must be paid from the operating budget. Revenue can cover other program
expenses. They manage these lines accordingly. Alternate revenue, including catering and providing food for other schools
(Strong Foundations), was also discussed
Louis Caron asked about the Special Education transportation costs. Mr. Wheeler stated that there was an increase in
Special Education Transportation costs of approximately $28,000. Louis noted that the School District Budget is very
personnel driven. He stated that approximately 70-72% of the budget can be attributed to this. It is a large, fixed cost that
could only be reduced by staffing cuts. Superintendent Bickford agreed
Sue asked if Pembroke is responsible for Special Education Services for charter, home or private school students.
Superintendent Bickford stated that the district is only responsible if the district places the child. In a home school
situation, it would only be responsible if the child was taking a class in the district and only for the time that they were in
class. She stated that in an Open Enrollment situation, the district would be responsible for Special Education costs.
Superintendent Bickford stated that they try to do as many Special Education services in-house as possible.
Gerry asked about McKinney-Vento. Superintendent Bickford explained that this program is meant for the homeless
student population. It mandates transportation if the parent cannot provide it. If they reside in another district, the cost is
split between districts. It was explained that this is an unpredictable expense.
Gerry asked how much the district anticipates in grant funding. Ms. Wheeler explained that (Elementary and Secondary
School Emergency Relief (ESSER) funding has concluded. They are anticipating approximately $287,000 in grant
funding for the upcoming year. There is also an anticipated decrease in State Adequacy Funding.
There was a discussion on State Adequacy Aid funding. Brian Seaworth provided an overview of his findings in looking
into the reduction in State SWEPT aid for the coming year, which appears tied to reduced enrollment. Amber confirmed
that reduced population of students qualifying for reduced/free lunch did impact SWEPT.
Mark stated that next meeting's discussion will focus on the Special Education Budget. Superintendent Bickford also
suggested any questions about open enrollment be discussed that night as well. Gerry requested information on reductions
and economies of scales employed in the Special Education Program.
Mark noted that there will be a Special School District Meeting on January 27, 2026, at 6:30 pm, regarding open
enrollment. As there is no specific dollar amount associated with the warrant article, the Budget Committee does not
formally vote on whether to recommend.
Adjourn
Clint made a motion to adjourn at 8:25 PM. Gerry seconded the motion, and it was approved unanimously.

With a total of 2,000’ of main piping, three hydrants and thirteen services. The most we have put in for a project was 1,580 of 6” on Whitten and Webster streets. Guests:

The regular meeting was called to order at 6:00pm.

OLD BUSINESS:

Potential Roadwork – 

PFC Monitoring- Remained consistent in the 3’s.

Concord Connection – Nothing new at this time. 

Strategic Planning Grant – Narrowed down to four sites. Working on approvals to go do geophysics. 

Lead Service Lines – Updated mailing list. However, still waiting on the new spreadsheet to be released from NHDES, to begin the updates to their database. No word from them as to when we should expect to see this. 

Bachelder Rd- Bridge work is complete. Matt had discussed with David, using the pipe we purchased somewhere else and we cannot do so. Since the money used to purchase the pipe and other materials was tied to the bridge work that must be used for Bachelder Rd project. The new 8” pipe has been run under the bridge and Matt is waiting on roads committee to see if they will be paving the entire road. If so, we do not need to pave the portion we will be utilizing for the new pipe. 

Glass St- Look in spring for any issues. Nothing new at this time.  

Wilkins Ave- Nothing new at this time. 

77 Turnpike (McDonald’s)- Nothing new at this time. 

Water Tariffs- Matt rewrote the tariff to clean up some template issues with the old format. Some minor changes are highlighted to reflect changes we’ve already made or future pricing increase to review. Matt printed pricing sheets with other towns pricing to compare and contrast. 

Motion: Chet Martel    Seconded: Larry Plourde. To approve the second reading of the Tariffs. 

All in favor, motion passed. 

**Tarriff changes must go through 3 meeting approvals**

NEW BUSINESS:     

MCSB Collateralization- Current collateralization is for $700,000 between all of our accounts. We are approaching this number so we may want to increase the insurance on our accounts. The bank said this doesn’t’ affect interest rates. So, Matt suggested bringing the total up to a million to be covered completely. This needs to be done by the town treasurer but, also wanted the board to be involved in the review. 

Motion: Chet Martel     Seconded: Larry Plourde. All in favor, motion passed

Office Roof- Matt reach out three roofers to get pricing on replacing the roof. In meeting with the first, Marquis Roofing, he looked from the outside and said to keep the chimney install plywood and re-shingle. After, Matt took him to the attic in which he had some concerns with this approach. He said the sides are blowing out and the center is settling. He also looked at the chimney, which has signs of fatigue from heat and water damage. He said he would not be comfortable adding weight to the roof without doing something to stop the current issues that will come to get worse. He offered some repairs but ultimately didn’t provide the price for the work. The second roofer, Adam Vaillencourt looked at the roof and said they would not feel comfortable with the job. They would just put new plywood all around and re-shingle. He did agree that the chimney should come down. As it is old, failing and would only be keeping for looks not for purpose. He also mentioned that he noticed the roof having a lot of fatigue and a lot of boards are broken or heavily nailed. It has as much as three layers up there currently. So, it would minimize some of the extra weight but, ultimately adds more. Metal roofs were also discussed but, the concern with that is controlling the snow and with it being a public building, it is simply not feasible. He also noticed some issues with the back section and recommends replacing that, since it’s 16 years old. Matt has noticed some leaks when there’s water backups. Some of the gutters have come loose, so they would fix that while here. Ultimately, they recommend a structural engineer to provide comment on the internals. He didn’t give an opinion on that and said it’s separate from what they do as roofers. The cost of the roof with Vaillencourt without repairs would be $35,000.  Bruce and Matt talked with Tom Hebert, and he recommended a contractor out of Bow to come take a look at the roof. 

Motion: Chet Martel    Seconded: Larry Plourde        All in favor, motion passed

Update office computer/monitors- The office computer is almost 13 years old and needs to be replaced. It glitches, shuts down, freezes, very frequently. The billing program doesn’t allow for opening other screens while in use with one monitor. Matt would recommend dual monitors to make the work flow easier. In addition, quick books online version has been implemented. We had to update from online version from desktop. Due to desktop version not supporting payroll as of May 29, 2025. There are some issues with the online version not supporting the 457 employer contributions. Michelle is temporarily doing payroll. Lynne will be doing the banking and taxes portion and Michelle would do the time inputs. Michelle has sent in a work order to intuit about the issue which also affects other functions that we don’t use but, means other companies are having issues as well. Intuit is working on the bug/issue but we do not have a timespan of how long this will take to fix said issue. Lynne emailed Brad for a quote to replace the computer and monitors. Brad, our IT contact, came back with a price to install the computer with all of the programs for $1,329. $2,000 is in the budget for office equipment. 

Motion: Chet Martel    Seconded: Larry Plourde   All in favor, motion passed. 

Tank work- Matt has a quote for tank repairs to the Hooksett tank as recommended from last year’s tank inspections/ Total cost $9,445 from aqueous. This includes installing fall prevention cable, flexible duckbill over the overflow pipes, OSHA compliant lockable ladder guard and replacing mesh screens to non-corrodible for vents and overflow. All other work requires draining the tank and that is not recommended at this time. This will be something to be planned with there is more work to do inside.  

Motion: Kevin Brasley        Seconded: Chet Martel          All in favor, motion passed.

Late Penalty Manifest – To approve the Late Penalty Manifest for May in the amount of $1,640.00. Motion by Chet Martel and Seconded by Ed Lavellee. All in favor, motion passed.

OTHER BUSINESS and CORRESPONDENCE:

Other Business – Corey’s Raise- Corey took the T1 and T2 exams and passed both. He’s now fully licensed as a system operator. The state only lists operators that are licensed to operate the system. Otherwise, the employee has to operate under the superintendent’s license, to do such jobs as pump-station batching or larger distribution system maintenance. Having another licensed person on staff is incredibly helpful to show that in in Matt’s absence, can operate the system. Typically, $1 raises are given for each license held. Bringing Corey from $29.08 to $31.08

Route 3 paving- Both crossings are completed and Same has paid all of his portions of the

Water Leak- No changes to Bartlett St. The crew had one sink hole that was filled in. The Library
St leak seems to have done more damage to the road. Matt will need to work with DOT on
what repairs they want for damaged road there.

Buck St townhouse- Nothing new at this time.
Cybersecurity- Matt met with the overwatch foundation on June 15, 2026 along with our
electricians. They asked us some questions about out current setup and took a look at the office
and Route 3. Given all the sites are generally the same, we didn't need to visit them all. They
will follow up with a report of recommended work and cost. They will then compare that to the
grant money available from NDES allocated to us. They hope to cover everything with the
grant money. If it does exceed, they can petition for more funds. If that doesn't work, we would
then need to decide if we want to also put money towards the project. At this point based off
our discussions in prior meetings, they are recommending redundancy for scada computer, so
we don't have another issue like we did last year. We discussed separating computers but
ultimately decided it would be best for us to have desktops tied into one monitor, mouse and
keyboard using a switch. If one computer goes offline, the other would just require flicking a
switch to keep everything running. This would also give the opportunity to upgrade to the latest
software. Some of the Fortnite security devices should be upgraded to newer models. We also
discussed how we access the system remotely. We currently use Google Chrome report
desktop, they suggested we utilize software from the scada company. Which they can set this
up with log ins for each person. Currently we all use one log in with the same authority to
make changes to the system. This is not recommended because they said we should all have
individual log ins by name. This allows to see what changes have been made and by what
operator. This not only helps with knowing who made the changes to the system but also if we
were to get hacked, they could track how they got in by knowing what device was used to log
in. Because of this, they suggested we don't use personal devices for logging in. Which is
primarily what we have been doing. Everyone has tablets from the Water Works they can use
but, getting them to carry those around everywhere they go after hours is not an option. The
work phones are flip phones so they will not work for this either. We either need to take our
chances with personal phones as we have been. Or upgrade the work phones to access the
scada system. Per board discussion to keep the board informed of any updates.

Academy Rd- There was a main water leak in February 2026. When the repair was made a

OLD BUSINESS:

Potential Roadwork – Nothing new at this time. Allenstown is still in discussion.

PFC Monitoring- Latest from EPA is that the rule for PFOA and PFOS remain the same with the original implementation date of 2029. They have proposed eliminating the other compounds for now and allowing an extension for PFOA and PFOS to 2031 with a request by the department. This rule is up for discussion in July. Last update from NHDES, as far as the litigation funding, we have been approved for an additional $210,000. Bringing the total to $1,035,634.

Concord Connection – Matt informed Concord of the issue at Route 106 and that we will still need a response. He was informed that it made the list for discussion but there is no meeting date that has been set. 

Groundwater Zones – This work is covered in the budget 100%. If the board wants to looks into continuing this work. 

Lead Service Lines – We have the approval for $60,000 in grant funds for potholing work to identify service line materials. This can also be used towards the collection of private line materials if we have known materials on our side. We can also use this money for hiring out vac trucks to limit the ground disturbance for potholing. The other option is to use the funds towards purchasing a vac trailer that we could use in house to do the same thing. In all scenarios $60,000 will not cover the full cost of identifying materials. 

ARD Water Lines- Matt received a few phone calls from a potential buyer of the property. He informed them we’re in the process of determining out remaining water capacity due to recent water quality changes. Matt looked at the recent demands the school has and determined they have capacity for 10 residential units under the current scenario. Any additional units may not be able to be approved until we know more about our remaining capacity. Which is under review by Underwood currently. Whatever is left would be used as first come first serve. It was also discussed the need to upgrade the water lines. Which they said they understood and agreed and still wanted to move forward per our last conversation and email chain. 

Concord Property- Jeff Eames at 6:15pm. 

Back Hoe- It was discussed with the board to approve a purchase of the 2025 Caterpillar 440 in the amount of $161,900 after trade in of the 200 JCB backhoe. Payment will be due when invoiced. The machine is being shipped from North Carolina. 

Motion by Kevin Brasley and seconded by Tom Petit. All in favor, motion passed. 

Route 3 paving- Work for the two drills across Route 3 are scheduled for May 27th and May 28th. We will do 352 Pembroke St first and Bow Lane second. The owner of 352 Pembroke St is responsible for all payments of that work. This leaves out patch up on Route 3, which we can do. 

Water Leak- The leak in Allenstown has been found on Bartlett St. This road has binder on it from last year. The main was sitting on the ledge with large broken up ledge over the top. With the road resurfacing and how cold the winter was, it looks like it was enough to partially split the main. We found both ledge, rock and drainage beneath and next to the main so it had places to run. We do have some settlement beyond the patch and did have a void down low where the water channeled to drainage in the road. With all of the rock, it may take time for things to settle into the voids. Matt informed Allenstown that we may have more damage to the road and recommended they wait on surfacing the road. Which it sounds like they will be doing. We also had a second main break on Sunday night, May 24th, which is separate from this on Library Street. This main blew out a hole in the main about the size of a golf ball. It took about an hour from breaking to responding and getting it shut down. This did more significant damage to School Street. So we may need to do repairs there as well.

Cybersecurity- The latest from EPA is cybersecurity evaluations. Grant money has been filtered down for the evaluations and some modifications that may be needed. One of the DES contractors is on the overwatch foundation. Matt has meant with them twice, along with our electricians and IT company Lakes Region Computer. We have a site visit scheduled in June, to take a look at our remote side and office. This is taking place because water infrastructure is becoming a target for hackers in recent years with various plc’s and Scada equipment being targeted. Once a hacker is in the system changes can be made to shutdown systems or change process controls to increase hazardous chemical dosages. Some of out equipment is 13 years old. Given this info, it is recommended that we hold off on any groundwater exploration that is in the budget for this year. This also affects the discussion we had about future capacity. The current recommendation from the engineers is to increase pumping from 350-500 gpm. Which is what is giving us the bulk of our additional capacity because of this, this is not an option. In the short term, we have lost 1/3rd of our capacity to PFAS contamination. Once the new rules take place and this trend remains in the 106 well, we then would lose half of our capacity. Matt recommends discussing with the engineers about this and future capacity. Matt recommends putting freezes on any new connections, after what has been approved already.

Concord Connection – Nothing back from Concord yet after the letters. 

Groundwater Zones – This work is covered in the budget 100%. If the board wants to looks into continuing this work. 

Lead Service Lines – The service line inventory list was approved by DES. With comments for correction to be made before this year’s submittal. Which is the final list before identifications need to start.

ARD Water Lines- Nothing new on the sale of the building.  

Concord Property- It was discussed with the board to move forward with the work to be done at this property. 

Motion by Ed Lavallee and seconded by Larry Plourde. All in favor, motion passed. 

Back Hoe- The crew went to look at the Deer and Cat machines and the Cat is the preferred machine of all 3 shown. With that they also looked at a different version of the Cat that has controls mounted to the sear that can control both the front and rear bucket at the flick of a switch. This allows the operator to sit at an angle, instead of turning their heads to operate at angles. This helps with the issue of the backhoe’s being bulky and sticking out into the road at times. The crew would be able to dig side ways if needed and still look in the same direction as the boom. It also helps with trenching in that you can move the machine without the need of spinning the chair because it also has a camera. We have two sperate prices for this option and the next size up machine that comes standard with this feature. All the other models have dedicated controls for the front and back that don’t have the same level of features of comfort for the operator. Prices have been given to the board to review and is was discussed to gather dimensions to triple check that the machine will fit in the garage for storage.  

Route 3 paving- Preconstruction meeting for this was on Monday April 13, 2026. Work is planned to start in May on Route 3. Matt informed them of our plans for two crossings and DOT said they would get the permit approved. Matt met with DBU for the excavation and drilling and they are working on pricing for this. They planned on getting it to Matt the same day but he hadn’t heard anything as of yet. Matt also looked at the fire hydrants and most of that work can be done without disturbing the roads. Some side walk repairs would be needed but that won’t be affected by the states project. So that can be done at a later date given the short timeframe. 

Water Leak- The crew checked the Bear Brook River crossing and re-walked the Pine Haven feed and neither are showing any signs of leaks. We fixed a service leak but this was not enough for what we have been seeing. We also made some adjustments to the pumping, which have reduced pumping by 20,000 a day.  

Buck St townhouse- Bruce Kudrick had mentioned that they’re meeting with the zoning board at the end of April. Other than that, nothing new. 

NEW BUSINESS:     

Fire system/ Back flow testing- Matt received a quote from Freedom Fire for fire systems backflow testing. We gave up the sure system testing years ago due to new rules form the state level and the liability of shutting down the sprinkler systems. We currently use Impact Fire but have been having ongoing issues with getting tests completed. As well as the lack of communication over the last few years. Freedom Fire is made up from a handful of ex-employees of Impact Fire, that weren’t in agreement with the way that things were going. So, they started their own company. They are offering to do the tests for $60 each, compared to Impact Fire, which has increased to $80 per test. We would have an account rep designated to us. Which we used to have with Impact Fire, which made things run a lot smoother and less communication issues. 

Water restriction letter- Restriction letter can remain the same with the start date of Monday May 18, 2026. Although, we may need to make adjustments if demands go any higher this summer. Lynne has emailed Mailways the letter and the mailing list. We’ve asked for this to be mailed out as soon as possible to allow people to get the letter well in advance of the date this starts to be implemented.

OLD BUSINESS:

Potential Roadwork – Fairview has been pushed off until 2027. Allenstown is still working on the list and needs to meet to discuss how they will be doing the roads. They’re still pushing for Ray Court and West St. Which is in our budget to replace the galvanized with plastic. 

PFC Monitoring- Two new PFAS compounds have been added to the list that we will be required to sample for. PFBS & Gen-X, which are the second versions of the compounds. EPA stated that these would be removed from requirement but, that hasn’t happened yet and they have not notified the states to include them in the sampling. The current timeframe for enforcement is 2029 but, EPA still plans on pushing this date back to 2031. However, we will be required to notify customers of an exceedance of the new limits, starting as soon as next year. Unless, EPA does push back the limits. PFBS has been detected in the Rt 3 wells in the past. Matt has asked the lab to begin testing for it on our weekly non- compliance sampling also. 

We have received notice from NHDES in regards to the funding from the state litigation against chemical companies. Including 3M, Dupont, Tyco & BASF. As we talked about the first payout has been made to NH with more to come. The dollar amount we will be receiving as part of the litigation is $824,739. As we discussed, this money will be used to pay down the loan portion of either the RLF or SRF funds. This brings down the total that doesn’t need to be paid back to 3,956,739 out of the $10,440,000 or roughly 38% of the cost.

Last note on the funding is that SRF needs to have the first request within 6 months of the final approval date of 11/12/2025. Which would be 5/12/2026. Matt has asked Underwood to send in the next bill to DES to meet this requirement. After that we can go back to sending the bills to David to use up the last of the ARPA funds. 

Concord Connection – Matt spoke with Tom, the city manager and he said he has approval to present the priority list to city council for meetings and he’ll be adding regional water sales to the list. Matt heard from NHDES that the town of Bow received approval for funding of the interconnection with Concord from the March meeting cote. DES has requested that we reach out to our executive councilor and senator for help in getting Concord to vote for the sale of water outside city limits. As we have discussed in the past, we can’t do anything with the approved funds until we have a yes or no from Concord. Executive John Stephen replied and will be sending a letter to Concord City council requesting that they vote for water sales. He will also be reaching out to Concord’s counselor for a letter as well. Matt also received a response from Howard Pearls office, stating they are working with city of Concord’s contacts, to see how to best approach the situation. To try and speed up the process.

Lead Service Lines – The grant approval is complete and has been signed by G & C. We will need to use the funds by the end of 2027. Given this will only cover a portion of the excavating, that shouldn’t be an issue. 

Glass St- Plants are closed. 

525 Pembroke St- Nothing new at this time.

Wilkins Ave- Nothing new at this time.

77 Turnpike- Nothing new at this time. 

Office Roof- Tabled

ARD Water Lines- Nothing new on the sale of the building.  

Concord Property- Matt heard from Jeff Eames, to say that the wood quality on this site is low grade chip wood only. Given this, if we do choose to cut the property, it wouldn’t generate any revenue for us. It would only get rid of the encampment on the site. If we wanted any revenue from this, he recommends we take a look at the Pembroke side and cut there at the same time. It has been about 12 years since the last cut, so we are almost due regardless. He did say, not is the time to start the paperwork if the board chooses to move forward with the work.

Back Hoe- Matt got a price from Milton Cat for comparison. They came in $4,000 under the Case but, are offering less from the old machine. The salesman said they have some wiggle room also. Case said he already sharpened his pencil. 

NEW BUSINESS:     

352 Pembroke St- The owner came in to the office to let Matt know he needs to go back to the original plan of connecting to water and installing a fire hydrant on his side of the property. Matt will start on the permit and work with DOT.

Water Leak- We have had increased demands since December 10, 2025. We have fixed three main breaks but none of them have been the ongoing issue we have seen. We’ve done every leak detection method and have not been able to pin point it. We have read all three zones’ meters and have seen a small increase in demands but, not enough to cover the total increase. If we aren’t able to find this before the May demand increase, we may need to restrict summer usage even more. 

Buck St Townhouses- We received conceptual plans from Keach Nordstrom for 47 units townhouses, located at Tina Dr that is being called Buck St Townhouses. This is all private according to the plan. With two roads connecting and a potential second phase in the future. This project is planned to remain private. They have requested individual services and meter for each unit. 8” water main with HDPE services. They’re looking for a letter of conditional approval for capacity. Board approved. 

307 Pembroke St- Property owner came in too the office to discuss a conversion of his barn into 6 residential units. He would be connecting 2-2” services. One for domestic and one for fire from the road. Matt informed him of the $2,500 per unit fee, plus the cost of the meter. He agreed and would like to continue with a conditional approval. Please give a detailed description of your proposal below. We are proposing
the construction of a single family home at 202-204 Fourth Range Road. Due to
the size of the lot and considering the location of other features of the lot such as a
patch of wetlands, a planned well and septic system, the house is proposed to be
built in a location where we can best comply with the town's setbacks. The front
and right side setbacks will be adequate, but the left side and rear borders of the
home will be within the setbacks, approximately 10-15 feet from the property
lines.

the neighborhood. Granting the variance will not threaten public health, safety,
or welfare. There will be no appreciable impact on traffic or the environment.
The location will not appear crowded as the neighboring lot to the side is
currently undeveloped.
2. The spirit of the ordinance is observed. The spirit of the ordinance is to
ensure adequate space between houses to maintain a comfortable rural setting.
We will be in compliance with the setbacks on the front and right sides of the
property which is what will be visible to passersby, so there should not be a
considerable aesthetic impact. Should our rear or left side neighbors have
concerns about privacy, we would be happy to work with them on a solution that
satisfies all parties.
3. Substantial justice is done. We do not believe that the granting of this
variance will cause harm to the public that would outweigh the benefit to the
property owner. The largest foreseeable concern would be if our rear neighbors
felt our home would be too close to their property line and had qualms about
privacy. We will cooperate with them on making sure privacy is preserved for
both their and our benefit.
4. The values of surrounding properties are not diminished; and We do
not believe that granting this variance will decrease the property values of our
neighbors' lots. The neighboring lots do not have structures built near the
property line, so our proposed home will not give the appearance of crowding
their property. We will match the aesthetics of the area as best as we are able to
by meeting the front and right side setbacks.
5. Literal enforcement of the provisions of the ordinance would result in an
unnecessary hardship. 202-204 Fourth Range Road is a grandfathered lot that

the neighboring lots in the area at .459 acres, where neighboring lots range from
1.76-2.8 acres. Due to the small size and a patch of wetlands near the rear
center, there is not a location available on this lot to build a home in compliance
with the setbacks on all 4 sides. Strict interpretation of the setback guidelines
would render this land unbuildable.

Chairman Kudrick reviewed safety protocols, microphone use, and explained that no new
cases will be started after 10:00 pm. He asked everyone to be courteous. He said he
would allow each audience member to speak for 3 minutes at one time then return to the
microphone to speak again if necessary. He indicated that no input from the public
would be allowed on the Rehearing Case.

Proposed Rehearing:
Case 26-02-2 A request has been made for a Variance under Article V, Dimensional
and Density Regulations, §143-20, D. (1). The applicant, DBH Homes, LLC (Bob
Meissner), 25 Buttrick Road, Unit A1, Londonderry, NH, 03053, is requesting a Variance
to allow more than (1) principal structure on a lot. A Variance is required because only
(1) principal structure on a lot is permitted. The property is located at Pembroke St. and
Broadway, Map 264 Lot 4 & 7, Map 266 Lot 25-4 & 26 and Map 567 Lot 1, in the R-1
Medium Density Residential district and is owned by the applicant.
Received: Letter dated April 10, 2026 from A. Eli Leino, Esq. of Bernstein, Shur,
Sawyer & Nelson, PA
Concerned Resident Letters Received: Susan Spezeski, 98 Broadway, Pembroke,
dated April 22, 2026; Karen Battistelli, 12 Brittany Circle, Pembroke, dated April 20.
2026; Valorie Faretra/Bob Lawliss, 98 Broadway, Pembroke, dated April 19, 2026.

Chairman Kudrick said that the Board will decide whether they made a mistake on the
hardship criteria and if there is anything unusual about this property compared to others
in the area.
Member Glisson said that in the letter from Attorney A. Eli Leino, dated April 10, 2026,
it showed that he looked at the case from a different angle from what the Board usually
does. The Board looks at cases as "this is the only reasonable way to develop it."
Attorney Leino explained the reasons why it is good to develop the property in their
proposed way.
Chairman Kudrick said that he did not think that the Board made a mistake because from
Broadway to Associated Grocers of NE, the land is very similar on the West side of
Route 3. The Whittemore property, golf course, French's Farm (the Donna Drive
development) were very large parcels that were developed. In his opinion, he saw
nothing different between the applicant's parcel and the others. In fact, the applicant
stated that he can develop it now without Zoning Board approval.
Member Carlucci agreed that it can be developed without a variance. The Board agreed.
MOTION: Vice Chairman Hebert moved to deny the request for rehearing. While
perhaps our articulation of the reasons for denial could have been clearer, a hardship
exists when special conditions of the land render the use for which the variance is sought
reasonable. The Applicant's representations in its application and at the hearing were
that the current proposal was more suitable for the property, and an effort to alleviate
what it believes are the town's concerns regarding development of the property, and that
given the property's location near Pembroke Academy, an age restricted development
would create less traffic. It also argued that clustering the houses on the property would
minimize impacts to the wetlands. However, none of these circumstances render
construction of 100 units on one lot "reasonable". Age restricted housing can be
developed on individual lots, and no wetlands relief is requested. The applicant would
simply prefer to develop the property as a Planned Unit Development and that is not a
special circumstance which justifies the grant of a variance. Seconded by Member
Carlucci.

V. Other Business / Correspondence
Vice Chairman Hebert distributed an article that he cut out of the paper regarding
conservation easements. He said that many developers like to "dangle the conservation
carrot in front of everyone's nose." The case, in the article, is in Newfield, New
Hampshire. The Charitable Trust Unit of the State decided that the Newfield
Conservation Commission can look at the easement that was in place on this particular
property and decide if the use being proposed, in their opinion, was agricultural and
indeed fitting with the terms of the conservation easement as it was laid out. They

decided that concerts, restaurant activities, and parking was an agricultural activity. The
Conservation Commission changed an existing conservation easement.
Vice Chairman Hebert said that it was a very slippery slope because there are thousands
of existing conservation easements with the State, and Pembroke has several as well. He
said that he found that it was a very interesting article. Years ago, there was legislation
proposed and the State immediately shot it down. Now, it has returned in a different
form, and is in front of a governing agency. It could have repercussions.
He said that Pembroke has a very dedicated Conservation Commission and he could not
imagine that they would go down this road, but he just wanted to share the article with
the Board.
Chairman Kudrick said that the normal ZBA meeting room, per Fire Code, has a capacity
of 33 audience members, not including the applicants and the Board. When a large group
of people attend, the Board is obligated to continue the meeting to another date and
find a new location. Town citizens have the right to speak on all hearings and if the Board
cannot provide a place large enough for the meeting, it must move to another meeting.
He also added that the ZBA has nothing to do with roads. The Planning Board discusses
roads, takes them to the Board of Selectmen and the Selectmen approve them.
Sometimes, when roads are first proposed to the Planning Board, it might be a private
road until the Board of Selectmen approves it.
Regional impact planning is mostly a Planning Board responsibility. The ZBA only
approves a use. The Planning Board discusses all the other things pertaining to a project.
Mr. Bacon said that he referred to the State statute, and the Planning Board and the
Zoning Board are allowed to have their own triggers for DRIs (Development of Regional
Impacts), but there are no "shalls". The only "shall" is if they are hearing a landfill case.
That becomes a DRI. The Planning Board does, in Pembroke, have things that trigger a
DRI and that is listed in their subdivision code.
Also, Chairman Kudrick said that the ZBA does not give conditional approvals. The
choice is to approve, disapproval, or continue an application.
With regards to voting, Chairman Kudrick said that the ZBA has always discussed each
application and then takes a vote - either for or against. Individual Board member votes
have never been taken.

(ADOPTED)

MEMBERS PRESENT: Bruce Kudrick, Chairman; Thomas Hebert, Vice Chairman;
Dana Carlucci, Blakely Miner III
ALTERNATES PRESENT: Safiya Wazir, Bruce Halliday
EXCUSED: Natalie Glisson
STAFF PRESENT: Jocelyn Carlucci, Recording Secretary and Paul Bacon, Code
Enforcement Officer
Chairman Kudrick called the public hearing to order at 7:00 p.m.
Roll call was taken by the Recording Secretary
Alternate Member Wazir recused herself. Chairman Kudrick assigned Bruce Halliday as
a voting member for Case 26-01-Z.
Case 26-01-Z A request has been made for a Variance under Article V, Dimensional
and Density Regulations, 8143-21, Setbacks. The applicants, Josh and Melissa Amyot,
31 Peaslee Dr., are requesting a Variance to allow an above ground swimming pool to be
10' from the rear lot line. A Variance is required because a swimming pool is not
allowed to be closer than 40' from a rear lot line in this district. The property is located at
31 Peaslee Dr., Map 565 Lot 51-11, in the R-1 Medium Density Residential District and
is owned by the applicants.
Applicant:
Josh and Melissa Amyot
Property Owners):
Josh and Melissa Amyot
Property Address:
31 Peaslee Drive
Tax Map 565-51, Lot 11
Included in the Member Packets: Fee Schedule Worksheet, Tax map, assessing card,
list of abutters
Present: Josh and Melissa Amyot
Mr. Bacon said that all abutters were notified.

Chairman Kudrick read aloud the rules governing the hearing: (1) Applicant will present
its case; (2) Those in favor of the application will speak; (3) Those opposed to the
application will speak; (4) Rebuttal by the applicant and those in favor of the application
will speak; (5) Rebuttal by those in opposition to the application will speak.
He stated that anyone wishing to speak must first give their name, address, and interest in
the case. All questions and comments will be directed to the Chairman. The Board will
base their decisions on facts presented by the applicant. If any of the presented facts are
found to be different than what was presented, the Board reserves the right to reconsider
its approval.
As requested by Chairman Kudrick, the Applicant read the application aloud:
Please give a detailed description of your proposal below. We would like to set up an
above-ground round 18 ft. pool in our yard. We meet the 15 ft. required to the side, the
30 ft. required from the road but do not meet the 40 ft. required to the back. We are 30 ft.
short.
1. The variance will not be contrary to the public interest. Installing an above-
ground pool on my property does not conflict with the public interest because it is a
temporary, non-permanent structure that does not affect public safety or the character of
the surrounding neighborhood. The pool will be fully contained on my property
boundaries, will comply with all safety requirements and will not create noise or traffic.
It is for private residential use.
2. The spirit of the ordinance is observed. Because the purpose of the 40 ft. rear
setback is to protect neighboring properties, maintain privacy, ensure safety and prevent
overcrowding. Even though my lot cannot meet the 40 ft. requirement, placing the pool
10 ft. from the rear boundary still meets the intent of the ordinance. It is temporary, will
meet all safety requirements, will not create noise, visibility or any safety concerns for
abutting properties.
3. Substantial justice is done. Allowing the pool at the proposed location does not
affect public safety, does not change character of the neighborhood and does not harm
neighboring properties. Granting the variance simply allows reasonable use of my
property, while denying it would prevent that use for no public gain.
4. The values of surrounding properties are not diminished. The values of
surrounding properties are not diminished because the pool is a typical residential
Pembroke Zoning Board of
Adjustment

Meeting Minutes (Adopted)
January 26, 2026

amenity, is fully contained within my property and will be installed and maintained in a
safe and attractive manner. It does not create noise or traffic. Above ground pools are
common in residential areas and do not reduce property values when properly placed.
Therefore, granting this variance will not harm the value or enjoyment of surrounding
properties
5. Literal enforcement of the provisions of the ordinance would result in an
unnecessary hardship. (A) For purposes of this subparagraph, "unnecessary
hardship" means that, owing to special conditions of the property that distinguish it
from other properties in the area: (i) No fair and substantial relationship exists
between the general public purposes of the ordinance provision and the specific
application of that provision to the property; and (i) the proposed use is a
reasonable one. My property is unusually shallow on the side where we want the pool
placed which makes it difficult to meet the 40 ft. rear setback and placing the pool closer
to the front of the house will not make the property visually appealing. Placing the pool
10 ft. from the rear boundary will still meet privacy, safety and property values. The pool
will meet safety requirements, properly maintained and will not create noise or visibility
issues. Applying the full setback will not serve the public interest and create an unfair
burden.
(B) If the criteria in subparagraph (A) are not established, and unnecessary
hardship will be deemed to exist if, and only if, owing to special conditions of the
property that distinguish it from other properties in the area, the property cannot
be reasonably used in strict conformance with the ordinance, and a variance is
therefore necessary to enable reasonable use of it. Due to the unusually shallow depth
of my lot, it is impossible to enjoy a reasonable residential use such as a backyard pool
without a variance. The pool will be safely installed, meet safety requirements and will
not negatively impact neighboring properties. Therefore, a variance is necessary to
enable reasonable use of my property
No one spoke in favor of the application.
Chairman Kudrick said that he was notified by the Superintendent of the Pembroke
Water Works who is an abutter, and the Pembroke Water Works Board had no problem
with the application.
No one spoke in opposition to the application.

egress would present safety issues for emergency vehicles access on any of the plans and

need to come up with plan(s) that have 2 egresses and cul-de-sacs are not recommended.

themselves to maintain. Any egress on Rt. 3 without a light would be dangerous. State
suggested a 4 way light at Academy Road. Original plan was denied and court upheld
Towns objections.
Another plan, 350-354 Third Range Road from Beauchesne's they are asking for a minor
subdivision but no reason has been given for this split. It may be for a single family
house for a family member but it has not been stated. There is a lot of wet land in the area
of this request. Applicant is going to do a presentation to the Conservation Commission.
They are expected to ask for a variance through the wetlands.

e. Wilkins Avenue Proposed Building
a. Paulette read the email regarding the citizen's (Zachary Taylor) concern about this area of
Pembroke Street at Riverview Way. Chief Gaskell had called the State regarding this
issue from a prior concerned citizen and was told that the Town would also have to install
a sidewalk which would also require sound alert and flashing light alert to meet current
regulations. The area of Riverview is not the best place for a cross walk, the closest place
to do that would Church Road. This would involve a new build (sidewalk) for the Town.
Adding this crosswalk would also encourage more parking on that street and there really
isn't enough room for the additional vehicles. The State specifications require 15 people
to cross within an hour. The police did a count during an event and only 7 within 30
1

minutes crossed there. During school hours only 6 students crossed. It would cost the
Town between $35,000.00 and $40,000.00 at a minimum to take on this project. It has
been observed that students cross anywhere they choose. They push the button at an
existing cross walk and cross before the light is ready for them. Then traffic waits for the
cross walk lights to clear because no one is there using them. His opinion was that it was
not feasible. VJ mentioned that some residents don't want kids parking on Riverview
Way because it does create a hazard. If we were to install a cross walk there, besides the
initial cost to install flashing light and sound warning, there is still the annual cost to paint
and service the lights and alarms, adding an unknown cost to the budget. Paulette also felt
it was cost prohibitive. Brian was concerned about the regular traffic having to stop
multiple times. And all agreed that the students cross where they want instead of where it
is safest to cross. If adding a cross walk there, then additional cross walks would be
probably be requested all along Pembroke Street. Possibly as many as 5 or 6 to do it
correctly. A letter of response will be drafted for the Committee to review before being
sent to Mr. Taylor.
b. Paulette was concerned that the Roads Committee did not meet before the deadline for
comments and suggestions for any projects coming before TRC meetings. She suggested
changing the Roads Committee meetings so that they could review those plans and get
their comments and recommendations to TRC before they meet. Whether the 1st or 2nd
Monday would be possible needed to be determined by what other committees meet on
those dates. Discussion continued as to when might be the best date and time. All agreed
that the Roads Committee needed to see any plans to allow input on the impact of the
roads. TRC is always the second Tuesday of the month.
c. The traffic count was discussed and they started with Cooperative Way (Kline) and
Commerce. After further discussion they felt it would be beneficial to look at 2026 roads
to get the counts done prior to work for that year. Since this list was not available tonight,
they decided to table this until the next meeting.
d. Crack Sealing Bid list was reviewed. The whole list should be within the $25,000.00
budget. The bid proposal will be sent out noting based on budget approval at Town
Meeting.
e. Wilkens Avenue project is proposing two 6-unit apartment buildings, 2 bedrooms each
and 24 parking spaces. Road is currently only 16' wide. VJ requested through TRC to
increase the lanes and shoulders to 24'width. It has also been suggested that the road be
extended to end of road not just to driveway or all the way to Smith Avenue to provide a
second egress. Access in the current plan does not provide enough area for Public Works
to snow plow or for emergency vehicles from Police, Ambulance or Fire Departments.
Planning Board has seen original plans but revised plans have not been presented to them
addressing these concerns. The plan is currently insufficient for the project to proceed as
proposed. Discussion tonight indicated that Wilkens Avenue needs to be brought up to
Town specifications. Possibly being reviewed by the Town engineer and engineers) from
both Water and Sewer since both will have to be extended from Buck Street. If and when
the Planning Board approves their plan, it is then up to the inspection process thereafter to
address any problems which need changes. Extensive discussion continued including
Right-of-Ways.

6. Any New Business:
a. Permit Fees
a. Recreation, driveway and other fees were discussed since they have not been
updated in some time need to be reviewed.
7. Accept Minutes:
a. February 4, 2025
Motion: Sandy motioned to accept the minutes
Seconded: Brian
Vote: All others in favor (Tom abstained)
8. Adjourn:
Motion: Sandy motioned to adjourn
Seconded: Brian
Vote: All in favor, adjourned: 7:17 PM.
Next meeting April 7, 2025 at 5:30 PM

Town of Pembroke
Roads Committee
311 Pembroke Street, Pembroke, NH 03275
MINUTES
Tuesday, February 4, 2025
Meeting called to order at 6:01 P.M.
1. Attendance: Buddy Curley, Sandy Goulet, Paulette Malo, VJ Ranfos, Adam Mendozza,
Brian Seaworth
Unavailable: Tom Gallo, Vincent Greco
Citizens Comments:
a. Jason Menard, 318 Pembroke Street: talked about sidewalks
a. He had talked with VJ, Adam and David about the Sidewalk Reserve Fund which
has about $47,000.00 in it. Since this is outside the roads budget, he suggested that
it be utilized in the rehab of sidewalks in town. Jason provided a detailed sidewalk
restoration proposal to the committee and discussed in detail the changes that are
needed to conform to the standards and practices required to meet public safety
regulations. His survey of roads that need sidewalk restoration included Pembroke
Hill Road, Third Range Road, Pleasant Street, Fairview Way, Academy Road and
Church Road. This would be a multi-year undertaking but as a concerned citizen, he
felt it should be given serious consideration.
3. Old Business:
a. Bachelder Road Bridge Replacement
b. 2024 Encumbrances
c. 2025 Road Budget
d. Finalize 2025 Road
a. Per VJ by the December meeting the permits from DES had been approved. The
structures have been ordered but delivery has not been determined. Once they are made
and delivered, the contractor would like to start as soon as possible. At this point we
need to wait for Spring.
b. We were able to encumber the funds for engineering the Thompson Road culvert,
engineering on Deerpath Lane, the guardrail at the intersection of Sixth Range Road and
Cross Country Road and the fog seal on Ricker Road and Horsecorner Road with indus.
c. The Budget Committee as reported by Sandy said that $150,000.00 needs to be cut. The
majority of that will probably come out of the Roads budget. The final amount has not
yet been decided.
d. Because the budget may be cut by $100,000.00 to $150,000.00 and the proposed roads
are a bit over the $800,000.00, it may be cut to $650,000.00. If necessary, VJ suggested
the first to be cut would be Plausawa Hill Road ($122,107.00) and the next would be
Beacon Hill Road ($63,957.00) to stay within the proposed final budget.
1

4. Any Old Business:
5. New Business:
a. Range Road Policy Subcommittee
b. Meeting Dates for David (camera schedule)
a. Brian explained why the "Subcommittee" was needed to deal with the new requests to
build on the range roads. Meant to guide the public meeting. They need a member of the
Roads Committee to be on it. Buddy will be on it.
b. The dates will be March 4, April 1, May 6, June 3, July -none, August 5, September 2,
October 7, November 4, December 2.
6. Any New Business:
a. Letter from KV Partners - Engineering estimate for Pembroke Hill Road sidewalks
from Grandview to Third Range Road
a. Unce the engineering is done, we will try to do Deerpath Lane (Fairview &
Renarl) in 2026 with a bond which may also include the sidewalk on Pembroke
Hill Road at that time.
7. Accept Minutes:
a. December 3, 2024
Motion: Sandy motioned to accept the minutes
Seconded: Brian
Vote: All others in favor

Motion: Buddy motioned to adjourn
Seconded: Sandy
